title: SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing for Labeled Property Graph Learning
summary: Labeled property graphs combine relational structure with heterogeneous textual and categorical properties attached to both nodes and relationships. Conventional graph neural networks typically represent these properties as static feature vectors, limiting their ability to determine which semantic evidence should influence message propagation for a particular prediction target. We propose SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing, an architecture that integrates a small language model directly into graph message selection. A topology GNN provides a stable structural representation and prediction anchor. For each target node, incident messages combine the neighbor's structural state, node-property encoding, relationship-property encoding, and relationship type. A parameter-efficient SLM processes structured graph soft tokens and produces a target-conditioned routing query. This query first selects relevant messages within each relationship type and subsequently routes information across relation-level summaries. The resulting representation provides a bounded residual update to the topology anchor, preserving structural evidence while allowing contextual semantic information to modify the prediction. The architecture supports interpretable analysis at both the neighbor and relationship-type levels and provides a general mechanism for integrating language-derived semantics into property-rich graph learning.

AI.tldr: SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing integrates a small language model into GNN-based Labeled Property Graphs to condition message routing by semantic cues, enabling targeted, interpretable, relation-type-aware information propagation while preserving topology.
AI.motivation: Conventional GNNs rely on static feature vectors, limiting the ability to dynamically select semantic evidence for a given prediction target in graphs with rich node/relationship properties. There is a need for target-conditioned, interpretable integration of language-derived semantics into property-rich graphs.
AI.method: A topology GNN provides stability; for each target node, messages combine neighbor structure, node-property encoding, relationship-property encoding, and relationship type. A parameter-efficient small language model processes structured graph tokens to produce a target-conditioned routing query. The query first selects relevant messages within each relation type and then routes information across relation-level summaries, yielding a bounded residual update to the topology anchor.
AI.result: Proposes a unified architecture that preserves structural evidence while allowing semantic information to modulate predictions. It enables interpretable analysis at both the neighbor and relation-type levels and offers a general mechanism to integrate language-derived semantics into property-rich graph learning.
AI.conclusion: The architecture advances graph learning by enabling language-informed, target-conditioned, relation-aware message routing with interpretable, topology-preserving updates.

title: NeuronFuzz: Safety Neuron Guided Fuzzing for LLM Safety Evaluation
summary:
Safety evaluation is critical for assessing whether aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) remain robust against jailbreak attacks. Existing automated testing methods, however, largely rely on response-level feedback: each candidate prompt typically requires generating a target-model response to evaluate its attack effectiveness. This process is expensive and, more importantly, provides only sparse guidance on strongly aligned models, where most candidates are rejected with the same failure outcome.
  This paper presents NeuronFuzz, a white-box fuzzing framework that exploits internal safety neurons as continuous execution feedback for LLM safety evaluation. A SafetyOracle converts safety-neuron activations into a continuous safety alarm score that serves as feedback for fuzzing and can be obtained during prefill, eliminating response generation from the fuzzing loop. To construct the SafetyOracle, NeuronFuzz uses template-invariant harmful and benign inputs and stability-aware selection to identify a compact set of safety neurons whose activations capture harmful-intent recognition. Moreover, since the safety alarm score is differentiable, NeuronFuzz uses its gradients to identify safety-sensitive template positions and a masked language model to generate fluent, context-compatible mutations while preserving original harmful payload and avoiding additional optimization variables. We evaluate NeuronFuzz across 21 text and multimodal models. Across five white-box source models, it achieves a 76-100% jailbreak discovery rate, outperforming baselines by up to 48 percentage points. Its optimized templates further transfer zero-shot to open-weight and six proprietary target models, achieving average ASR and top-5 ensemble ASR (EASR) of 69.6%/92.6% and 44.1%/60.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: NeuronFuzz is a white-box fuzzing framework that uses internal safety neurons and a SafetyOracle to provide a continuous safety score during prefill, enabling efficient jailbreak discovery across many models and achieving strong transfer to open-weight and proprietary targets.
AI.motivation: Evaluate and improve LLM safety against jailbreak attempts when response-level feedback is expensive and sparse for strongly aligned models; need continuous internal feedback to guide fuzzing.
AI.method: Construct a differentiable SafetyOracle that maps safety-neuron activations to a continuous alarm score; identify a compact safety-neuron set via template-invariant harmful/benign inputs and stability-aware selection; use gradients to locate safety-sensitive template positions; employ a masked language model to generate fluent, context-consistent mutations preserving payload; perform prefill-based fuzzing without requiring target responses.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 text and multimodal models; across five source models, jailbreak discovery rate is 76–100%, outperforming baselines by up to 48 percentage points; zero-shot transfer of optimized templates to open-weight and six proprietary targets with ASR 69.6%/92.6% and EASR 44.1%/60.0%.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective white-box, prefill-based safety evaluation leveraging differentiable internal signals, yielding high jailbreak discovery and transferability while reducing reliance on response generation.

title: Pruning Binarized Neural Networks: A Dedicated Framework and Globally Weighted Algorithms
summary: Extreme compression of deep neural networks, up to full binarization, dramatically reduces memory footprint and arithmetic complexity, facilitating deployment on constrained edge hardware with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and microcontrollers. Although combining binarization with pruning promises additional efficiency gains, existing pruning strategies are ill-suited to binarized representations and rarely translate into meaningful hardware savings. We introduce a PyTorch-based, research-oriented framework that incorporates freezing and pruning mechanisms for designing and optimizing binarized neural networks. The framework enables rapid and reproducible evaluation of state-of-the-art approaches and the fast prototyping of new ones. Leveraging this framework, we propose a novel pruning method that accounts for the relative importance of learned parameters across abstraction levels. Such a global weighting mechanism consistently achieves a superior trade-off between model accuracy and pruning rate, achieving a 70% pruning rate on VGG11 with constant accuracy, while state-of-the-art results reach only 41% in the binarized setting.

AI.tldr: A PyTorch framework for pruning and freezing binarized neural networks (BNNs) and a global-importance pruning method that cross-weights across abstraction levels, achieving 70% pruning on VGG11 with unchanged accuracy—outperforming the previous 41% in the binarized setting.
AI.motivation: BNNs offer extreme storage and compute savings, but pruning them often fails to yield hardware savings or maintain accuracy. A reusable framework and a pruning strategy that accounts for parameter importance across abstraction levels are needed to realize practical gains on constrained edge hardware.
AI.method: Introduce a PyTorch-based framework that supports freezing and pruning for BNNs to enable rapid, reproducible evaluation. Propose a global weighting mechanism to measure parameter importance across multiple abstraction levels, guiding pruning decisions. Validate on VGG11 and compare against state-of-the-art binarized pruning results.
AI.result: The framework enables rapid experimentation in BNN pruning; the proposed global-weighting pruning method consistently yields better trade-offs between accuracy and sparsity, achieving ~70% pruning on VGG11 with constant accuracy, outperforming the prior 41% reported for binarized settings.
AI.conclusion: A cross-layer, global-importance pruning strategy, when paired with a PyTorch-based BNN framework, delivers superior sparsity-accuracy trade-offs and closer alignment with hardware efficiency goals than previous binarized pruning approaches.

title: Muon with Finite Newton-Schulz: The Smoothing Benefit in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization
summary: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for the matrix-valued parameters in large language model pretraining, approximately orthogonalizing its momentum with a few Newton-Schulz iterations. Existing theory either replaces this iteration with the exact polar factor it approximates, or treats its finite depth as an approximation error, and thus the iteration Muon actually runs can only hurt the guarantees. We show that finite Newton-Schulz can instead be beneficial for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization. To this end, we analyze Muon through the online-to-nonconvex conversion, which views the update rule as an online learner and converts its regret bound into a stationarity guarantee. The finite Newton-Schulz iteration smooths the discontinuous polar map into a Lipschitz map of the singular values, and Muon with finite Newton-Schulz can be regarded as an online learner with a smoothed spectral potential. This smoothing is exactly what the conversion needs: we prove that a Newton-Schulz depth growing only logarithmically in the target accuracy suffices for convergence to stationary points in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, whereas Muon with the exact-polar update may fail to converge. The resulting sample complexity bounds match the best-known guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and are optimal for smooth nonconvex optimization up to problem-dependent factors. The argument extends beyond Newton-Schulz to general spectral maps with the same smoothing property.

AI.tldr: Finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations in Muon act as a beneficial smoothing of the polar map, enabling convergence guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization with logarithmic-depth NS; exact-polar or shallow depth can fail, while NS-depth growing logarithmically in target accuracy achieves optimal sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Current analyses either replace the NS step with the exact polar factor or treat finite depth as an error, leaving potential benefits of finite-depth smoothing unexplored. The goal is to understand whether finite-depth NS can improve convergence guarantees for Muon in nonsmooth nonconvex settings.
AI.method: Apply online-to-nonconvex conversion to Muon, modeling the update as an online learner with a smoothed spectral potential induced by finite NS smoothing of the polar map. Prove that NS depth can grow only logarithmically with target accuracy to guarantee convergence to stationary points; generalize to other spectral maps with similar smoothing properties.
AI.result: Finite NS depth yields convergence guarantees with sample complexity matching the best-known bounds for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization; for smooth nonconvex problems the bounds are optimal up to problem-dependent factors. The smoothing effect of NS is key to the online-to-nonconvex conversion, and the argument extends beyond NS to general spectral maps having the same smoothing property.
AI.conclusion: Finite-depth NS in Muon can be advantageous rather than detrimental: it smooths the spectral operator just enough to enable stationarity guarantees in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, with logarithmic-depth sufficing and exact-polar updates potentially failing under some conditions; the approach broadens to general spectral maps and deepens understanding of spectral-operator-based optimizers.

title: WALL-SS: Scaling Long-horizon World Models via Next-Scale Autoregression
summary: Generative world models provide robots with predictive models of how the world evolves under interaction, with growing potential for simulation, planning, policy evaluation, and robot learning. Beyond clip-level future prediction, a unified generative formulation should relate actions to consequences, support flexible horizons and continuous interaction, and enable reward-driven optimization. We introduce WALL-SS, a world model that generates visual futures through Scale-wise autoregressive Scaling, enabling action-controllable and long-horizon robotic simulation. WALL-SS represents embodied trajectories as causal sequences of temporally interleaved observations and actions, making action-dependent state transitions explicit while naturally supporting variable-length generation, streaming extension through reusable causal states, and direct optimization through sequence probabilities. To make this formulation effective over long horizons, we generate each future observation in a coarse-to-fine manner and develop three complementary components within the same hierarchy. Action-conditioned next-scale prediction injects scale-aligned action representations to improve action-future coupling and model both successful and failed behaviors. Scale-compressed long-horizon memory retains recent interactions at fine resolution while compressing distant observations and actions, with scale-wise dream forcing enhancing robustness to self-generated context. Finally, on-policy alignment optimizes autoregressive visual dynamics with action-following and long-term consistency rewards while preserving the pretrained visual distribution. Experiments show that WALL-SS improves action following and trajectory accuracy, supports coherent minute-long streaming rollout under bounded memory, and consistently benefits from on-policy alignment in reducing action drift and long-horizon inconsistency.

AI.tldr: WALL-SS: a scale-wise autoregressive, action-conditioned world model for long-horizon, visual robotic prediction; enables controllable, streaming simulation with a coarse-to-fine generation pipeline and three hierarchical components.
AI.motivation: Addresses the need for unified, action-aware generative world models that support variable horizons, streaming rollout, and reward-based optimization in robotics.
AI.method: Proposes Scale-wise Autoregressive Scaling (WALL-SS) with causal sequences of observations and actions; coarse-to-fine future observation generation; three components: action-conditioned next-scale prediction, scale-compressed long-horizon memory with scale-wise dream forcing, on-policy alignment; streaming extension via reusable causal states; training via optimizing sequence probabilities.
AI.result: Improved action following and trajectory accuracy; minute-long streaming rollout under bounded memory; on-policy alignment reduces action drift and long-horizon inconsistency; robust to self-generated context.
AI.conclusion: WALL-SS enables action-controllable, long-horizon robotic simulation; supports variable-length generation, streaming, and reward-driven optimization; effective for long-horizon planning and policy evaluation in robotics.

title: Surgical Video Generation From Diffusion to World Models: A Survey
comment: 4 pages, 1 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the 2026 3rd International Conference on Intelligent Perception and Pattern Recognition (IPPR 2026)
summary: Surgical video data provides the primary training resource for models of intraoperative perception, surgical workflow understanding, and robotic decision-making. However, clinical data acquisition remains constrained by privacy, cost, and class imbalance. Surgical video generation has emerged as a transformative approach to addressing data scarcity and as a foundation for surgical simulation, training, and robotic policy learning. The field has developed rapidly without a clear conceptual framework. This survey organizes the 2024-2026 literature into three categories: unconditional generation, conditional generation, and world modeling generation, revealing a fundamental shift in how the task is defined from synthesizing visually plausible frames to modeling the causal dynamics of surgical scenes. We examine the persistent gap between pixel-level fidelity and clinical plausibility, and identify generalization, physical realism, controllability, and interpretability as bottlenecks. We further summarize experimental results of representative methods on public datasets to provide a quantitative reference for the field. This survey provides a structured overview of the current state and open challenges, offering a reference for researchers working at the intersection of intelligent perception, multi-modal fusion, generative AI, and surgical data science.

AI.tldr: A 2024-2026 survey on surgical video generation categorizes methods into unconditional, conditional, and world-modeling approaches, emphasizing a shift from visual frame synthesis to causal dynamics; it discusses gaps (generalization, realism, controllability, interpretability), summarizes experimental results on public datasets, and outlines open challenges for surgeon AI.
AI.motivation: Data scarcity due to privacy, cost, and class imbalance motivates synthetic data generation to support intraoperative perception, workflow understanding, and robotic decision-making; generation enables simulation, training, and policy learning while mitigating clinical data constraints.
AI.method: Systematic review of 2024-2026 literature; classify work into three generation paradigms; analyze the progression from pixel realism to causal modeling; assess clinical plausibility vs pixel fidelity; identify bottlenecks; compile results on public datasets; provide structured overview.
AI.result: Collates representative methods and their experimental results on public datasets; provides quantitative references and benchmarks; offers a structured framework to compare unconditional, conditional, and world-modeling approaches for surgical video generation.
AI.conclusion: Provides a structured overview of current state and open challenges; highlights the shift to causal dynamics in surgical scene modeling; identifies bottlenecks—generalization, physical realism, controllability, interpretability—and calls for research addressing these issues; serves as a reference for researchers in intelligent perception, multi-modal fusion, generative AI, and surgical data science.

title: EduRiskX: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework with F-Logic Reasoning for Early Academic Risk Prediction
comment: Previously available on Research Square: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8877832/v1. This version presents the complete neuro-symbolic framework, EduRiskX, integrating temporal Transformers with F-Logic reasoning
summary: Predicting students' academic risk in online education is crucial for enabling timely interventions that can improve retention and learning outcomes. However, existing models often suffer from limited early detection capability and insufficient interpretability, leading to a "black-box" trust crisis that hinders their adoption in real-world pedagogical settings. To address these challenges, we propose EduRiskX, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates a temporal Transformer-based predictor with F-Logic symbolic reasoning. The neural component models longitudinal student activity sequences using temporal attention, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation. Acting as a data-driven expert system, an F-Logic rule base -- grounded in established educational theories (Engagement Theory and Student Integration Model) to mimic the diagnostic logic of human educators -- is constructed exclusively from the training data. The neural risk probability and the symbolic confidence score are then combined through a logistic regression-based fusion mechanism that learns the relative contribution of each signal. Experiments on the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) using a strict 80/10/10 student-level split show that EduRiskX achieves an accuracy of 0.900 and an F1-score of 0.894 at the end of the semester (Week 38), with an average early detection week of 9.32 and a detection rate of 94.30 percent. Compared with state-of-the-art time-series models (PatchTST, iTransformer) and common deep learning baselines (LSTM, CNN), EduRiskX yields improved recall and earlier risk identification under identical conditions. Beyond predictive performance, the F-Logic module provides structured rule-based explanations linking predictions to observable behavioral patterns and educational theories.

AI.tldr: EduRiskX is a neuro-symbolic framework that blends a temporal Transformer predictor with F-Logic symbolic reasoning to predict student risk in online education, achieving high accuracy, early detection, and explainable rule-based insights.
AI.motivation: Current risk-prediction models suffer from limited early detection and poor interpretability (black-box). This hinders trust and adoption in real-world teaching. A transparent, data-driven diagnostic framework aligned with educational theory is needed.
AI.method: A temporal Transformer-based predictor models longitudinal student activity with temporal attention, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation. An F-Logic rule base, grounded in Engagement Theory and the Student Integration Model, is constructed solely from training data to mimic human diagnostic reasoning. A logistic regression fusion combines the neural risk probability with the symbolic confidence score, estimating their relative contributions. Evaluation on OULAD with an 80/10/10 split.
AI.result: End-of-semester performance: accuracy 0.900, F1 0.894 (Week 38). Early warning: average detection week 9.32, detection rate 94.30%. Outperforms state-of-the-art time-series models (PatchTST, iTransformer) and common DL baselines (LSTM, CNN) in recall and earlier risk identification. The F-Logic module also offers structured, theory-linked explanations.
AI.conclusion: The EduRiskX framework demonstrates that integrating neural sequence modeling with data-driven symbolic reasoning yields better predictive performance and interpretability, delivering actionable explanations and robust early detection in online learning analytics.

title: Quadratic Complexity of Voronoi Diagrams in $\mathbb{R}^3$ for Lines in a Single Ruling of a Regulus
summary: We study nearest and farthest Voronoi diagrams of lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$ under the Euclidean metric when all $n$ lines belong to one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled real quadric. For arbitrary line sites, the combinatorial complexity of the nearest Voronoi diagram is known only to lie between $Ω(n^2)$ and $O(n^{3+\varepsilon})$. Under general-position assumptions, we prove that both diagrams in the ruling class have at most $4n(n-3)$ vertices and $O(n^2)$ total combinatorial complexity. Conversely, for every $n \ge 4$, one ruling of a fixed non-rotational one-sheeted hyperboloid contains a general-position set of $n$ lines with at least $(n-2)(n-3)/2$ distinct regular nearest vertices, where regular means that exactly four lines support the vertex and their three defining bisectors meet transversely. Thus the worst-case complexity of the nearest Voronoi diagram in this class is $Θ(n^2)$, while the farthest diagram has $Θ(n^2)$ complexity for every general-position input, since it has exactly $n(n-1)$ three-dimensional cells. Under the Plücker embedding, the ruling is a conic, and the condition for a line to be tangent to a Euclidean sphere restricts to a binary quartic. At a regular vertex, the four supporting parameters exhaust its roots, and sign alternation forces two arcs of the parameter circle to be site-free. This leaves only $n(n-3)/2$ possible cyclic support types, while Bézout's theorem bounds the number of centers for each type by eight. The same reduction yields an exact $O(n^2)$-time algorithm that, after cyclically sorting the site parameters, enumerates all finite nearest and farthest vertices as constant-degree real univariate representations.

AI.tldr: In the setting where n lines lie on a ruling of a smooth doubly ruled real quadric in R^3, the nearest and farthest Voronoi diagrams have quadratic complexity under general position; the nearest diagram has at most 4n(n-3) vertices; worst-case is Theta(n^2); the farthest diagram also Theta(n^2) with n(n-1) 3D cells; an exact O(n^2) algorithm enumerates all finite vertices via real univariate representations after sorting parameters.
AI.motivation: Understand the combinatorial and algorithmic aspects of Voronoi diagrams for line sites constrained to a ruled quadric, a natural extension beyond point sites; derive tight complexity bounds and efficient computation strategies under a structured geometric assumption.
AI.method: Leverage the Plücker embedding to transform the ruling into a conic; analyze tangency conditions to spheres as a binary quartic; classify regular vertices (4-site support with transversely intersecting bisectors); use sign alternation to bound site-free arcs; enumerate cyclic support types (≤ n(n-3)/2); apply Bézout to bound centers; deduce O(n^2) bounds; construct lower bounds by explicit configuration; derive an O(n^2) algorithm via cyclic parameter sorting and real univariate representations.
AI.result: Nearest Voronoi diagram within the ruling has at most 4n(n-3) vertices; total complexity O(n^2). There exist general-position configurations on a non-rotational one-sheeted hyperboloid yielding Omega(n^2) nearest vertices; farthest Voronoi diagram has Theta(n^2) complexity for every general-position input and comprises n(n-1) three-dimensional cells. An exact O(n^2)-time enumeration algorithm is provided.
AI.conclusion: The quadratic complexity under the ruling constraint is tight for both diagrams; the structured algebraic approach yields precise combinatorial counts and a practical O(n^2) algorithm, while the general case without the ruling constraint may exhibit higher complexity.

title: Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading
summary: Modern machine learning models rely on large amounts of labeled data. However, manual annotation of large-scale datasets is expensive and time-consuming. Label spreading is a semi-supervised learning technique that addresses this challenge by propagating information from a few labeled examples to a larger pool of unlabeled data. Despite its effectiveness, its application to large-scale, high-dimensional datasets is limited by computational costs and memory constraints. To address these limitations, we propose Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading (AMELS), an efficient label spreading framework that improves scalability by fast construction of neighborhood graphs and the incorporation of algebraic multigrid solvers. The latter is an iterative solver that replaces the ordinary random walk iteration typically performed in label spreading. Due to the multilevel nature of algebraic multigrid solvers, AMELS spreads given label information across a graph of any size in a single multigrid cycle. We demonstrate that AMELS achieves significant runtime reductions compared to existing implementations while also being more robust to hyperparameter choices in terms of both runtime and classification accuracy. Our framework therefore enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets and produces accurate labels even when only a few labeled samples are available.

AI.tldr: AMELS accelerates label spreading for large-scale, high-dimensional data using fast neighborhood graph construction and algebraic multigrid solvers, achieving faster runtimes and robustness with limited labeled data.
AI.motivation: Label spreading is effective for semi-supervised learning but scales poorly to large, high-dimensional datasets due to computational and memory constraints; a scalable solution is needed for practical large-scale applications.
AI.method: Construct neighborhood graphs efficiently and replace the standard random-walk iteration with an algebraic multigrid (AMG) solver. The multilevel AMG framework propagates given labels across graphs in a single cycle, enabling scalable label spreading on graphs of arbitrary size.
AI.result: AMELS delivers significant runtime reductions compared to existing implementations and exhibits greater robustness to hyperparameter choices in both runtime and classification accuracy. It enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets with few labeled samples.
AI.conclusion: AMELS provides a scalable, robust framework for label spreading on large graphs, combining fast graph construction with AMG-based propagation, and is applicable to large-scale SSL tasks beyond the studied image datasets.

title: Constraint-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Static Shape Estimation of Co-Manipulative Continuum Robots
summary: Static shape estimation of co-manipulative continuum robots (CCRs) is challenging because the continuum arms and manipulated flexible object form a closed chain that must satisfy both static equilibrium and geometric loop-closure constraints. This paper presents a constraint-aware physics-informed neural network (PINN) for static shape estimation of a tendon-driven CCR modeled using the geometric variable strain formulation. The proposed method incorporates a projected static equilibrium residual and a configuration-level geometric residual to enforce the governing mechanics and closed-chain geometry. In simulation, the PINN is compared with a purely data-driven artificial neural network (ANN) under limited and noisy training data. With 140 samples and 50% label noise, the PINN reduces the relative configuration error, equilibrium residual, and closed-chain residual by 67.88%, 67.35%, and 88.06%, respectively. Using the full dataset, the PINN achieves 0.1597% relative configuration error with an inference time of 0.1773 ms, compared with 17.97 s for an iterative nonlinear solver. Experimental fine-tuning reduces the marker RMSE from 2.657 mm to 0.497 mm and increases R2 from -0.788 to 0.937. These results demonstrate accurate, physically consistent, and computationally efficient static shape estimation of closed-chain CCRs.

AI.tldr: Constraint-aware physics-informed neural network (PINN) for static shape estimation of tendon-driven co-manipulative continuum robots (CCRs) with closed-chain geometry.
AI.motivation: Static shape estimation of CCRs is challenging due to closed-chain constraints requiring both static equilibrium and loop-closure; data-driven methods struggle to enforce physics and geometry, especially with limited/noisy data.
AI.method: A PINN incorporating a projected static equilibrium residual and a configuration-level geometric residual, built on the geometric variable strain formulation for tendon-driven CCRs; compared against a purely data-driven ANN under limited/noisy data; evaluated with both simulated and experimental data.
AI.result: With limited/noisy data (140 samples, 50% label noise), PINN reduces relative configuration error by 67.88%, equilibrium residual by 67.35%, and closed-chain residual by 88.06% compared to ANN. With full data, PINN achieves 0.1597% relative configuration error and 0.1773 ms inference time (vs 17.97 s for an iterative solver). Experimental fine-tuning lowers marker RMSE from 2.657 mm to 0.497 mm and raises R2 from -0.788 to 0.937.
AI.conclusion: The proposed constraint-aware PINN yields accurate, physically consistent, and computationally efficient static shape estimation for closed-chain CCRs, robust to label noise and applicable to real-time inference.

title: Procedura: Agentic 3D Modeling with Procedural Control
summary: Native 3D generators now recover impressive mesh geometry from a single image. However, a dense mesh stays soft where a machined object should be sharp, it carries no part decomposition, and it exposes no parameter a user could edit. To address this, we explore the paradigm of 3D shape as code, leveraging and scaling the coding ability of an LLM for 3D modeling. We introduce Procedura, a novel 3D modeling agent framework that writes an object as a procedural assembly, a parametric program whose named parts are joined by typed, machine-checkable mates. From a text prompt, the agent plans the object as an assembly graph and writes the program part by part, solving each placement from the mated frames rather than guessing it, and admitting a part only once compile, mate, and connectivity checks pass. A decoupled vision critic then refines the assembly one diagnosed fix at a time. Moreover, the same graph carries per-part materials and a simulator-validated articulation. We evaluate on P3D-Bench under its assembly judge, and with the same judge on MechBench-36, our hard-surface benchmark. On both, Procedura outperforms state-of-the-art native 3D generators and every prior 3D-code agent on judged quality, produces the sharpest edges of any method we evaluate, and is the only one whose output is an editable, part-structured program.

AI.tldr: Procedura introduces a 3D modeling agent that encodes objects as parametric assemblies (a programmable, part-based model) with mates and materials, enabling editable, sharp-edged outputs. It outperforms native 3D generators and prior 3D-code agents on standard benchmarks and yields a fully editable, part-structured program.
AI.motivation: Dense meshes from single images are often soft, lack part decomposition, and offer no user-editable parameters. There is a need for explicit, machine-checkable representations that preserve machinability and editability, leveraging LLMs for procedural 3D design.
AI.method: From a text prompt, Procedura plans an assembly graph and writes a parametric program part by part. Each placement is solved via mated frames and part inclusion requires successful compile, mate, and connectivity checks. A decoupled vision critic performs iterative fixes. The graph encodes per-part materials and simulator-validated articulation.
AI.result: On P3D-Bench (assembly judge) and MechBench-36 (hard-surface benchmark), Procedura outperforms state-of-the-art native 3D generators and prior 3D-code agents in judged quality, produces the sharpest edges among evaluated methods, and yields an editable, part-structured program.
AI.conclusion: Procedura demonstrates that planning and writing a parametric assembly as code, with constraint-based placement and vision-based refinement, yields higher-quality, machinable, and editable 3D models compared to existing approaches.

title: Standalone LLM and a Pre-specified Agentic Pipeline for Explaining ICU Mortality Predictions: a Feasibility Study on the eICU Demo Dataset
summary: Machine-learning models can predict ICU mortality accurately, but feature-attribution methods alone rarely provide the clinical narrative needed for bedside use. Large language models (LLMs) may bridge this gap, and multi-step agentic pipelines are a plausible extension because they separate data interpretation, guideline checking, and final explanation. This revised feasibility study preserves the original standalone-versus-agentic comparison while making the main clinical findings more explicit. Using the retained local eICU Demo artifact set (2,353 ICU stays; 8.1\% mortality), XGBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.855 (95\% CI 0.796--0.906) and an AUPRC of 0.332 (95\% CI 0.217--0.494). On a stratified 38-case explanation subset, the standalone LLM produced 1 explanation with explicit outcome leakage, whereas the four-step agentic pipeline produced none. Among the 14 cases that overlapped with the SHAP review subset, the standalone LLM showed higher SHAP alignment (mean Jaccard 0.171 versus 0.077) and higher direction consistency (92.9\% versus 78.6\%), while the agentic pipeline showed higher guideline grounding (0.762 versus 0.143), higher value specificity (0.236 versus 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 versus 0.671). Clinically, the results suggest that agentic decomposition may improve safety-relevant grounding and patient-specific detail, but it should be paired with attribution-based checks before use in high-stakes risk explanation.

AI.tldr: Feasibility comparison of standalone LLM explanations versus a four-step agentic pipeline for ICU mortality risk explanations, using XGBoost baseline. Agentic decomposition improves safety grounding and patient-specific detail, but requires attribution checks; standalone LLM shows higher SHAP alignment/direction consistency on overlapping cases, while agentic shows stronger guideline grounding, value specificity, and plausibility.
AI.motivation: Bridge predictive performance and clinical narrative for bedside use; address insufficiencies of attribution methods by leveraging LLMs with structured, multi-step reasoning and guideline-considerate checks.
AI.method: Evaluate on the local eICU Demo artifact set (2,353 ICU stays; 8.1% mortality). Baseline XGBoost: AUROC 0.855 (CI 0.796–0.906), AUPRC 0.332 (CI 0.217–0.494). On a stratified subset of 38 cases: standalone LLM produced 1 explanation with outcome leakage; four-step agentic pipeline produced none. For 14 overlapping SHAP-review cases: standalone LLM had higher SHAP alignment (mean Jaccard 0.171) and higher direction consistency (92.9% vs 78.6%), while agentic pipeline had higher guideline grounding (0.762 vs 0.143), higher value specificity (0.236 vs 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 vs 0.671).
AI.result: Quantitative findings show a trade-off: standalone LLM can align with SHAP and maintain directional consistency, whereas the agentic pipeline enhances safety-related grounding and patient-specific detail through structured reasoning steps.
AI.conclusion: Agentic decomposition may improve safety-grounding and patient-specific detail, but must be paired with attribution-level checks before deployment in high-stakes explanations.

title: Lunar Generalizations of the Euclidean Minimum Spanning Tree in the Plane and their Expected Costs
summary: Motivated by the recent introduction of chromatic persistent homology, we generalize the Euclidean minimum spanning tree (EMST) for $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the lunar EMST for the case in which the points come in $s+1$ colors. Calling the intersection of $s+1$ disks of radius $r$ centered at points with pairwise different colors a \emph{lune}, the generalized EMST reflects the history of the union of lunes as $r$ goes from $0$ to $\infty$, and its \emph{cost} is twice the difference between the radii when the arcs and nodes of the tree are formed. If the points are chosen uniformly at random in $[0,1]^2$ and colored randomly, the expected cost converges to some constant (that depends on $s$) times $\sqrt{n}$, as $n$ goes to infinity. The main contribution of this paper is a proof that this constant exists, however similar to the case of the classic EMST, its precise value remains elusive.

AI.tldr: Proves the existence of a scaling constant for the lunar EMST in colored point sets; the constant exists and scales with sqrt(n), but its exact value is not determined.
AI.motivation: Generalize the Euclidean MST to a chromatic/persistent setting (lunar EMST) and understand its asymptotic behavior in random colored point ensembles.
AI.method: Geometric-probabilistic analysis of the lunar EMST as the radius r grows, using random uniform points in [0,1]^2 colored with s+1 colors; apply subadditive-type arguments to show a finite limit for the normalized cost; parallel to Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley framework for EMST.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the expected lunar EMST cost converges to a constant (dependent on s) times sqrt(n) as n→∞; the constant exists but is not explicitly computed.
AI.conclusion: Extends EMST to a chromatic persistent framework and establishes a universal sqrt(n) scaling with an existence result for the limiting constant; leaves the exact value open and invites determination of c_s and extensions to broader models.

title: Privacy Without Regret: Differentially Private Inference-Time Alignment
summary: Best-of-N (BoN) sampling is the simplest and most widely deployed inference-time alignment strategy, but it suffers from two distinct problems: reward hacking, in which the selected response exploits errors in the proxy reward model, and the absence of any privacy protection for the sensitive human preference data used to train that reward model. We show that a single intervention-adding calibrated noise to reward scores before selection-resolves both. Our first result, Private Best-of-N (PrivBoN), establishes that Gumbel noise at an appropriate scale simultaneously provides $ε$-differential privacy and implements KL-regularized alignment. Whenever the privacy budget exceeds a critical threshold $ε^*$, the privacy-mandated noise is the regret-optimal regularization, and privacy imposes zero additional alignment cost-matching the information-theoretic skyline of Huang et al. (2025). Because $ε^*$ depends on an unknown coverage coefficient, we introduce Private Inference-Time Pessimism (PrivITP), which combines $χ^2$-regularized rejection sampling with a two-phase Gaussian mechanism. PrivITP achieves ex-post $(ε,δ)$-DP with a privacy cost independent of the number of responses $n$, cleanly decouples the regularization parameter from the privacy parameter, and attains the skyline up to a noise-inflation term. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm our results: PrivBoN and PrivITP are scaling-monotonic (unlike BoN, which degrades past a critical $n$), and PrivITP matches or outperforms PrivBoN at equivalent privacy levels, with the largest gains in the strong-privacy regime.

AI.tldr: Calibrated noise added to reward scores at inference time yields Private Best-of-N (PrivBoN) and PrivITP, achieving differential privacy and KL-regularized alignment while mitigating reward hacking; PrivITP offers ex-post (ε,δ)-DP with privacy cost independent of the number of responses and strong-privacy gains.
AI.motivation: Address two core issues in Best-of-N inference: (1) reward hacking due to proxy reward models and (2) lack of privacy protection for sensitive human preference data used to train those rewards.
AI.method: Introduce calibrated noise to reward scores before selection. PrivBoN uses Gumbel noise at an appropriate scale to deliver ε-differential privacy and KL-regularized alignment; identify a critical privacy budget threshold ε* beyond which privacy is the regret-optimal regularization and matches the information-theoretic best. To handle unknown ε*, PrivITP combines χ^2-regularized rejection sampling with a two-phase Gaussian mechanism to achieve ex-post (ε,δ)-DP with privacy cost independent of n and decouples the regularization and privacy parameters.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple language models, datasets, and reward models show both methods scale monotonically, unlike vanilla BoN. PrivITP either matches or outperforms PrivBoN at the same privacy level, with larger gains in the strong-privacy regime; privacy costs do not grow with the number of responses.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated inference-time noise provides a practical, scalable path to privately aligned BoN inference. PrivBoN establishes privacy and KL-regularization via Gumbel noise, while PrivITP offers a robust ex-post DP approach with a decoupled regularization/privacy design and favorable performance relative to PrivBoN across privacy levels.

title: Dispersive Forward Tree Search for Optimal Control: Coverage, Complexity, and Computation
summary: Steering-based planners require solutions to state-to-state boundary value problems, which can be inaccessible for nonlinear platforms. Forward propagation evades the steering requirement, but the finite-sample behavior of the associated planners remains uncharacterized and their implementations underperform in practice. This paper develops a propagation-based kinodynamic planner with deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees. We work within the large class of differentially flat nonlinear systems and show that a forward tree of locally dispersive control commands contains a near-optimal trajectory at a certified tree size. We provide a general mechanism to construct dispersive command sets for control-affine systems, which are necessary to implement the search algorithm prescribed by the theory. We show that covering the certified trajectory class irrespective of cost provably demands a tree exponentially sized in the problem horizon, and present a cost-conditioned dominance pruning procedure that retains near-optimality at a tree size polynomial in the horizon. We implement the resulting search algorithm, Dispersive Forward Tree search (DFT*), as breadth-first expansion of the forward tree, which maps naturally onto parallel hardware. We design efficient dispersive samplers for the unicycle, the trailer car, and the quadrotor and evaluate challenging planning tasks for these platforms. DFT* delivers consistently competitive and often substantially better solution quality than state-of-the-art kinodynamic planners at comparable solution times on embedded-tier processors, accelerating further as parallel compute is scaled. We also implement DFT* in a receding-horizon loop to demonstrate real-time planning in dynamic environments at embedded-tier compute budgets.

AI.tldr: Propagation-based kinodynamic planning with deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees for differentially flat nonlinear systems using forward trees of dispersive control commands, cost-conditioned pruning to achieve polynomial growth, and a parallelizable algorithm (DFT*) that demonstrates real-time planning on embedded hardware across unicycle, trailer car, and quadrotor.
AI.motivation: Steering-based planners require solving state-to-state boundary value problems, which is difficult for nonlinear platforms. Forward propagation avoids this but lacks finite-sample guarantees and has underwhelming practical performance. The paper seeks theoretically grounded, scalable, forward kinodynamic planning with practical performance.
AI.method: Develop forward-tree planner with locally dispersive control commands. Establish that a forward tree contains a near-optimal trajectory if the tree reaches a certified size. Provide a mechanism to construct dispersive command sets for control-affine systems. Prove that covering the certified trajectory class (independent of cost) requires exponential tree size, then introduce a cost-conditioned dominance pruning that preserves near-optimality with a tree size polynomial in the horizon. Implement DFT* as breadth-first forward-tree expansion, with dispersive samplers for unicycle, trailer car, and quadrotor.
AI.result: DFT* achieves competitive or superior solution quality versus state-of-the-art kinodynamic planners at similar solution times on embedded-tier processors, benefits from parallel compute, and enables real-time planning in dynamic environments via a receding-horizon loop.
AI.conclusion: Propagation-based planning with dispersive commands and pruning offers deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees for a broad class of nonlinear systems and is practically viable for real-time, embedded planning through parallel implementation.

title: Modality Maturity Index: A benchmark for assessing multimodal capabilities of omni models
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures. Code and dataset available
summary: Frontier language models are increasingly marketed as omni systems that can perceive and respond across modalities. Existing evaluation frameworks, however, focus almost exclusively on bimodal understanding, typically text plus one other modality. We propose the Modality Maturity Index (MMI), a benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal capabilities of large language models across five modalities (text, image, audio, video and document) and combinations of up to three modalities in both inputs and outputs. MMI consists of 893 questions, each carefully crafted to require the model to demonstrate its understanding of multiple input modalities and to generate responses that incorporate various output formats. The questions are designed to be self-contained, with clear expectations for the correct modality or mix of modalities required for an accurate response. Every MMI prompt carries human-authored rubric criteria for each output modality expected in the response; a model's MMI Value expresses the average of the per-modality scores for each prompt. Because low scores can reflect either failure to generate a modality (lack of presence) or failure to generate correct content, we introduce also a supplementary Modality Presence Score (MPS), a per-prompt F1 over the expected output modalities. Applying MMI to five frontier multimodal models, we find that the MPS ranges from only 15.6 (Claude Opus 4.6) to 34.9 (GPT-5.4). Given the low availability of returned modalities to even grade, we report MPS as our main result pending model improvements. To assess the viability of judging output correctness with LLM judges and rubrics, we run a separate experiment with custom generation tools. On the assets that generates, we find that an LLM judge applying the rubrics agrees with rubric-blind human annotators (who score the outputs directly and never see the criteria) on 70.8% of judgments.

AI.tldr: Proposes Modality Maturity Index (MMI), a benchmark to evaluate LLM multimodal capabilities across five modalities (text, image, audio, video, document) and up to three modalities in inputs/outputs, using 893 questions with rubrics; introduces Modality Presence Score (MPS); evaluates five frontier models showing limited modality presence; LLM judges align with human annotators ~71% of the time.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal evaluations focus on bimodal setups, neglecting broader cross-modal understanding. A comprehensive, standardized benchmark is needed to assess true multimodal maturity and generation across multiple modalities and outputs.
AI.method: Construct 893-item benchmark covering five modalities and combinations up to three modalities; attach per-output modality rubric criteria; compute MMI Value as average per-modality scores; define MPS as per-prompt F1 over expected output modalities; apply to five frontier models; perform a separate experiment with LLM judges using rubrics and compare to rubric-blind human annotators.
AI.result: MMI results show limited modality presence: MPS ranges from 15.6 to 34.9 across models ( Claude Opus 4.6 to GPT-5.4 ); low modality return leads authors to report MPS as the main result; an auxiliary study shows LLM judges using the rubrics agree with rubric-blind human annotators on 70.8% of judgments.
AI.conclusion: MMI provides a standardized framework to assess multi-modal maturity beyond bimodal evaluations; current frontier models exhibit limited modality presence, underscoring the need for improvements in cross-modal generation; rubric-based LLM judging demonstrates partial alignment with human judgments and can be viable for scalable evaluation.

title: Large Models for Battery Prognostics and Health Management: A Review and Future Roadmap
comment: Published in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews
summary: Battery Prognostics and Health Management (BPHM) is critical for ensuring the safe, reliable, and cost-effective operation of batteries across electric vehicles, grid storage, and consumer electronics. Conventional BPHM approaches, including physics-based models and task-centric deep learning methods, face challenges in computational efficiency and parameterization, cross-domain generalization, dependence on extensive labeled run-to-failure data, and model interpretability. Recent Large Models (LMs), built upon Transformer architectures and self-supervised pre-training, offer a transformative new paradigm to overcome these long-standing bottlenecks. This review provides the first comprehensive survey of LM applications in BPHM, systematically examining how these models address challenges in the field. We begin by elucidating the foundational technologies enabling LMs, including Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, large-scale multimodal datasets, and PEFT techniques. We then categorize recent progress along four critical dimensions: mitigating data scarcity, enhancing generalization and robustness, integrating domain knowledge for interpretability, and enabling system-level automation. Despite promising results, significant challenges remain across data accessibility, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility. To guide future research, we propose a roadmap focused on building collaborative data ecosystems, validating intelligence for industrial applications, enhancing trustworthiness with physics-informed designs, and enabling efficient on-device deployment. This review establishes a systematic approach to understand and advance LM-driven BPHM, providing researchers and practitioners with essential insights for developing next-generation battery management systems capable of safe, reliable, and autonomous operation throughout battery lifecycles.

AI.tldr: LMs offer a transformative paradigm for BPHM, addressing data scarcity, generalization, and interpretability, but practical deployment remains challenging; a roadmap is proposed.
AI.motivation: To survey and synthesize how large models can overcome long-standing BPHM bottlenecks and to define a research agenda.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of LM applications in BPHM; framework-based analysis along four dimensions; articulation of foundational tech and a future roadmap.
AI.result: Compiles evidence that LM approaches can mitigate data and robustness issues, enhance interpretability via physics-informed designs, and enable automation; identifies gaps in data access, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility.
AI.conclusion: LM-driven BPHM has the potential to enable safer, more reliable autonomous battery operation across lifecycles, contingent on addressing data sharing, validation, and deployment challenges.

title: CLIPPER: Replayable Shortlisted Optimization for Repeated Spatial Coverage Planning
comment: Accepted at ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Operational requirements developed with the City of Braunschweig frame municipal micromobility planning under geofenced exclusions, mandatory retained sites, spacing rules, and area-level caps. Each policy edit requires a new feasible plan; full-set greedy takes tens of seconds per alternative at city scale. We present CLIPPER (Constraint-exact Low-latency Iterative Planning with Pooled Evaluation and Replay). It forms bounded candidate pools but recomputes exact current gains and checks every active constraint before selection. Coverage from each candidate alone sets the initial order. Offline full-set scans measure gains omitted by the pool; online, a conservative bound triggers expansion or audit. CLIPPER-F gives each proposal group the same number of candidate slots. Across Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, its mean coverage over complete chains stays within 0.245 percentage points of full-set greedy under the same policy, with 13.6--28.9 times lower mean rollout time. CLIPPER-A instead distributes one shared candidate budget across the groups. Under its coverage-prioritized policy, it uses 9--15% of full-set greedy's rollout time under the same policy, with mean gaps of 1.82 percentage points in Braunschweig, 0.12 in Munich, and 0.27 in Berlin. Together, CLIPPER enables rapid, replayable comparison of recorded city-scale planning states while enforcing every encoded model constraint.

AI.tldr: CLIPPER provides constraint-exact, low-latency planning for city-scale micromobility with two variants (CLIPPER-F and CLIPPER-A) that closely match full-set greedy coverage while dramatically reducing rollout time.
AI.motivation: Need to plan under complex constraints (geofenced exclusions, retained sites, spacing, area caps) at city scale where full-set greedy is too slow.
AI.method: Form bounded candidate pools, recompute exact gains, enforce constraints, initial ordering from individual candidate coverage; offline full-set scans to detect omissions; online bound to expand/audit; CLIPPER-F fixes slots per group; CLIPPER-A shares budget across groups; rollout policy is coverage-prioritized.
AI.result: Mean coverage within 0.245 percentage points of full-set greedy; 13.6–28.9x faster rollout across Braunschweig, Munich, Berlin. CLIPPER-A achieves 9–15% of full-set time with gaps: Braunschweig 1.82 pp, Munich 0.12 pp, Berlin 0.27 pp.
AI.conclusion: CLIPPER enables rapid, replayable comparison of city-scale planning states while enforcing encoded constraints; practical for city planning workflows.

title: Beyond Capability Benchmarks: Learning Operational Fingerprints of LLM Cloud Services from Production Incident Metadata
summary: Managed LLM services are now part of real production systems, but model selection and service planning still rely heavily on capability benchmarks that reveal little about operational behavior after deployment. We present Operational Embedding (OpEmbed), a framework for learning compact operational fingerprints of LLM cloud services from structured, privacy-preserving support-case metadata, without using case text. OpEmbed aggregates model--time windows into an eight-channel operational signature and learns a low-dimensional representation via temporal contrastive learning, cross-view reconstruction, and generational-ordinality regularization. Evaluated on more than 33,000 production support cases spanning seven LLM families over 26 months at Google Cloud, OpEmbed recovers interpretable family- and version-level structure, improves leave-one-model-out operational forecasting over non-learned baselines, remains useful under limited early-window data, and supports cross-model fault-type transfer. We report the practical lessons learned from building and evaluating this tool for model onboarding, support readiness assessment, and operational monitoring.

AI.tldr: OpEmbed learns compact, privacy-preserving operational fingerprints for LLM cloud services from structured support-case metadata, enabling interpretable model-family structure, cross-model forecasting, and fault-type transfer.
AI.motivation: Production LLM services require understanding operational behavior post-deployment; capability benchmarks miss operational dynamics and privacy constraints; need scalable, privacy-preserving signals from metadata to guide onboarding, planning, and monitoring.
AI.method: Developed eight-channel OpEmbed signatures and train with temporal contrastive learning, cross-view reconstruction, and generational-ordinality regularization to obtain a low-dimensional representation from support-case metadata; evaluated on 33k+ cases across seven LLM families over 26 months at Google Cloud.
AI.result: OpEmbed recovers interpretable family- and version-level structure; improves leave-one-model-out operational forecasting versus non-learned baselines; robust with limited early data; enables cross-model fault-type transfer.
AI.conclusion: Offers practical lessons for model onboarding, readiness assessment, and operational monitoring, demonstrating real-world utility and guidance for deployment decisions.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmark of Neural 3D Reconstruction for Autonomous Laboratory Robots
comment: This manuscript is peer-reviewed from the committees in the workshop "VAxAutoSci: Visual Analytics in the Age of Autonomous Scientific Discovery" in conjunction with 2026 IEEE Visualization & Visual Analytics
summary: Autonomous robots performing laboratory tasks depend on 3D reconstruction pipelines that can turn raw camera streams into actionable object representations within the latency budget of a physical control loop. Neural 3D reconstruction methods have demonstrated high-quality view synthesis, but their real-time viability across the compute platforms on which laboratory robots actually run remains poorly characterized. In this work, we present a systematic compute-platform benchmark of neural 3D reconstruction methods, evaluating NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting training and rendering on GPU-enabled computing devices ranging from single-board computers to server-class nodes, and place Meta's SAM3D single-image reconstruction on the same axes to quantify its latency and fidelity gap relative to per-scene optimization. Our results show that Gaussian Splatting yields higher rendering quality than NeRF at greater GPU cost, and that onboard compute is insufficient for full per-scene optimization at interactive rates. Our preliminary assessment on SAM3D indicates that it delivers plausible object geometry within seconds, but with detail mismatches that can compromise downstream manipulation. Together, these findings motivate tiered pipelines in which lightweight feed-forward reconstruction sustains the real-time perception-and-tracking loop for laboratory robots, while heavier neural reconstruction is scheduled selectively on suitable compute.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking neural 3D reconstruction for lab robots across devices shows Gaussian Splatting offers better rendering quality than NeRF at higher GPU cost, while onboard compute struggles with per-scene optimization. SAM3D is faster but less detailed. Suggest tiered pipelines with lightweight real-time reconstruction and heavier neural methods scheduled on capable hardware.
AI.motivation: To characterize the real-time viability and hardware requirements of neural 3D reconstruction methods in autonomous laboratory robots, and to quantify trade-offs between quality, latency, and compute platform.
AI.method: Systematically benchmark NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting for training and rendering on GPUs spanning from single-board computers to server-class nodes; evaluate SAM3D single-image reconstruction on the same axes; assess latency and fidelity relative to per-scene optimization.
AI.result: Gaussian Splatting yields higher rendering quality than NeRF but requires more GPU resources; onboard compute is insufficient for interactive per-scene optimization; SAM3D can generate plausible object geometry within seconds but with noticeable detail mismatches.
AI.conclusion: Suggest tiered pipelines: real-time perception with lightweight feed-forward reconstruction, while heavier neural reconstruction is scheduled on suitable high-end compute to maintain loop latency and reliability.

title: Finding the Right Evidence: Factor-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Reasoning for Long Videos
summary: While LVLMs rapidly improve, long-video question answering still remains challenging: relevant evidence is sparse, and question-relevant context often fails to provide cues that discriminate the correct answer from plausible alternatives. Diagnostic analysis on a manually annotated subset of MMR-V shows that prior agentic systems substantially improve cue retrieval over direct VLM inference yet fail to achieve a corresponding gain in answer accuracy, indicating that the bottleneck lies in option-discriminative evidence rather than topical relevance alone. We propose PACE (Progressive Acquisition of Critical Evidence), a factor-guided framework for long-video evidence acquisition. PACE proceeds in two stages: it first indexes clip-level descriptions guided by question-derived factors without observing the candidate answers; it then uses the candidate answers to derive contrastive cues and queries the index for verification. On MMR-V with the open-source Qwen3-VL backbone, PACE achieves 42.6% accuracy, outperforming direct inference and prior agentic baselines including Deep Video Discovery (DVD). On the same diagnostic subset, PACE recovers 66.9% of the annotated cues, providing empirical evidence that its gains are associated with improved evidence recovery rather than stronger answer-side priors alone. Consistent gains over DVD on LVBench, Video-MME, EgoSchema, and LongVideoBench suggest that option-aware evidence acquisition transfers beyond MMR-V. Code is available at https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/PACE.

AI.tldr: PACE is a two-stage, factor-guided framework for long-video evidence acquisition in LVLM-based QA. It indexes clip-level descriptions guided by question factors without seeing candidate answers, then uses the candidate answers to derive contrastive cues and queries the index for verification. It achieves 42.6% accuracy on MMR-V using Qwen3-VL, outperforms direct inference and prior agentic baselines like DVD, and recovers 66.9% of annotated cues, with consistent gains on LVBench, Video-MME, EgoSchema, and LongVideoBench. Code is available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.motivation: Long-video question answering suffers from sparse relevant evidence and limited discriminability among answer options. Although prior agentic systems improve cue retrieval, this does not translate to higher answer accuracy, suggesting the bottleneck is option-discriminative evidence rather than topical relevance alone.
AI.method: PACE operates in two stages. Stage 1 indexes clip-level descriptions guided by question-derived factors without observing candidate answers. Stage 2 uses the candidate answers to derive contrastive cues and queries the index to verify evidence against options. This factor-guided, two-stage, option-aware approach aims to retrieve evidence that discriminates between answer choices.
AI.result: Empirical results show 42.6% accuracy on MMR-V with the Qwen3-VL backbone, outperforming direct inference and prior agentic baselines including Deep Video Discovery (DVD). On a diagnostic subset of MMR-V, PACE recovers 66.9% of annotated cues, indicating improved evidence recovery. Across LVBench, Video-MME, EgoSchema, and LongVideoBench, PACE shows consistent gains over DVD, suggesting good transfer of option-aware evidence acquisition beyond MMR-V. Code is available at https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/PACE.
AI.conclusion: Option-aware, two-stage evidence acquisition can improve long-video QA by focusing on discriminative evidence rather than solely topical relevance, with demonstrated gains on multiple benchmarks and transferability beyond the initial dataset.

title: PICasso: An AI-Enabled Design Framework for Autonomous Optimization of Silicon Photonic Devices
summary: We present PICasso, an AI-assisted framework for automated synthesis, verification, and optimization of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) from natural-language specifications. PICasso couples a structured NL -> YAML -> GDS generation pipeline with PDK aware knowledge injection, automated placement and routing, DRC/LVS validation, and SAX-based photonic simulation. To systematically evaluate AI-driven photonic design, we introduce PIC-Set, a benchmark of 36 parameterized PIC design tasks spanning core photonic primitives and multi-component circuits. Using PIC-Set, we benchmark several state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) under a unified evaluation protocol, including new metrics such as structural and functional $Spec@k$, optimization efficiency, and robustness under perturbations. Across the benchmark, PICasso significantly improves end-to-end specification satisfaction compared to vanilla LLM generation. Structural $Spec@3$ reaches up to 92.7% and functional $Spec@3$ up to 52% on high-complexity circuits. In addition, PICasso consistently reduces circuit insertion loss, lowering the mean loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (1.74 dB improvement) through simulation-guided optimization. These results demonstrate that structured domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback transform LLMs from brittle netlist generators into practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts with competitive runtimes relative to manual GUI-based workflows.

AI.tldr: PICasso is an AI-assisted framework that auto-generates manufacturable photonic integrated circuit (PIC) designs from natural language through a structured NL->YAML->GDS pipeline, with verification and optimization. It introduces PIC-Set, a 36-task benchmark, and shows LLM-guided design improvements in specification satisfaction and reduced insertion loss compared to vanilla LLMs and manual workflows.
AI.motivation: To overcome brittleness and engineering gaps in LLM-driven PIC design by enforcing domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback, and by providing a standardized benchmark to evaluate AI-assisted PIC design.
AI.method: Integrated pipeline: NL to YAML to GDS generation; PDK-aware knowledge injection; automated placement and routing; DRC/LVS validation; SAX-based photonic simulation; PIC-Set benchmark of 36 parameterized PIC tasks; unified evaluation protocol with Spec@k, optimization efficiency, and perturbation robustness.
AI.result: PICasso achieves high specification satisfaction (Spec@3 up to 92.7% structural, up to 52% functional) on high-complexity circuits; mean insertion loss reduced from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (≈1.74 dB improvement) via simulation-guided optimization; runtimes competitive with manual GUI workflows.
AI.conclusion: Structured domain constraints, verification, and feedback loops enable LLMs to function as practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts, surpassing vanilla LLMs in specification adherence and achieving better performance with efficient runtimes.

title: CG4AI: A Column Generation Framework for Training AI Models Under Constraints
summary: Standard machine-learning training minimizes a loss function over a dataset, but does not guarantee that the resulting model will satisfy predefined rules or constraints on its outputs. In many real-world applications, ranging from autonomous systems to network routing, such guarantees are essential. We propose CG4AI, a framework that builds a convex combination of AI models while enforcing linear constraints on the combined output. A master linear program (LP) determines the optimal mixture weights, while a pricing subproblem generates new models guided by LP dual variables, focusing attention on the most violated constraints. A cutting-plane procedure extends feasibility guarantees beyond the training set. We apply CG4AI to two problems: (i) digit classification on MNIST, where we demonstrate four distinct uses of constraints, learning from constraints alone, improving adversarial robustness, correcting misclassified examples, and enforcing output relabeling; and (ii) the multi-commodity flow problem, where link capacity constraints are enforced on neural-network routing predictors. Experiments on MNIST and standard SNDLIB benchmark networks show that CG4AI reliably produces feasible predictors while achieving better accuracy than single-model baselines.

AI.tldr: CG4AI builds a convex ensemble of models under linear output constraints using a master LP for weights and a pricing subproblem to generate models guided by duals, with a cutting-plane extension to guarantee feasibility beyond the training data.
AI.motivation: In many real-world tasks, it is essential to guarantee that model outputs satisfy predefined linear constraints. Standard training rarely ensures such guarantees, limiting reliability in safety- or resource-critical applications like autonomous systems and network routing.
AI.method: CG4AI constructs a convex combination of candidate models. A master linear program (LP) selects the mixture weights to satisfy linear constraints on the combined output. A pricing subproblem generates new models by exploiting LP dual variables, focusing search on the most violated constraints. A cutting-plane procedure extends constraint feasibility beyond the training set.
AI.result: Applied to MNIST and SNDLIB: (i) MNIST demonstrated four uses of constraints (learning from constraints, improving adversarial robustness, correcting misclassifications, and enforcing output relabeling); (ii) multi-commodity flow with neural routing predictors enforcing link-capacity constraints. In experiments, CG4AI yielded feasible predictors and outperformed single-model baselines in accuracy while maintaining feasibility.
AI.conclusion: CG4AI offers a general, optimization-driven framework for enforcing linear-output constraints in machine learning ensembles, delivering reliability guarantees without sacrificing (and often improving) predictive performance across classification and routing tasks; it shows promise for broader safety-critical applications and invites exploration of scalability and non-linear constraint extensions.

title: RTNav: Towards Real-Time Zero-Shot Object Navigation
summary: Navigation in unknown environments to find unforeseen objects has become increasingly feasible with capable vision and language foundation models. However, these models also introduce non-negligible inference latency, which becomes an important concern when agents must operate continuously in the real world. Most state-of-the-art methods are still developed in synchronous simulators, where the environment waits for the agent to act and inference time is effectively free. As a result, agents are often designed around the sequential execution of perception, reasoning, and action, with little regard for time constraints. Under real-time execution, where wall-clock time counts towards the task budget, the inefficiencies of these architectures become clear. We show that recent zero-shot object navigation methods suffer consistent performance degradation under such realistic timing conditions. Motivated by this observation, we propose RTNav, a simple but effective architecture that treats inference latency, asynchronous environment stepping, and bounded compute as explicit design considerations. Evaluated on real-time variants of HM3D-v1, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON, RTNav improves the success rate by up to 11% and the Success weighted by Completion Time by up to 5.1 points over prior work.

AI.tldr: RTNav is a latency-aware, asynchronous, bounded-compute architecture for real-time object navigation that improves performance under wall-clock constraints.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot object navigation methods show degraded performance when wall-clock time matters; current work largely assumes free inference time in synchronous simulators, which is unrealistic for real-world continuous operation.
AI.method: Proposes RTNav, a simple yet effective architecture that explicitly accounts for inference latency, asynchronous environment stepping, and bounded compute, enabling real-time navigation rather than a strictly sequential perception–reasoning–action loop.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-time variants of HM3D-v1, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON; RTNav yields up to 11% higher success rate and up to 5.1 points higher Success weighted by Completion Time (SWCT) compared with prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for latency and timing constraints in the architecture substantially improves real-time navigation performance, highlighting the importance of time-aware design in vision–language navigation.

title: A Unified Framework for the Mechanics of Information in Convolutional Neural Network Image Space
summary:
This paper introduces a unified mathematical framework for modeling information propagation through convolutional neural networks (CNNs), with the aim of connecting descriptions of physical space and information space.
  A correspondence is presented linking discrete filter symmetry and the relativistic energy--momentum relation under the widely used nonlinear rectified convolution operation. Specifically, symmetric filter components (e.g. the sum $Σ= [1,1]$) operate analogously to rest energy $mc^2$ in preserving the image centre of mass (e.g. isotropic diffusion), whereas antisymmetric components (e.g. the gradient $\nabla = [-1,1]$) operate analogously to the momentum term $pc$ in generally inducing a displacement (e.g. vibration or translation). For typical small discrete filters, this displacement is determined by the ratio of antisymmetric to total filter energy, analogously to how the displacement of a relativistic particle relates to a Lorentz transform with beta parameter $β= \frac{v}{c}=\frac{pc}{E}$ equal to the ratio of momentum $pc$ to total energy $E$.
  Repeated filtering leads to the Gaussian scale-space and emergent scale-invariant features. These constructions share a Laplacian-driven structure with the classical heat (diffusion) equation and, via standard mathematical correspondences, with the Schrödinger equation and aspects of the Friedmann equations, together with emergent Morse topological structure. Demonstrations in 3D images reveal blob-like, scale-invariant Morse critical points in images spanning a wide range of physical scales, including organic sugar molecules and inorganic silicon crystals, human and primate brains in magnetic resonance images (MRI), galaxies and the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

AI.tldr: A unified mathematical framework links CNN filter symmetry in nonlinear rectified convolution to relativistic energy–momentum, deriving a scale-space and scale-invariant features via diffusion-like processes; connects to Schrödinger and cosmological equations, with 3D demonstrations showing Morse-type critical points across scales.
AI.motivation: To unify descriptions of information propagation in CNNs with physical space, enabling interpretation of filter components as rest energy and momentum, and to explore emergent scale-invariant structures across diverse physical datasets.
AI.method: Establish a correspondence between discrete symmetric/antisymmetric filter components and energy terms; define ratio of antisymmetric energy to total energy as beta-like displacement; show repeated filtering yields Gaussian scale-space; relate to Laplacian-driven diffusion, Schrödinger equation, Friedmann equations; perform 3D image experiments across multiple scales.
AI.result: Framework yields blob-like Morse critical points across scale, consistent with patterns in organic/inorganic materials, brain MRI, galaxies, and CMB; demonstrates emergent scale-invariance and Morse topology in images.
AI.conclusion: Approach unifies information propagation in CNNs with fundamental physical laws, offering a novel lens to analyze scale-invariance and topological structures; suggests broad applicability across scientific imaging and data analysis.

title: CIFQA: A Deterministic Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Financial Query Answering
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, submitted for academic dissemination
summary: Calculation-intensive financial question answering requires exact reasoning over structured rates, temporal conditions, numerical formulas, and rule-based constraints.
