Although Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on natural language tasks, they often produce numerically incorrect yet plausible answers when solving multi-step financial calculations. To address this limitation, we introduce CIFQA (Calculation-Intensive Financial Query Answering), a deterministic tool-grounded multi-agent LLM framework for financial question answering. CIFQA separates language understanding from numerical execution by assigning specialized agents to query interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, and response generation, while deterministic Python-based tools perform financial calculations and rule application. We instantiate CIFQA for fixed deposit query answering and evaluate it on a curated benchmark of fixed deposit queries. CIFQA achieves 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy, substantially outperforming direct LLM baselines even when provided with complete formulas, rate cards, and benchmark instructions. Ablation studies show that deterministic components such as exact rate lookup, tenure computation, rolling-year adjustment, and premature-withdrawal logic are critical contributors to performance. Notably, a 17B open-source backbone operating within CIFQA outperforms substantially larger frontier models evaluated with the same financial information, demonstrating that architectural design is a more important determinant of numerical reliability than model scale. While evaluated on fixed deposit queries, CIFQA provides a generalizable framework for calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: CIFQA is a deterministic, multi-agent framework that channels numerical finance tasks through Python-based tools to ensure exact calculations, achieving high accuracy on fixed-deposit queries and outperforming larger LLM baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs often produce numerically plausible but incorrect multi-step financial calculations. A tool-grounded, deterministic architecture is needed to guarantee numerical reliability in calculation-intensive financial QA.
AI.method: CIFQA decomposes the problem into specialized agents (interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, response generation) with deterministic Python tools performing exact calculations and rule applications; evaluated on fixed deposit queries with a 17B open-source backbone integrated to show architectural efficacy.
AI.result: Achieves 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy; substantially outperforms direct LLM baselines even with full financial inputs; ablations reveal critical contributions from exact rate lookup, tenure computation, rolling-year adjustments, and premature-withdrawal logic; smaller open-models within CIFQA can surpass larger frontier models with the same data.
AI.conclusion: The CIFQA framework generalizes to calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks and demonstrates that architectural design and deterministic components can outweigh model scale in achieving numerical reliability.

title: The Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy: A Framework for Constructing Classifiers and Diagnosing Their Decisions, Applied to Prompt Injection Detection
summary: This paper proposes a framework for constructing a classifier as a safeguard layer, and for developing a complementary diagnostic that identifies which of the classifier's confident decisions can be trusted. This framework, the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, consists of (i) constructing a dimensionality-optimized classifier, in which the embedding dimensionality is empirically selected via cross-validated performance rather than fixed a priori, (ii) locating a relatively small set of latent support vectors (~ 29% of total training examples) representing influential prompts for identifying tokens that alter the classifier's predicted labels, and (iii) utilizing such tokens and their associated attack magnitudes for constructing a diagnostic taxonomy. This diagnostic taxonomy provides an end-to-end guideline for flagging prompts that require different treatments: rely Safely on the classifier's decision; flag Heuristic Bias and Heuristic Override cases; route Insufficient Context cases for further human/safety review. Applying the framework to a classifier trained on a public prompt injection dataset, we find that a substantial fraction of its confident decisions (~ 77%) are not robust to removing a single token, and that this brittleness separates into two distinct failure patterns: a confidence calibration failure and a genuinely exploitable shortcut. For each zone of the taxonomy, we also recommend strategies for remediating diagnosed prompts. We illustrate the framework as a series of steps, demonstrating how each step operates.

AI.tldr: Proposes Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy (LDT) to add a safeguard layer for classifiers, using dimensionality-optimized embeddings, latent support vectors (~29% of training data) to identify influential prompts, and a diagnostic taxonomy to classify prompts into safe, heuristic bias/override, or insufficient context; empirical results show ~77% of confident decisions are vulnerable to single-token removal, revealing calibration and shortcut failures; provides remediation steps and a step-by-step framework.
AI.motivation: Address brittleness and unreliability of classifier decisions under adversarial or misleading prompts. Provide a principled, end-to-end framework to diagnose when confident decisions can be trusted and how to remediate problematic prompts.
AI.method: 1) Build dimensionality-optimized classifier by selecting embedding dimensionality via cross-validated performance rather than fixed dimensionality. 2) Identify latent support vectors representing influential prompts (~29% of training examples) that influence label changes. 3) Use tokens and their attack magnitudes to construct a diagnostic taxonomy that flags: Safe reliance, Heuristic Bias, Heuristic Override, and Insufficient Context, with remediation strategies. 4) Demonstrate with a classifier trained on a public prompt injection dataset and illustrate steps.
AI.result: Empirical findings: about 77% of confident decisions are not robust to removing a single token; brittle decisions separate into two failure modes: confidence calibration failure and exploitable shortcut. The taxonomy yields actionable remediation strategies per zone and is demonstrated as an end-to-end pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy provides a practical, end-to-end framework for diagnosing and remediating prompts that affect classifier trust, enabling safer deployment of prompt-based systems through dimensionality optimization, latent prompts analysis, and structured remediation guidance.

title: Closing the Loop on the Poppy Humanoid: Bipedal Locomotion with Linear-Quadratic Control and Learned Cost Functions
comment: Accepted by International Conference on the AI Revolution: Research, Ethics, and Society (AIR-RES 2026)
summary: The Poppy Humanoid is an open-source, low-cost robot suitable for research and education in artificial intelligence. However, we are unaware of any published methodology that achieves reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on the standard Poppy hardware. This paper contributes a functional closed-loop walking controller for Poppy, based on the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) framework for trajectory tracking. Starting with data collected from open-loop playback of a nominal walking trajectory, our proposed method learns a quadratic cost function for an LQR controller that substantially improves the reliability of the motion. The closed-loop controller is validated empirically, demonstrating statistically significant improvements in walking performance compared to open-loop trajectory playback.

AI.tldr: Learned a quadratic cost for an LQR-based closed-loop walking controller to achieve reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on Poppy, with significant gains over open-loop walking.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on the open-source Poppy platform, addressing the gap in methodologies for stable walking on standard hardware and supporting AI research/education.
AI.method: Data are collected from open-loop playback of a nominal walking trajectory. A quadratic cost function for an LQR controller is learned to perform trajectory tracking, yielding a closed-loop controller that stabilizes locomotion on the Poppy robot.
AI.result: Empirical validation shows statistically significant improvements in walking performance with the closed-loop LQR controller compared to open-loop trajectory playback.
AI.conclusion: A functional, closed-loop walking controller for Poppy can be learned by shaping the LQR cost, improving reliability of locomotion on standard hardware and supporting accessible research/education in legged robotics.

title: VIPER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Veterinary Pathology
summary: Pathology vision-language models are advancing rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain focused on human tissue, particularly oncology, leaving non-human pathology largely unaddressed. This gap is especially important in toxicologic pathology, where microscopic tissue examination of laboratory animals is a core component of preclinical drug safety assessment. To address it, we introduce VIPER, the first expert-curated benchmark for vision-language model evaluation in toxicologic pathology. VIPER contains 1,251 questions associated with 419 H&E-stained rat histology images across seven organ systems, covering multiple-choice, KPrim, and free-text formats. All questions were curated and validated by board-certified veterinary pathologists. In total, we benchmarked 16 models, including two newly introduced veterinary-pathology models, seven human pathology-specialized models, and seven general-purpose frontier models. The results identify a substantial domain gap between veterinary and human pathology, expose the risk of over-diagnosis of normal tissue in frontier models, and show that domain-specific training remains critical for visually grounded predictions. VIPER data and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/mahmoodlab/viper.

AI.tldr: VIPER: the first expert-curated veterinary-toxicologic vision-language benchmark with 1,251 questions linked to 419 rat histology images across seven organ systems; evaluates 16 models (veterinary, human pathology, and general frontier); reveals domain gaps, over-diagnosis risk in frontier models, and the need for domain-specific training; data and code released.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of benchmarking resources for non-human, toxicologic pathology in vision-language models, which is crucial for preclinical safety assessment.
AI.method: Curated 1,251 questions associated with 419 H&E-stained rat images across seven organ systems, covering MC, KPrim, and free-text formats. Validation by board-certified veterinary pathologists. Evaluated 16 models: 2 veterinary-pathology models, 7 human-pathology models, 7 general frontier models.
AI.result: Disclose a substantial domain gap between veterinary and human pathology; frontier models tend to over-diagnose normal tissue; domain-specific training is essential for accurate visually grounded predictions.
AI.conclusion: VIPER provides a robust, expert-validated benchmark for veterinary-toxicologic pathology VLMs and highlights the importance of domain adaptation; data and evaluation code are publicly available to drive future model development.

title: The Artificial Experimentalist: Discovery and Control of Self-Organizing Phenomena with Autotelic Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at ALIFE 2026. Companion website: https://developmentalsystems.org/carl/
summary: Existing methods for exploring cellular automata and other complex systems mostly operate in open loop: they set initial conditions, execute a full simulation, and observe the outcome, without intervening during execution. We introduce a closed-loop framework based on autotelic reinforcement learning, in which an agent autonomously samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene in a complex system through minimal, local perturbations. We instantiate this framework on Lenia, a continuous cellular automaton known for life-like self-organizing patterns, in an agentic system we call CARL, and demonstrate three capabilities. First, CARL discovers stable solitons across a wide range of Lenia update rules at a higher rate than heuristic baselines. Second, it learns to steer the movement direction of existing solitons with few interventions, showing that CARL can control self-organizing patterns, not only create them. Third, humans can use trained agents to guide solitons through maze environments in real time by specifying high-level directional commands that the agent translates into low-level interventions. Trained across diverse goals, update rules, and random initial states, the agents acquire policies that generalize zero-shot to various out-of-distribution conditions. These results suggest a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that, autonomously or with human guidance, discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems.

AI.tldr: Closed-loop autotelic RL (CARL) for Lenia: an agent learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene via minimal local perturbations, enabling rapid discovery of solitons, steering of patterns, and real-time human-guided navigation, with zero-shot generalization across goals, update rules, and random inits; suggests autonomous experimentalists for emergent phenomena.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of open-loop exploration of cellular automata and other complex systems by enabling autonomous, goal-driven interventions that discover and control emergent structures.
AI.method: Train an agent in a closed-loop autotelic reinforcement learning framework (CARL) that samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to apply minimal local perturbations in Lenia. Evaluate on (i) discovery of stable solitons across Lenia update rules, (ii) steering soliton movement with few interventions, and (iii) real-time human-guided navigation through maze environments using high-level commands translated into low-level actions. Demonstrate zero-shot generalization across goals, update rules, and random initial states.
AI.result: CARL discovers stable solitons more rapidly than heuristic baselines; learns to steer existing solitons with few actions; enables humans to guide solitons in mazes in real time via high-level commands; policies generalize to out-of-distribution goals, rules, and initial conditions (zero-shot).
AI.conclusion: Autonomous agents with autotelic, goal-conditioned policies can discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems, offering a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that operate with or under human guidance.

title: FedCMAPSS: A Benchmark for Federated Learning in Remaining Useful Life Estimation
comment: Accepted at the 21st IEEE Conference on Industrial Electronics and Applications (ICIEA 2026)
summary: Data-driven prognostics and health management has emerged as a key enabler for Industry 4.0, yet the development of robust remaining useful life (RUL) estimation models is often limited by the scarcity of run-to-failure data. While federated learning offers a promising paradigm to collaboratively train predictive models without sharing sensor data, research efforts have operated so far in the absence of a common evaluation framework. To address this gap, this paper introduces FedCMAPSS, a benchmark for federated RUL estimation based on the commonly-used NASA C-MAPSS dataset. We define a set of five standardized tasks designed to simulate real-world industrial challenges, ranging from ideal IID settings to extreme statistical heterogeneity, and conduct a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art federated optimization algorithms across multiple neural architectures. By establishing reproducible baselines and making the source code and data splits publicly available, this work aims to provide a standard foundation for developing and comparing federated predictive maintenance solutions.

AI.tldr: FedCMAPSS is a standardized federated RUL benchmark (NASA C-MAPSS) with five tasks spanning IID to extreme heterogeneity, enabling reproducible evaluation of federated optimization across multiple neural architectures; source code and data splits are released.
AI.motivation: Addresses the scarcity of run-to-failure data and privacy concerns by enabling collaborative learning; fills the lack of a common evaluation framework for federated predictive maintenance.
AI.method: Define five benchmark tasks on the NASA C-MAPSS data to simulate real-world industrial heterogeneity, evaluate state-of-the-art federated optimization algorithms across multiple neural architectures, and establish reproducible baselines with publicly available source code and data splits.
AI.result: Introduction of the FedCMAPSS benchmark with standardized tasks and baseline evaluations; demonstrates feasibility of federated RUL estimation under varied data heterogeneity and provides a reproducible evaluation platform for future methods.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark creates a standard foundation for developing and comparing federated predictive maintenance solutions and will facilitate fair, reproducible progress in federated RUL estimation.

title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
summary: Robot policies deployed in the wild should have the capability to continually learn new tasks without forgetting existing behaviors. A common approach to combat such catastrophic forgetting is to train on new task data with a replay buffer of previously learned task data. Although this buffer is commonly sampled randomly from all prior experiences, we show that a small set of these experiences contributes greatly in anchoring past performance. We call these experiences Memory Anchors. We identify Memory Anchors in regions where representations of new-task observations collapse onto those of old-task observations even though the tasks require conflicting actions, like when a familiar object must be manipulated in a new way. Rehearsing old data in this region plays a key role in preventing destructive overwriting of past task knowledge, serving as this critical Memory Anchor role. Excluding only 10% Memory Anchors before sampling the buffer leads to more than a 4.5x increase in catastrophic forgetting on the LIBERO benchmark suites. Conversely, enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors can decrease high-conflict task forgetting by 63% and enables successful continual learning of two task sequences on a real robot. Videos and additional visualizations can be found at https://robot-adaptation.github.io/MemoryAnchors

AI.tldr: Memory Anchors: a small, impactful subset of past experiences used to anchor past task performance during continual learning for robots, identified where new-task representations collapse onto old-task ones despite conflicting actions; replaying these anchors prevents forgetting.
AI.motivation: Overcome catastrophic forgetting in continual robot learning by identifying and prioritizing a small set of informative past experiences that stabilize representations across tasks.
AI.method: Identify Memory Anchors as experiences where representations of new-task observations collapse onto old-task representations despite conflicting actions. Enrich or prune the replay buffer with Memory Anchors and evaluate effects on forgetting. Experiments on LIBERO benchmarks and real robots, including removing 10% of anchors and observing impact, and increasing anchor presence to reduce forgetting in high-conflict tasks.
AI.result: Removing 10% of Memory Anchors leads to >4.5x more catastrophic forgetting on LIBERO benchmarks. Enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors reduces high-conflict forgetting by 63% and enables continual learning of two task sequences on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: Memory Anchors are critical anchors for preventing catastrophic forgetting in continual robotic learning; targeted replay buffer design around anchor samples substantially improves retention and enables more robust continual adaptation.

title: Mapping Woody Vegetation from Multi-Source Imagery and Prediction Fusion for Enhanced Data Efficiency and Accuracy
comment: Published in IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing
summary: Tree cover maps are a fundamental remote sensing product, used to derive ecological insights about the landscape and are essential to change detection, vegetation mapping and fire monitoring programs. However, comprehensive tree cover mapping requires reliable and high-quality imagery, free of cloud and weather defects to ensure accurate model outputs. Deep learning approaches can generate high quality maps with minimal human intervention but require large amounts of human annotated data to be successful. In this work we propose a framework consisting of methods that aim to improve the data efficiency and robustness of deep learning models using data fusion techniques to segment woody vegetation defined as vegetation over the height of 2m across the state of New South Wales, Australia. To improve robustness against varying image quality, we propose an image composition method that normalizes the imagery and removes defects, whilst also minimizing the reliance on individual image quality by proposing a prediction fusion method. The two methods resulted in an error reduction of 38.2% and 53.6% respectively compared to single-source imagery. To address deep learning approaches' limitation of requiring large amounts of data, we apply label transfer to multiple sources of imagery as a form of data augmentation to improve data efficiency. Learning from multiple image sources was shown to be the biggest improvement in performance, resulting in an error reduction between 28.1% to 76.2% across the different validation experiments, whilst reducing the standard deviation of performance across image dates by a factor of 13.

AI.tldr: The work enhances data efficiency and robustness of deep-learning tree cover mapping via data fusion across imagery sources, image normalization/prediction fusion to mitigate defects, and label transfer for augmentation, achieving large error reductions and reduced variability across dates.
AI.motivation: Tree cover maps require high-quality imagery free of cloud/defects, but such data are scarce and labeled data are costly. The study targets woody vegetation (>2 m) over New South Wales to improve mapping accuracy with less data and more robust performance under varying image quality.
AI.method: 1) Image composition: normalize imagery and remove defects to reduce sensitivity to image quality. 2) Prediction fusion: combine predictions from multiple sources to further reduce reliance on a single image. 3) Label transfer/data augmentation: transfer labels across multiple imagery sources to improve data efficiency; evaluate across validation experiments.
AI.result: Image composition reduced error by 38.2% and prediction fusion by 53.6% compared with single-source imagery. Learning from multiple image sources (label transfer) yielded 28.1%–76.2% error reductions across experiments, and reduced the standard deviation of performance across image dates by a factor of 13.
AI.conclusion: Data fusion and cross-source learning substantially improve robustness and data efficiency in deep-learning tree cover mapping, enabling high-quality woody-vegetation maps with less dependence on pristine, single-source imagery.

title: The Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox Quantifying Net Energy Loss in on-Device Energy Forecasting
comment: The 5th International Conference on Mobile, Military, Maritime IT Convergence (ICMIC 2026)
summary: Energy forecasting aims to maximize accuracy to ensure energy efficiency by reducing energy waste, an objective that applies equally to on-device forecasting for mission-critical edge environments, including military systems. However, this paper identifies the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox: high-precision energy forecasting models can ironically trigger a net energy deficit. This stems from both edge AI's inference energy consumption and battery aging. We propose a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework for energy forecasting, designed to minimize net energy loss. This framework treats not only inference energy consumption but also battery aging as a unified form of energy loss, as degradation represents a physical dissipation of the system's future energy-carrying capacity. We demonstrate that in thermally sensitive edge environments, energy saved by the superior precision of complex architectures is often outweighed by the total energy lost through their high operational intensity.

AI.tldr: High-accuracy edge energy forecasting can incur higher net energy use due to inference energy and battery aging; a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework unifies these losses to minimize net energy dissipation.
AI.motivation: Address the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox in edge energy forecasting, where pursuing precision may increase overall energy consumption. Propose a framework that accounts for both runtime inference energy and battery aging as energy losses.
AI.method: Introduce a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework for energy forecasting. Model energy loss from inference energy and battery aging as a single cost. Evaluate in thermally sensitive edge environments, comparing architectures with varying accuracy and intensity to identify configurations that minimize net energy loss.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates that, in thermally sensitive edge settings, the energy saved by higher-precision models is often outweighed by increased operational intensity and accelerated battery aging, leading to a net energy deficit.
AI.conclusion: A TCO-based approach can guide model and system design to minimize net energy loss in edge forecasting, suggesting selective deployment of simpler models or energy-aware training to balance accuracy and total energy cost.

title: NeoTriFuse: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Fusion under Missingness Heterogeneity for Neonatal Mortality Risk Prediction
summary: Neonatal mortality risk prediction from bedside monitoring data remains challenging due to extreme class imbalance, heterogeneous clinical risk factors, multi-scale temporal dynamics, and substantial missingness. We propose NeoTriFuse, a reliability-aware multimodal fusion framework for missingness-heterogeneous neonatal monitoring data. Unlike conventional multimodal approaches that treat missingness primarily as a preprocessing issue, NeoTriFuse models missingness as an explicit reliability signal that dynamically modulates modality contributions during fusion. The framework integrates static perinatal variables, local-global temporal encoders, and patient-level statistical summaries through reliability-guided gating mechanisms, while jointly optimizing mortality prediction and an auxiliary length-of-stay objective. NeoTriFuse achieves competitive performance, with an F1 score of 0.6736 +/- 0.0216 and an AUROC of 0.9454 +/- 0.0056. Ablation studies indicate that the local-global temporal architecture and patient-level summary branch contribute most substantially to predictive performance, while reliability-aware gating provides additional improvements on threshold-dependent metrics under heterogeneous observation completeness. Sensitivity analyses further suggest stable performance across nearby hyperparameter settings. Overall, the findings support reliability-aware multimodal fusion as a practical approach for neonatal mortality prediction under realistic clinical missingness conditions.

AI.tldr: NeoTriFuse is a reliability-aware multimodal fusion framework for neonatal mortality prediction that treats missing data as a reliability signal and integrates static perinatal data, local-global temporal encoders, and patient-level summaries to improve performance under realistic missingness.
AI.motivation: Neonatal mortality prediction from bedside data faces extreme class imbalance, heterogeneous clinical risk factors, multi-scale temporal dynamics, and substantial missingness. Conventional multimodal approaches often treat missingness as a preprocessing issue rather than a reliability signal.
AI.method: NeoTriFuse introduces reliability-guided gating to modulate modality contributions during fusion. It integrates static perinatal variables, local-global temporal encoders, and patient-level statistical summaries, and jointly optimizes mortality prediction with an auxiliary length-of-stay objective.
AI.result: On evaluation, NeoTriFuse achieves F1 = 0.6736 ± 0.0216 and AUROC = 0.9454 ± 0.0056. Ablation shows the local-global temporal architecture and the patient-level summary branch contribute most to performance; reliability-aware gating yields additional improvements on threshold-dependent metrics under heterogeneous observation completeness. Sensitivity analyses indicate stable performance across nearby hyperparameter settings.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware multimodal fusion is a practical and effective approach for neonatal mortality prediction under realistic clinical missingness conditions.

title: TrapVLA: Trapping Vision-Language-Action Models in Configured Failure Modes
summary: This work introduces Configured Failure Trapping, a novel backdoor attack task against Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which aims to activate attacks through stealthy textual triggers and induce configured failure modes. Unlike prior backdoor attacks that treat any task failure as a successful attack, Configured Failure Trapping requires the attacker to control how the robot fails (e.g., causing the robot to grasp with a specified positional offset), making it substantially more challenging and hard to detect. To support the new task, we propose an effective data engine for synthesizing high-quality target trajectories and an automated suite for measuring configured-failure fidelity. Then, based on this foundation, we construct two new benchmarks, namely Trap-LIBERO and Trap-RoboTwin, that instantiate Configured Failure Trapping across four representative failure modes. To address this task, we identify sparse action deviation as a critical challenge and accordingly propose a novel method named TrapVLA, which explicitly learns trigger-induced action residuals to steer the policy toward the configured failure behavior. Extensive experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic settings show that TrapVLA effectively injects configured failure modes into VLA models while largely preserving performance on clean data. Project page: https://john-liua.github.io/TrapVLA/

AI.tldr: Proposes Configured Failure Trapping (CFT) as a backdoor task for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. Introduces data synthesis for target trajectories, evaluation of configured-failure fidelity, and two benchmarks (Trap-LIBERO, Trap-RoboTwin). Presents TrapVLA to learn trigger-induced action residuals to steer policies into a predefined failure after textual triggers. Demonstrates effectiveness in simulation and real-world with preserved clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: To raise the bar for backdoor attacks by not only causing any failure but controlling the specific failure mode of a robot, making detection harder and enabling stealthy, task-specific manipulation.
AI.method: Develop a data engine to synthesize high-quality target trajectories; create an automated suite to measure fidelity of configured failures; construct two benchmarks Trap-LIBERO and Trap-RoboTwin spanning four failure modes; propose TrapVLA, a method that explicitly learns trigger-induced action residuals to steer policy toward the configured failure.
AI.result: TrapVLA successfully injects configured failure modes in VLA models while largely preserving performance on clean data, across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotics settings. The benchmarks enable evaluation of configured-failure fidelity under various modes.
AI.conclusion: Configured Failure Trapping represents a novel, more controllable backdoor paradigm for VLA systems, highlighting new security risks and the need for defenses that detect or mitigate trigger-induced action residuals. The work provides datasets, benchmarks, and a baseline method, with a project page for reproducibility.

title: Zero-Shot Video Restoration and Enhancement with Text-to-Image Latent Diffusion Models and Multi-Modal References
summary: Zero-shot image restoration methods with text-to-image latent diffusion models have achieved great success in universal image restoration tasks without training. However, applying them to video restoration will result in severe temporal flickering. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for zero-shot video restoration and enhancement which uses a text-to-image latent diffusion model and multi-modal references. Through the proposed dual prompt tuning inversion and sampling, the inference time can be reduced to nearly 1/3 of the original. The performance and temporal consistency can be also significantly stregthened. By using the proposed texture-aware video token merging, the temporal correlation between frames can be further utilized to improve the temporal consistency. We futher propose the referenced self-attention and referenced token merging to support image reference. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in restoring and enhancing temporally consistent videos.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot video restoration framework using a text-to-image latent diffusion model with dual prompt tuning inversion and sampling, texture-aware video token merging, and referenced attention/token merging, achieving faster inference (~1/3) and improved temporal consistency using multi-modal references.
AI.motivation: Address temporal flickering when applying zero-shot image-to-image diffusion for video restoration by leveraging temporal cues and references to enhance consistency and efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce dual prompt tuning inversion and sampling; texture-aware video token merging to exploit temporal correlations; referenced self-attention and referenced token merging to support image references; operate within a zero-shot framework using a text-to-image latent diffusion model and multi-modal references.
AI.result: Inference time reduced to about one-third; improved temporal consistency and restoration quality; experimental results demonstrate superiority in producing temporally consistent videos.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively extends zero-shot diffusion-based video restoration with enhanced temporal stability and efficiency, validated by experiments, and highlights the importance of texture-aware token merging and reference-guided attention mechanisms.

title: LLMs for Academic Workflows: An Evaluation of Literature Reviews Generated with Short and Long Context Windows of LLMs
summary: Our research focuses on evaluating literature reviews generated in short and long context settings of large language models (LLMs) to investigate the impact of context window on the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and the role of AI in supporting literature review writing. Twenty AI-generated literature reviews based on research sources from Semantic Scholar and Arxiv were evaluated by two researchers across 15 dimensions. Our findings reveal that AI-generated literature reviews require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. As context windows increase, LLMs can incorporate broader information and maintain coherence across longer inputs, but they also exacerbate issues such as content repetition, omission of critical work, and a tendency towards descriptiveness over synthesis. Our work shows that AI-generated reviews can provide foundational overviews, but their output must be critically evaluated and refined by domain experts. Future research should consider integrating other LLMs and fine-tuned models in different domains with hybrid approaches that combine human expertise with AI capabilities to address the limitations identified in this study.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated literature reviews can be useful as starting points but require human oversight; larger context windows improve coverage and coherence but increase repetition and omission risks and tend toward description over synthesis; future work favors hybrid human–AI approaches with multiple models.
AI.motivation: To evaluate how context window size in LLMs impacts the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and to elucidate the role of AI in assisting literature-review writing.
AI.method: 20 AI-generated literature reviews, sourced from Semantic Scholar and ArXiv, were evaluated by two researchers across 15 dimensions.
AI.result: AI reviews require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. As context windows enlarge, LLMs incorporate broader information and maintain coherence, but issues rise: content repetition, omission of critical works, and descriptiveness over synthesis. AI can provide foundational overviews, but outputs must be critically evaluated and refined by domain experts.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated reviews are useful as foundational overviews but are not ready-to-publish; integrating other LLMs and fine-tuned models in different domains and employing hybrid human–AI approaches can address identified limitations.

title: Subgraph Filtering for Fair Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can exhibit unfair behavior even when sensitive attributes are excluded from node features, because graph topology and message passing propagate group-correlated signals under sensitive homophily. Existing fairness-aware GNN methods mainly constrain representations or prediction distributions at a global level, without explicitly controlling the local structural pathways through which biased information propagates during aggregation. We propose Subgraph Filtering for Fair Graph Neural Networks (SF-GNN), a lightweight and architecture-agnostic framework that mitigates structural bias at its source. SF-GNN identifies bias-prone edges by combining sensitive homophily with structural propagation amplifiers, including hub participation and triadic closure. It then incorporates stochastic edge filtering into each message-passing step to selectively downweight or remove these edges while preserving the remaining graph structure. Training further incorporates a statistical-parity regularizer with a warm-up schedule to stabilize optimization. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show that SF-GNN achieves consistent fairness improvements while maintaining competitive predictive performance, leading to a better fairness--accuracy trade-off than recent fairness-aware GNN baselines.

AI.tldr: SF-GNN uses subgraph-level edge filtering to mitigate structural bias in GNNs, improving fairness with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Biased information can propagate via graph topology even when sensitive attributes are removed; existing methods operate globally and miss local propagation pathways.
AI.method: Identify bias-prone edges via sensitive homophily and structural propagation amplifiers (hub participation, triadic closure); apply stochastic edge filtering during message passing; add warm-up-based statistical-parity regularizer.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on five benchmarks shows consistent fairness gains and competitive accuracy, better fairness-accuracy trade-off than baselines.
AI.conclusion: SF-GNN provides a lightweight, architecture-agnostic approach that targets the source of structural bias and yields robust fair performance with preserved predictive power.

title: SOLO: Stable Omni-terrain Long-Horizon Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Humans traverse complex terrain over long distances without losing balance, whereas perceptive humanoid policies become fragile as perception and control errors accumulate. We present SOLO, a unified framework addressing two compounding causes of this long-horizon fragility: dense terrain reconstruction smooths action-critical details, and pointwise imitation lacks temporal credit assignment. Its Query Reconstructor (QR) uses Fourier-encoded cell queries to retrieve spatially specific evidence from depth-proprioception tokens, preserving sharp terrain boundaries. Trajectory-Aware MSE (TA-MSE) Distillation adds next-state teacher-student disagreement to the PPO reward, enabling Generalized Advantage Estimation to propagate future disagreement penalties to preceding actions. In simulation, QR reduces height-map L1 error by factors of 3.3-4.0, while TA-MSE surpasses PPO and MSE+PPO in curriculum progression. On stress-test terrains, SOLO achieves 97.5% mean traversal success and 96% stepping-stone success, versus 75.0-75.6% and 0-3% for dense-reconstructor variants. Deployed zero-shot with only a chest-mounted depth camera and proprioception, SOLO completes a continuous 1.5-km outdoor route and an indoor mixed-terrain course. Project page: https://sunpihai-up.github.io/solo/

AI.tldr: SOLO unifies terrain reconstruction and temporal credit assignment to improve long-horizon legged locomotion, achieving large gains in terrain boundary preservation, prediction accuracy, and zero-shot real-world traversal.
AI.motivation: Perception–control fragility in long-horizon locomotion arises from (i) dense terrain reconstruction blurring action-relevant details and (ii) lack of temporal credit assignment in pointwise imitation policies. A unified approach is needed to maintain sharp terrain cues and propagate future penalties to prior actions.
AI.method: Introduce Query Reconstructor (QR) with Fourier-encoded cell queries to retrieve spatially specific evidence from depth-proprioception tokens, preserving sharp terrain boundaries. Introduce Trajectory-Aware MSE (TA-MSE) Distillation that augments PPO rewards with next-state teacher–student disagreement, enabling Generalized Advantage Estimation to propagate future disagreement penalties to earlier actions.
AI.result: QR reduces height-map L1 error by 3.3–4.0x in simulation. TA-MSE outperforms PPO and MSE+PPO in curriculum progression. On stress-test terrains, SOLO attains 97.5% mean traversal success and 96% stepping-stone success, vs 75.0–75.6% and 0–3% for dense-reconstructor variants. Zero-shot deployment with only chest-mounted depth camera and proprioception achieves a continuous 1.5-km outdoor route and an indoor mixed-terrain course.
AI.conclusion: A unified SLAM-perception-control framework with temporally-aware imitation substantially improves long-horizon locomotion robustness on challenging terrains, preserving terrain boundaries and enabling real-world zero-shot deployment. QR and TA-MSE are the key components enabling improved perception fidelity and credit assignment across time.

title: Learning Woody Clearing With Loss Alignment for Zero-Shot Regrowth and Woody Segmentation
comment: Published in IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Detecting woody clearing is vital for managing biodiversity. Deep learning models can detect change in woody vegetation from bitemporal remote sensing imagery, however generated products may not meet end-user specifications due to unaligned loss definitions. Further limitations of deep learning models are the reliance on large datasets which can be difficult to attain for spatially rare and ambiguous events such as regrowth detection. In this work we train a model to detect woody change using bitemporal Sentinel-2 imagery consisting of 7 years' worth of annual imagery across the state of New South Wales, Australia. To align the objective of the model with end-user metrics, we introduce the loss scaling coefficient $α$ which transforms the objective to optimize for specific $F_β$ scores. Introducing $α$ was found to increase precision by 1.85x or recall by 1.12x. We propose input imagery augmentation and generation techniques that allow the woody change detection model to zero-shot transfer to regrowth and woody segmentation tasks. For woody segmentation, image generation techniques using activation maximization with low $α$ values for stability and image generation techniques derived from handcrafted features utilizing a mosaic of clearing patches and artificial trees for contextual grounding were found to outperform prior woody segmentation works of the study area, reducing the overall error by up to 18.2%. For zero-shot woody regrowth, creating pseudo-post and prior images resulted in the model achieving an F1 score of 0.845, creating a foundation for future regrowth detection work.

AI.tldr: Proposes a loss-scaling factor α to align change-detection DL objective with specific Fβ end-user metrics for woody clearing using Sentinel-2; shows precision/recall gains; introduces input augmentation and synthetic-generation to enable zero-shot transfer to woody regrowth and segmentation; achieves F1=0.845 for regrowth with pseudo-post/prior images and up to 18.2% error reduction in segmentation.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between DL training objectives and practical end-user metrics in woody vegetation change detection, while addressing data scarcity for regrowth events and enabling transfer to related tasks.
AI.method: Train a model on 7 years of annual Sentinel-2 bitemporal imagery across New South Wales. Introduce a loss scaling coefficient α to optimize for chosen Fβ scores. Apply input imagery augmentation and generation techniques. For woody segmentation, use activation maximization at low α for stability and handcrafted-features-based contextual grounding via a mosaic of clearing patches and artificial trees. For regrowth, create pseudo-post/prior images to enable zero-shot learning.
AI.result: α increased precision by 1.85x or recall by 1.12x. Woody segmentation achieved up to 18.2% reduction in overall error over prior work. Zero-shot regrowth reached F1=0.845 using pseudo-post/prior images.
AI.conclusion: Loss scaling enables alignment of DL models with user-centric metrics in woody change detection. Augmentation and synthetic-context techniques support zero-shot transfer to regrowth and segmentation, demonstrating substantial performance gains and establishing a foundation for future regrowth detection work.

title: Methodological and Conceptual Framework for 5D Multi-Table Analysis: A Unified Approach for Complex Data Reuse
summary: Multi-table learning remains a major challenge in machine learning for healthcare and other complex information systems. Relational data combine several sources of complexity, including large data volume, high-dimensional variables, high-cardinality categorical features, complex inter-table dependencies, and repeated temporal observations. We introduce the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a unified architecture that represents relational databases as hypergraphs, learns pentadimensional embeddings (PentE), and performs sparse relational attention with complexity proportional to the average relational degree rather than the square of the number of entities. We formally define the architecture, derive the complexity of its attention mechanism, and provide an open-source reference implementation. We evaluate RHT on the public Synthea synthetic electronic health record dataset using multi-label prediction of SNOMED CT condition codes per encounter, a task characterized by high categorical cardinality and long-tailed label distributions. Comparisons with tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines show that RHT produces more semantically coherent embeddings while remaining computationally scalable. In this benchmark, the highest rare-code recall is achieved by XGBoost, whereas RHT attains the strongest embedding semantic coherence. We also report ablation studies quantifying the contribution of each architectural component. Clinical validation on MIMIC-IV is planned following PhysioNet credentialing. Source code and experimental protocols are provided in the accompanying repository.

AI.tldr: Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT) models relational databases as hypergraphs, learning pentadimensional embeddings (PentE) and performing sparse relational attention with complexity tied to average relational degree, enabling scalable multi-table learning in healthcare. Open-source implementation and ablation studies accompany the evaluation on Synthea for multi-label SNOMED codes; clinical validation on MIMIC-IV planned.
AI.motivation: To tackle multi-table learning in healthcare with complex relational structures (large data, high-cardinality features, inter-table dependencies, temporal repeats) while avoiding quadratic attention costs.
AI.method: Represent relational data as hypergraphs; learn PentE embeddings; implement sparse relational attention whose cost scales with average relational degree; provide theoretical complexity analysis and open-source code; evaluate on Synthea for multi-label SNOMED CT prediction per encounter; compare with tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines; perform ablations; plan clinical validation on MIMIC-IV.
AI.result: RHT produces more semantically coherent embeddings and remains computationally scalable compared to baselines; strongest embedding semantic coherence; XGBoost achieves the highest rare-code recall in the benchmark; ablations quantify component contributions; open-source code and protocols available.
AI.conclusion: RHT advances scalable, semantically meaningful representation learning for relational healthcare data; demonstrated gains in embedding quality and scalability; clinical validation on MIMIC-IV planned; implementation released for reproducibility.

title: Toward Equitable Low-Carbon Mobility: Fairness-Aware Demand Prediction for Expanding Bike-Sharing Systems
summary: Bike-sharing systems are an important component of low-carbon urban mobility, but continued expansion creates challenges in both cold-start prediction and equitable resource allocation. Newly deployed stations lack historical ridership records, causing a mismatch between training and inference for graph-based models on evolving networks. Historical demand may also encode structural inequalities, as lower ridership in low-income neighborhoods can reflect limited infrastructure access rather than weak latent demand. Models trained directly on such data may therefore reinforce existing mobility disparities. We propose FairGIN, a fairness-aware graph neural network for demand prediction in expanding bike-sharing systems. FairGIN integrates three components. Expansion-Simulated Increment Training stochastically simulates network expansion during training to reduce the cold-start distribution gap. Attention-Based Knowledge Transfer combines station-adaptive temperature scaling with orthogonal embedding alignment to transfer representations from data-rich existing stations to data-sparse new stations. Fairness-Aware Optimization introduces income-stratified regularization and an equity-calibrated deployment score to support more inclusive station placement. Experiments on NYC and Seattle demonstrate that FairGIN achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy across diverse expansion scenarios while substantially reducing income-based disparities without compromising overall system efficiency.

AI.tldr: FairGIN is a fairness-aware GNN for demand prediction in expanding bike-sharing systems, addressing cold-start and equity: it uses expansion-simulated incremental training, station-adaptive attention transfer with orthogonal embedding alignment, and income-aware regularization with an equity-calibrated deployment score, achieving strong accuracy and reduced income-based disparities in NYC and Seattle.
AI.motivation: Address cold-start and fairness challenges in expanding bike-sharing networks: new stations lack data, and historical demand may encode inequities that propagate through predictive models.
AI.method: (1) Expansion-Simulated Increment Training to simulate network expansion during training; (2) Attention-Based Knowledge Transfer using station-adaptive temperature scaling and orthogonal embedding alignment to transfer representations from data-rich stations to data-sparse ones; (3) Fairness-Aware Optimization with income-stratified regularization and an equity-calibrated deployment score for fair station placement.
AI.result: Experiments on NYC and Seattle show state-of-the-art predictive accuracy across expansion scenarios and substantial reductions in income-based disparities without sacrificing overall system efficiency.
AI.conclusion: FairGIN effectively combines expansion-aware training, transfer learning, and explicit fairness constraints to improve predictive performance while promoting more equitable bike-sharing deployment.

title: Relaxation-Aware Multimodal Sensing of Soft Gripper Driven by Structure-Perception-Learning
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures. Published in Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS 2026)
summary: Achieving stable, sustained grasping with soft robotic hands remains a fundamental challenge. Compliance enables safe and adaptive contact, yet the intrinsic viscoelasticity of soft polymers leads to stress relaxation and a continuous decay of grasping force during holding. Inspired by human grasping, which combines phase-dependent stiffness regulation with continuous sensing and feedback, this paper presents an integrated structure--perception--learning framework. We develop a variable-stiffness soft gripper that uses onboard vision and infrared thermography to track deformation and the temperature field in real time, preserving continuous tracking of the interaction state. To mitigate relaxation-induced force decay, we propose a temperature-coupled viscoelastic force representation, together with a physics-informed learning model, to reconstruct the force trend and provide explicit compensation during holding. Experiments show that, in a 280s force-controlled grasp-and-hold task, the proposed method maintains the desired force with a mean absolute error of 0.066N, outperforming fixed-aperture and instantaneous-only baselines by 80% and 95%, respectively. Overall, the results support a mechanism--AI co-design view: mechanisms shape feasible interactions, while learning compensates remaining uncertainty in viscoelastic dynamics, together enabling stable, sustained grasping.

AI.tldr: Variable-stiffness soft gripper with real-time vision and infrared sensing, plus physics-informed learning, to counter viscoelastic force decay and enable stable grasping with MAE 0.066 N over 280 s; outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Address stress relaxation in soft polymers that causes force decay during holding; mimic human grasping with phase-dependent stiffness and continuous sensing to maintain stable contact.
AI.method: Develop a variable-stiffness soft gripper equipped with onboard vision and infrared thermography to track deformation and temperature in real time. Introduce a temperature-coupled viscoelastic force representation and a physics-informed learning model to reconstruct the force trend and provide explicit holding-force compensation.
AI.result: Experiment: 280 s force-controlled grasp-and-hold task achieving mean absolute error of 0.066 N, outperforming fixed-aperture and instantaneous-only baselines by 80% and 95%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a mechanism–AI co-design view: physical mechanisms define feasible interactions, while learning compensates remaining viscoelastic dynamics uncertainty, enabling stable, sustained grasping.

title: Video-FLAIR: Not Whether to Reason, But How
summary: Multimodal queries can require different types of reasoning. Some can be answered via perceptual reasoning, extracting information directly from the visual signal, while others require compositional reasoning that combines observations or deliberative reasoning that evaluates competing hypotheses. However, many existing methods apply a uniform reasoning strategy across queries, leading to unnecessary computation on simple tasks and insufficient reasoning on complex ones. We introduce Video-FLAIR, a training framework that learns to select the appropriate reasoning mode for each query using reinforcement learning. During training, the model generates responses under all three modes for the same prompt, enabling direct comparison. A composite reward compares these responses to favor the most effective one based on correctness, grounding, and cost, while discouraging unsupported or misaligned deliberation. This yields a supervision signal for learning adaptive reasoning without per-query annotations. Video-FLAIR improves accuracy over the Qwen2.5-VL base model by +5.4 on MathVista, +4.8 on Video-Holmes, and +4.8 on Video-MMMU, while reducing average token usage to 95 compared to 417 for always-thinking baselines.

AI.tldr: Video-FLAIR is an RL-based framework that adaptively selects among perceptual, compositional, and deliberative reasoning modes for multimodal queries. It trains by generating responses in all modes per prompt and uses a composite reward to identify the most effective mode, achieving higher accuracy with lower token usage.
AI.motivation: Uniform reasoning strategies across queries waste computation for simple tasks and underperform on complex ones. There is a need for adaptive, per-query reasoning without expensive per-example annotations.
AI.method: During training, the model produces responses under all three modes for each prompt. A composite reward—assessing correctness, grounding, and cost—guides learning and discourages unsupported deliberation. This reinforcement-learning signal trains a mode selector without per-query annotations. Baseline: Qwen2.5-VL.
AI.result: Accuracy gains on evaluated datasets: MathVista +5.4, Video-Holmes +4.8, Video-MMMU +4.8. Average token usage reduced to 95 (vs. 417 for always-thinking baselines).
AI.conclusion: Adaptive RL-driven mode selection yields improved accuracy and reduced compute across diverse video QA benchmarks, demonstrating effective per-query reasoning strategy selection.

title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Systematic Literature Review of Disease Spread Models
comment: To be published in the Winter Simulation Conference 2026
summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have created new opportunities to streamline and potentially automate many research processes, including systematic literature reviews (SLRs). This study reports an LLM pipeline development for extracting model-relevant information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers. We compare the results with those of a human-conducted SLR. Our results show paper-level accuracies of approximately 77.95% for GPT-4.1 and 81.67% for GPT-5.0. Field-level accuracy ranges from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex or subjective fields performing less reliably. Importantly, we find that agreement between LLMs is a potential indicator of output quality: low agreement may signal hallucinations, whereas high agreement combined with low accuracy may point to noise or errors in the human dataset. Overall, our study provides practical insights into prompt development and highlights both the potential and limitations of using LLMs for full-scale SLRs in the modeling and simulation domain.

AI.tldr: LLMs can assist systematic literature reviews in agent-based modeling with moderate accuracy; inter-model agreement may indicate quality; results vary by field, with higher complexity reducing reliability; careful prompt design and quality checks are essential.
AI.motivation: Assess feasibility and reliability of using large language models to perform or assist in systematic literature reviews in the modeling and simulation domain, and compare against human-conducted SLR.
AI.method: Developed an LLM-based pipeline to extract model-relevant information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers; compared outputs with a human-conducted SLR; evaluated paper-level and field-level accuracy; analyzed inter-LLM agreement as a quality signal.
AI.result: Paper-level accuracies: ~77.95% (GPT-4.1) and ~81.67% (GPT-5.0). Field-level accuracy ranges from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex/subjective fields less reliable. Inter-LLM agreement correlates with output quality; high agreement with low accuracy may indicate noisy human data; low agreement may signal hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs have potential for automating or assisting full-scale SLRs in modeling and simulation but require robust prompt engineering, verification, and domain-specific adaptations to handle variability across fields and mitigate hallucinations and data quality issues.

title: Distributed Training using an Intelligent Network
summary: Distributed training across a wide area network (WAN) is challenging, as continuous parameter exchange by islands of compute is constrained by limited bandwidth, high latency, and uneven topology. We propose making the network an active participant in training. On the systems side, such networks should leverage (i) multicast technology to replicate outbound traffic and (ii) in-line FPGAs to aggregate inbound traffic, to ease egress and ingress bottlenecks. These technologies are used for training across workers within a data center, but this paper extends them to the WAN. On the algorithms side, we develop an optimization framework that produces rich synchronization schedules (namely, rotating cliques of islands) around the underlying network topology and these technologies, to maximize information exchange. Finally, we illustrate this on a nine-city topology modeled on the DoubleZero network, a live programmable WAN equipped with both technologies, and show how the optimal schedules shift with the network's capabilities. Together, these can narrow the gap to the gold standard of colocated training.

AI.tldr: WAN distributed training under network-aware schedules using multicast and FPGA aggregation across rotating cliques to maximize information exchange; demonstration on a nine-city DoubleZero-like WAN improves toward colocated training.
AI.motivation: WAN-scale training suffers from limited bandwidth, high latency, and uneven topology; existing approaches replicate data within data centers but struggle across wide areas; need network-aware methods to coordinate synchronization.
AI.method: System design with multicast to replicate outbound traffic and inline FPGAs to aggregate inbound traffic; algorithmic framework that constructs rich synchronization schedules (rotating cliques) aligned to topology and hardware capabilities; evaluation on a nine-city topology based on DoubleZero live programmable WAN.
AI.result: Optimized schedules depend on network capabilities; the proposed framework narrows the gap to gold-standard colocated training; demonstrates feasibility and schedule shifts with topology and bandwidth changes.
AI.conclusion: Network-aware active participation can substantially improve WAN training efficiency; extending data-center techniques to WAN with hardware-assisted routing and topology-aware schedules can approach colocated performance.

title: FLARE: A Failure-Aware Framework for Autonomous Correction and Recovery in Visual-Language Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action Models~(VLAs) have demonstrated significant promise in generalizing to complex, long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks. However, their performance remains brittle, as they are typically trained on trajectory-monotonic, failure-free demonstrations. This reliance on ``perfect" data leaves them unable to recover from common execution errors, such as a missed grasp, a dropped object, or an unexpected collision. In this paper, we propose FLARE, a novel framework that endows VLAs with robust error recovery capabilities through a ``Retry" and ``Reset" paradigm. First, we introduce a ``Retry" mechanism by injecting perturbation and bridging segments that decouple robot pose from environment state into demonstrations, enabling the policy to autonomously handle execution deviations. Second, to address critical, state-breaking (OOD) failures, we introduce a ``Reset" pipeline. We leverage an MLLM for offline failure analysis to automatically identify OOD states from execution videos. This analysis enables the efficient, targeted collection of a small library of object-centric ``Reset" skills, which are trained to restore the environment to a task-valid state. Our full framework integrates these learned policies. At inference, an online MLLM monitor arbitrates between task execution and ``Reset" skills. Experiments on challenging, contact-rich manipulation tasks show our approach significantly improves task success and robustness.

AI.tldr: FLARE strengthens Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) with dedicated error-recovery through a Retry and Reset framework. By injecting perturbation/bridging segments into demonstrations, it enables autonomous recovery from execution deviations; and by using an offline Multi-Lingual/Large Language Model? MLLM? (likely multimodal LLM) to analyze failures and curate a library of object-centric Reset skills, it addresses state-breaking (OOD) failures. An online MLLM monitor arbitrates between task execution and Reset actions, yielding improved success and robustness on challenging, contact-rich tasks.
AI.motivation: VLAs are brittle because they are trained on trajectory-monotonic, failure-free demonstrations. They struggle to recover from common execution errors (missed grasps, dropped objects, unexpected collisions) during long-horizon tasks. A robust recovery mechanism is needed to improve reliability in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Introduce a two-pronged framework: 1) Retry: augment demonstrations with perturbation and bridging segments to decouple robot pose from environment state, enabling autonomous handling of deviations during execution. 2) Reset: perform offline failure analysis with an MLLM on execution videos to identify out-of-distribution (OOD) states; collect a small library of object-centric Reset skills trained to restore the environment to a task-valid state. At inference, an online MLLM monitors and arbitrates between task execution and Reset policies.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on challenging, contact-rich manipulation tasks shows substantial gains in task success and robustness compared with baseline VLAs.
AI.conclusion: FLARE provides a practical framework for robust error recovery in VLAs by combining Retry-based deviation handling with targeted Reset skills, mediated by an online MLLM monitor, leading to improved performance in complex manipulation.

title: Systematic Literature Review of Machine Learning Models and Applications for Text Recognition
comment: Published in IEEE Access, 2025. 24 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables
summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for text recognition using machine vision has significantly improved, particularly when handling heterogeneous textual data. Traditional OCR models struggle with script variations, writing styles, and degraded documents. Advancements in technology are leading to new AI models with improved architecture for handling multiple languages and complex data formats. Despite this progress, a comprehensive evaluation of OCR advancements remains limited. Based on the established preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines, this literature review presents an extensive assessment of OCR research to trace the evolution of AI models over the past decade. It explores the transition in AI models, application domains, data types, linguistic coverage, and challenges. Through a detailed analysis of 97 selected studies published during January 2015 - January 2025, key OCR models are identified, and their performance, strengths, and limitations are analyzed. The findings highlight how OCR technologies have evolved to address structured and unstructured text, scene text recognition, and multilingual processing. Unresolved challenges include limited resources for underrepresented languages, high variability in handwritten text, visual similarity among characters, and constraints in real-time OCR applications. To address these issues, several promising approaches are proposed. Key suggestions include self-supervised learning, multimodal AI, automated machine learning (AutoML), AI-assisted postprocessing, tiny machine learning (TinyML), and the creation of joint corpora for script matching. The future recommendations aim to enhance OCR accuracy and tackle the challenges identified for real-time industrial applications. This study will guide future research and establish a foundation for OCR field.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of OCR research from 2015 to 2025 analyzing 97 studies; maps the evolution of AI models, application domains, data types, and languages; identifies unresolved challenges and proposes future directions (self-supervised learning, multimodal AI, AutoML, post-processing, TinyML, and joint corpora).
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive synthesis of OCR advances across diverse scripts, languages, and data formats, addressing gaps in evaluation and guiding future OCR research.
AI.method: Systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines; selection of 97 studies published Jan 2015–Jan 2025; qualitative analysis of models, performance, strengths, and limitations; thematic categorization by domain, data type, and linguistic coverage; identification of key OCR models and trends.
AI.result: OCR research shows a shift from single-language/structured text to multi-language, scene text, and multilingual processing with evolving architectures; persistent challenges include limited resources for underrepresented languages, handwriting variability, visual similarity among characters, and real-time constraints; proposed directions include self-supervised learning, multimodal AI, AutoML, AI-assisted postprocessing, TinyML, and joint corpora for script matching.
AI.conclusion: The review provides a foundation for OCR research, highlighting progress and outlining actionable directions to improve accuracy and real-time performance for real-world industrial applications.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Customer Churn Prediction in Telecommunications: A Framework for CRM Integration
summary: Subscriber attrition is a costly, persistent challenge for telecommunications providers, with monthly churn of roughly 1.9% in mature markets eroding billions in revenue annually. Predictive models can flag at-risk customers accurately, yet they are routinely excluded from frontline CRM workflows because high-performing ensemble and non-linear architectures are opaque: a retention specialist cannot design a personalised intervention from a probability score alone, without knowing why a subscriber is at risk. This paper addresses that gap. We benchmark four classifiers--Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM--on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (7,043 records; 19 features; 26.5% churn, balanced to 50% via SMOTE on the training partition only). Logistic Regression attains the strongest AUC-ROC (0.8411) and LightGBM the highest accuracy (78.42%); all four fall within a 0.011 AUC band (0.831--0.841), and 5-fold cross-validation confirms the leading models are effectively tied. Explanations are delivered at two granularities: a global SHAP ranking identifying tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract as the dominant churn signals, and instance-level SHAP and LIME decompositions that expose the drivers behind each prediction. Building on these outputs, we introduce a four-layer CRM integration architecture that converts risk scores and attribution vectors into tiered segmentation, maps top features to structured retention-action templates, and routes campaign outcomes into a retraining feedback loop. Targeting the highest-risk quintile is projected to cut overall churn by 3.3--5.3 percentage points, preserving an estimated $199K--$319K per campaign cycle.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks four classifiers on IBM Telco Churn; LR best AUC; SHAP/LIME explanations; CRM integration; potential churn reduction with quantifiable savings.
AI.motivation: Address the interpretability gap in predictive churn models, enabling actionable CRM interventions based on risk scores and feature attributions.
AI.method: Compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM on the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records, 19 features; 26.5% churn; SMOTE on training to balance to 50%). Evaluate AUC-ROC and accuracy; 5-fold cross-validation; provide global SHAP rankings and instance-level SHAP/LIME explanations; propose a four-layer CRM integration architecture mapping risk scores and attributions to retention actions; simulate impact on churn/revenue and feedback loop for retraining.
AI.result: Logistic Regression achieves the highest AUC-ROC of 0.8411; LightGBM achieves the highest accuracy at 78.42%; all models fall within a narrow AUC band (0.831–0.841); 5-fold cross-validation suggests the models are effectively tied. Global SHAP identifies tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract as dominant churn signals; instance-level SHAP and LIME explain individual predictions. A four-layer CRM integration converts risk scores and attribution vectors into tiered segmentation, links top features to retention-action templates, and routes outcomes into a retraining loop. Targeting the top quintile is projected to reduce churn by 3.3–5.3 percentage points, preserving ~$199K–$319K per campaign cycle.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability is operationalized via SHAP/LIME explanations and wired into a CRM deployment, enabling actionable targeting and a feedback loop for continuous improvement, with estimated tangible business impact.

title: Diff Mining: Logit Differences Reveal Finetuning Objectives
comment: 37 pages, 7 figures. ICLR 2026 Workshop: Principled Design for Trustworthy AI. Code available at https://github.com/science-of-finetuning/diffing-toolkit
summary: Finetuning has become the gold standard for refining existing behaviors and inducing new ones in language models, yet it often remains unclear exactly which behaviors emerge during this process. As models grow ever more capable, understanding finetuning better becomes increasingly important, particularly since unwanted behaviors may arise during finetuning. In this paper, we introduce Diff Mining, a simple yet effective framework for identifying what a finetuned model has learned by comparing its logits to those of its base model. Diff Mining effectively surfaces salient tokens that are amplified in the finetuned model, serving as a fingerprint of its training -- even on text unrelated to the finetuning domain. Unlike many existing model diffing methods which require model internals, Diff Mining only needs access to output logits and scales to large models. The framework consists of two modular stages: (i) extracting per-context logit differences between the finetuned and base models on a reference corpus, and (ii) aggregating the resulting signals to construct an interpretable token set representing the finetune. For aggregation, we explore both a simple Top-K frequency method and a Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)-based approach for disentangling multiple finetuning objectives into distinct token clusters. Empirically, Diff Mining succeeds across diverse settings: on finetune domain detection, it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art model diffing methods both in identifying relevant tokens and in downstream performance when an interpretability agent is given access to the extracted token set; on models with injected biases, it identifies more than one third of the biases without targeted probing. Overall, our framework shows promise in developing auditing tools to detect finetuning objectives.

AI.tldr: Diff Mining is a logit-difference framework that detects what a finetuned model has learned by comparing its output logits to its base model on a reference corpus, then aggregates differences into interpretable token sets using Top-K or NMF. It scales to large models and does not require access to model internals.
AI.motivation: As models are finetuned, unintended behaviors can emerge; understanding exactly what changes during finetuning is hard, especially without access to internal parameters. A lightweight, scalable method that only uses output logits to identify finetuned objectives is valuable for auditing and mitigating unwanted behaviors.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (i) compute per-context logit differences between finetuned and base models on a reference corpus; (ii) aggregate these signals to form interpretable token sets. Aggregation uses (a) Top-K frequency to surface most amplified tokens and (b) Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to disentangle multiple finetuning objectives into token clusters.
AI.result: Empirically, Diff Mining outperforms state-of-the-art model diffing methods in finetune-domain detection and improves downstream performance when an interpretability agent uses the extracted tokens. It identifies more than one third of injected biases without targeted probing. It is scalable to large models and only requires access to output logits, not internals.
AI.conclusion: Diff Mining offers a simple, scalable, and effective auditing tool for identifying finetuning objectives and the behaviors learned during finetuning, with practical impact on detecting domains and biases across models.

title: Beyond the Proving Ground: Independent Public-Road Testing of Assisted Lane Change Systems using LiDAR
summary: Testing of commercial Advanced Driver Assistance Systems is essential to ensure safety and compliance during type approval and in service operation. However, proving ground scenarios may not reflect real world driving complexity, while geo fencing can require manufacturer collaboration and limit assessment independence. This work presents a methodology for independently testing Assisted Lane Change systems on public roads. A campaign on the A31 French motorway used a test vehicle equipped with a LiDAR based vehicle detection and tracking system. Tests covered combinations of inter vehicle distance and speed between the test vehicle and the take over vehicle. Real time kinematic global navigation satellite system receivers assessed detection and tracking performance. Recorded lane change trajectories were compared with the lane change suppression requirements of UNECE Regulation Number 79. Of 27 predefined lane change manoeuvres, 18 were completed and 9 suppressed. In 6 cases, the system allowed manoeuvres that did not meet regulatory minimum distance requirements. In 3 cases, the deviation remained statistically significant after accounting for measurement uncertainty. To the authors knowledge, this is the first public road campaign designed to assess Assisted Lane Change compliance with Regulation Number 79 safety distance requirements. The results demonstrate the suitability of LiDAR based sensing for this purpose. The methodology can support market surveillance and future regulatory revisions by revealing real world behaviours not covered by approval procedures.
