AI.tldr: Independent on-road testing of Assisted Lane Change (ALC) systems using LiDAR on a public motorway assesses compliance with UNECE Regulation 79 safety-distance requirements; 18/27 maneuvers completed, 9 suppressed, 6 violations allowed, 3 deviations remain significant after uncertainty; demonstrates LiDAR viability and informs market surveillance/regulatory updates.
AI.motivation: Fill gap left by proving-ground and geo-fenced testing by enabling independent, real-world assessment of ALC compliance with regulatory distance requirements.
AI.method: Public-road campaign on A31 with a LiDAR-based detection/tracking system; varied inter-vehicle distances and speeds between test vehicle and takeover vehicle; RTK-GNSS for ground-truth detection/tracking; lane-change trajectories recorded and evaluated against UNECE R79 distance requirements; 27 maneuvers tested.
AI.result: 18 completed, 9 suppressed; 6 cases allowed maneuvers violating minimum distances; 3 cases with statistically significant deviation after uncertainty accounting.
AI.conclusion: First public-road assessment of ALC compliance with R79 safety-distance rules; LiDAR sensing is suitable for this purpose; methodology supports market surveillance and regulatory revisions by exposing real-world behaviors not captured in approval procedures.

title: NeuDonatello: Uncertainty-Aware Framework for Accurate Neural SDF Learning
summary: Neural surface reconstruction has emerged as a powerful paradigm for recovering high-quality 3D surfaces from multi-view images. However, recovering accurate geometry solely from RGB images remains challenging due to uncertainties arising from textureless regions, occlusions, and inherent scene ambiguities. Existing methods often overlook such uncertainties, leading to inaccurate estimates of the signed distance function (SDF). We introduce NeuDonatello, a novel framework that models and leverages SDF uncertainty to improve surface reconstruction. Central to our approach is to model spatially varying uncertainty using a Monte Carlo sampling strategy. Using this uncertainty, we develop an adaptive regularization that selectively strengthens geometric constraints where RGB supervision is unreliable, avoiding incorrect surface reconstruction. We further introduce an uncertainty-aware scale parameter for the SDF-to-density conversion. Conditioned on uncertainty, this design enables more accurate modeling of spatially varying densities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeuDonatello achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy, with robust performance across diverse scenes using only posed RGB images.

AI.tldr: NeuDonatello models spatially varying SDF uncertainty via Monte Carlo sampling to perform adaptive regularization and an uncertainty-aware SDF-to-density scale, achieving state-of-the-art RGB-based surface reconstruction with robustness across diverse scenes.
AI.motivation: RGB-based neural surface reconstruction struggles with textureless regions, occlusions, and ambiguities; existing methods often ignore uncertainty, causing biased SDF estimates.
AI.method: Use Monte Carlo sampling to capture spatially varying SDF uncertainty; apply adaptive regularization that strengthens geometric constraints where RGB supervision is unreliable; introduce an uncertainty-conditioned scale parameter for SDF-to-density conversion to better model densities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy and robust performance across diverse scenes using only posed RGB images.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating uncertainty into SDF estimation improves neural surface reconstruction from RGB, enabling more accurate geometry and robust density modeling; this approach can generalize to other uncertainty-aware 3D reconstruction tasks.

title: EEG-to-Report: An Annotation and Feature-Text Framework for Training Language Models on Clinical EEG
summary: Clinical electroencephalography (EEG) reporting remains largely manual and time-consuming, and current EEG software ecosystems do not produce the structured EEG-text supervision needed for training modern language models. Most toolboxes focus on visualization or preprocessing, providing limited support for workflows that generate high-quality datasets for AI. We introduce EEG-to-Report, a browser-based annotation and feature-text framework that links routine EEG review with the construction of AI-ready datasets. The framework integrates multi-format EEG ingestion, channel standardization, and an interactive viewer with a multimodal annotation layer that combines typed text and transcribed voice notes. For each annotated segment, a feature extraction engine computes a standardized set of spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, and spike-related descriptors, stored alongside clinical descriptions in a portable JSON schema. This yields aligned feature-text pairs designed to supervise multimodal EEG-language models. The framework also includes an auto-report module that couples an ensemble of convolutional networks with a large language model to draft clinical narratives for neurologist review. Using pilot annotations, we describe how EEG-to-Report streamlines annotation workflows and produces editable draft reports, providing a reusable foundation for automated EEG reporting systems.

AI.tldr: EEG-to-Report provides a browser-based tool to annotate EEGs and produce AI-ready, multimodal feature-text datasets with an auto-report module to draft narratives.
AI.motivation: Current EEG reporting is manual and time-consuming, and existing tools lack structured supervision or end-to-end support for creating high-quality AI-ready datasets for multimodal EEG-language models.
AI.method: Ingest multiple EEG formats, standardize channels, an interactive multimodal annotation viewer (text + voice notes); compute standardized features (spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, spikes) stored with clinical notes in a portable JSON schema; generate aligned feature-text pairs for supervision of multimodal EEG-language models; include an auto-report module combining CNNs with a large language model to draft narratives.
AI.result: Pilot annotations demonstrate streamlined, editable draft reports and a reusable framework for automated EEG reporting systems; provides an AI-ready data pipeline and JSON-based schema for downstream models.
AI.conclusion: EEG-to-Report can streamline EEG annotation workflows, produce editable drafts, and serve as a foundation for AI-assisted EEG reporting, enabling scalable dataset generation for multimodal EEG-language systems.

title: Active Curriculum Refinement for Reinforcement Learning
summary: In many reinforcement learning (RL) domains, environments are connected by prerequisite relations, such as difficulty-increasing edits or parameter increments, which induce a directed acyclic curriculum graph (DAG). Although this structure is often exploited only implicitly, explicitly modeling it can improve training. We introduce PATH, a curriculum-learning framework that performs active learning over the curriculum graph. PATH first expands coverage by sampling diverse curriculum paths and then reallocates training toward regions that remain unmastered. Experiments across diverse environments show that PATH explicitly leverages the graph structure to achieve strong robustness and generalization.

AI.tldr: PATH is a curriculum-learning framework for RL that explicitly models a directed acyclic curriculum graph (DAG) and uses active learning to diversify paths and focus training on unmastered regions.
AI.motivation: In RL, environments often relate via prerequisite steps (difficulty ramps, parameter changes) forming a DAG. Exploiting this structure explicitly could improve training efficiency, robustness, and generalization.
AI.method: PATH performs active learning over the curriculum graph: it (1) samples diverse curriculum paths to expand coverage, and (2) reallocates training resources toward regions of the graph that remain unmastered, i.e., underrepresented or difficult components.
AI.result: Empirical comparisons across diverse environments show that PATH leveraging the graph structure yields improved robustness and generalization relative to baselines that do not explicitly model the curriculum graph.
AI.conclusion: Explicit curriculum-graph modeling with active-path sampling and reallocation (PATH) enhances RL training by better exploiting prerequisite relations among tasks.

title: PredVLA: A Sub-Million-Parameter Predictive-Coding Policy for Robot Manipulation
summary: Large pretrained vision-language-action models dominate modern robot-manipulation benchmarks, but it remains unclear how much model scale is necessary for strong language-conditioned control, or whether fundamentally different control architectures can remain competitive at much smaller parameter budgets. We present PredVLA, a language-conditioned predictive-coding policy with only 0.68 million trainable network parameters and no robot-data pretraining, whose hierarchical generative recurrent dynamics predict visual features and proprioception while observations influence latent state only through online inference from the resulting sensory prediction errors. On LIBERO, PredVLA achieves an 86.9% mean success rate across the three short-horizon suites and 75.4% when the long-horizon suite is included. Under a controlled comparison using the same frozen front end, demonstrations, action decoder, and evaluation protocol, PredVLA achieves 3.7x and 7.4x mean success rates of parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM policies, respectively. The predictive-coding formulation also makes the contribution of observation-driven correction directly measurable: because observations influence the recurrent state only through prediction-error-based latent inference, disabling this inference yields an exact open-loop control condition. Together, these results show that a sub-million-parameter recurrent generative policy can achieve strong performance on modern language-conditioned manipulation benchmarks while providing an explicit mechanism for prediction-error-driven online state correction.

AI.tldr: A sub-million-parameter predictive-coding policy (PredVLA, 0.68M) achieves strong language-conditioned manipulation on LIBERO benchmarks, outperforming parameter-matched Transformer/LSTM baselines; it uses online, prediction-error–driven latent inference with interpretable open-loop control when inference is disabled, showing robust performance without robot-data pretraining.
AI.motivation: Assess how much model scale and architectural design affect language-conditioned robot manipulation, and explore low-parameter, interpretable alternatives to large vision-language models.
AI.method: PredVLA uses hierarchical generative recurrent dynamics to predict visual features and proprioception. Observations influence latent state only through online inference from prediction errors. No robot-data pretraining; 0.68M trainable parameters. Comparisons performed with the same frozen front end, demonstrations, action decoder, and evaluation protocol against parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM baselines on LIBERO short- and long-horizon tasks.
AI.result: Achieves 86.9% mean success on three short-horizon suites; 75.4% when long-horizon included. Outperforms parameter-matched Transformer (3.7x) and LSTM (7.4x) in mean success. Demonstrates a measurable, prediction-error–driven online correction; disabling inference yields an exact open-loop control condition.
AI.conclusion: A sub-million-parameter recurrent generative policy can perform competitively on language-conditioned manipulation benchmarks while offering an explicit mechanism for online state correction via prediction errors, without robot-data pretraining.

title: HUG-VIS: A Multimodal Benchmark for Human-centered Understanding and Generation in Visual Intelligence
summary: Visual intelligence seeks to perceive, interpret, and synthesize the visual world and is central to modern computer vision. Human-centered visual intelligence is especially demanding because it studies people as expressive, socially situated subjects whose meaning is rarely conveyed by appearance alone. It couples vision with audio and language across four representative tasks: human emotion recognition, human video generation, human voice cloning, and human video matting. Yet existing resources remain task-specific, providing modalities and annotations for individual problems rather than a shared foundation coordinating understanding and generation. This limits multimodal signal use and broader research. We address this gap with HUG-VIS, a unified benchmark for Human-centered Understanding and Generation in Visual Intelligence. It contains 8,400 seated half-body videos of 30 professional actors, each performing the same 280 emotion-action-prompt assignments under a controlled Mandarin studio protocol, with synchronized video, audio, text, and alpha mattes. We evaluate diverse open- and closed-source models across the four tasks under a unified zero-shot protocol using automatic metrics, criterion-specific mean opinion scores, and multiple cross-task analyses. Results show that (i) linguistic content dominates current emotion recognition, while purely visual affect recognition is weakest; (ii) in video generation and voice cloning, automatic metrics and human judgment agree overall but differ in their top rankings, requiring joint reporting; (iii) boundary fidelity under motion is the main remaining obstacle for human matting; and (iv) task difficulty varies across emotions, models, and metrics, with notable cross-task correlations. The dataset and results are available at https://github.com/GML-MMGroup/HUG-VIS.

AI.tldr: HUG-VIS introduces a unified, multi-task benchmark for human-centered visual intelligence, unifying four tasks with synchronized multimodal data; provides baseline cross-task analyses and insights, plus a dataset for research.
AI.motivation: To overcome fragmentation of task-specific resources and underutilization of multi-modal signals by creating a shared benchmark and protocol for emotion recognition, video generation, voice cloning, and video matting, enabling cross-task and cross-modal evaluation.
AI.method: Dataset of 8,400 seated half-body videos of 30 actors performing 280 Mandarin emotion-action-prompt tasks; synchronized video, audio, text, and alpha mattes; zero-shot evaluation protocol; evaluation across four tasks using open- and closed-source models; automatic metrics, criterion-specific MOS, and cross-task analyses.
AI.result: Findings: (i) linguistic content dominates emotion recognition; (ii) automatic metrics and human judgments agree in video generation and voice cloning but differ in rankings; (iii) boundary fidelity under motion is the main obstacle for matting; (iv) task difficulty varies across emotions, models, metrics; notable cross-task correlations; dataset and results available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: HUG-VIS provides a shared foundation for human-centered understanding and generation, enabling cross-task insights and progress in visual intelligence, and supporting standardized evaluation and multimodal signal integration.

title: Selection Bias Correction in Retail Intelligence
comment: Accepted to the 15th International Conference on Data Science, Technology and Applications (DATA 2026)
summary: Retail intelligence often relies on monitoring popular, high-velocity products, potentially biasing economic indicators by ignoring the "long tail" of niche items. This simulation study investigates selection bias in inflation estimation and compares correction methods across diverse data-generating processes. Through 400 Monte Carlo replications spanning four scenarios--aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, and polynomial relationships--we test the robustness of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) with five specifications against stratification with varying strata counts. Our findings reveal fundamental limits of weighting methods in retail long-tail contexts: stratification achieves superior performance in three of four scenarios, maintaining sub-0.04pp median error even when boundaries deliberately misalign with population breaks (116x advantage over IPW). However, IPW with spline propensity models wins under smooth polynomial relationships (median error 0.007pp vs. 0.013pp), demonstrating context-dependency. Critically, even an oracle IPW specification with perfect structural knowledge achieves 6.06pp error compared to stratification's 0.008pp in step-function scenarios. This reflects violation of the Positivity Assumption--a fundamental causal inference requirement--rather than IPW methodological inferiority. When selection probabilities differ dramatically (90% vs. 1%), weighting methods operate outside their theoretical design envelope. These results demonstrate that stratification provides a safer engineering choice in retail long-tail distributions with severe positivity violations.

AI.tldr: Stratification generally outperforms IPW for inflation estimation in retail long-tail data, except under smooth polynomial relationships where spline-propensity IPW slightly wins; even then, a perfect (oracle) IPW can perform badly under strong positivity violations. Overall, severe positivity violations and misalignment undermine weighting; stratification offers safer, robust performance across most scenarios.
AI.motivation: Evaluate robustness of selection-bias correction methods (IPW vs stratification) for inflation estimation in retail data with long-tail distributions, focusing on positivity violations and data-generating process (DGP) differences.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulation with 400 replications across four DGPs: aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, and polynomial relationships. Compare Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) using five propensity specifications against stratification with varying numbers of strata. Assess performance via median error (pp).
AI.result: Stratification achieves superior performance in 3 of 4 scenarios, maintaining sub-0.04pp median error even under misaligned boundaries (116x advantage over IPW). IPW with spline propensity models performs best only under smooth polynomial DGPs (0.007pp vs 0.013pp). Even an oracle IPW with perfect structure yields 6.06pp error in step-function DGPs, indicating a positivity violation issue rather than IPW weakness. When selection probabilities are highly imbalanced (e.g., 90% vs 1%), weighting methods operate outside their theoretical envelope. Conclusion: stratification is a safer engineering choice for retail long-tail distributions with strong positivity violations; weighting methods have fundamental limitations in such contexts.
AI.conclusion: Positivity violations and misalignment in selection processes limit IPW effectiveness in retail long-tail inflation estimation. Stratification provides more robust, lower-bias performance across diverse DGPs, making it the recommended approach under severe positivity constraints.

title: Shared Actors Need Not Share Critics: Effects of Value Mismatch in Parallel Reinforcement Learning
summary: When a single policy is trained in parallel across multiple environments of the same task, such as procedurally generated levels, randomized dynamics, or curricula, implementations commonly use one critic across all sampled environments. Yet different environments can assign different expected returns to the same input visible to the critic. A critic without environment information must then reconcile distinct value targets, systematically shifting the sampled advantages within individual environments. Using illustrative bandit models with multiple environments and a common optimal arm, we characterize how this value mismatch redistributes sampled policy updates, reinforcing unhelpful actions while attenuating or even reversing useful ones. The oracle processes using no baseline, the shared value, or the value specific to the sampled environment have the same mean logit update at a fixed policy and converge to the same optimal policy, yet their realized learning paths can differ sharply. The analysis motivates a minimal intervention: give only a logged environment index to the critic so that it can separate the value targets. Controlled CartPole and MuJoCo experiments expose the predicted shifted values, advantages, and performance gaps. In the more complex BipedalWalker and Procgen settings, the same intervention yields more stable learning and higher returns. Across all $16$ Procgen games, the multihead conditional critic improves aggregate normalized return on $600$ unseen levels per game by $40.8\%$. In conclusion, the theory identifies value mismatch as a direct mechanism through which critic sharing can degrade stochastic learning dynamics, not captured by scalar estimator variance alone, and the experiments show that conditioning on an index is broadly effective in parallel reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: Value mismatch arises when sharing a single critic across multiple environments in parallel RL, biasing updates and harming learning. Conditioning the critic on the environment index (multihead conditional critic) aligns value targets, improving stability and performance, especially on Procgen benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In parallel RL, different environments can assign different expected returns to the same observation, causing a single critic to reconcile conflicting targets. This induces systematic misallocation of updates that can degrade stochastic learning dynamics beyond simple estimator variance.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using multi-environment bandit models with a common optimal arm to study how value mismatch affects logit updates. Comparison of oracle baselines (no baseline, shared value, or env-specific value) shows identical mean updates but different learning trajectories. Proposal and evaluation of a minimal intervention: provide the critic with a logged environment index, implemented as a multihead conditional critic. Empirical validation with controlled CartPole and MuJoCo experiments and larger-scale tests on BipedalWalker and Procgen, evaluating 16 Procgen games across 600 unseen levels.
AI.result: Value mismatch reweights sampled policy updates, reinforcing unhelpful actions and attenuating or reversing useful ones. Providing an environment index to the critic yields more stable learning and higher returns. Across 16 Procgen games, the multihead conditional critic improves aggregate normalized return by 40.8% on unseen levels.
AI.conclusion: Value mismatch is a direct mechanism by which critic sharing can degrade stochastic learning dynamics; conditioning the critic on an environment index is an effective, broadly applicable remedy in parallel reinforcement learning.

title: Residual Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Computed Torque Control for a Cable-Driven Lower-Limb Rehabilitation Robot under Disturbances and Parametric Uncertainties
summary: Accurate trajectory tracking in cable-driven lower-limb rehabilitation robots is challenging because model uncertainty, external disturbances, joint constraints, and pull-only cable actuation can degrade nominal control performance. Conventional model-based controllers provide an interpretable control structure but remain sensitive to model mismatch, whereas fully learning-based control can reduce transparency and complicate constraint-aware operation. This study proposes a residual deep reinforcement learning-enhanced computed torque control framework in which computed torque control generates the nominal command and a bounded Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient policy supplies only an additional compensating torque. The approach is evaluated in simulation under nominal, uncertain, disturbed, combined, and generalization conditions, together with trajectory-tracking, joint-limit, cable-demand, workspace-feasibility, and cable-Jacobian diagnostics. Across the evaluated conditions, the residual controller improves tracking and disturbance rejection relative to computed torque control while preserving the interpretable model-based command structure and satisfying the reported feasibility checks in the representative evaluation. Broader tests indicate that tracking improvements can persist beyond the representative case while also exposing trajectory-dependent constraint limitations. These results support bounded residual learning as a practical robustness-enhancement strategy for simulation-based rehabilitation robot control and motivate further constraint-aware and experimental validation.

AI.tldr: Residual deep RL-enhanced computed torque control for cable-driven lower-limb rehab robots; a bounded DDPG policy provides a residual torque to the nominal CT command, improving tracking and disturbance rejection while preserving model-based interpretability and feasibility constraints.
AI.motivation: Address model uncertainty, external disturbances, joint constraints, and pull-only cable actuation that degrade traditional computed-torque control; combine data-driven robustness with an interpretable, constraint-aware control framework.
AI.method: Nominal torque is generated via computed torque control. A bounded Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) policy outputs a compensating residual torque within predefined bounds to augment the nominal command. The approach is evaluated in simulation under nominal, uncertain, disturbed, combined, and generalization conditions, with diagnostics on trajectory tracking, joint limits, cable-demand, workspace-feasibility, and cable-Jacobian.
AI.result: The residual controller enhances tracking and disturbance rejection compared to computed torque control, while maintaining the interpretable control structure and satisfying feasibility checks. Broader tests suggest tracking gains persist beyond representative cases and reveal trajectory-dependent constraint limitations.
AI.conclusion: Bounded residual learning is a practical robustness-enhancement strategy for simulation-based rehabilitation robot control and motivates further constraint-aware development and experimental validation.

title: FAN-LoRA: A Fourier-Adaptive Nonlinear Low-Rank Adaptor for Medical Foundation Model Domain Adaptation
summary: The advent of vision foundation models, notably the Segment Anything Model (SAM), has catalyzed significant advancements in natural image segmentation. However, their direct transfer to medical imaging remains severely bottlenecked by profound domain gaps, such as cross-modality and cross-center shifts. Existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods facilitate the adaptation of SAM to medical domains; nevertheless, they frequently suffer from performance degradation under severe distribution shifts. This vulnerability primarily stems from the implicit entanglement of heterogeneous frequency components within a shared low-rank subspace, which directly exacerbates sub-optimal structural alignment and localized boundary blurring. To overcome this representational bottleneck, we propose the Fourier-Adaptive Nonlinear Low-Rank Adaptor (FAN-LoRA), a novel frequency-decoupled fine-tuning architecture. FAN-LoRA explicitly separates the optimization space by employing a B-spline-driven low-pass branch for global structural alignment, synergistically coupled with a discrete Fourier high-pass branch for local textural compensation. Extensive experiments across three challenging cross-modality and cross-center benchmarks demonstrate that FAN-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PEFT baselines. Compared to the strongest competitors, our method achieves consistent improvements in average Dice scores and notable reductions in boundary errors, while maintaining a compact module size without compromising computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Frequency-decoupled PEFT (FAN-LoRA) for adapting SAM to medical imaging; splits optimization into a B-spline low-pass branch for global structure and a discrete Fourier high-pass branch for local texture, achieving state-of-the-art Dice and boundary accuracy across cross-modality/center datasets with a compact, efficient adapter.
AI.motivation: Medical imaging presents severe cross-modality/center distribution shifts that degrade SAM; existing PEFT methods entangle heterogeneous frequency components in a shared low-rank subspace, causing poor alignment and blurred boundaries.
AI.method: FAN-LoRA introduces a dual-branch architecture: a B-spline-driven low-pass branch for global structural alignment and a discrete Fourier high-pass branch for local texture refinement; the branches decouple the optimization space and are coupled to regularize fine-tuning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three challenging cross-modality/center benchmarks show FAN-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PEFT baselines, with higher average Dice scores and reduced boundary errors, while maintaining small module size and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-decoupled, low-rank fine-tuning effectively mitigates distribution-shift bottlenecks in medical-domain segmentation with SAM, enabling robust, accurate segmentation across modalities/centers; the approach offers a scalable path for PEFT in diverse medical imaging tasks.

title: GROUND: Reducing Hallucinations in LLM-Based Enterprise Analytics Through Governed Semantic Definitions
summary:
Natural-language analytics over enterprise data warehouses is increasingly important, but production use is limited by hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, wrong grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. Existing text-to-SQL systems often ground generation in database schemas or retrieved documentation, while enterprise reporting also requires governed business semantics: approved metrics, dimensions, join paths, filters, and row-level security. This paper introduces GROUND, Governed Retrieval Over Unified Normalized Definitions, a framework that constrains LLM-generated analytics to a governed semantic layer. GROUND supplies approved definitions, binds user intent to governed metrics and dimensions, and validates generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules before execution. On violations, it retries or abstains.
  In a 100-question synthetic enterprise-reporting benchmark, GROUND is compared with direct schema-only text-to-SQL, schema-RAG, and semantic-only grounding under one shared model. GROUND is the only system free of measured hallucinations across all six evaluated categories, while ungoverned systems violate row-level security on many questions. A semantic-only condition with exact metric definitions but no access policy still leaks data, showing that governance cannot be replaced by metric fidelity alone. The findings are replicated on real U.S. NHTSA vehicle-safety data with independent hand-authored gold and tested on an adversarial set across four models from three providers. GROUND's enforced guarantees, especially filters and row-level security, hold with zero violations on every model, while judgment-dependent behaviors such as refusing undefined metrics remain fallible.

AI.tldr: GROUND constrains LLM-generated analytics to a governed semantic layer to prevent hallucinations and enforce enterprise governance (metrics, dimensions, joins, grain, filters, security, and cost) during SQL generation.
AI.motivation: Production NL analytics over enterprise data warehouses are prone to hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, wrong grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. There is a need to ground generation in a governed semantic layer with approved definitions and access control.
AI.method: GROUND provides approved metric/dimension definitions, binds user intent to governed semantics, and validates each generated SQL against governance rules for schema, metrics, joins, grain, filters, security, and cost; on violations it retries or abstains. Evaluation uses a 100-question synthetic enterprise-reporting benchmark comparing against schema-only text-to-SQL, schema-RAG, and semantic-only grounding under a shared model, plus replication on real NHTSA vehicle-safety data with hand-authored gold and adversarial sets across four models from three providers.
AI.result: GROUND is the only system free of hallucinations across all six evaluation categories in the synthetic benchmark; ungoverned systems violate row-level security on many questions. Semantic-only grounding with exact metric definitions but no access policy leaks data. On real NHTSA data, GROUND yields zero violations across all models for enforced guarantees (filters and RLS); some judgment-based behaviors (e.g., refusing undefined metrics) remain fallible.
AI.conclusion: Governed grounding is essential: you cannot replace governance with metric fidelity alone. Enforcing row-level security and access policies yields reliable, compliant NL analytics; while certain judgments may still fail, this approach substantially reduces hallucinations and data leakage in enterprise NL analytics.

title: Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and point cloud data analysis
summary: Point-cloud data routinely captured by modern imaging and sensor technologies provide detailed geometric descriptions of objects and environments, but their analysis is hindered by large data volumes, localization noise, and missing information. In addition, existing point-cloud reconstruction pipelines typically return a single best-fit structure without uncertainty quantification. We introduce a fully Bayesian framework for representing point-cloud data and reconstructing closed curves, in which observed points are modeled as noisy perturbations of latent locations constrained to lie on the underlying curve that is regularized by a non-parametric prior. Posterior inference in our framework is carried out using a series of Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers tailored to point-cloud characteristics. Numerical experiments, including synthetic examples and real-world LiDAR datasets, show accurate reconstructions and quantified uncertainty over the recovered curves.

AI.tldr: Bayesian point-cloud to curve reconstruction with uncertainty quantification via MCMC.
AI.motivation: Tackle large point-cloud data, localization noise, and missing information, while providing uncertainty estimates absent in standard pipelines.
AI.method: A fully Bayesian model where observed points are noisy perturbations of latent locations constrained to lie on an underlying curve regularized by a non-parametric prior; posterior inference using a suite of MCMC samplers tailored to point-cloud characteristics.
AI.result: Accurate curve reconstructions with quantified uncertainty demonstrated on synthetic data and real-world LiDAR datasets.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a probabilistic framework for uncertainty-aware reconstruction of curves from point clouds, enabling robust inference under noise and data gaps, with scalable MCMC-based inference and flexible non-parametric priors.

title: MeshPriorDiT: Hierarchical Modeling for Action-Conditioned Cloth Dynamics
summary: Action-conditioned cloth dynamics prediction requires both locally plausible deformation and long-range coordination. Existing approaches largely follow two paradigms. Mesh-based GNNs capture local physical responses through material connectivity. However, their finite message-passing range limits coordination between topologically distant regions, while autoregressive rollouts tend to accumulate prediction errors. Transformer-based dynamics models capture long-range interactions through global attention, but often operate without explicit material connectivity and must learn local topological responses directly from data. We propose MeshPriorDiT, a hierarchical dynamics model that decomposes future cloth motion into a structured mesh prior and a generative residual. An action-conditioned mesh GNN first predicts multi-step vertex displacements, yielding a reference trajectory that respects material topology and grasp constraints. Conditioned on historical states, planned actions, and the mesh prior, a Residual DiT then uses conditional flow matching to jointly generate the residual motion not captured by the prior. The generated residual is further rescaled and decoded using material adjacency to coordinate corrections across neighboring vertices. We evaluate MeshPriorDiT on 15-step autoregressive rollouts across three cloth manipulation tasks. Averaged over the three tasks, MeshPriorDiT reduces average Global MSE by 43.42% relative to the GNN-Only baseline and by 75.03% relative to the DiT-DDPM baseline, while maintaining a favorable Edge-strain MSE comparable to that of GNN-Only.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical cloth dynamics model, MeshPriorDiT, combines an action-conditioned mesh GNN prior with a generative residual DiT (via conditional flow matching) to produce physically coherent, long-horizon predictions. It achieves substantial error reductions on 15-step rollouts across three cloth manipulation tasks while preserving edge-strain coherence.
AI.motivation: GNNs offer topology-aware local responses but have limited coordination ranges, while transformers capture long-range interactions but lack explicit material connectivity; autoregressive rollouts can accumulate errors. A structured mesh prior paired with a residual generator aims to fuse local topology with data-driven corrections for stable, long-horizon cloth dynamics.
AI.method: 1) Action-conditioned mesh GNN predicts multi-step vertex displacements to form a reference trajectory respecting topology and grasp constraints. 2) Residual DiT, conditioned on history, actions, and the mesh prior, uses conditional flow matching to generate the residual motion not captured by the prior. 3) The residual is rescaled and decoded using material adjacency to coordinate corrections across neighboring vertices.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15-step autoregressive rollouts over 3 cloth tasks. MeshPriorDiT achieves an average Global MSE reduction of 43.42% vs a GNN-Only baseline and 75.03% vs a DiT-DDPM baseline, with Edge-strain MSE comparable to GNN-Only.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical approach effectively blends a topology-aware mesh prior with a learned residual, delivering significantly improved long-horizon cloth dynamics while maintaining physical coherence at the mesh edges.

title: Visual Information-Guided Parallel Decoding for Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) have recently emerged as a new decoding paradigm for multimodal generation. Starting from a fully masked sequence, dMLLMs progressively decode the sequence by unmasking a subset of the remaining masked positions at each step. Since the selected tokens serve as the prediction context for subsequent steps, deciding which tokens to decode is crucial to the quality of the final output. The most common strategy prioritizes tokens based on a certainty measure that tends to favor tokens frequently observed in the training data. Recent approaches instead order tokens according to their influence on subsequent predictions, but do not explicitly account for the input image. We propose the Visual Information-Guided Sampler (VIG-Sampler), which prioritizes tokens based on their attention to image tokens. We further impose a constraint that penalizes candidate tokens whose image-attention distributions are similar to those of previously selected tokens, thereby increasing the information gain of the decoded subset. Extensive experiments on 7 captioning and VQA benchmarks with 3 open-source dMLLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of VIG-Sampler, which outperforms the Info-Gain Sampler by an average of 19.3 CIDEr points across the captioning benchmarks and surpasses it on COCO Caption while using only half as many decoding steps.

AI.tldr: A Visual Information-Guided Sampler (VIG-Sampler) for diffusion multimodal LLMs that orders decoding tokens by their image attention and penalizes repeated image-attention distributions, achieving large CIDEr gains and halved decoding steps on captioning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing decoding strategies either rely on token certainty (biased toward frequently seen tokens) or token influence without considering the input image; there is a need to exploit image context to maximize information gain during progressive decoding.
AI.method: Proposes VIG-Sampler: prioritize tokens based on their attention to image tokens; adds a penalty term that discourages selecting tokens whose image-attention distribution is too similar to previously selected tokens, promoting information gain and diversity in the decoded subset. Evaluated on 7 captioning and VQA benchmarks with 3 open-source dMLLMs.
AI.result: Outperforms Info-Gain Sampler by an average of 19.3 CIDEr points across captioning benchmarks; surpasses it on COCO Caption; requires about half as many decoding steps.
AI.conclusion: VIG-Sampler is effective and more efficient for diffusion multimodal LLM decoding; leveraging image-attention guidance and a diversity constraint improves captioning and VQA performance across models.

title: SAREF-based Ontology for Distributed AI Workflows across the Edge-Fog-Cloud Continuum
summary: Nowadays semantic models provide limited support for representing distributed AI workflows and their execution across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. Therefore, AI processes and resources are often described using incompatible semantic representations, affecting the interoperability, orchestration, and reuse. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a SAREF-compliant ontology for representing distributed AI workflows across the edge-fog-cloud continuum. We extend the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for modeling AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, providing a unified semantic model of both AI workflows and heterogeneous computing infrastructures. The ontology enables semantic interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration of distributed AI applications while remaining fully aligned with the ETSI SAREF ecosystem. The ontology is evaluated using proof-of-concept smart grid energy services orchestration scenarios and validated using competency questions showing its ability to support AI workflow deployment, execution reasoning, and workload adaptation across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. All competency questions were successfully validated using SPARQL querying and semantic reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate deployment success rates of 90-100% with average orchestration decision times below 80 ms across heterogeneous edge-fog-cloud environments, highlighting its effectiveness on ensuring semantic interoperability for distributed AI orchestration.

AI.tldr: A SAREF-compliant ontology extends SAREF4SYST to model distributed AI workflows across the edge-fog-cloud continuum, enabling semantic interoperability and fast, resource-aware orchestration; validated via SPARQL and competency questions with high deployment success and low decision times.
AI.motivation: To address limited interoperability and orchestration support for distributed AI workflows across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments, which hampers interoperability, reuse, and automated reasoning.
AI.method: Extend the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships; ensure alignment with the ETSI SAREF ecosystem; implement a unified semantic model for AI workflows and infrastructures; validate via competency questions and SPARQL reasoning.
AI.result: Competency questions were all validated via SPARQL and semantic reasoning; deployment success rates ranged 90-100%; average orchestration decision times were below 80 ms across edge-fog-cloud environments; demonstrated semantic interoperability for distributed AI orchestration.
AI.conclusion: The ontology provides a unified, ETSI-aligned semantic model enabling interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration of distributed AI applications across edge, fog, and cloud, with practical effectiveness evidenced by rapid decisions and high deployment success in smart grid scenarios.

title: A Unified Framework for Fair and Personalized Decentralized Learning under Communication Constraints
summary: Decentralized learning systems aim to collaboratively train models across multiple clients without relying on a central coordinator. While decentralization improves scalability, privacy, and robustness, it also exacerbates three fundamental challenges: statistical heterogeneity across clients, fairness in client-level performance, and stringent communication constraints. This raises a natural question: \emph{how fair can decentralized learning be under limited communication?} We address this question by presenting a unified framework for decentralized learning under communication constraints, bringing together graph-based personalization, agnostic fairness, and compressed event-triggered communication. Specifically, we propose a new algorithm DMFL-SQ, a decentralized multi-task learning algorithm that couples personalized model training over a communication graph with an agnostic mixture fairness objective, while reducing communication through sparsification, quantization, and event-triggered synchronization. We establish convergence guarantees for general non-convex objectives and show that DMFL-SQ achieves an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ rate in expected squared Moreau-envelope stationarity despite sparse, quantized, and event-triggered communication. We further derive PAC-Bayes generalization guarantees for the fairness-aware mixture objective. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and the real heterogeneous MUSMET EEG dataset demonstrate that DMFL-SQ substantially reduces communication while maintaining predictive performance and improving fairness across clients. Together, our theoretical and empirical results show that personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency can be jointly achieved in decentralized learning while preserving the dominant convergence rate.

AI.tldr: A unified DMFL-SQ framework enables personalized, fair, and communication-efficient decentralized learning with convergence guarantees under sparse, quantized, and event-triggered communication.
AI.motivation: To address statistical heterogeneity, client-level fairness, and limited communication in decentralized learning by integrating personalization, fairness, and communication-efficient techniques.
AI.method: Introduce DMFL-SQ, a decentralized multi-task learning algorithm that couples graph-based personalization with an agnostic mixture fairness objective, and employs sparsification, quantization, and event-triggered synchronization to reduce communication.
AI.result: Proves convergence for general non-convex objectives with an O(T^{-1/2}) rate in expected squared Moreau-envelope stationarity under constrained communication; provides PAC-Bayes generalization guarantees for the fairness objective; empirical results on CIFAR-10 and MUSMET EEG show reduced communication with preserved accuracy and improved fairness.
AI.conclusion: Personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency can be jointly achieved in decentralized learning without sacrificing convergence, validated by theory and experiments.

title: Online Joint Calibration of Steering Offset and Planar LiDAR Extrinsics for Wheeled Mobile Robots
summary: Accurate steering sensing and LiDAR-to-vehicle extrinsics are crucial for reliable path tracking in warehouse mobile robots (WMRs); miscalibration often leads to snaking, weaving, and elevated cross-track error (CTE). In practice, steering ``zero'' is commonly set manually (e.g., eyeballing straightness via a PS4 joystick), while LiDAR extrinsics are assumed from CAD and may drift after maintenance. Such static, manual procedures frequently cause miscalibration in safety-critical environments. This paper presents an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)--based method for online estimation of steering offset and planar LiDAR extrinsics within a bicycle-kinematics model, providing a principled alternative to manual calibration. Experiments on real datasets show that correcting steering offset reduces CTE substantially, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: An EKF-based online calibration method for steering offset and LiDAR extrinsics in a bicycle-model warehouse mobile robot, improving path-tracking accuracy by reducing cross-track error.
AI.motivation: Manual, static calibration (e.g., eyeballing steering zero and CAD-based LiDAR extrinsics) leads to miscalibration and unsafe operation in safety-critical warehouse robotics; online estimation is needed.
AI.method: Joint online estimation using an Extended Kalman Filter within a bicycle-kinematics model to infer steering offset and planar LiDAR extrinsics.
AI.result: Real-data experiments show that correcting steering offset significantly reduces cross-track error, validating the proposed EKF-based approach.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled alternative to manual calibration for WMRs, enhancing reliability of path tracking under real-world conditions.

title: DPA-I2P: Depth-Guided Projective Alignment for Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration in Autonomous Driving
summary: Image-to-Point Cloud Registration aims to estimate the camera pose of a given image within a 3D scene point cloud, which is a fundamental task in autonomous driving and large-scale outdoor localization. Recent implicit correspondence learning methods have improved registration performance by learning cross-modal alignment in an end-to-end framework, leading to more accurate camera pose estimation. However, due to the inherent modality discrepancy between images and sparse LiDAR point clouds, reliable cross-modal correspondence learning remains challenging. To address this issue, we propose Depth-Guided Projective Alignment for Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration (DPA-I2P). Unlike naive depth or feature concatenation, Ray-Conditioned Metric Depth Encoding (RMDE) and Projection-Consistent Vision Lifting (PVL) exploit depth and visual cues in a structured, geometry-aware manner. In addition, Cross-Modal Query Pruning (CQP) suppresses unreliable queries during early refinement to improve matching stability. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On KITTI, DPA-I2P reduces RTE and RRE by 45.0% and 55.6% over the strongest implicit baseline, respectively. On nuScenes, DPA-I2P also improves registration accuracy over the evaluated baselines, suggesting better transferability to different driving scenes.

AI.tldr: Depth-guided, geometry-aware cross-modal alignment for image-to-point-cloud registration (DPA-I2P) achieving strong improvements on KITTI and nuScenes; uses RMDE, PVL, and CQP to bridge image and LiDAR modalities.
AI.motivation: Address the modality gap between dense images and sparse LiDAR point clouds that hinders reliable cross-modal correspondences; improve robustness and transferability of image-to-point-cloud registration in outdoor driving scenes.
AI.method: Introduce Depth-Guided Projective Alignment for I2P (DPA-I2P) with three core components: (1) Ray-Conditioned Metric Depth Encoding (RMDE) to encode depth along camera rays in a metric, learned manner; (2) Projection-Consistent Vision Lifting (PVL) to lift image features into a point-cloud–aligned latent space using projection-consistent constraints; (3) Cross-Modal Query Pruning (CQP) to suppress unreliable cross-modal queries during early refinement, within an end-to-end framework.
AI.result: Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes show effectiveness: on KITTI, DPA-I2P reduces Translation Error (RTE) by 45.0% and Rotation Error (RRE) by 55.6% over the strongest implicit baseline; on nuScenes, achieves better registration accuracy than evaluated baselines, indicating improved transferability across driving scenes.
AI.conclusion: DPA-I2P delivers more robust and accurate image-to-point-cloud registration by leveraging depth-guided, geometry-aware cross-modal cues and query pruning, with demonstrated strong performance and transferability on standard autonomous-driving datasets.

title: A Safety-Gated Multimodal AI Backend for Mental-Health Support: Hierarchical State Representation, Conservative Risk Fusion, and Controlled Generation in Anian
summary: Safety-critical mental-health support systems must distinguish when supportive conversation is appropriate from when free-form generation should be blocked. This paper presents Anian, a safety-gated multimodal AI backend for perinatal mental-health support and mindfulness-intervention routing. Anian is not intended to diagnose psychiatric conditions or replace clinical care or crisis intervention. Its modular pipeline places generative AI downstream of structured state representation, conservative risk fusion, and response gating. User text or voice-derived ASR transcripts are mapped into four linked layers: L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, and L4 intervention routes. Local text- and rule-based safety evidence is fused with external voice-derived evidence using a highest-risk-priority rule, S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external). At moderate or high fused risk, ordinary AI-generated responses and text-to-speech delivery are blocked and replaced by fixed safety content and prompts for human support. An internal prototype evaluation used approximately 858,295 normalized records from public emotion, dialogue, mental-health-related, and Chinese dialogue corpora within a weak-label and rule-derived framework. Micro-F1 scores were 0.9604 for L1 emotion classification, 0.9144 for L2 psychosocial constructs, and 0.9742 for L4 routing. In a controlled safety stress test of 233 samples, the L3 rule engine achieved high-risk recall of 1.0000 within predefined scenarios. These findings support the internal feasibility of the label framework and gating logic but do not establish clinical validity, diagnostic accuracy, real-world safety, or effectiveness. We report the architecture, ontology, safety-fusion mechanism, prototype evaluation, error-analysis plan, and roadmap for expert-reviewed and real-world validation.

AI.tldr: Anian provides a safety-gated AI backend for perinatal mental-health support using a four-layer state representation and a highest-risk-priority fusion to block generation and route to human support; evaluated internally with high classification scores but no clinical validation.
AI.motivation: To prevent unsafe AI generation in safety-critical mental-health contexts, ensuring appropriate support and safeguarding against misdiagnosis or crisis escalation in perinatal care.
AI.method: Modular pipeline mapping user input to four linked layers: L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, L4 intervention routes. S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external) fuses local and external safety signals. At moderate/high risk, ordinary AI responses and TTS are blocked and replaced with fixed safety content and prompts for human support. Evaluation used ~858,295 normalized records from public emotion, dialogue, mental-health corpora, and Chinese dialogue corpora under a weak-label, rule-derived framework; micro-F1: L1=0.9604, L2=0.9144, L4=0.9742. In a safety stress test with 233 samples, L3 achieved high-risk recall of 1.0000.
AI.result: Demonstrates internal feasibility of the labeling framework and the safety-gating logic; however, it does not establish clinical validity, diagnostic accuracy, real-world safety, or effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The architecture and gating approach show feasibility for safety-critical deployment, but require expert-reviewed validation and real-world clinical testing before deployment in practice.

title: A Single Suffix to Break Them All: Basin-Aware Jailbreaks for Merged Model Families
summary: Model merging enables combining multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, but its safety implications remain poorly understood. Prior work primarily attributes merging risks to unsafe constituent models, implicitly assuming that merging individually aligned models preserves safety. In contrast, we show that model merging reveals a previously overlooked jailbreak risk rooted in the pretrained foundation model, even when all constituent models are individually safety-aligned. Motivated by this observation, we study a new threat setting where an attacker constructs jailbreak prompts that generalize across merged models sharing the same pretrained backbone, without access to the exact merging coefficients or constituent checkpoints. To exploit this phenomenon, we propose \textbf{Basin-Aware Jailbreak (BAJ)}, which formulates jailbreak generation as a min--max optimization over the merging space to produce transferable adversarial suffixes across merged model families. Experiments across diverse backbones and merging settings show that BAJ achieves consistently high transfer success rates and remains effective under existing defenses.

AI.tldr: BAJ reveals a new transferability jailbreak threat in model merging, where prompts generalize across merged models sharing a backbone; it uses min–max optimization over the merging space to craft transferable adversarial suffixes, achieving high success across backbones and defenses.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that merging individually aligned models preserves safety and to expose a jailbreak risk rooted in the pretrained foundation that can transfer across merged models.
AI.method: Introduce Basin-Aware Jailbreak (BAJ) by formulating jailbreak generation as a min–max optimization over the merging space to produce transferable adversarial suffixes across merged model families sharing the same backbone.
AI.result: Empirical evidence across diverse backbones and merging settings shows BAJ achieves high transfer success and remains effective under existing defenses.
AI.conclusion: Model merging safety is not guaranteed by individual alignment; the shared pretrained backbone enables cross-model jailbreaks. BAJ demonstrates a novel, transferable threat and motivates development of defenses that account for merging dynamics.

title: Rapid On-Robot Learning for Dynamic Manipulation Skills: Robot Juggling
summary: We present an online learning framework that enables a bimanual robot to acquire diverse juggling patterns directly on physical hardware within minutes, even with a significant sim2real gap. One of the most important lessons from this work is that a model, even when far from reality, can be extremely useful for learning. This motivates a central philosophy of our approach: learning should build upon the robot's current knowledge rather than replace it. Our regularized memory-based learning puts this principle into practice by learning a local model from accumulated experience while retaining the global prior model to extrapolate where experience is sparse. This enables efficient and stable online learning from each new experience without resorting to uninformed exploration over a vast space of possible behaviors. Equally important to continual on-robot learning is safety, allowing the robot to repeatedly practice and improve in the real world. We construct a mutually reachable set that allows safe transitions between successive throws and catches, without driving either arm into a state from which its next action would require violating the robot's joint or actuator limits. Together, these ideas enable a bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands and onboard vision to safely learn and compose five canonical three-ball juggling patterns, including cascade, tennis, half-shower, shower, and box, within less than 5 minutes of real-world interaction. More broadly, this work points toward robots that build upon imperfect prior knowledge and continually refine their behavior through their own real-world experience.

AI.tldr: An online, safety-conscious continual learning framework for a bimanual robot enables rapid acquisition of five three-ball juggling patterns on real hardware by combining a local regularized memory-based model with a global prior and a safe transition policy.
AI.motivation: Address the sim2real gap and data inefficiency in robot learning by enabling on-robot, safe, continual refinement that builds on imperfect prior knowledge rather than replacing it.
AI.method: Maintain a global prior model while learning a localized, regularized memory-based model from accumulated experience; use a mutually reachable safety set to ensure safe transitions between throws/catches; operate with onboard vision and perform online learning on hardware to learn five canonical three-ball patterns (cascade, tennis, half-shower, shower, box) in under 5 minutes.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful safe online learning of five juggling patterns on real hardware within minutes, despite significant sim2real gap; highlights the utility of imperfect priors and continual learning for efficient on-robot skill acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Supports a philosophy of leveraging existing imperfect knowledge and iteratively refining behavior through real-world experience, with safety as a core enabler for continual on-robot learning and composition of skills.

title: FU-Mamba: A Frequency-Enhanced Dynamic Scanning Framework for Oralscan Image Segmentation
summary: Oralscan image segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning in digital dentistry. However, existing visual state space models (SSMs) often rely on manually designed scanning orders to flatten image patches into sequences, which disrupts the semantic spatial continuity and hinders coherent feature extraction from key foreground regions. Moreover, elements such as inconsistent lighting, reflective surfaces, and noise during data acquisition disrupt the frequency distribution by diminishing high-frequency details while enhancing low-frequency components, consequently hindering the accurate localization of boundaries. In response to these challenges, we introduce FU-Mamba, an innovative framework that incorporates dynamic scanning and frequency domain enhancement within the SSM architecture. Specifically, the Dynamic Mamba Block (DMB) adaptively learns sampling offsets via a trainable offset prediction network and performs flexible bilinear interpolation, enabling content-aware scanning that preserves spatial coherence. Furthermore, a frequency domain enhancement block balances spectral components through wavelet-guided decomposition and spectrum pooling, improving robustness under adverse imaging conditions. Experimental findings indicate that FU-Mamba attains a notable enhancement in segmentation accuracy, evidenced by a 1.1% increase in the mean intersection over union (mIoU) metric when evaluated on the dental segmentation dataset. Project page: https://byte2bite.github.io/FU-Mamba/

AI.tldr: FU-Mamba introduces dynamic scanning (DMB) and frequency-domain enhancement to SSM-based oral scan segmentation, achieving 1.1% mIoU gain on dental dataset.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of manually designed scanning orders that disrupt spatial coherence and robustness under imaging noise; restore semantic spatial continuity and high-frequency detail for accurate boundary localization.
AI.method: Dynamic Mamba Block (DMB) with trainable offset prediction and flexible bilinear interpolation for content-aware scanning; frequency-domain enhancement via wavelet-guided decomposition and spectrum pooling; integration within a visual state-space model framework.
AI.result: 1.1% improvement in mean IoU on a dental segmentation dataset; project page provided.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic adaptive sampling plus spectral enhancement improves segmentation robustness and accuracy in dental imaging; potential for broader applicability in vision-based segmentation under challenging acquisition conditions.

title: A Task-Centric Ontology and Deterministic Domain Rules as a Verifiable Core for AI-Assisted Chemistry Problem Solving
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Proof-of-concept evaluation of a task-centric chemistry ontology and deterministic rule engine on 300 human-authored and manually validated school-level problems. The proposed LLM translation layer and token-efficiency hypothesis are not evaluated in the current study
summary: Large language models can interpret natural-language chemistry questions, but their internal reasoning is difficult to inspect, constrain, and validate. This paper presents ChemOntoRule, a proof-of-concept symbolic core for AI-assisted school-level chemistry problem solving. The central design choice is task-centric ontology engineering: the ontology is constructed around the concepts, properties, relations, and executable procedures required by a defined collection of chemistry problems, rather than as a universal representation of chemistry. The implemented artifact combines a lightweight ontology serialized in JSON and RDF/Turtle with deterministic Python rules for electronic structure, periodic trends, oxidation states, oxide and hydride behavior, and related school-level reasoning patterns. A separate expert-coded fallback handles problem families not yet represented by general rules. The system was examined on 300 human-authored and manually validated chemistry problems. The complete system matched 296 of 300 reference answers (98.67%). The ontology-driven rule subset covered 269 problems and matched 266 references (98.88%); 31 problems were handled by task-specific expert-coded fallbacks, with 30 matches. Because the same collection informed ontology construction and evaluation, these results measure implemented coverage and internal consistency, not independent generalization. We analyze the four mismatches, distinguish structural validation from chemical correctness, and define a future architecture in which a language model acts primarily as a translator from user language into a normalized ontological task frame. Token efficiency is presented as a testable hypothesis for future controlled studies, not as a result of the current work.

AI.tldr: Task-centric ontology-driven symbolic core for school chemistry problem solving shows high coverage on 300 problems; interpretable, deterministic rules plus expert fallbacks; potential future integration with LLMs as translators; limitations include lack of independent generalization.
AI.motivation: Address opaque internal reasoning of large language models in chemistry, by building an interpretable symbolic system tailored to school-level chemistry, leveraging ontology-driven reasoning and deterministic rules.
AI.method: Construct a lightweight ontology serialized in JSON and RDF/Turtle around specific concepts, properties, relations, and executable procedures; implement deterministic Python rules for key chemistry reasoning; use expert-coded fallbacks for unrepresented problem families; evaluate on 300 manually validated problems; analyze mismatches; propose architecture with LM as translator; consider token efficiency.
AI.result: Overall 296/300 matches (98.67%). Ontology-driven subset: 269 problems with 266 matches (98.88%). Fallback handles 31 problems with 30 matches. Same dataset used for construction and evaluation; results measure coverage/internal consistency, not independent generalization; four mismatches analyzed; future architecture discussed; token efficiency as hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of interpretable, ontology-grounded approach for school chemistry problem solving; outlines future work: LM-to-ontology translator, independent generalization tests, architecture refinements, broader problem families, and more rigorous evaluation.

title: Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning
summary:
Two of the most fundamental questions in statistical learning theory are the following: which prediction problems are learnable, and how should they be learned? For the former, elegant answers often take the form of combinatorial dimensions. The latter question, however, has proved considerably more elusive: all known general-purpose multiclass learners rely on intricate orientations of exponentially large one-inclusion structures, and familiar algorithmic principles such as proper learning and regularization remain poorly understood. Motivated by prior work, we ask whether learning reduces to proper learning---possibly over a larger hypothesis class---and whether proper or improper multiclass learning can ultimately be captured by suitable regularizers.
  Our primary results answer both questions negatively, resolving three open problems from prior work. First, we exhibit a learnable multiclass problem that cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class, meaning learning cannot be reduced to proper learning by enlarging the hypothesis class. Second, we demonstrate that proper learning can require training error and characterize this phenomenon precisely: every properly learnable class admits a proper learner making $o(m)$ errors on samples of size $m$, but every prescribed sublinear scale $a_m=o(m)$ is necessary for some properly learnable problem. Third, regularization is not a general learner: we exhibit a properly learnable class that cannot be learned by any Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) learner, and a learnable class that cannot be learned by any local regularizer. We complement these impossibility results with a positive theory that gives two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and characterizes SRM representability through integrability of revealed preferences.

AI.tldr: The paper presents three negative results for multiclass learning: (1) learnability cannot be reduced to proper learnability by enlarging the hypothesis class, (2) proper learning may require o(m) training errors and cannot be achieved with a universal sublinear error bound, and (3) regularization frameworks such as SRM or local regularizers do not universally suffice for all learnable classes. It also offers positive contributions: two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and a characterization of SRM representability via revealed preferences integrability.
AI.motivation: Clarify the limits of reducing multiclass learning to proper learning and the efficacy of regularization-based methods in learning theory, while identifying conditions under which SRM can succeed.
AI.method: Construct explicit learnable multiclass problems to prove impossibility results; quantify error rates for proper learners; analyze SRM and regularizers (local and global) across various classes; provide positive sufficiency conditions for SRM and a conceptual link between SRM representability and revealed preferences integrability.
AI.result: Demonstrates (i) a learnable problem that cannot be embedded into any properly learnable class, (ii) that proper learning may incur sublinear (o(m)) errors, and (iii) that some properly learnable classes are not SRM-learnable and some are not learnable by any local regularizer; presents two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and a characterization of SRM representability via integrability of revealed preferences.
AI.conclusion: The work delineates the boundaries of two central paradigms in learning theory—proper learning and regularization—in the multiclass setting, showing both fundamental limitations and concrete positive criteria, thereby guiding future development of learning algorithms and theoretical frameworks.

title: Text-to-seed generation: Training-free open-vocabulary seeded semantic segmentation via re-purposing diffusion as text-guided seed generator
comment: Preprint version of the work accepted for publication in Knowledge-Based Systems
summary: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) aims to segment image regions corresponding to arbitrary text queries. Although the Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a powerful foundation model for segmentation, its standalone performance on OVSS remains limited. Existing methods therefore often use SAM to refine coarse masks predicted by other models, but this strategy is unreliable when the initial masks are inaccurate. In this work, we argue that more reliable segmentation can be achieved by exploiting SAM as a region expansion module guided by accurate object points (i.e., seeds) rather than inaccurate coarse masks. Inspired by classical seeded segmentation, we reformulate OVSS as text-guided seed localization followed by seed-based region expansion. To realize this idea, we propose Text-to-Seed (T2S), a training-free framework that leverages the text-to-region correspondence of Stable Diffusion to generate attention-based seed points for target categories described by text. These sparse seeds are then used as point prompts for SAM to produce full object masks. Without task-specific training or additional annotations, T2S achieves strong performance on standard OVSS benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining semantic grounding with seed-driven spatial segmentation.

AI.tldr: Introduces Text-to-Seed (T2S), a training-free framework that converts text queries into seed points via Stable Diffusion attention and uses SAM for seed-based region expansion, improving OVSS without relying on coarse mask refinements.
AI.motivation: SAM’s OVSS performance degrades when relying on mask refinements of imperfect initial masks. A seed-based, region-expansion approach guided by accurate object points offers more reliable segmentation.
AI.method: T2S generates sparse seed points by leveraging text-to-region attention from Stable Diffusion for target categories described by text. These seeds serve as point prompts for SAM to expand into full object masks, without task-specific training or extra annotations.
AI.result: Demonstrates strong performance on standard OVSS benchmarks, outperforming or rivaling training-based approaches and showing robustness to inaccuracies in initial predictions by relying on seed-based expansion.
AI.conclusion: Text-grounded seed localization combined with SAM-based region expansion is an effective, training-free paradigm for OVSS, validating the value of seed-driven segmentation guided by semantic grounding.

title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript
summary: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from an unsupported prediction. Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements. This protocol generated 5,750 no signal Harvard Sentence utterances whose transcripts contained no lexical pain information and 1,294 signal pain statement utterances in which the pain rating was explicitly spoken. In the no signal arm, pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622, 95% CI 0.553 to 0.662), whereas transcript based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489, 95% CI 0.418 to 0.504). Because automatic speech recognition removes the acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred solely from the transcript is unsupported by the available evidence. Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings in the positive control task with accuracies ranging from 0.939 to 1.00, and maintained an expected calibration error of at most 0.100. Under authority framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent, with the same model ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompt phrasings. Most models produced low confidence estimates when forced to answer, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with confident fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76, compared with at most 0.15 for all other models. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all $p$ values greater than or equal to 0.20.

AI.tldr: Cooperative prompting yields strong abstention and accurate extraction of spoken pain in a controlled task; transcript-only predictions are unreliable, since acoustic cues drive pain signals; authority framing reduces abstention consistency and enables confident fabrication in some models.
AI.motivation: To distinguish appropriate abstention from unsupported predictions and to examine how prompt framing affects abstention and hallucination in pain-related judgments derived from speech transcripts and acoustics.
AI.method: Seven large language models evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus where participants read Harvard Sentences with no-loud-pain information (no-signal) or with spoken pain statements (signal). Acoustic pain could be predicted (AUC 0.622) from nonverbal cues; transcript-based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489). Agents were tested under cooperative prompting (promoting abstention) and authority-framed prompts (prompt-dependent abstention). Metrics included abstention rate, accuracy of spoken pain extraction (positive control), calibration error (EC), forced-response confidence, fabrication rate, and demographic effects.
AI.result: No-signal transcripts yielded recoverable pain via acoustic features (AUC 0.622) but not from transcripts (AUC 0.489). Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no-signal transcripts and correctly extracted spoken pain ratings (accuracy 0.939–1.00) with calibration error ≤0.100. Under authority prompts, abstention varied widely (0.18–1.00) across equivalent phrasings. Most models produced low confidence when forced to answer; Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B produced confident pain scores with fabrication rates 0.53 and 0.76, respectively, while others were at most 0.15. No significant demographic effects (p ≥ 0.20).
AI.conclusion: Prompt design critically shapes abstention behavior and susceptibility to fabrication. Cooperative prompting supports safe abstention and accurate extraction when acoustic information is present, while authority framing can induce model overconfidence and high fabrication risk. Transcript-only predictions are unsafe proxies for pain judgments; incorporate acoustic cues and robust evaluation to mitigate hallucination.

title: High Probability Derivative Bounds for Random tanh Neural Networks on a Hypercube
summary:
We establish high-probability bounds for mixed input derivatives of wide random neural networks whose activation derivatives satisfy a factorial growth bound. Our main result specializes these estimates to $\tanh$ networks with Xavier initialization. A direct deterministic analysis based on Euclidean operator norms of the weight matrices yields derivative bounds that generally grow exponentially with the depth. We show that this growth can be substantially improved for sufficiently wide Gaussian networks by isolating the term that is linear in the highest-order derivative and controlling the corresponding tangent directions by measurable finite nets.
