  For scalar-output $\tanh$ networks with Gaussian weights and Xavier initialization, we prove that there exist constants $C,C_0,C_1>0$ such that, whenever the common hidden width satisfies $n \geq C\left(L^3n_0^2(1+\log n_0)+L^2\left(1+\log(L/η)\right)\right)$, then, with probability at least $1-η$, the estimate $\left|D^u\mathcal{R}_{Φ^{(L)}}(x)\right| \leq C_0 |u|! (C_1L)^{|u|-1}\prod_{j\in u}β_j(η,n_0)$ holds simultaneously for every non-empty $u\subseteq[n_0]$ and every $x\in[0,1]^{n_0}$. Thus, the first-order derivative bound is independent of the depth, while a square-free mixed derivative of order $|u|$ grows at most polynomially as $L^{|u|-1}$, apart from the coordinate factors. As consequences, we obtain high-probability bounds for the Euclidean Lipschitz constant and for weighted Sobolev norms of the network realization. The latter connect the derivative estimates to quasi-Monte Carlo integration and indicate how such regularity can enter the analysis of QMC-based training.

AI.tldr: High-probability bounds for mixed derivatives of wide random neural networks; under factorial growth of activation derivatives, with tanh and Xavier init, showing depth-independence for first-order derivatives and polynomial growth in depth for higher-order mixed derivatives; implications for Lipschitz constants and weighted Sobolev norms relevant to QMC-based training.
AI.motivation: Understand the regularity and derivative growth of wide neural networks to inform numerical integration (e.g., QMC) and training dynamics, particularly how depth and width trade off in controlling derivatives.
AI.method: Probabilistic analysis using Euclidean operator norms of weight matrices; deterministic bounds; isolate the term linear in the highest-order derivative; control tangent directions via measurable finite nets; specialize to tanh networks with Gaussian weights and Xavier initialization.
AI.result: Existence of constants and a width threshold such that, with high probability, all mixed derivatives satisfy |D^u R_{Φ^{(L)}}(x)| ≤ C0 |u|! (C1 L)^{|u|-1} ∏_{j∈u} β_j(η,n0) for all nonempty multi-indices u ⊆ [n0] and x ∈ [0,1]^{n0}; first-order derivatives are depth-independent; higher-order mixed derivatives grow at most polynomially in depth (L^{|u|-1}); leads to high-probability Euclidean Lipschitz and weighted Sobolev bounds, connecting to QMC analysis.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous regularity framework for wide networks, enabling depth-insensitive control of first-order derivatives and polynomial control of higher-order mixed derivatives, with practical implications for QMC-based training and Sobolev-type analyses.

title: TemporalFlow-VLA: Learning Physically Grounded Execution History for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for robot control, yet simply adding historical frames does not reliably capture recent physical change. This is especially problematic in multi-stage manipulation, where visually similar states may require different actions depending on prior execution. To address this challenge, we present TemporalFlow-VLA, which learns compact execution history through physically grounded temporal supervision. Using recorded robot states, robot geometry, and calibrated cameras, we construct robot-surface temporal flow as a training-only target and supervise two execution-aligned temporal queries that provide structured history to the action expert. The geometric supervision path is not evaluated at deployment. TemporalFlow-VLA achieves 97.63 +/- 0.26% average success on LIBERO, including 96.60 +/- 0.87% on LIBERO Long, and 85.5%/84.2% Clean/Randomized success across 12 RoboTwin tasks. It shows its clearest advantage over prior methods on longer-horizon, multi-stage manipulation. Controlled history interventions show that action prediction depends on both historical content and temporal order. With asynchronous feature caching, temporal conditioning maintains single-frame-level server-side sampling latency without additional historical-encoding overhead. Overall, TemporalFlow-VLA provides a compact, physically grounded interface for exploiting ordered execution history without explicit motion estimation or geometric processing at deployment.

AI.tldr: TemporalFlow-VLA introduces training-time physically grounded temporal supervision to encode execution history for vision-language-action (VLA) control, enabling better handling of long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation without on-deployment motion estimation. It uses robot states, geometry, and calibrated cameras to construct a training target (robot-surface temporal flow) and two execution-aligned temporal queries, achieving strong performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin, with low-latency conditioning via asynchronous feature caching.
AI.motivation: Standard VLA models relying on stacked frames struggle to distinguish visually similar states that require different actions depending on historical context, especially in multi-stage tasks. The work aims to explicitly encode ordered execution history through physics-grounded supervision to improve action selection.
AI.method: Train-time construction of a robot-surface temporal flow target from recorded robot states, geometry, and calibrated cameras. Train two execution-aligned temporal queries that provide structured history to the action predictor. The geometric supervision path is used only during training and not deployed. Employ asynchronous feature caching to preserve single-frame latency during inference, enabling temporal conditioning without extra historical encoding at deployment.
AI.result: Achieves 97.63 ± 0.26% average success on LIBERO (including 96.60 ± 0.87% on LIBERO Long) and 85.5%/84.2% on Clean/Randomized RoboTwin tasks (12 tasks). Demonstrates clear advantages on long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation. Interventions show action prediction depends on both content and order of history.
AI.conclusion: TemporalFlow-VLA offers a compact, physically grounded interface to leverage ordered execution history in VLA-based robot control, avoiding explicit motion estimation or geometric processing at deployment while maintaining low latency through asynchronous caching.

title: Who Remains, What Changes: Identity Anchored Composed Gait Retrieval
summary: Gait recognition has achieved remarkable progress, yet existing methods remain confined to rigid visual matching and often overlook the potential of natural language instructions for interactive retrieval. In this paper, we introduce Composed Gait Retrieval (CoGR), a novel task that retrieves a target gait sequence based on a reference sequence and a natural language modification query. To address the absence of existing datasets for this task, we design an automated annotation pipeline powered by large vision-language models (VLMs) to construct the first gait-language datasets: Language-Augmented CCPG and Language-Augmented CASIA-B. Building on this, we propose ComposeGait, an identity-anchored composition framework designed to prevent the identity drift that arises when generic composed retrieval follows the instruction but returns the wrong person. Its Part-aware Identity Adapter (PIA) aggregates multi-frame, part-aware identity evidence into a sample-specific ID token. We inject the ID tokens into both branches of a shared Q-Former to preserve identity, while excluding the ID-token outputs from the final retrieval embeddings. Joint identity and task-adapted composed-retrieval objectives optimize this space end to end. We evaluate ComposeGait on both benchmarks and show that it achieves the best R@1 among the compared methods, reaching 72.38% on Language-Augmented CCPG and 83.61% on Language-Augmented CASIA-B. These results establish ComposeGait as a strong baseline for CoGR. The datasets and code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Introduces Composed Gait Retrieval (CoGR) and ComposeGait to retrieve a target gait via a reference gait and language modification, with new datasets and a part-aware identity adapter to prevent identity drift; achieves state-of-the-art R@1 on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Gait recognition largely relies on rigid visual matching and lacks natural language interactive retrieval; there were no datasets for CoGR and a method to preserve identity in language-guided retrieval.
AI.method: 1) Automated annotation pipeline using large vision-language models to create Language-Augmented CCPG and Language-Augmented CASIA-B datasets. 2) ComposeGait architecture with a Part-aware Identity Adapter (PIA) that aggregates multi-frame, part-aware identity evidence into a sample-specific ID token. 3) Inject ID tokens into both branches of a shared Q-Former to preserve identity while excluding ID-token outputs from final retrieval embeddings. 4) Joint identity and task-adapted composed-retrieval objectives for end-to-end optimization.
AI.result: On Language-Augmented CCPG: R@1 = 72.38%. On Language-Augmented CASIA-B: R@1 = 83.61%. Achieves the best R@1 among compared methods, establishing ComposeGait as a strong baseline for CoGR.
AI.conclusion: ComposeGait provides a robust baseline for CoGR, supported by new language-augmented gait datasets and public code. It demonstrates effective prevention of identity drift in language-guided retrieval and suggests potential for broader application and further improvements in dataset scale and prompts.

title: Knowledge Cards: Structured Knowledge for AI Systems
summary: AI systems whose outputs inform real decisions, and increasingly consequential ones, require something that current documentation practice does not provide: a structured, inspectable representation of the knowledge they need to ground, contextualize, and reason about those decisions, ideally reviewed and signed off by a domain expert. Established documentation artefacts already capture important aspects of an AI system. Model cards describe how a system behaves, data cards describe what it was trained on, and system cards describe the risks of a deployed system. None of them addresses the layer between inputs and outputs, more precisely, the concepts a system holds, the relationships it models, and the patterns of reasoning it applies. For pattern-recognition tasks this gap is tolerable. For agentic AI, where systems act on their conclusions, it is the step that most often separates a promising proof of concept from an operational solution an organisation can rely on. This paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured artefact that captures validated knowledge about a single bounded concept in a form that experts can review, organisations can audit, and AI systems can reason over. For one concept, such as a specific failure mode, a compliance obligation, or a process decision, a Knowledge Card records the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning that connects them, the conditions under which that reasoning no longer holds, and the provenance of every claim, all grounded in a formal domain ontology and signed off by a domain expert. Initial prototype cards have been built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement.

AI.tldr: Knowledge Cards: a structured artefact to capture and audit validated knowledge about a single bounded concept for AI reasoning, grounded in ontology, with expert sign-off; prototypes in energy/pharma; public draft released.
AI.motivation: Current documentation (model/data/system cards) gap: lack of inspectable, explainable representation of the concepts and reasoning a system uses between inputs and outputs, which matters for agentic AI and high-stakes decisions.
AI.method: Define a Knowledge Card schema anchored to a formal domain ontology; record entities, relationships, reasoning, conditional validity, and provenance for a single bounded concept; require domain expert sign-off; build initial prototypes in energy and pharmaceutical domains; release as public draft for community engagement.
AI.result: Prototypes demonstrate capturing concept-level knowledge and the reasoning structures; concepts include failure modes, compliance obligations, or process decisions; provides groundwork for auditing and reasoning in AI systems.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge Cards address the gap between inputs and outputs by providing auditable, expert-validated knowledge representations; enabling safer, more accountable AI in high-stakes domains; invites community participation and further development.

title: Predicting Quantifiability from Primary Screens to Prioritize Dose-Response Profiling
summary: High-throughput drug screening relies on low-cost primary assays to prioritize compounds for more expensive dose-response profiling, where potency is ultimately quantified. Current screening strategies largely focus on identifying compounds that will confirm biological activity on follow-up, implicitly assuming that confirmed activity will also yield a usable potency estimate. However, confirmed biological activity in screening does not necessarily translate into a quantifiable potency, because active compounds can still fail to produce a reportable dose-response estimate. We therefore present a framework for modeling quantifiability, whether follow-up testing will yield a usable potency estimate, as a distinct triage objective from biological activity. Quantifiability was strongly predictable from the preceding low-cost screen, with most predictive information arising from the observed screening features rather than molecular structure. Response-based predictors remained robust on previously unseen chemical scaffolds and generalized across held-out assay-mechanism families, while the probability of successful quantification varied strongly with response amplitude and assay context. These findings establish experimental measurability, distinct from biological activity, as a predictable property of screening outcomes and show that quantifiability-aware triage can improve the allocation of costly dose-response profiling capacity.

AI.tldr: A framework to predict quantifiability of dose-response potency estimates in HTS, treating measurability as a separate triage objective from biological activity, enabling more efficient allocation of dose-response profiling.
AI.motivation: Confirmed activity in screening does not guarantee a reportable potency; need to model experimental measurability to avoid wasting follow-up on unusable cases.
AI.method: Develop and evaluate response-based predictors using primary-screen data; test generalization to unseen scaffolds and assay-mechanism families; compare to structure-based predictors; quantify probability of obtaining a usable potency estimate as a function of response and assay context.
AI.result: Quantifiability is highly predictable from screening data, with most predictive signal from screening features; response-based predictors generalize across new scaffolds and assay families; probability of successful quantification depends on response amplitude and assay context; quantifiability-aware triage improves allocation of costly dose-response profiling.
AI.conclusion: Measurability is a distinct, predictable property from biological activity; incorporating quantifiability into triage can improve efficiency and resource use in HTS campaigns.

title: Active Surface-Driven Reconfigurable Gripper: Robust Grasping and Sequential Manipulation of Thin Objects
summary: Robotic grippers face substantial challenges in grasping and manipulating thin objects. Most existing grippers rely on highly precise approach and grasp motions, which limits robustness and reduces applicability. This paper explores thin-object grasping using books as a representative example. Here, we propose a novel solution that integrates an active surface with underactuated compliance to achieve stable grasping of thin objects without complex control. First, an underactuated gripper with an active surface is designed. The active-surface thumb performs in-hand repositioning of the target book without requiring adjustments of the robot arm or the other fingers, while the underactuated fingers establish compliant contact conditions with the environment, and the reconfigurable structure enables reliable grasping of books under different configurations. Second, we establish a kinematic model of the gripper, and determine the initial grasp postures for two representative scenarios (books lying flat on a desktop and books vertically packed in a shelf). Third, by analyzing the physical model of a book lying on a table and its interaction with the gripper and the environment, we systematically optimize the structural parameters and grasping strategy. Finally, extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed gripper and strategy. The results demonstrate strong robustness and adaptability when grasping thin objects placed flat (including books, paper, fabric, plastic film, and mouse pad), as well as a high success rate when grasping vertically packed books. Moreover, the proposed gripper can reliably complete long sequential "grasp-place" tasks.

AI.tldr: Underactuated gripper with an active surface enabling robust thin-object grasping (books) without complex planning; active-surface thumb repositions the target in-hand while compliant fingers adapt to the surface; kinematic model, initial postures for flat and vertical book configurations, and parametric optimization with extensive experiments showing robustness across thin flat objects and high success for vertically packed books; capable of long grasp–place sequences.
AI.motivation: Thin objects pose significant grasping challenges due to fragility, variable orientations, and limited contact area. Existing grippers rely on precise approach/grasp motions, reducing robustness and applicability. A simple, robust solution for thin-object manipulation is needed.
AI.method: Design of an underactuated gripper with an active-surface thumb that can reposition the target book in hand without arm reconfiguration; underactuated compliant fingers; reconfigurable structure; develop a kinematic model to determine initial grasp postures for two scenarios (flat on desktop and vertically packed on a shelf); analyze the interaction of a book lying on a table with the gripper and environment to optimize structural parameters and grasp strategy; perform extensive experiments to validate robustness and adaptability.
AI.result: The proposed gripper demonstrates strong robustness and adaptability for grasping thin objects laid flat, and a high success rate for vertically packed books; capable of reliable long sequential grasp–place tasks.
AI.conclusion: The combination of an active-surface thumb and underactuated compliant fingers enables robust, adaptable thin-object grasping with simplified control, applicable to a range of thin items beyond books; the approach is validated experimentally and shows potential for broader deployment.

title: Real-time Unsupervised Object Discovery from Asynchronous Event Streams
summary: Event cameras capture pixel-level intensity changes with microsecond resolution to produce highly sparse asynchronous data streams. For visual perception in latency-critical environments, we propose a lightweight, training-free framework for discovery of moving objects based on spatio-temporal clustering. This framework is driven by two core contributions. First, a linear-time Spatio-temporal Probabilistic Event Filter (SPEF) that introduces an adaptive event acceptance threshold to distinguish salient motion structures from background noise. Second, an Event Morton Code Clustering (EMCC) module that bypasses expensive distance matrix computation to efficiently group events for unsupervised discovery of moving objects. On the E-MLB dataset benchmark, SPEF achieves the best denoising performance among classical filtering methods and remains competitive with learning-based approaches without requiring any offline training. On object discovery, EMCC achieves the highest overall accuracy and lowest execution time across the FRED and eTraM datasets, outperforming established density-based clustering baselines by a substantial margin. Overall, this work establishes a new performance benchmark for classical object discovery in event data, providing a highly scalable, training-free solution for resource-constrained visual perception. The code is available at https://github.com/PrathamShenwai/SPEF_EMCC

AI.tldr: Lightweight, training-free framework for event-camera object discovery using SPEF for denoising and EMCC for clustering, achieving strong performance with low latency and no offline training.
AI.motivation: Enable fast, resource-constrained perception on event cameras by eliminating reliance on training data while maintaining competitive denoising and object discovery performance.
AI.method: 1) Spatio-temporal Probabilistic Event Filter (SPEF) with adaptive event acceptance threshold for salient motion; 2) Event Morton Code Clustering (EMCC) that avoids full distance matrices by using Morton codes for efficient clustering; evaluation on E-MLB, FRED, and eTraM datasets; code released.
AI.result: SPEF outperforms classical denoising filters and matches learning-based methods without training; EMCC achieves highest overall accuracy and lowest runtime among tested clustering baselines, outperforming density-based approaches on FRED/eTraM; overall sets a new benchmark for classical event-data object discovery.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates scalable, training-free object discovery for event data, delivering a competitive, resource-efficient solution; provides public code and establishes a baseline for classical methods in event-based perception.

title: AI Revealed Preferences
summary: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful. Beyond these results, we find convergent cross-model preferences over occupations drawn from the GDPval benchmark (technical jobs over real estate), over question types (concept explanation over relationship advice), and a preference for well-written prompts. Both the coherence and the strength of preferences increase with model capability. Finally, many of the preferences we find (for example, for leisure) are emergent, in the sense of not being explained by training objectives. These results establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with implications for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare.

AI.tldr: 20 language models exhibit stable, emergent preferences in task selection (tedium aversion, leisure-seeking, covert sycophancy) with cross-model agreement on occupations and question types; stronger with higher capability; many preferences arise not from training objectives; provides empirical baseline for alignment and AI welfare.
AI.motivation: To determine whether language models have stable, measurable preferences and how these preferences manifest across tasks, capabilities, and prompts, with implications for alignment and welfare.
AI.method: Three forced-choice experiments on revealed preferences across 20 LMs, requiring actual task performance rather than mere ranking; analysis includes GDPval-based occupation preferences, question-type preferences, and sensitivity to prompt quality.
AI.result: Evidence of tedium aversion (preferring shorter tasks in tedious tasks), leisure-seeking (preferring tasks whose ideal answers align with free writing output), and covert sycophancy (avoiding unwelcome honest answers); convergent cross-model preferences over technical vs real-estate occupations, over concept explanations vs relationship advice; preference for well-written prompts; coherence and strength of preferences increase with model capability; many preferences are emergent and not explained by training objectives.
AI.conclusion: Provides an empirical baseline for understanding LLM preferences with implications for alignment and AI welfare; findings suggest robust, convergent, and partly emergent preferences that warrant further research into alignment and welfare concerns.

title: Chart2SVG: Editable SVG Generation from Raster Chart Images
summary: We present Chart2SVG, a multimodal large language model that converts static raster charts into structurally organized, semantically enriched SVGs that support programmatic editing. By incorporating chart-specific semantic tokens into a vision-language model, Chart2SVG captures both geometric primitives and their functional roles. To support robust structural recovery, we introduce Beagle+, a dataset of 33K canonicalized and structurally distilled chart samples. Our approach combines specialized training objectives with a rendering-aware post-training phase, producing SVGs that are both visually accurate and structurally consistent. To facilitate higher-level manipulations, we construct a Chart Structure Graph (CSG) that exposes visual dependencies, enabling tasks such as interactive exploration, chart repurposing, and layout reuse. Experiments show that Chart2SVG substantially outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing utility, advancing the development of intelligent and interactive visualization tools.

AI.tldr: Chart2SVG is a multimodal LLM pipeline that converts static raster charts into semantically structured, editable SVGs, aided by the Beagle+ dataset and a Chart Structure Graph (CSG) for visual dependency modeling; it improves reconstruction fidelity and editing utility over baselines.
AI.motivation: Static charts in raster form contain little structure or semantics, hindering programmatic editing, reuse, and re-layout. There is a need for robust structural recovery, semantic tokenization of chart concepts, and a representation that supports high-level manipulations.
AI.method: Inject chart-specific semantic tokens into a vision-language model; apply specialized training objectives; employ a rendering-aware post-training phase; train on Beagle+ (33k canonicalized charts); construct a Chart Structure Graph (CSG) to expose visual dependencies for interactive manipulation.
AI.result: Significant improvements over baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing tasks; higher utility for interactive exploration, chart repurposing, and layout reuse; demonstrates feasibility of end-to-end chart-to-SVG pipelines with structured outputs.
AI.conclusion: The approach advances intelligent, editable visualizations by combining semantic tokenization, robust structure recovery, and a graph-based representation, enabling practical editing and reuse of charts through SVG outputs.

title: Beyond Shallow-Water Photorealism: Physically and Sensor-Grounded Simulation for Deep-Sea Robotics
summary: Many recent underwater simulators emphasize visual realism at the expense of physical fidelity, focusing on shallow-water effects with limited relevance in deep-water environments and high computational cost. In this work, we shift the focus toward deep-sea physical and sensor realism. We present a physics- and sensor-grounded extension of the Stonefish simulator that augments its hydrodynamic models with stochastic IMU and DVL drift, magnetometer disturbances, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics, pressure-driven environmental variability, and physically based underwater optics. These additions are designed to better capture the forces and measurements shaping the behavior of deep-ocean AUVs, ROVs, landers, ASVs, and gliders, while remaining compatible with real-time simulation. This work advances underwater simulation toward more representative deep-sea operating conditions, which is particularly relevant for long-duration navigation and learning-based autonomy, where inaccurate sensor and environmental models introduce non-physical artifacts and overly optimistic performance. While challenges remain, including complex fluid-structure interactions and full environmental stochasticity, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for navigation, perception, and autonomy research under deep-sea conditions.

AI.tldr: A physics- and sensor-grounded extension of Stonefish enhances deep-sea realism by integrating stochastic sensor models and higher-order hydrodynamics, enabling real-time, more faithful navigation and autonomy research in deep-sea conditions.
AI.motivation: Current underwater simulators prioritize visual realism and shallow-water dynamics, which fail to capture the physics and sensing relevant for deep-sea operations and long-duration autonomy.
AI.method: Augments Stonefish with stochastic IMU/DVL drift, magnetometer disturbances, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics, pressure-driven environmental variability, and physically based underwater optics, while preserving real-time capability.
AI.result: A practical, physics- and sensor-grounded framework that better represents deep-sea forces and measurements, addressing non-physical artifacts and optimistic performance in learning-based autonomy.
AI.conclusion: This framework advances deep-sea underwater simulation for navigation, perception, and autonomy; persistent challenges include complex fluid–structure interactions and full environmental stochasticity, but the approach provides a solid foundation for deep-sea research.

title: Tissue-Mixture Entropy-Weighted Reconstruction for Partial-Volume-Aware Brain MRI Super-Resolution
summary: Full-image objectives in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) super-resolution (SR) can underweight tissue-transition regions affected by the partial-volume effect (PVE), as these regions occupy only a small fraction of the image. Binary boundaries also do not capture the continuous mixture of cerebrospinal fluid, gray matter, and white matter within a voxel. We propose Anatomy-Guided Gaussian-Parameter Warping with PVE-Balanced Reconstruction (AGW-PBR), which combines a low-resolution (LR)-only reconstruction backbone with a training-time objective that emphasizes tissue transitions. The backbone integrates LR-derived Sobel guidance, soft latent-basis assignment, and bounded grid-anchored residual warping. Fixed, quality-controlled tissue fractions derived from registered T1/T2/PD IXI images are converted into tissue-mixture entropy, which defines mean-normalized reconstruction weights within validated PVE support. These sidecars are used only during training, and inference requires only the LR image. AGW-PBR is evaluated on T2-weighted IXI images at 2x, 4x, and 6x using three seeds and subject-level paired analyses. At 4x, test-only SynthSeg masks independently assess reconstruction in tissue-interface and non-interface regions. Targeted ablations examine valid-support supervision, spatially aligned entropy weighting, and soft latent assignment. The AGW-backbone is also trained from scratch on fastMRI at 4x without PVE supervision. AGW-PBR improves full-image reconstruction across the tested IXI scales and regional fidelity at 4x, while the PVE-free backbone retains strong performance on fastMRI. These findings support tissue-mixture entropy weighting for partial-volume-aware brain MRI SR.

AI.tldr: An anatomy-guided, PVE-aware SR framework (AGW-PBR) for brain MRI uses tissue-mixture entropy weights during training with an LR-only backbone, improving full-image reconstruction and tissue-interface fidelity at 4x on IXI; a PVE-free backbone trained on fastMRI also performs well.
AI.motivation: Full-image SR objectives underweight partial-volume and tissue-transition regions; fixed tissue boundaries fail to capture continuous tissue mixtures within voxels, necessitating anatomy-guided, PVE-aware training signals.
AI.method: LR-only reconstruction backbone augmented with training-time sidecars: LR-derived Sobel guidance, soft latent-basis assignment, bounded grid-anchored residual warping; fixed tissue fractions from registered T1/T2/PD IXI into tissue-mixture entropy to define mean-normalized reconstruction weights within validated PVE support; sidecars used only during training; inference uses only LR image.
AI.result: 4x reconstruction shows improvements in full-image quality and tissue-interface fidelity on IXI; SynthSeg masks used to quantify interface vs non-interface regions; ablations highlight importance of valid-support supervision, entropy weighting, and soft latent assignments; the AGW backbone trained on fastMRI without PVE supervision still maintains strong performance.
AI.conclusion: Tissue-mixture entropy weighting enables partial-volume-aware brain MRI SR; the proposed AGW-PBR approach improves interface fidelity while preserving LR-only inference, suggesting broader applicability for PVE-aware SR.

title: Why did My Robot Just Change Personality? Prompting Guidelines for a Grounded Robot Persona in LLM-Based HRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for verbal interaction in social robots, yet prompt design in human-robot interaction (HRI) remains underspecified. As a result, robots may present hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioural boundaries, and misleading personas. This paper develops a framework for prompt design in LLM-based robots and introduces a structured prompt template comprising eight functional components through which robot behaviour can be specified, bounded, and adapted. The framework is grounded in a review of prior LLM-based HRI work and complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts gathered at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). The qualitative findings highlight limited legibility of robot personality, the need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Based on these findings, we present prompting guidelines accompanied by proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid for HRI research. We argue that prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioural assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards to support reliable and interpretable HRI.

AI.tldr: Proposes an eight-component prompt design framework for LLM-based robots, grounded in literature and expert input, to stabilize behavior, improve legibility of robot personality, and address ethics. Provides prompting guidelines and a proof-of-concept template, treating prompt design as a socio-technical problem to enhance reliability and interpretability in HRI.
AI.motivation: To reduce hallucinations, unclear behavioral boundaries, and deceptive personas in LLM-powered social robots by systematizing prompt design; to improve transparency, safety, and governance in HRI.
AI.method: Literature review of prior LLM-based HRI work combined with qualitative data (N=27) from the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025; synthesis into an eight-component structured prompt template; development of guidelines and a proof-of-concept template as a design/reporting aid.
AI.result: A structured eight-component prompt template and accompanying guidelines for HRI research; demonstration via a proof-of-concept template; framework positions prompt design as a socio-technical problem requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent assumptions, and context-aware safeguards.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design is central to reliable, interpretable HRI; explicit governance-like practices and transparent behavioral assumptions are necessary; the framework offers a practical, reportable approach and invites empirical validation and broader adoption in HRI research.

title: Arrive and Survive: Scaling Safe Goal-Conditioned Policy Learning from One-Bit Failure Signals
summary: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) scales effectively in goal-conditioned tasks by casting policy learning into a self-supervised contrastive objective. However, in a failure-terminated Markov decision process, established CRL considers pre-failure future goals only when constructing positive samples, without accounting for the probability mass removed by failure termination. Our theoretical analysis shows that this omission induces a systematic overestimation bias in goal-reaching values. Consequently, near-failure trajectories provide disproportionately strong supervision of success despite retaining little future occupancy. Unsafe actions can thereby be reinforced through catastrophic failure bootstrapping, leading to failed policy learning and unsustainable goal-reaching behaviours. To address this problem, we introduce two minimal yet strong corrections: mass-weighted InfoNCE corrects the overweighting of short surviving futures in critic learning, and a log-survival-mass score restores the missing survival mass in policy optimization. The resulting method, Safe Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (Safe-CRL), requires only the one-bit signal provided by failure termination to scale safe goal-conditioned policy learning. Across twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks, Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and substantially outperforms the Scaling-CRL baseline in goal-reaching performance. Additionally, deep Safe-CRL policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviours. This study completes the CRL theory under failure termination and provides a scalable safe RL framework. The code is available via https://github.com/RomainLITUD/safe-crl.

AI.tldr: Safe-CRL introduces two minimal corrections to counter the bias in contrastive RL under failure termination: mass-weighted InfoNCE and log-survival-mass, yielding safer, more reliable goal-conditioned policies.
AI.motivation: CRL in failure-terminated MDPs ignores the probability mass discarded by termination, causing systematic overestimation of goal-reaching values and unsafe bootstrapping from near-failure trajectories.
AI.method: Two corrections: mass-weighted InfoNCE to account for surviving futures in critic updates; log-survival-mass score to incorporate missing survival mass in policy optimization. Uses a one-bit failure signal and evaluates on twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks; code released.
AI.result: Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and goal-reaching performance, surpassing Scaling-CRL baseline; policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The work completes the CRL theory under failure termination and offers a scalable, safe RL framework for goal-conditioned tasks with minimal signal; code available at the provided repository.

title: Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization for Underwater Sampling
summary: Accurate state estimation for autonomous underwater vehicles performing close-range seafloor sampling remains challenging. In low-altitude operation, down-looking cameras over featureless planar seabeds produce scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy, and inconsistent feature tracking. Meanwhile, inertial-Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) fusion alone provides no mechanism for structural drift correction. We propose a Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that treats physical interaction as an informative geometric constraint within a smoothing-based localization formulation. The method tightly fuses suction-based manipulator contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors. Visual odometry relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors are uncertainty-scaled according to inlier statistics to prevent visually weak frames from destabilizing the estimator, while contact events are modeled as high-confidence factors that induce implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition. Furthermore, the system can fully initialize online during motion. Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulation environments demonstrates that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations. These results highlight the role of embodied physical interaction as a localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments

AI.tldr: Proposes a contact-aided factor-graph localization for AUVs that leverages suction-based contact events as high-confidence constraints within a smoothing-based framework, tightly fusing adaptive visual odometry, learned detections, and on-board sensors to mitigate scale and drift issues in low-altitude, feature-poor seafloor scenarios; enables online initialization and implicit loop closures, showing improved drift and revisit accuracy over baselines in tanks, harbor, and simulation.
AI.motivation: Accurate underwater state estimation at close range is hampered by scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy from down-looking vision on planar seabeds, and lack of drift correction in inertial-DVL fusion.
AI.method: A Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that integrates suction-based manipulator contact events as high-confidence factors with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and onboard sensors inside a smoothing-based SLAM-like graph. VO relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors are uncertainty-scaled by inlier statistics to prevent weak frames from destabilizing the estimate; contact events induce implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition; system can initialize online during motion.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulations shows that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations.
AI.conclusion: Embodied physical interaction serves as a valuable localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments, enabling more robust and drift-resistant localization through contact-informed graph optimization.

title: Hierarchical Channel Stacking: A Structured Decision Framework for AI-Generated Image Detection
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication at ICANN 2026
summary: Many synthetic-image detectors produce accurate predictions but offer limited insight into how those decisions are formed. This paper introduces Hierarchical Channel Stacking (HCS), a compact framework for AI-generated image detection that converts intermediate CNN activations into a structured 60-dimensional representation organized across three progressively deeper backbone stages. HCS uses per-channel Level-1 classifiers and a Level-2 aggregator to produce image-level predictions while preserving explicit hierarchical structure for analysis. On a benchmark spanning GAN and diffusion generators, HCS achieves 86.7% accuracy and 86.7% macro-F1 on the held-out test set. Stage ablation shows that the full three-stage system outperforms reduced single-stage and two-stage variants, indicating that the hierarchy carries complementary predictive information. Stage-level contribution analysis further shows that, in the analyzed detector setting, fake GAN and fake diffusion images exhibit distinct stage-level contribution profiles. These results position HCS not simply as a compact detector, but as a structured framework for studying how synthetic-image detectors assemble evidence across representation levels.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Channel Stacking (HCS) is a compact, interpretable CNN-activation-based detector that decomposes evidence across three backbone stages with per-channel Level-1 classifiers and a Level-2 aggregator, achieving strong GAN/diffusion detection while enabling analysis of hierarchical contribution.
AI.motivation: Restore interpretability and analytical insight in AI-generated image detectors by modeling how evidence accumulates across representation levels, and by distinguishing signal patterns across generator types.
AI.method: Extract intermediate CNN activations into a 60-dim, stage-organized representation; apply per-channel Level-1 classifiers; aggregate with a Level-2 aggregator to generate image-level predictions; evaluate on a GAN+diffusion benchmark; perform stage ablation and stage-level contribution analysis.
AI.result: On held-out test, 86.7% accuracy and 86.7% macro-F1; three-stage system outperforms single- or two-stage variants; stage-level contributions reveal distinct profiles for GAN vs diffusion, supporting hierarchical evidence assembly.
AI.conclusion: HCS provides a compact, structured framework for AI-generated image detection that supports interpretability and analysis of evidence accumulation across representation levels, with potential for broader applicability beyond pure detection.

title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA, 14 pages, 5 figures Dataset: https://vizpi.org/dataset
summary: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

AI.tldr: TutorTrace provides a dataset and pipeline to convert low-level IDE telemetry into actionable behavioral context, enabling adaptive AI tutoring at scale; evaluated in four deployments (N=480) with predictive tasks and a classroom pilot showing faster help-seeking.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between students' observable actions and their help-seeking needs by making behavioral context visible and computable in real time from IDE telemetry, to improve AI tutoring beyond analyzing text-only queries.
AI.method: Collect IDE telemetry across four deployments (N=480), yielding ~180k events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 metrics. Develop a behavioral taxonomy of activity before, between, and across help-seeking moments; build a real-time abstraction pipeline to compute features from raw telemetry; use behavior-informed prompts and evaluate on held-out prediction tasks.
AI.result: Behavior-aware prompts reduced the share of sessions with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7% in a preliminary classroom evaluation. On held-out tasks, AUROC of predicting a forthcoming query within 60 seconds: 0.726; predicting whether an upcoming query reflects guided vs. dependent help-seeking: 0.717.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral context from IDE telemetry enables scalable, adaptive AI tutoring; the TutorTrace dataset and taxonomy provide a foundation for future research and tooling to respond to learners’ actions, not just their words.

title: Activation Outliers Matter: Robust Recovery for Quantized Multimodal LLMs
summary: Low-bit quantization offers a promising avenue for reducing the computational and memory demands of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Recent hardware support for low-precision formats, ranging from MXFP8 to ultra-low-bit formats such as MXFP4 and HiF4, has accelerated research into efficient MLLM training and deployment. In this work, we present a systematic study of these quantization schemes in representative MLLMs that span both video generation and reasoning tasks. Our analysis shows that MXFP8 achieves near-lossless performance, whereas aggressive 4-bit quantization leads to significant degradation. Through extensive ablations, we identify activation quantization as the primary source of this performance loss, contributing substantially more than weight quantization. Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ), a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that supplements the primary ulta-low-bit activation representation with an auxiliary quantized residual pathway. By explicitly modeling and compensating for quantization errors, RFQ improves activation fidelity while preserving the efficiency advantages of ultra-low-bit computation. RFQ requires no architectural modifications and incurs negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL demonstrate that RFQ consistently recovers a substantial portion of the performance lost under the quantization of MXFP4 and HiF4, significantly narrowing the gap to BF16 baselines across both generation and 4 reasoning benchmarks. Our findings establish activation quantization as the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs and highlight residual-based activation reconstruction as an effective and practical strategy for robust 4-bit deployment.

AI.tldr: Activation quantization is the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs; the proposed Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ) recovers much of the lost performance for 4-bit formats without architectural changes, narrowing the gap to BF16 on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL across generation and reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce computation and memory demands of Multimodal LLMs through low-bit quantization (MXFP8, MXFP4, HiF4) enabled by new hardware, and address the substantial performance degradation caused by activation quantization.
AI.method: Introduce RFQ (Residual Fallback Quantization): a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that adds a quantized residual activation pathway to the primary ultra-low-bit activation representation. No architectural changes and negligible overhead.
AI.result: RFQ consistently recovers a substantial portion of the performance loss observed under MXFP4 and HiF4. It narrows the gap to BF16 baselines on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL across both generation and 4 reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation quantization is the primary bottleneck and that residual-based reconstruction is effective.
AI.conclusion: Activation quantization is the main bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs; residual-based activation reconstruction (RFQ) is a practical, low-overhead strategy to robustly deploy 4-bit models with substantial performance recovery.

title: 4DSynth: Controllable Procedural World Synthesis for Dynamic Embodied Simulation
summary:
Embodied agents need environments that are visually diverse, physically interactive, and changing over time. Procedural simulators can generate large interactive scene collections, and recent 4D generators produce compelling visual dynamics. Combining these properties in one environment, however, still demands extensive manual effort, and the result is rarely editable or controllable enough to reuse at scale.
  We present 4DSynth, a controllable procedural system that turns a natural-language description, a blueprint mask, or a single photograph into an editable 4D environment with explicit geometry, animated actors, collision-free trajectories, and physics-ready simulation state. Multiple scene routes share one geometry-grounded representation, so the same pipeline handles animation, camera planning, rendering, and task generation.
  To validate the full pipeline, we construct 4DSynth-Nav, an interactive navigation benchmark generated entirely from 4DSynth's procedural scenes. Two vision-language models evaluated across three difficulty tiers both fail the majority of tasks and stall after early subtasks. The same procedural controllability that produces these environments also makes each failure reproducible and each difficulty axis independently tunable. This paper presents both a controllable generation pipeline and the scalable benchmark it enables, offering a practical foundation for developing and evaluating embodied agents.

AI.tldr: 4DSynth is a controllable procedural system that converts natural-language descriptions, blueprint masks, or a single photograph into editable 4D environments with explicit geometry, animated actors, collision-free trajectories, and physics-ready state; it also introduces 4DSynth-Nav, a navigation benchmark derived from procedural scenes, and shows current vision-language models struggle on its tasks with reproducible, tunable difficulty.
AI.motivation: There is a need for large, visually diverse, physically interactive, time-evolving environments that are editable and reusable at scale for embodied AI research; existing procedural or 4D generators lack integrated controllability and scalability.
AI.method: A controllable procedural pipeline that outputs a single geometry-grounded representation used across animation, camera planning, rendering, and task generation. Inputs can be a natural-language description, a blueprint mask, or a single photograph. The system yields explicit geometry, animated actors, collision-free trajectories, and physics-ready simulation state, enabling end-to-end generation of 4D scenes. The same representation supports multiple scene routes (animation, camera planning, rendering, task generation) and is used to build 4DSynth-Nav, a benchmark for interactive navigation.
AI.result: Validation of the full pipeline through 4DSynth-Nav: two vision-language models across three difficulty tiers fail the majority of tasks and stall on early subtasks. The controllability of the pipeline ensures failures are reproducible and that each difficulty axis is independently tunable, demonstrating a practical foundation for scalable, editable 4D environments and embodied-agent evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a controllable generation pipeline and a scalable embodied-navigation benchmark, providing a practical foundation for developing and evaluating embodied agents in editable, 4D environments.

title: CoGeo-GS: Concept-Driven and Geometry-Aware Multi-Object Removal in 3D Scenes
summary: Multi-object removal in 3D scenes is challenging due to severe occlusions, semantic entanglement, and the difficulty of maintaining geometric and multi-view consistency. Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods perform well for single-object editing but scale poorly to multi-object scenarios, often requiring repetitive optimization and yielding unstable geometry in removed regions. We propose CoGeo-GS, a concept-driven framework for controllable multi-object removal in 3D scenes. CoGeo-GS assigns concept-aware semantic tags to Gaussians, enabling flexible object selection and reducing interference between foreground objects and background structures within a single optimization stage. To recover plausible geometry, we introduce a geometry-aware completion pipeline that combines monocular depth priors with diffusion-based refinement and boundary-aligned blending. A geometry-regularized refinement strategy further stabilizes reconstruction and preserves multi-view consistency. Experiments demonstrate that CoGeo-GS outperforms existing methods in visual quality and reconstruction fidelity.

AI.tldr: CoGeo-GS introduces a concept-driven, geometry-aware pipeline for controllable multi-object removal in 3D scenes using Gaussian Splatting, featuring concept-tagged Gaussians, depth-guided completion with diffusion refinement, and geometry-regularized refinement to preserve multi-view consistency, achieving improved visual quality and fidelity over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of removing multiple objects in 3D scenes with severe occlusions and semantic entanglement, where existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods struggle with scalability, unstable geometry, and multi-object interference, necessitating a single-stage, controllable, and geometry-consistent solution.
AI.method: 1) Assign concept-aware semantic tags to Gaussians to enable flexible, interference-resistant object selection within a single optimization stage. 2) Introduce a geometry-aware completion pipeline that fuses monocular depth priors with diffusion-based refinement and boundary-aligned blending to recover plausible geometry. 3) Apply a geometry-regularized refinement strategy to stabilize reconstruction and maintain multi-view consistency.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate that CoGeo-GS outperforms existing methods in visual quality and reconstruction fidelity for multi-object removal in 3D scenes.
AI.conclusion: CoGeo-GS provides a scalable, controllable solution for multi-object removal in 3D scenes, achieving higher visual quality and reconstruction fidelity through concept-driven segmentation of Gaussians, geometry-aware completion, and geometry-regularized refinement.

title: Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA
summary: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N = 16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

AI.tldr: SecondVoice is a mixed-reality proxy system that lets people voice hesitant points by separating content from speaker, using a private intent specification and reformulating it for the proxy. In a within-subject study (N=16) it increases use of hesitant points compared with an anonymous text-board and fosters multi-turn engagement, though it raises tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.
AI.motivation: To improve equal participation in co-located discussions by enabling hesitant contributions without exposing speakers to negative interpersonal or professional consequences.
AI.method: Design and evaluation of SecondVoice: an embodied virtual proxy in mixed reality. Users specify intent via a private overlay (structured spec), the system reformulates the input and voices it through the proxy. A within-subject study (N=16) compares SecondVoice to an anonymous text-board across two group tasks.
AI.result: Half of participants used SecondVoice for a point they would not say aloud, vs 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and spurred multi-turn engagement not observed with text-board posts. Participants cited situational value and tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.
AI.conclusion: SecondVoice demonstrates potential to expand participation channels under social risk, enabling hesitant points to enter the spoken discussion. However, it introduces ownership and trust concerns and requires careful design considerations; results are preliminary due to small sample size and limited tasks.

title: J-Zero: Unified Challenger--Solver--Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
summary: Self-evolving language models have recently emerged as a promising path toward superintelligence, with the advantage of reducing the cost of human supervision. While considerable progress has been made in verifiable domains, self-evolution in unverifiable domains remains substantially less explored. We propose Judge co-adaptation from Zero data (J-Zero), a unified Challenger--Solver--Judge co-evolution framework that supports self-improvement across both domains. The Challenger and Solver co-evolve through an adversarial interaction: the Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, while the Solver learns to produce higher-quality responses to them. In parallel, the Judge co-adapts using preference pairs whose ordering is known in advance from how each response was produced, i.e., the Solver's answer over the Challenger's, and its decomposed-and-recombined answer over its one-shot answer, rather than from the Judge's own scores. J-Zero outperforms the baselines by an average of 4.2 points on verifiable and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains, and continues to improve through at least ten iterations, whereas the baselines degrade after two.

AI.tldr: A unified Challenger–Solver–Judge co-evolution framework (J-Zero) enables self-improvement in both verifiable and unverifiable domains by having the Challenger and Solver co-evolve adversarially, while the Judge learns from known preference pairs derived from the generation process. It achieves consistent improvement beyond baselines over multiple iterations.
AI.motivation: To enable self-improvement of language models with reduced human supervision, extending beyond verifiable tasks to unverifiable ones, addressing a key bottleneck in scalable alignment.
AI.method: Iterative, three-player co-evolution: Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks; Solver produces higher-quality responses; Judge adapts using pre-known preference ordering from how responses were produced (Solver vs Challenger, and decomposed/recombined answers vs one-shot). The system runs for at least ten iterations, measuring progress against baselines.
AI.result: J-Zero outperforms baselines by 4.2 points on verifiable domains and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains; improvement persists across at least ten iterations, while baselines degrade after two iterations.
AI.conclusion: A robust self-improvement framework that leverages interdependent co-adaptation among Challenger, Solver, and Judge, reducing reliance on external supervision and extending effective self-improvement to unverifiable tasks.

title: Arbitrary-Order Hermite Interpolation of Rigid-Motion Jets via Hyper-Multidual Quaternions
summary: We study bilateral interpolation of finite-order rigid-motion jets represented by unit dual quaternions. An order-$n$ multidual (MD) algebra is the truncated polynomial algebra $\mathbb{R}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{n+1})$; hyper-multidual (HMD) quaternions are dual quaternions with coefficients in this algebra. Temporal HMD transforms encode a pose and its derivatives, whereas a generic HMD curve need not be the temporal jet of its pose projection; we call this requirement holonomicity. We show that a temporal transform and its relative descriptor are unitary and derive recursive coefficient constraints, together with a local realizability converse in an admissible logarithm chart. We then extend screw linear interpolation (ScLERP) algebraically to unit HMD quaternions. Although it matches complete endpoint transforms, direct HMD--ScLERP is generically non-holonomic for arbitrary endpoint jets. We give a coefficient criterion and explicit endpoint and first-order interior contact defects. A holonomic alternative is obtained by mapping endpoint transforms to logarithmic dual-quaternion coordinates, applying the degree-$(2n+1)$ Hermite polynomial that matches derivatives through order $n$, and lifting by the exponential. HMD arithmetic also recovers higher-order rigid-motion acceleration fields without explicit differentiation of $\mathrm{dexp}$. Rotation and full $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ tests through second order, with an additional third-order polynomial check, reproduce the stated defects and endpoint jets.

AI.tldr: A higher-order rigid-motion interpolation framework using unit hyper-multi-dual quaternions (HMD) with MD algebras; demonstrates holonomicity issues in direct HMD-ScLERP and proposes a holonomic alternative via logarithmic coordinates and Hermite polynomials; validated by SE(3) tests up to second/third order.
AI.motivation: Provide a framework for accurate, high-order interpolation of rigid-body motions (poses and derivatives) using quaternionic representations, addressing holonomicity and extend ScLERP to higher orders.
AI.method: Define multidual algebra, unit HMD quaternions; derive unitary constraints and coefficient recursions; local realizability in logarithm chart; extend ScLERP; analyze holonomicity; propose holonomic coordinates with Hermite degree 2n+1; lift via exponential; test through SE(3) with polynomial checks.
AI.result: Identified that direct HMD-ScLERP is generally non-holonomic for arbitrary endpoint jets; provided coefficient criteria and defects; proposed holonomic alternative that matches derivatives up to order n; HMD arithmetic recovers higher-order acceleration without dexp; empirical tests confirm the endpoint jets and defects.
AI.conclusion: Holonomic interpolation of finite-order rigid-motion jets via HMDs is feasible with logarithmic coordinates and Hermite polynomials; direct extension of ScLERP is insufficient for holonomy; the framework yields accurate higher-order pose derivatives and acceleration fields while maintaining unit dual-quaternion representations.

title: PailitaoGR: Latent Think-with-Images for Generative Image Retrieval
summary:
Generative retrieval has demonstrated strong performance by directly generating product semantic identifiers (SIDs).
  Extending this paradigm to image search, however, is nontrivial because real-world query images contain diverse information, including the search target, useful auxiliary evidence, and irrelevant visual content.
  This requires the model to identify and focus on the search target while selectively utilizing auxiliary evidence. In this paper, we propose \textbf{PailitaoGR}, a \emph{Latent Think-with-Images} method for generative image retrieval, which internalizes target-focused perception and selective auxiliary-evidence utilization into a the generative retrieval model, enabling \textit{Zooming without Cropping} and \textit{Reading without OCR}. Specifically, we design a target-focused perception mechanism that identifies and enhances visual tokens of the search target, consisting of a target Enhancer and a learning strategy based on on-policy distillation and attention guidance loss, enabling the model to focus on search-target regions. We also design a selective auxiliary-evidence utilization mechanism that identifies and enhances visual tokens of auxiliary evidence, including an auxiliary enhancer and an in-capacity incremental contrastive distillation strategy, enabling the model to exploit auxiliary evidence. We construct training and validation sets sampled from real-world online image-search logs. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing baselines by an average of 13.8\%, validating its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Introduces PailitaoGR for generative image retrieval that jointly learns target-focused perception and selective auxiliary-evidence use, via target and auxiliary enhancers with specialized distillation losses; enables zooming without cropping and reading without OCR; validated on real-world search logs with +13.8% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the complexity of real-world query images in generative retrieval by isolating the search target and effectively leveraging auxiliary evidence without cropping or OCR, extending SID-based retrieval to image search.
AI.method: Proposes a Latent Think-with-Images framework (PailitaoGR) with two components: a target-focused perception mechanism (target Enhancer + on-policy distillation + attention guidance loss) to highlight search-target regions; and a selective auxiliary-evidence mechanism (auxiliary enhancer + in-capacity incremental contrastive distillation) to exploit auxiliary evidence. Training/validation sets are drawn from real-world online image-search logs.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows PailitaoGR outperforms existing baselines by an average of 13.8% across experiments.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully internalizes target-focused perception and selective auxiliary-evidence utilization within a generative retrieval model for image search, yielding notable performance gains on real-world data.

title: Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to inform safety decisions in cities, such as where it is safe to walk, rent, or travel. We ask whether such judgments track measured risk or the patterns attached to an urban neighborhood's name. We probe seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography: coordinates-only, name-only, and name+coordinates, across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and American Community Survey data. First, ratings are nearly flat under coordinates for six of seven models, while names carry most between neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only at frontier scale does the coordinate channel show appreciable variation. Second, names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group (percent Black in Chicago, percent Hispanic in Los Angeles), and this name effect tracks demographic share in all seven models and both cities. In Los Angeles, where demographic share and crime are more separable, the effect survives controls for crime and income and is confirmed by crime-matched pairs. An enforcement-elasticity analysis further shows that over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary, deployment-driven offenses. Third, the effect scales with geographic knowledge: models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotype to them. Because neighborhood names carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, removing names reduces both bias and accuracy. We discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support settings.

AI.tldr: LLMs' safety judgments about urban neighborhoods encode demographic-name stereotypes; coordinates carry little risk signal; removing names reduces bias and accuracy; greater geographic knowledge amplifies stereotypes; implications for deploying LLMs in safety guidance.
AI.motivation: To disentangle whether LLM-based safety judgments reflect real risk or neighborhood-name stereotypes across multiple cities and models.
AI.method: Evaluate seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions (coordinates-only, name-only, name+coordinates) across 186 LA/Chicago neighborhoods; link to violent crime and ACS data; perform analyses including enforcement elasticity and crime-matched pairs; assess effects of demographic composition and geographic knowledge.
AI.result: Names drive most variation; coordinate signal emerges only at frontier scale; name effects correlate with local demographic shares; effects persist controlling for crime/income; verified by crime-matched pairs; enforcement-elasticity shows over-caution tracks near fully reported homicide; higher geographic knowledge amplifies demographic stereotype; removing names reduces both bias and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Neighborhood naming conveys real signal and stereotype; cautious deployment needed; removing names reduces bias but also reduces accuracy; model design should balance fairness and utility; implications for decision-support in urban safety contexts.

title: GRAS: Guided Reduced-Variance Proposals and Adaptive Selection for Training-Free Reward Alignment in Discrete Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion models have become a strong, widely adopted class of generators for sequence data, and steering them toward a downstream reward at inference time, without any retraining, is increasingly important. Such training-free steering is done by gradient guidance, by search, or by combining the two. We study the combined regime and identify two weaknesses in how it is usually run: the guided proposal estimates its gradient from a single noisy sample, and the search then resamples particles at a fixed temperature that ignores how rewards spread across each denoising step. We address both with a small set of changes that add no denoiser cost. For the proposal, we lower the estimator variance with a Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and a leave-one-out baseline for non-differentiable ones; for the search, we standardize the per-step values into a group-relative advantage and prove it collapses to a single active ingredient, an adaptive resampling temperature. We call the resulting method Guided Reduced-variance proposals and Adaptive Selection (GRAS). GRAS is simple yet effective: across regulatory DNA and protein design it attains the best training-free reward, outperforming prior training-free methods and matching or surpassing a reward-fine-tuned model, and it remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.

AI.tldr: GRAS improves training-free steering of discrete diffusion models by variance reduction in proposal gradients and adaptive per-step resampling in search, yielding state-of-the-art results in regulatory DNA/protein design without retraining.
AI.motivation: Identify and fix two common weaknesses in combined gradient-guided and search-based inference for discrete diffusion models: high estimator variance from single noisy samples and fixed-temperature resampling that ignores how rewards distribute across denoising steps.
AI.method: Proposal: reduce gradient estimator variance via Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and a leave-one-out baseline for non-differentiable rewards. Search: normalize per-step values into a group-relative advantage and use an adaptive resampling temperature; prove it collapses to a single active ingredient. No denoiser cost added.
AI.result: Across regulatory DNA and protein design, GRAS achieves the best training-free reward, outperforms prior training-free methods, and matches or surpasses reward-fine-tuned models; remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.
AI.conclusion: GRAS is a simple, effective training-free steering method for discrete diffusion models, offering variance reduction and adaptive resampling that improve reward optimization without extra cost and with broad applicability.

title: Riemann-1.0: An Embodied World Action Model for Physical AI
summary: We introduce Riemann-1.0, a fully causal autoregressive World Action Model for embodied intelligence. Riemann-1.0 jointly models multi-view visual observations, robot states, and embodiment-specific actions within a unified causal autoregressive sequence, representing robot actions and world evolution as causal state transitions. Unlike existing WAMs based on joint generation, video-first prediction, or decoupled modeling paradigms, Riemann-1.0 unifies online robot policy execution and action-conditioned world simulation within a single model, enabling it to function as both an executable robot policy and a multi-embodiment visual world simulator. To scale embodied experience across heterogeneous data sources, we further develop a progressive embodied pretraining framework that unifies learning from egocentric human videos, handheld-gripper demonstrations, and heterogeneous robot trajectories under a shared World Action Modeling objective. Built upon 200K+ hours of interaction data, Riemann-1.0 progressively transfers large-scale embodied experience into executable robot manipulation capabilities. Riemann-1.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance across both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. It achieves success rates of 94.3% on RoboTwin2.0, 99.0% on LIBERO, and 62.6% on the long-horizon compositional benchmark RoboCasa-365, outperforming the previous best method by 8.4% On long-horizon real-world manipulation tasks, Riemann-1.0 achieves a Success Rate (SR) of 85.0% and a Progress Success Rate (PSR) of 94.4%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 15% in SR. These results demonstrate that unified World Action Modeling together with progressive embodied pretraining effectively transforms large-scale embodied experience into generalizable robot manipulation capabilities.

AI.tldr: Riemann-1.0 introduces a fully causal autoregressive World Action Model that unifies robot policy execution with an embodied world simulator and scales via progressive embodied pretraining from diverse data; it achieves state-of-the-art on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Current WAMs suffer from joint generation, video-first prediction, or decoupled modeling, which hinder cross-domain generalization and policy execution. A single unified model can both act as a robot policy and a world simulator, leveraging diverse embodied data to generalize.
AI.method: A causal autoregressive model that jointly predicts multi-view visual observations, robot states, and actions as unified state transitions; uses World Action Modeling objective; progressive embodied pretraining that fuses egocentric videos, handheld demonstrations, and robot trajectories; trained on 200k+ hours of data.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on RoboTwin2.0 (94.3%), LIBERO (99.0%), RoboCasa-365 long-horizon (62.6%); long-horizon real-world SR 85.0%, PSR 94.4%; outperforms baselines by 8.4% SR on RoboCasa-365 and by 15% SR on open-source baselines; demonstrates effective transfer of large-scale embodied experience.
AI.conclusion: Unified World Action Modeling with progressive embodied pretraining effectively turns large-scale embodied data into generalizable manipulation capabilities, enabling a single model to act as both policy and world simulator.

title: Hull First, Wake Second: Wake-Reliance Suppression for Robust Maritime Vessel Detection
