comment: Accepted by ICIG 2026 (The 14th International Conference on Image and Graphics)
summary: Maritime vessel detectors often face scenes where hulls are small, low-contrast, or blurred, while wakes are longer and easier to detect. This creates a wake-reliance problem: detectors may miss slow or stationary vessels with weak wakes, or produce false positives on wake-like water clutter. We propose HullWake, a hull-first wake-second framework for robust maritime vessel detection. HullWake separates proposal-centered hull evidence from directional wake context, extracts wake cues with bidirectional proposal-anchored corridors, and suppresses wake-dominant predictions through wake response supervision, wake-attenuated consistency, wake-only confidence suppression, and hull--wake decorrelation. We also introduce a wake-oriented evaluation protocol covering weak/no-wake vessels, wake-like hard negatives, worst-group AP, and confidence drop after wake attenuation. Experiments are conducted on Curated-Wake, a wake-oriented maritime dataset of about 10,000 images curated from Ships/Vessels in Aerial Images, the SMD benchmark, and SeaDronesSee, with newly added detection- and segmentation-level wake annotations. Compared with box-only detectors and mask-supervised segmentation baselines, HullWake improves overall AP, weak/no-wake robustness, wake-like false positives, worst-group AP, and confidence stability after wake attenuation.

AI.tldr: HullWake is a hull-first, wake-second framework that decouples hull evidence from wake context to robustly detect maritime vessels, addressing wake-reliance, and evaluated with wake-oriented metrics and new annotations.
AI.motivation: Maritime detectors struggle with small, low-contrast, or blurred hulls while wakes are more detectable; this leads to missed vessels and wake-like false positives. A hull-centric approach can improve robustness to weak/no-wake scenarios.
AI.method: HullWake separates hull evidence from wake context, uses bidirectional proposal-anchored corridors to extract wake cues, and applies wake-focused supervision and decorrelation techniques (wake response supervision, wake-attenuated consistency, wake-only confidence suppression, hull–wake decorrelation). It also introduces a wake-oriented evaluation protocol and new wake annotations across multiple datasets (Curated-Wake, Ships/Vessels in Aerial Images, SMD, SeaDronesSee).
AI.result: Compared with box-only detectors and segmentation baselines, HullWake improves overall AP, weak/no-wake robustness, wake-like false positives, worst-group AP, and confidence stability after wake attenuation.
AI.conclusion: A hull-first, wake-second design mitigates wake-dominant predictions, yielding more robust maritime vessel detection across varied wake conditions and enabling a wake-centric evaluation framework.

title: Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using agents fail two ways: choosing the wrong tool, or forming wrong arguments, and an early failure of either kind can silently corrupt everything downstream. We measure a correct-invocation rate that separates the two, under both a clean teacher-forced context and the model's own free-running context, on five open-weight models over contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's own clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Our central finding concerns the measurement itself. Under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, a propagation model's severity and recovery parameters are not merely hard to estimate - they are fixed by the scoring rule. Severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct); recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps returned on-track, against an expected 0.0058 by chance). Both follow from one mechanism: post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool constants the model never sees, so it is information the model cannot derive. A fit run anyway returns 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000 - confident numbers for a parameter the scoring rule already determined. We give the mechanism and a remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero additional cost, which un-pins severity to interior estimates excluding zero (+0.149, +0.316).

AI.tldr: Exact-match scoring in tool-use evaluation can mask the propagation of early tool-use and argumentation errors, showing spurious severity/recovery estimates; a conditional-on-state scoring remedy reveals interior severity and can be applied at zero cost to cached outputs.
AI.motivation: Understand how early mistakes in tool-use tasks propagate downstream and how scoring rules bias measurements; propose a remedy that decouples observed metrics from a fixed gold trajectory.
AI.method: Empirical study across five open-weight models on contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1–8), comparing clean teacher-forced vs self-generated contexts. Measure correct-invocation rate to separate wrong-tool vs wrong-argument errors. Analyze severity and recovery parameters, their observability under exact-match scoring, and the effect of post-divergence gold values. Apply conditional-on-state scoring retrospectively to cached completions at zero cost.
AI.result: By depth 6, roughly 0.686 and 0.684 of a model’s clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes. Under exact-match scoring, the severity parameter is forced to a boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct) and the recovery parameter becomes structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps on track). The mechanism is that post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool-constants the model never sees, making it unattainable. A separate fit yields 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000, illustrating spurious precision. The remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions, un-pins severity to interior estimates, yielding +0.149 and +0.316.
AI.conclusion: Scoring artifacts can severely distort measured tool-use reliability; conditional-on-state scoring provides a plausible remedy by biasing estimates away from hard-zero/1 bounds and can be applied post hoc to existing data without cost.

title: SimCast-S2S: An Efficient Generative Model for Subseasonal Precipitation Forecasting via Transfer Learning from Climate Simulations
summary: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) precipitation forecasting has substantial financial and societal impact, yet remains challenging because of weak predictive signals, high associated uncertainty, and the computational cost of operational systems, which constrains simulation fidelity. We introduce SimCast-S2S, a generative latent-diffusion framework for probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting that addresses three major bottlenecks in data-driven prediction. First, because S2S prediction requires uncertainty quantification rather than only deterministic point forecasts, SimCast-S2S is the first data-driven system that uses a diffusion-based generative pipeline for S2S prediction, enabling effective sampling from the underlying conditional distribution. Second, since generating large probabilistic ensembles is computationally costly in physical space, SimCast-S2S instead operates in a compact latent space learned by variational autoencoders, enabling efficient large-ensemble generation. Third, diffusion models typically require large training datasets; SimCast-S2S overcomes this via transfer learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), pretraining on large ensembles of climate simulations before fine-tuning on limited reanalysis data. On reanalysis data, SimCast-S2S outperforms deep learning baselines, including convolutional neural networks and U-Net architectures. Notably, despite using only a subset of atmospheric input variables and no post-processing, bias correction, or calibration, SimCast-S2S remains competitive with, and in many cases outperforms, state-of-the-art operational systems such as the ECMWF-S2S baseline. These results indicate that latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning offers an efficient and scalable path toward data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based latent generative model, SimCast-S2S, enables probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting via latent-space diffusion, VAEs, and LoRA transfer learning, achieving strong probabilistic forecasts with large ensembles and data efficiency, outperforming DL baselines and rivaling ECMWF-S2S without extra post-processing.
AI.motivation: Address the need for uncertainty-aware S2S forecasts under weak predictive signals, high forecast uncertainty, and computational constraints that limit simulation fidelity.
AI.method: Use a diffusion-based generative pipeline operating in a compact latent space learned by variational autoencoders; generate large probabilistic ensembles efficiently; employ transfer learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) pretrained on large climate ensembles and fine-tuned on limited reanalysis data.
AI.result: On reanalysis data, SimCast-S2S outperforms deep learning baselines (CNNs, U-Net) and is competitive with, and often superior to, the ECMWF-S2S baseline, even with a subset of inputs and no post-processing.
AI.conclusion: Latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning offers an efficient and scalable path toward data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting.

title: GRAFT: Grounded and Efficient Online Reinforcement Adaptation for Fine-Grained Robot Manipulation
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide strong priors for robot manipulation, yet adapting them online to fine-grained biomedical tasks remains challenging. Task success often hinges on subtle, view-dependent visual cues, while task-level rewards provide little guidance about which regions matter, making it difficult to learn task-relevant visual grounding from limited real-robot interaction. Online adaptation is further constrained by the computational cost of VLA inference and replay-based updates. We introduce GRAFT (Grounded Reinforcement Adaptation for Fast Task Learning), a framework for efficient online VLA adaptation through grounded perception. GRAFT uses region-level supervision to learn view-specific visual anchors that focus perception on task-relevant local cues without requiring region proposals at deployment. It further combines single-step action generation with cached visual-language prefix reuse to accelerate online learning. Across four biomedical manipulation tasks, GRAFT improves success rates by 25 percentage points under matched adaptation budgets, while reducing the computational overhead of online policy updates.

AI.tldr: GRAFT enables fast online adaptation of vision-language-action policies for biomedical manipulation by grounding perception to region-specific cues and reusing VLA prefixes, improving success by ~25 percentage points with lower online compute.
AI.motivation: Adapt pretrained VLA policies to fine-grained biomedical tasks where subtle view-dependent cues and sparse rewards hinder learning from limited real-robot data; online adaptation is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Region-level supervision to learn view-specific visual anchors without deployment-time region proposals; single-step action generation; cached visual-language prefix reuse to accelerate online learning.
AI.result: Across four biomedical manipulation tasks, GRAFT achieves a 25 percentage-point improvement in success under matched adaptation budgets and reduces the computational overhead of online policy updates.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT demonstrates efficient, grounded online adaptation for VLA policies, improving task success while lowering compute; effective for fine-grained manipulation with limited data.

title: RECAP-Forcing: Retaining Content Appearances for Long Video Generation
summary: Long autoregressive video generation faces a fundamental memory challenge: with a finite attention window, a model must decide which information from an ever-expanding history to retain. Existing methods organize memory temporally, preserving recent frames while compressing or discarding older ones. We instead propose RECAP-Forcing, organizing memory by appearance novelty. A long video is not merely a sequence of frames, but an evolving cast of subjects, objects, and scenes whose identities must remain consistent over time. We organize memory by retaining the KV cache associated with newly appearing content--such as entering subjects, disoccluded regions, and newly introduced scenes--at the moment it first becomes visible, prioritizing novelty over recency. Memory should scale with the amount of newly introduced content, rather than with video length. This appearance-indexed memory makes long-range consistency an explicit property of the memory structure. Our framework unifies two mechanisms under this single principle. At the beginning of a video, when all visible content is novel, an attention sink preserves the initial scene. As the video evolves, an optical-flow-based novelty bank extends the same principle by selectively retaining newly revealed content. As a training-free inference method with no additional learnable parameters, RECAP-Forcing consistently improves visual quality and semantic fidelity across multiple strong baselines and outperforms existing memory methods.

AI.tldr: RECAP-Forcing proposes appearance-novelty memory for long AR video generation, storing KV caches of newly appearing content rather than sliding window-based recency; training-free and improves quality across baselines.
AI.motivation: Finite attention window makes long video generation challenging; existing memory schemes rely on temporal recency and compression; need explicit long-range consistency tied to appearance changes.
AI.method: Organize memory by appearance novelty; retain KV cache for newly appearing content at first visibility; attention sink preserves initial scene at video start; optical-flow-based novelty bank retains newly revealed content; no learnable parameters;Inference-time only.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in visual quality and semantic fidelity across baselines; outperforms existing memory methods.
AI.conclusion: Appearance-indexed memory enables explicit long-range consistency; unifies two mechanisms; scalable memory tied to content novelty rather than video length; training-free method.

title: Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models
summary: World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at https://wzm206.github.io/latent-world-model-nav.

AI.tldr: Latent World Model (LWM) predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility for robot navigation, avoiding observation reconstruction; supports counterfactual training, unlabeled video supervision, and RL within the world model; shows strong gains on real-world navigation datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing world models primarily reconstruct future observations, adding unnecessary complexity and not directly aiding decision making. A latent-space compatibility view leverages spatial proximity as a proxy for feature similarity, enabling evaluation of action consequences directly in latent space; facilitates counterfactual training and annotation-free RL.
AI.method: Propose a compatibility-prediction latent world model that predicts which action-conditioned latent features are compatible with progress toward the goal. It relies on spatial proximity as a proxy for feature similarity, evaluating action consequences directly in latent space. For counterfactual training, it samples action sequences across trajectories to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. The learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and enable reinforcement learning entirely within the world model, removing the need for action annotations and extra environment interaction.
AI.result: Outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance on multiple robot navigation datasets; code, pretrained models, and materials provided.
AI.conclusion: An imagination-driven latent-world model can substitute observation-reconstruction approaches for decision making, enabling counterfactual training and action-annotation-free RL within the world model, improving sample efficiency and real-world navigation performance.

title: Technical Comparative Benchmarking Study: Advanced AI Hybrid Methods for Renewable Energy Farm Optimization and Forecasting
summary: This study provides a comprehensive benchmarking of conventional machine learning (ML), ensemble learning, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph based models, and hybrid ensemble deep learning approaches under complementary renewable energy scenarios. Three datasets are considered: a large scale WEC dataset, a 16 WEC dataset, and operational 10 min SCADA measurements at the Penmanshiel wind farm. For structured WEC layout data, tree ensembles exhibited a clear advantage over conventional ML and neural predictors because randomized partitioning and boosting efficiently captured nonlinear layout power interactions without requiring explicit feature representation learning. The Extra Trees was the strongest model, achieving considerable results. Relative to the MLP baseline, this corresponds to an approximately 63.7% reduction in MAE, demonstrating the suitability of randomized tree ensembles for high dimensional structured WEC data. Also, STGCN reduced the MAE to approximately 167.0 kW and achieved R = 0.93 by explicitly learning spatial and temporal turbine interactions. The best overall forecasting accuracy was obtained by the RF BiLSTM hybrid, with an MAE=150.5 kW. Compared with standalone LSTM, this represents an approximately 75% reduction in MAE, while improving on STGCN by approximately 10.0%. Finally, the experiments reveal that no single AI architecture is universally optimal: randomized and boosted ensembles are particularly effective for structured WEC surrogate modeling, graph networks become advantageous when explicit spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble recurrent hybrids provide the strongest balance when nonlinear tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist.

AI.tldr: Benchmark across ML, ensemble, deep, recurrent, Transformer, graph, and hybrid models for renewable energy surrogate modeling using WEC datasets and SCADA; no single architecture dominates. Randomized tree ensembles excel on structured data; graph nets help when spatial interactions dominate; RF-BiLSTM hybrid offers best overall MAE.
AI.motivation: Assess the relative performance of a wide range of AI architectures on diverse WEC-related datasets to identify effective modeling strategies for structured, spatial, and temporal dependencies in renewable energy forecasting.
AI.method: Evaluate conventional ML, ensemble methods, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph-based models, and hybrid ensemble approaches on three datasets: a large-scale WEC dataset, a 16-WEC dataset, and 10-minute SCADA data from Penmanshiel wind farm. Use MAE and R metrics to compare models such as Extra Trees, Random Forests, STGCN, RF-BiLSTM, and LSTM baselines.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Tree ensembles (especially Extra Trees) outperform conventional ML and neural predictors on structured WEC data, achieving ~63.7% MAE reduction vs MLP baseline. (2) STGCN attains MAE ≈ 167.0 kW with R ≈ 0.93 by learning spatial-temporal turbine interactions. (3) RF-BiLSTM hybrid yields best overall forecasting with MAE = 150.5 kW, about a 75% reduction vs standalone LSTM and ~10% better than STGCN. (4) No single architecture is universally optimal: ensembles excel on structured data, graph networks shine when explicit spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble recurrent hybrids balance nonlinear tabular and temporal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Recommendations: use randomized boosted ensembles for high-dimensional structured WEC data; deploy graph networks when explicit spatial interactions are crucial; prefer ensemble recurrent hybrids when nonlinear tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist. Model choice should be guided by data characteristics (structure, spatial coupling, and temporal dependencies).

title: Pass the Bucket: Efficient, Robust, Local Load Balancing for Teams of Heterogeneous Robots
comment: This paper was submitted to IROS 2026 on March 2nd and accepted on June 17th
summary: We study the problem of decentralized, self-organized task sharing for a swarm of heterogeneous robots that collaborate in transportation or other objectives that require coordinated motion planning. To this end, we present theoretical and practical results for the simple but effective mechanism of \emph{bucket brigades} for load balancing, in which a team of heterogenous robots share a spatial task in a confined, one-dimensional space, while only being able to sense collisions with neighbors or walls. The goal is to optimize throughput of the overall system, without central control or information, aiming at an interval partition proportional to robot velocities. We address possible chaotic system behavior by developing a stabilization mechanism based on simple local aid, a ``token'', that temporarily decelerates robots after an encounter. This purely local change eliminates persistent oscillations, resulting in convergence towards a stable system state. We accelerate system convergence by comparing a single boundary token to ubiquitous two-directional tokens and optimizing the deceleration factor. Event-driven simulations report convergence times and robustness: For a large variety of perturbations (such as robot deletion, position or velocity jittering), the system reliably re-converges. The results suggest a local, practical mechanism for robust load balancing for heterogeneous teams of robots that promises an effective tool as basis for more complex scenarios.

AI.tldr: Decentralized, self-organized load balancing for a heterogeneous robot swarm in a 1D setting using bucket brigades, stabilized by local token-based deceleration to suppress oscillations; shows convergence and robustness; two-directional tokens outperform a single boundary token in accelerating convergence; no central control required.
AI.motivation: Address scalable, robust coordination of heterogeneous robots performing shared spatial tasks in constrained environments, without central control; aim to maximize throughput by partitioning the interval proportional to robot velocities.
AI.method: Employ bucket brigades for 1D spatial task sharing, with robots only sensing collisions with neighbors or walls. Partition the interval proportional to robot velocities to optimize throughput. Introduce a simple local stabilization mechanism using a token that temporarily decelerates robots after encounters to eliminate persistent oscillations. Compare a single boundary token to two-directional tokens and optimize the deceleration factor. Validate via event-driven simulations across perturbations (robot deletion, position/velocity jitter) to assess convergence and robustness.
AI.result: The token-based stabilization removes persistent oscillations and leads to convergence toward a stable state. Two-directional tokens offer faster convergence and robustness across perturbations. The system exhibits reliable re-convergence after disruptions, indicating a practical, local mechanism for robust load balancing in heterogeneous robot teams.
AI.conclusion: A purely local, practical approach can achieve robust load balancing in heterogeneous multi-robot systems without central control, providing a viable foundation for more complex, higher-dimensional or dynamic scenarios.

title: Reason in the Words You Speak: Idiolectal Paraphrasing Off-Policy Traces for Reasoning Distillation in VideoLLMs
summary: Recent large language models achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, where reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has emerged as a leading paradigm for optimizing models on self-generated trajectories. However, the on-policy nature of GRPO bounds the model to the reasoning skills it can already produce, restricting to learn more advanced capabilities. Prior works inject privileged reasoning traces from a stronger teacher policy to guide training, yet these traces are inherently out of distribution with respect to the student policy. We observe that this mismatch between on-policy and off-policy causes gradient clipping on semantically critical reasoning tokens, ultimately rewarding correct answers while leaving the reasoning that justifies them unlearned. Hence, we propose \textbf{Echo-GRPO}, a framework that lets the model reason in the words it speaks. Rather than imitating low-probability privileged traces from the teacher model, Echo-GRPO rewrites them into the student policy's own \textit{idiolect}, that is, its own characteristic vocabulary and expression patterns, while preserving their semantics via Dual-Reference Decoding. We instantiate this framework as \textbf{VideoEcho-R1} for video reasoning distillation, achieving consistent improvements across three multimodal LLM backbones and five benchmarks. Finally, we show that our idiolectal paraphrasing is a plug-in module that consistently improves both RL and supervised fine-tuning frameworks for reasoning distillation, demonstrating that policy-aligned supervision extends beyond GRPO.

AI.tldr: Echo-GRPO rewrites privileged teacher traces into the student policy's idiolect via Dual-Reference Decoding to align reasoning traces with the student distribution, addressing on-policy/off-policy mismatch. VideoEcho-R1 demonstrates improvements across three multimodal LLMs and five video-reasoning benchmarks; the approach acts as a plug-in to improve both RL and supervised fine-tuning for reasoning distillation.
AI.motivation: On-policy GRPO confines learning to the agent's current reasoning and capabilities. Using off-policy privileged traces can cause gradient clipping on semantically critical tokens, hindering the justification steps for correct answers. A method is needed to transfer useful semantics from teachers while staying within the student’s linguistic style.
AI.method: Introduce Echo-GRPO, a framework that paraphrase-primes teacher traces into the student policy's idiolect using Dual-Reference Decoding, preserving semantics while aligning with the student's vocabulary. Instantiate as VideoEcho-R1 for video reasoning distillation and evaluate across three multimodal LLM backbones on five benchmarks. Treat the idiolect paraphrase as a plug-in module compatible with RL and supervised fine-tuning frameworks.
AI.result: Echo-GRPO yields consistent improvements across three multimodal LLM backbones and five benchmarks in video reasoning distillation. The idiolectal paraphrase module consistently boosts performance for both reinforcement learning-based training and supervised fine-tuning, indicating the approach's generality beyond GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Policy-aligned supervision via idiolect paraphrasing is a general and effective strategy for reasoning distillation, reducing gradient clipping and enabling higher-level reasoning capabilities to be learned. The VideoEcho-R1 instantiation demonstrates practical gains and suggests broader applicability as a plug-in module for various training paradigms.

title: Structured Evidence Routing for Incident Risk Prediction from Multimodal Longitudinal EHRs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. We propose structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that separates full-record access from disease-specific assessment. The router organizes the complete pre-index EHR into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form an evidence-linked risk assessment, which the reviewer critiques. For comparison with supervised EHRSHOT baselines, we pair the routed evidence summaries with a supervised classifier readout. Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, our method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal pre-readout ablations further suggest that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces a router-predictor-reviewer workflow for incident risk prediction from longitudinal EHRs, achieving AUROC comparable to supervised EHRSHOT baselines while offering a patient-specific evidence trail via structured evidence routing and ablation-supported contributions.
AI.motivation: EHR-based incident risk signals are multimodal, weak individually, and irregularly distributed; current models struggle with explainability and efficient access to relevant evidence.
AI.method: Router creates a compact summary of full pre-index EHR and targeted evidence slices; predictor uses evidence to produce an evidence-linked risk assessment; reviewer critiques the output; for comparison, routed evidence is paired with a supervised classifier readout; five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks; internal pre-readout ablations examine routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review.
AI.result: AUROC is in the range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC; patient-specific evidence trail exposed; ablations indicate contributions from routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review.
AI.conclusion: Structured evidence routing with a router-predictor-reviewer workflow can achieve competitive predictive performance while enhancing interpretability through an explicit evidence trail; components such as routing and evidence slices contribute to performance, suggesting applicability to multimodal EHR tasks and potential for broader use with further refinements.

title: Robust Neural Stimulation Response Modeling Through Meta-Learning and Pretraining
comment: Open source code available: github.com/mmattb/py-tbfm/tree/multisession. 15 pages, 10 figures
summary: Objective: Model-based closed-loop neural stimulation holds promise for therapeutic applications ranging from Parkinson's disease to sensory restoration, but deployment has been limited by two obstacles: 1) forecasting models for predicting the consequences of stimulation fail catastrophically on a meaningful fraction of sessions, and 2) per-session calibration requirements are often incompatible with clinical constraints. We address both by demonstrating, for the first time, that meta-learning and pretraining can be applied to neural stimulation response modeling. Methods: Temporal basis function models (TBFMs) forecast state-dependent neural responses to stimulation. We extend TBFMs with cross-session pretraining using a novel architecture and algorithm based on model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), evaluating them on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates. Results: Meta-learning substantially reduces catastrophic forecast failure: for a 1k calibration set size, sessions with test R-squared < 0.05 drop from 16 of 40 (single-session training) to 1 (MAML-pretrained), and prediction intervals become significantly narrower (p < 0.05). Calibration requirements are reduced by 50-90% at matched accuracy, enabling experiments otherwise infeasible within clinical session-time constraints. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that cross-session structure in stimulation responses is consistent enough to support pretraining, providing the first empirical evidence that meta-learning approaches are viable for neural stimulation. Significance: The robustness and sample efficiency gains directly address known obstacles to deploying model-based stimulation controllers. Our results motivate community efforts to assemble standardized multi-site stimulation datasets and to further explore meta-learning for robust closed-loop stimulation.

AI.tldr: Meta-learning with MAML improves robustness and data efficiency of temporal basis function models for closed-loop neural stimulation; cross-session pretraining reduces catastrophic forecast failures and calibration burden in NHP optogenetic experiments.
AI.motivation: Forecasting models for stimulation often fail catastrophically and per-session calibration is burdensome; leveraging cross-session structure via pretraining may address both.
AI.method: Extend temporal basis function models (TBFMs) with cross-session pretraining using model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML); evaluate on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates.
AI.result: Significant reduction in catastrophic forecast failure: test R^2 < 0.05 sessions drop from 16/40 (single-session training) to 1 (MAML-pretrained); prediction intervals narrower (p<0.05); calibration requirements reduced by 50–90% at matched accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Cross-session structure in stimulation responses supports pretraining; first empirical evidence that meta-learning is viable for neural stimulation; motivates community data-standardization and further meta-learning exploration.

title: Active sensing to characterize the heterogeneity of plant stress
summary:
While most phenotyping platforms rely primarily on image-based measurements, advanced plant characterization requires the integration of active physiological sensing modali- ties such as chlorophyll fluorescence. We present an autonomous robotic platform designed to perform targeted fluorescence measurements on plant leaves. The system combines 3D plant reconstruction, geometric analysis, and motion planning to localize suitable measurement points and generate collision-free trajectories for a robotic manipulator.
  A dense 3D model of the plant is reconstructed from multi-view data and used to extract candidate leaf surfaces based on orientation, accessibility, and sensing constraints. These targets are then integrated into a task-level planning framework that guides the end-effector to precise contact or near-contact configurations required for point-based fluorescence acquisition. The platform enables automated, repeatable, and spatially resolved physiological measurements that go beyond passive imaging. By tightly coupling perception, geometric reasoning, and manipulation, the proposed system provides a robotics-driven approach to high-resolution plant phenotyping and opens new directions for autonomous agricultural inspection and plant-aware manipulation.

AI.tldr: Autonomous robotic platform enables targeted chlorophyll fluorescence measurements on plant leaves by integrating dense 3D plant reconstruction, geometric reasoning, and motion planning to generate collision-free trajectories for point-based sensing.
AI.motivation: To extend plant phenotyping beyond passive image-based measurements by incorporating active physiological sensing (chlorophyll fluorescence) with precise, repeatable, and spatially resolved data collection.
AI.method: Reconstruct a dense 3D plant model from multi-view data to identify candidate leaf surfaces based on orientation, accessibility, and sensing constraints; integrate targets into a task-level planner that guides a robotic end-effector to contact or near-contact configurations for point-based fluorescence acquisition; generate collision-free trajectories for measurement.
AI.result: Demonstrates automated, repeatable, and spatially resolved fluorescence measurements enabled by tight coupling of perception, geometry, and manipulation; showcases a robotics-driven approach to high-resolution plant phenotyping and autonomous agricultural inspection.
AI.conclusion: Presents a scalable framework that expands phenotyping capabilities beyond passive imaging by enabling targeted, automated fluorescence sensing through integrated perception and manipulation, with potential implications for autonomous plant monitoring and manipulation.

title: Domain-Specific Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Retinal Fundus Classification
summary: Despite the growing number of public datasets, annotated medical images remain scarce. Supervised learning methods achieve strong performance on many benchmarks, however require large amounts of labeled data, which are costly and time-consuming to obtain in the medical domain. To address this limitation, contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising alternative for learning useful representations from unlabeled data. In this work, we investigate two SSL frameworks, SimSiam and SimCLR, for retinal disease classification from fundus images. We focus on understanding how augmentation strategies and training parameters influence representation learning under resource-constrained settings. Given limited data and computational capacity, we explore the feasibility of training SSL models with small batch sizes incorporated with retinal-specific augmentation techniques. Through a series of experiments, we assess the quality of learned representations via linear evaluation and fine-tuning across downstream tasks, including multi-disease classification and diabetic retinopathy grading. Our results show that tailoring augmentation strategies to the characteristics of retinal images plays a critical role in improving performance. Even under constrained settings, lightweight SSL frameworks can learn transferable representations that reduce dependence on large annotated datasets and achieve competitive results.

AI.tldr: Evaluates contrastive self-supervised learning (SimSiam and SimCLR) for retinal disease classification under resource constraints, emphasizing retinal-specific augmentations and small-batch training to learn transferable representations for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Annotated medical retinal images are scarce; SSL offers a data-efficient path to learning useful representations from unlabeled data. The study probes how augmentation choices and training parameters affect representation quality in low-resource regimes.
AI.method: Systematic experiments with SimSiam and SimCLR using varying augmentation strategies and small batch sizes, incorporating retinal-specific augmentations. Evaluation via linear probes and fine-tuning on downstream tasks including multi-disease classification and diabetic retinopathy grading.
AI.result: Tailoring augmentations to retinal image characteristics improves representation quality; lightweight SSL models can learn transferable representations under data/computation constraints and achieve competitive performance on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: Appropriate retinal-specific augmentation and small-scale SSL training can reduce reliance on large annotated datasets for retinal disease classification, enabling effective learning from unlabeled fundus images.

title: AffectOmni: RL-Verifiable People-Centric Grounded Affective Reasoning for Social and Art-Related Scenes
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on VQA and scene understanding, yet affective reasoning remains vulnerable to shortcut behavior. Models may predict correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues such as micro expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and external verification. Prior reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context or logical coherence without explicitly enforcing attention to human evidence. In addition, LLM as a Judge scoring often suffers from score clustering, which reduces reward discriminability. We propose AffectOmni, a GRPO trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning. AffectOmni introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, and it adopts within-group comparative scoring to produce more stable and discriminative reward signals. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel level evidence regions via SAM3 to provide an externally auditable interface outside the training loop. Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open source 7B scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/eliot127825-rgb/AffectOmni_nobody.

AI.tldr: AffectOmni is a GRPO-trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning in multimodal LLMs, introducing People Focus and Temporal Order rewards, within-group comparative scoring, and a Thinking Summarizer with SAM3 grounding to pixel-level evidence, enabling external auditable verification and improved performance on emotion recognition and temporally sensitive tasks.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal LLMs for affective reasoning can rely on shortcut cues and lack verifiable, human-centric evidence. LLM-based judges often produce clustered scores, reducing reward discriminability. A framework that enforces attention to people cues and provides external verifiability is needed.
AI.method: AffectOmni employs GRPO training with (i) People Focus rewards to emphasize people-centric evidence, (ii) Temporal Order rewards to enforce temporally structured reasoning, and (iii) within-group comparative scoring for stable, discriminative rewards. A Thinking Summarizer converts free-form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3, yielding an externally auditable interface outside the training loop.
AI.result: On IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense, AffectOmni outperforms open-source 7B baselines, including a +4.66% gain in emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: AffectOmni demonstrates verifiable, people-centric affective reasoning with improved reward discriminability and traceability across multiple benchmarks; it enables external auditing and shows strong gains, with potential directions in efficiency, generalization, and robustness.

title: When Privacy Hurts Mergeability: Geometry-Aware Model Merging under Differential Privacy
summary: Model merging promises to construct a single multi-task model from independently fine-tuned task models without accessing the original task data. This makes it attractive when task data cannot be centralized, but released task models may still leak private fine-tuning data. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled mechanism for limiting such leakage, yet its effect on model merging remains poorly understood. In this paper, we study the geometry of differentially private model merging and identify two geometric obstacles that make private task models difficult to merge: \emph{local sharpness}, which makes task losses sensitive to the parameter displacement induced by merging, and \emph{reference drift}, which measures the displacement of private task models from the shared pretrained initialization and amplifies cross-task interference. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{DP-Merging}, a geometry-aware framework that improves the mergeability of differentially private task models. DP-Merging uses a DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to guide each private task model toward flatter loss regions, and a reference-based alignment regularizer to keep task models close to the shared pretrained initialization. We derive a merge-gap upper bound showing that reducing local curvature and reference drift tightens the bound on the loss increase induced by merging. Experiments on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show that DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving the privacy guarantees of the underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware DP-based model merging framework (DP-Merging) improves the mergeability of privately finetuned task models by addressing local sharpness and reference drift, using a sharpness-aware objective and a reference alignment regularizer; it provides a merge-gap bound and shows consistent gains across vision and language tasks under differential privacy budgets.
AI.motivation: Model merging without access to original task data is appealing but privacy constraints (DP) introduce geometry-induced obstacles. Local sharpness amplifies parameter displacement effects during merging, and reference drift causes cross-task interference. Reducing these factors should improve merge performance while preserving DP.
AI.method: DP-Merging combines (i) a DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to steer each private task model toward flatter loss regions, and (ii) a reference-based alignment regularizer to keep models close to a shared pretrained initialization. The authors derive a merge-gap upper bound showing how decreasing local curvature and reference drift tightens the bound on the loss increase caused by merging.
AI.result: Empirical results on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show DP-Merging consistently improves the performance of private merged models, while maintaining the privacy guarantees of the underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.
AI.conclusion: A geometry-aware approach effectively enhances private model merging under differential privacy by mitigating local sharpness and reference drift; the method yields theoretical tightening via a merge-gap bound and practical gains across tasks and budgets.

title: Planning a Shared Modular Fixture Layout Across Robotic Disassembly Stages
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering (T-ASE)
summary: Stable support remains challenging in robotic disassembly of irregularly shaped products. As components are progressively removed, the available support surfaces, mass distribution, and task loads change throughout the process. A fixture layout designed for one workpiece state may therefore become infeasible at later stages, motivating unified support planning over the complete disassembly sequence. This paper presents a modular vacuum-based fixturing system that plans one shared support configuration for the complete disassembly sequence of a screwdriver or shaver, allowing each sequence to proceed without fixture reconfiguration. To search the mixed continuous--discrete layout space under repeated cross-stage evaluation, a denoising diffusion probabilistic model generates physics-informed initial configurations that are refined through Bayesian optimization. Robotic screw and component-removal experiments verified the disassembly feasibility of the planned layouts, while 11 directional-load tests quantified their stability. Comparisons between the measured operational loads and directional responses yielded mean empirical stability margins of 66.9% for the screwdriver and 81.6% for the shaver. These results demonstrate that a product-specific shared layout can provide stable support throughout the tested robotic disassembly sequence.

AI.tldr: A product-specific, shared vacuum fixturing layout enables stable robotic disassembly across all stages without reconfiguration, using a diffusion model to generate initial layout candidates and Bayesian optimization to refine them; validated on screwdriver and shaver with favorable stability margins.
AI.motivation: Disassembly of irregularly shaped products requires adjusting fixtures as mass distribution and loads evolve; reconfiguring fixtures is costly and time-consuming. A single, stable, stage-spanning fixturing solution could streamline automated disassembly.
AI.method: A modular vacuum-based fixturing system that searches a mixed continuous–discrete layout space for a single plan covering the complete disassembly sequence. Initial configurations are produced by a denoising diffusion probabilistic model incorporating physics-informed constraints, then refined via Bayesian optimization. Experimental validation includes robotic screw/ component removal and 11 directional-load tests.
AI.result: The planned layouts supported disassembly feasibility for both devices without fixture reconfiguration. Empirical stability margins averaged 66.9% for the screwdriver and 81.6% for the shaver, indicating robust stability under staged removal loads.
AI.conclusion: A product-specific shared fixturing layout can provide stable support throughout a robotic disassembly sequence. The combination of diffusion-based initialization and Bayesian optimization effectively navigates the mixed (continuous–discrete) layout space to produce feasible, stable fixtures.

title: AesCanvas: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Aesthetic Critique and Contextual Suitability
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material included
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have extended Image Aesthetic Assessment (IAA) beyond scalar scores toward interpretable critique and guidance. Yet existing benchmarks mainly assess intrinsic visual quality or fixed domain criteria, leaving open whether an appealing image is appropriate for a specific purpose, audience, cultural setting, or domain convention. We introduce AesCanvas, a unified suite with two complementary components: CritiqueCanvas with 519,136 instruction-response pairs from 54,300 images supports long-form, multi-dimensional critique across photography, painting, and virtual imagery, whereas ContextCanvas with 301 expert-reviewed use scenarios evaluates contextual aesthetic suitability in realistic use scenarios. Under a unified protocol, we evaluate closed-source frontier, open-weight general, and aesthetic-specific MLLMs. Results reveal a clear separation between critique generation and context-sensitive judgment: reference-based lexical and semantic metrics only partially capture critique quality, while aesthetic specialists remain competitive on selected critique metrics yet substantially lag strong general-purpose MLLMs on ContextCanvas. Further analyses show that aesthetic specialization does not reliably transfer to contextual suitability and that model decisions may fail to track or ground themselves in decisive contextual visual cues. These findings establish culturally situated, evidence-grounded suitability as a distinct objective for aesthetic modeling.

AI.tldr: AesCanvas introduces CritiqueCanvas and ContextCanvas to evaluate image aesthetics in two dimensions: quality of critique and contextual suitability, revealing a split between critique generation and context-sensitive judgment; generalist MLLMs excel in contextual evaluation, while aesthetic specialists lag, and specialization does not reliably transfer to contextual grounding.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for Image Aesthetic Assessment (IAA) emphasize intrinsic visual quality or single-domain criteria, neglecting cultural, audience-specific, or domain-specific suitability; there is a need for culturally grounded, context-aware evaluation suites for aesthetic models.
AI.method: Proposes two datasets: CritiqueCanvas (519,136 instruction-response pairs from 54,300 images) for long-form, multi-dimensional critique across photography, painting, and virtual imagery; ContextCanvas (301 expert-reviewed use scenarios) for contextual suitability in realistic use cases; uses a unified evaluation protocol across closed-source frontier, open-weight general, and aesthetic-specific MLLMs.
AI.result: Critique quality metrics based on references and semantics are only partially captured; aesthetic specialists perform well on some critique metrics but are outperformed by strong generalist MLLMs on ContextCanvas; specializing in aesthetics does not reliably transfer to contextual suitability; model decisions may fail to ground in decisive contextual cues.
AI.conclusion: Culturally situated, evidence-grounded contextual suitability is a distinct objective for aesthetic modeling, requiring evaluation frameworks that separate critique generation from context-aware judgment.

title: Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization
summary: Operating a scientific instrument such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) requires continuous expert decision-making. A trained user defines the experimental intent, translates it into instrument commands, assesses incoming data, adjusts imaging parameters, and post-processes the final image. Existing automation usually addresses only parts of this workflow through hard-coded routines, task-specific controllers, or trained machine-learning models. Here we present an agentic-AI framework that operates the executable part of the AFM workflow using a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework consists of 3 MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot assesses image quality through a large language model (LLM) and, if necessary, adapts imaging parameters; and AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. Because the language model performs image assessment rather than a fixed scalar objective or external optimizer, the same strategy can be applied across sample types and imaging modes without specific retraining. Safe hardware operation is enforced through an ambiguity check layer before execution. Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that this guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference. These results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

AI.tldr: Agentic-AI framework for AFM control using three MCP-based LLM agents to cover intent translation, image quality assessment and artifact post-processing, with a guarded execution layer that yields zero wrong commands; matches expert performance in live tests.
AI.motivation: Automate the executable AFM workflow end-to-end while preserving human-defined experimental intent, enabling generalization across samples and imaging modes without task-specific retraining, and ensuring safe hardware operation.
AI.method: Three MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger translates natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot uses an LLM to assess image quality and adapt imaging parameters; AFM Doctor diagnoses artifacts and applies transparent, pre-approved post-processing. A pre-execution ambiguity-check layer enforces safety. Evaluation benchmarks compare against fine-tuned and generic tool-using models; live experiments test across samples.
AI.result: Guarded execution reduces wrong-command execution to zero. AFM Pilot achieves expert-like image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference from human operators across samples.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a safe, generalizable path to agentic operation of scientific instruments—human intent guides commands while AI handles execution, tuning, and post-processing—potentially extendable to other instruments and modalities.

title: Simple Actors and Deep Critics for Scalable Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining these ingredients with a lightweight deterministic actor, we propose LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic). On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. Its critic recipe also transfers across actor parametrizations.

AI.tldr: LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic) trains a deep critic with a lightweight deterministic actor in offline RL to gain inference-time efficiency; achieves strong performance with up to 4x lower latency than diffusion/flow-matching actors and transfers across actor parametrizations.
AI.motivation: Offline RL benefits from powerful, multimodal actors but their deployment cost is high. Since the critic is only needed during training, allocating capacity to the critic (instead of the actor) can improve deployment efficiency. However, deep critics in offline RL face instabilities that hinder performance, necessitating stabilizing techniques.
AI.method: Introduce LAC: a deep critic with a residual MLP backbone to mitigate optimization and bootstrap-noise issues, combined with n-step bootstrap targets and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Use a lightweight deterministic actor. The critic design is made to be transferable across actor parametrizations.
AI.result: On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x faster inference; performance is comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. The critic recipe transfers across actor parametrizations.
AI.conclusion: Shifting capacity to the trainer (deep critic) while keeping a lightweight actor yields efficient offline RL with strong performance and deployment efficiency. The proposed stabilizing ingredients enable training deep critics in offline settings and the approach generalizes across actor types.

title: Task-space model-based control of pneumatic soft actuators
summary: Soft actuators enable dexterous and compliant interaction, but closed-loop task-space control remains challenging due to strong nonlinearities, distributed deformation, and uncertainty in their dynamics. This paper presents a real-time dynamic-model-based task-space feedback and estimation framework based on a non-minimal coordinate discrete elastic rod model formulated in absolute coordinates with holonomic constraints. The resulting structure preserves distributed mechanics while maintaining computational efficiency through sparse system matrices, enabling real-time control with up to 10 discretized rods. A quasi-static feedforward inverse model is combined with a task-space PI controller and a dynamic observer that fuses measurement residuals as virtual forces, enabling full-state estimation from sparse sensing. The approach is experimentally validated on three planar pneumatic soft actuators with varying geometries. Across five tasks, including drawing the digits 0-9 across the workspace (3-18 mm/s tip speed), tracking periodic motion (up to 37 cm/s), cross-platform generalization, reduced sensing conditions, and real-time user-defined references, our method achieves 1.5-2.3 mm root mean square error (RMSE) for precision motions and 5.5-12.4 mm RMSE at 1-2 Hz. Results demonstrate that structured, non-minimal dynamic models can enable real-time, high-precision, moderate-bandwidth task-space control of planar soft pneumatic actuators in free space.

AI.tldr: Real-time task-space control for soft actuators using a non-minimal coordinate discrete elastic rod model with holonomic constraints; combines a quasi-static inverse model, task-space PI control, and a dynamic observer; validated experimentally on planar pneumatic soft actuators with mm-scale accuracy.
AI.motivation: Soft actuators exhibit strong nonlinearities, distributed deformation, and uncertain dynamics, making closed-loop task-space control difficult; a real-time, accurate, and scalable control framework is needed.
AI.method: Non-minimal coordinate discrete elastic rod model in absolute coordinates with holonomic constraints; sparse system matrices for computational efficiency; supports up to 10 discretized rods; integrates a quasi-static feedforward inverse model, a task-space PI controller, and a dynamic observer that fuses residuals as virtual forces for full-state estimation from sparse sensing.
AI.result: Experimental validation on three planar pneumatic soft actuators with varying geometries across five tasks (drawing digits 0-9 at 3-18 mm/s, tracking periodic motion up to 37 cm/s, cross-platform generalization, reduced sensing, real-time user-defined references). Achieves 1.5-2.3 mm RMSE for precise motions and 5.5-12.4 mm RMSE at 1-2 Hz.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that structured, non-minimal dynamic models enable real-time, high-precision, moderate-bandwidth task-space control of planar soft pneumatic actuators in free space, with computational efficiency from sparse matrices.

title: LiveVVT: High-Fidelity Video Virtual Try-On in Real Time
summary: Diffusion-based Video Virtual Try-On (VVT) achieves high visual fidelity through bidirectional spatio-temporal modeling, but complete-clip dependence incurs prohibitive latency and computational overhead in practical continuous deployment. Naively enforcing causality disrupts pretrained bidirectional priors and substantially degrades synthesis quality. We introduce LiveVVT, a rolling streaming diffusion framework that preserves bounded bidirectional modeling within causal recurrent generation. Within a fixed-size window, LiveVVT jointly denoises multiple video chunks under bounded look-ahead, preserving local bidirectional interactions while emitting one clean chunk per iteration. Beyond the window, two complementary memories sustain long-term consistency: a bounded temporal memory propagates recent dynamics and occlusion context, whereas a persistent global appearance memory, constructed once from the target garment and a frontal try-on keyframe, anchors garment details and dressed appearance throughout the stream. We further introduce a progressive distillation framework integrating bidirectional VVT learning, teacher-trajectory regression for causal few-step adaptation, and Collaborative Matching Distillation, which couples teacher-distribution matching with rolling flow matching on real videos to align optimization with recurrent inference. Experiments on paired and unpaired long-sequence benchmarks demonstrate superior generation quality over similarly sized models, with $26\times$ lower latency and $11\times$ higher throughput, enabling high-fidelity real-time streaming VVT.

AI.tldr: LiveVVT introduces a rolling streaming diffusion approach with a fixed-size causal window and dual memories to enable real-time, high-fidelity video virtual try-on (VVT) while preserving long-term consistency.
AI.motivation: Overcome the prohibitive latency and computational overhead of complete-clip diffusion-based VVT and the degradation caused by naive causality enforcement, by preserving bounded bidirectional priors within a streaming framework.
AI.method: A rolling streaming diffusion framework that denoises multiple video chunks within a fixed window with bounded look-ahead. It uses (1) a bounded temporal memory for recent dynamics and occlusion context and (2) a persistent global appearance memory anchored to the target garment and a frontal try-on keyframe. It also introduces progressive distillation: bidirectional VVT learning, teacher-trajectory regression for causal few-step adaptation, and Collaborative Matching Distillation (teacher-distribution matching with rolling flow matching on real videos) to align training with recurrent inference.
AI.result: Experiments on paired and unpaired long-sequence benchmarks show superior generation quality versus similarly sized models, with about 26× lower latency and 11× higher throughput, enabling high-fidelity real-time streaming VVT.
AI.conclusion: LiveVVT achieves high-fidelity, real-time streaming VVT with sustained long-term consistency via bounded bidirectional modeling and memory-augmented diffusion, validated by efficient training through progressive distillation.

title: Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling
summary: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations---such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections---through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Results show that strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends strongly on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments.

AI.tldr: Locally deployed LLM agents can automate expert hardware design workflows in a realistic tool-calling setting using a Model Context Protocol; with thorough tool descriptions and careful agent design, near-complete call coverage is achievable, but reliability hinges on task structure and configuration.
AI.motivation: Confidentiality constraints prevent hosted proprietary APIs and motivate local models; evaluating how LLMs can manage stateful, dependency-ordered hardware-design workflows through tool calls in a realistic setting.
AI.method: Build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that emulates the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool; create a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspellings, and multi-server tool contexts; evaluate seven open-source models across variations in prompts, tool descriptions, context scope, and single-agent vs multi-agent architectures.
AI.result: Strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmark; reliability depends on task structure and agent configuration; comprehensive tool descriptions reduce failures; few-shot prompting can cause inaction for some models; cumulative context harms constrained models; multi-agent decomposition helps weaker workers or long sessions but increases the number of calls.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments, highlighting the importance of detailed tool descriptions, context management, and agent architecture tradeoffs to achieve reliable automation.

title: Neural Regression with Embeddings for Numerical Attribute Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
summary: In recent years, transductive knowledge graph embedding models have been applied to tasks such as link prediction and query answering. Although knowledge graphs often contain rich numerical attributes, most embedding models neglect them, limiting their ability to represent real-world knowledge graphs with diverse information. In this work, we propose a neural regression model (LitEm) that enables transductive knowledge graph embedding models to predict numerical attributes within knowledge graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that LitEm achieves the best or second-best results on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, and Mutagenesis. Furthermore, we propose a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive knowledge graph embedding models with LitEm, which improves link prediction performance mainly for bilinear models and simultaneously enables them to predict numerical attributes. In addition, the literal-awareness evaluation demonstrates that co-training helps models to encode and exploit attribute information in a "literal-aware'' manner, suggesting that the observed gains are not merely due to additional parameters. We publicly release our implementation at https://github.com/dice-group/dice-embeddings.

AI.tldr: LitEm extends transductive KGE with a neural regression model to predict numerical attributes; co-training with LitEm improves link prediction and yields literal-aware representations; code released.
AI.motivation: KGs often contain rich numerical literals that are underutilized by existing embedding models; integrating literals can improve expressiveness and downstream tasks.
AI.method: Introduce LitEm neural regression to predict numerical attributes; propose a co-training framework jointly training LitEm with state-of-the-art transductive KGE models; evaluate literal-aware capabilities.
AI.result: LitEm achieves best or second-best on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, Mutagenesis; co-training boosts link prediction mainly for bilinear models and enables numerical attribute prediction; literal-aware evaluation shows encoded attribute information beyond extra parameters.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating numerical literals via LitEm and co-training enhances KGE performance and representation; code released.

title: Tensegrity Continuum Robots Enable Task-Adaptive Morphologies for Cooperative Behaviors
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, Accepted to Nature Machine Intelligence
summary: Robots that can change their morphologies and behaviors for different tasks and environments hold great promise for adaptable, multifunctional systems. Modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) can achieve such functionalities by docking and rearranging individual units, but most rely on rigid modules that lack structural compliance, resulting in limited capabilities. Continuum robots offer compliance through flexible backbones, yet they cannot self-reconfigure into task-adaptive multi-robot configurations. Here, we introduce an MRR that unifies the advantages of both architectures by combining a tensegrity-based compliant body with claw-based connection mechanisms. Each robot can manipulate and locomote independently, and multiple robots can self-reconfigure into different morphologies (e.g., chains, loops, branches) for cooperative manipulation and locomotion. We demonstrate the robots' capability across diverse tasks and environments, including coordinated object manipulation and transport, multimodal locomotion, and loco-manipulation in real-world scenarios. These results lay a foundation for adaptable and multifunctional robotic collectives, with broad potential applications in manufacturing, space exploration, and search-and-rescue operations.

AI.tldr: MRR architecture combining tensegrity-compliant bodies with claw docking enables self-reconfigurable morphologies for cooperative manipulation and locomotion; demonstrated across chains, loops, and branches and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the rigidity and limited morphologies of traditional modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) and the lack of reconfiguration in continuum robots; enable adaptable, compliant multi-robot systems.
AI.method: Develop tensegrity-based compliant modules with claw-based connectors; each unit can operate independently and reconfigure into chains, loops, branches; demonstrate manipulation, locomotion, and loco-manipulation across diverse tasks and environments, including real-world scenarios.
AI.result: Robots can self-reconfigure into multiple morphologies (chains, loops, branches); achieve coordinated object manipulation and transport; display multimodal locomotion and loco-manipulation capabilities; validated in real-world tests.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a unified architecture that blends compliant continuum-like behavior with modular reconfigurability, laying groundwork for adaptable, multifunctional robotic collectives with broad applications (manufacturing, space, search-and-rescue).

title: Beyond Atomic Layouts: Compositional Design Understanding with Vision-Language Models
summary: Layout understanding, or the interpretation of element organization, is essential for document analysis, user interface (UI) creation, and graphic design. While recent vision-language models (VLMs) excel at interpreting atomic layouts composed of independent elements, they struggle with compositional layouts that require reasoning over visually entangled elements within hierarchical multi-layer structures. In this paper, we introduce a new task, compositional layout understanding, and present CoDeLayout, a VQA dataset of ~20K real-world multi-layer layouts annotated with compositional element pairs and design intent. Through empirical analysis on CoDeLayout, we identify two key challenges for existing VLMs: semantic drift between textual metadata and visual content, and structural ambiguity in hierarchical inter-element relationships. To address these challenges, we propose MASON, a post-training paradigm that integrates multimodal alignment (MA) and structural perception (SP). MA enhances element interpretation by grounding metadata-defined elements to their visual counterparts, mitigating semantic drift, while SP models layer-aware inter-element spatial relationships to improve hierarchical understanding and reduce structural ambiguity. Experiments reveal substantial gaps in existing VLMs: even the strongest baseline, GPT-o3, achieves only 79.68% accuracy, whereas Qwen2.5-VL 7B with MASON reaches 91.66%. Notably, MASON surpasses full-data Direct Finetune using only 30% of the training data and scales better with additional data.

AI.tldr: CoDeLayout introduces a compositional layout understanding task with a ~20k real-world multi-layer VQA dataset; proposes MASON (multimodal alignment + structural perception) to address semantic drift and hierarchical structure; achieves 91.66% with MASON, outperforming full-data fine-tuning with only 30% data.
AI.motivation: Need to extend layout understanding beyond independent, atomic elements to compositional, hierarchically entangled layouts. Existing VLMs struggle with semantic alignment and structural reasoning in layered designs.
AI.method: Introduce CoDeLayout dataset of ~20k real-world, multi-layer layouts for compositional VQA. Propose MASON, a post-training paradigm with two components: multimodal alignment (grounding metadata-defined elements to visuals) and structural perception (layer-aware modeling of inter-element spatial relationships). Apply to Qwen2.5-VL 7B; evaluate against baselines including GPT-o3.
AI.result: Baseline GPT-o3 achieves 79.68% accuracy; Qwen2.5-VL 7B with MASON attains 91.66% accuracy. MASON surpasses full-data Direct Finetune using only 30% of training data and scales better with more data.
AI.conclusion: MASON effectively reduces semantic drift and structural ambiguity, yielding strong performance gains for compositional layout understanding and enabling data-efficient training for complex hierarchical layouts.

title: GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games
summary: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization.
