For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

AI.tldr: Introduce GameWAM, a World-Action Model (WAM) for native closed-loop gameplay that jointly generates future visuals and executable actions, with mode-aware control and long-horizon planning; reveals LASI failure mode.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between world-dynamics models and task policies in video-game agents. Existing models either predict visuals from actions or map visuals to actions but do not couple world dynamics with control in a unified, open-ended gaming setting.
AI.method: Propose GameWAM with parallel visual and action generative processes, block-causal conditioning, flow matching, and synchronized gameplay/GUI trajectories. It detects gameplay/GUI mode at each step, uses mode-specific action distributions, and normalizes continuous actions. Employs block-cycle control for long-horizon planning with replanning from new observations; preserves temporal continuity via within-cycle context and cross-cycle history. Also analyzes LASI, a low-frequency action source imprinting effect.
AI.result: Demonstrates competitive task success with fewer native actions required than compared agents. Identifies LASI as a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control.
AI.conclusion: GameWAM advances World-Action Models for native closed-loop gameplay by integrating world dynamics with control in dynamic, heterogeneous-action environments and highlights LASI as a caution for future development.

title: Rethinking Message Passing as Retrieval for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically conceptualized as message-passing neural networks, yet it remains unclear why neighborhood aggregation reliably outperforms node-wise multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Despite its empirical success, this paradigm can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. In this work, we present a retrieval-augmented view of GNNs: each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation together with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context. Motivated by this perspective, we propose RTA, a simple MLP-based framework that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. We provide theoretical insights that (i) connect retrieval-based aggregation to softmax-attention message passing, and (ii) establish the robustness of retrieved-context supervision to mis-retrieved outliers. Experiments on multiple text-attributed graph benchmarks show that RTA matches or even outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

title: STEP: State-Aware Task Estimation and Planning with Multi-Modal LLMs for Human-Robot Collaboration
comment: Published in IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN), 2026, 8 pages, 4 figuers, 5 tables
summary: Effective human-robot collaboration in industrial settings requires robots to understand human intentions and assist with task planning, reducing workload. Recent works have explored the use of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MM-LLMs) for task planning in such data-scarce scenarios, leveraging in-context learning to interpret user actions and generate long-horizon action plans in natural language. However, MM-LLMs inherently lack an understanding of system states and do not track state transitions, often leading to hallucinated actions that deviate from the intended goal. Additionally, generating action plans in natural language tends to limit the generated plans to a high level, introducing ambiguity in action execution. To address these limitations, we propose the State-aware Task Estimator and Planner (STEP), which prompts a MM-LLM to explicitly estimate the state of the system and predict the state transitions resulting from executed actions. By forecasting future states alongside actions, STEP ensures task-convergent planning while also providing additional assistance parameters necessary for executing the predicted actions. We evaluate STEP in a simulated environment using a robot assembly task. Our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art by 32.8% in action executability and 14.8% in final-state error.

AI.tldr: A state-aware planner for MM-LLMs (STEP) forecasts system state and state transitions to enable convergent, executable action plans, outperforming SOTA in simulation.
AI.motivation: MM-LLMs in task planning suffer from lack of system-state understanding and plan hallucinations; natural-language plans tend to be high-level and ambiguous. Explicit state estimation and transition forecasting are needed for goal-oriented planning and reliable execution.
AI.method: Introduce STEP, which prompts a MM-LLM to (1) estimate the current system state, (2) predict the state transitions caused by executed actions, and (3) forecast future states alongside actions, providing actionable execution parameters.
AI.result: In a robot assembly simulation, STEP outperforms the state-of-the-art by 32.8% in action executability and 14.8% in final-state error.
AI.conclusion: STEP enhances task-convergent planning, reduces hallucinations, and supplies execution cues, demonstrating clear benefits of explicit state-awareness in MM-LLMs for human-robot collaboration.

title: Parameter Efficient Continual Learning for Sparse Event-Based Transformers
summary: Robotic and edge intelligence systems operate in dynamic environments where data arrives continuously, requiring models to adapt while preserving previously learned knowledge under strict memory and energy constraints. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning has shown promise for continual learning with vision transformers, conventional architectures rely on dense computation and remain costly for real-world deployment. Sparse event-based vision transformers provide energy-efficient event-driven computation, yet their continual learning capabilities remain largely unexplored. We here introduce sLoTh, a parameter-efficient continual learning framework for pretrained sparse event-based (spiking) vision transformers. sLoTh freezes the backbone and restricts plasticity to scalable-efficient low-rank attention updates (seLoRA) and shared neuronal threshold modulation, enabling adaptation without replay buffers by updating less than 1% of model parameters. Experiments across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-R with up to 100 tasks demonstrate competitive rehearsal-free performance in class-incremental learning and online continual learning, while enabling approximately 6.5x lower energy consumption than conventional dense vision transformers.

AI.tldr: sLoTh enables rehearsal-free continual learning in sparse event-based vision transformers by freezing the backbone and using seLoRA low-rank attention updates plus shared threshold modulation, updating <1% of parameters, with ~6.5x energy savings vs dense ViTs.
AI.motivation: Real-world robotic/edge systems require continual adaptation in dynamic environments under strict memory and energy constraints; sparse event-based architectures offer energy-efficient computation, but their continual learning capabilities are underexplored.
AI.method: Freeze pretrained sparse spiking ViT backbone; restrict plasticity to (i) seLoRA low-rank attention updates and (ii) shared neuronal threshold modulation; no replay buffers; update <1% of parameters; evaluate on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-100, ImageNet-R across up to 100 tasks.
AI.result: Achieves competitive rehearsal-free performance in class-incremental and online continual learning across datasets; ~6.5x energy reduction compared with conventional dense ViTs.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a practical, highly parameter-efficient continual learning framework for sparse event-based transformers, enabling adaptation with minimal memory and energy without replay buffers.

title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Software and study artifacts: https://github.com/sydches/yuj
summary:
A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
  Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

AI.tldr: Changing the harness while keeping the model and task fixed can substantially alter outcomes in coding-agent benchmarks; results imply the harness and model must be treated as a coupled solver rather than independent components.
AI.motivation: Test whether harness design (context management, tool usage, continuation strategy) changes results when the model and task are fixed, across multiple benchmarks and context windows.
AI.method: Directly compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, FeatureBench). Use tight and wide context windows, with fixed token and time constraints; measure per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF), complete solutions, and prompt-token usage; report across multiple models without retuning.
AI.result: Under tight context, the treatment increases per-task F2PF across all three benchmarks and raises complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro; specific numbers show an increase in F2PF from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72 in the Verified cohort (169 tasks, 20,480-token window, 480s). Similar positive effects on other models with the frozen treatment; in wide-window settings, outcomes are more mixed, with some benchmarks showing comparable results and others retaining higher F2PF under treatment; the treatment also reduces prompt tokens per turn in some cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Harness design materially influences coding-agent performance; evaluations should treat the model and harness jointly as the tested solver.

title: Self-Augmented Diffusion Guidance for Physics-Informed Generation
summary: Diffusion models can be used to generate spatiotemporal signals of physical phenomena, such as time-series images of fluid dynamics. However, a major limitation of standard diffusion models is that they do not incorporate constraints derived from the underlying physical laws. Consequently, generated samples may appear visually plausible while deviating substantially from the true dynamics. In this study, we propose a simple yet effective physics-informed approach based on diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. The proposed method learns the data distribution conditioned on the degree of deviation from the physically correct dynamics and generates samples by explicitly setting the deviation condition to be zero. The method decouples the evaluation of the governing equations from the diffusion model training and sampling processes, avoiding the need to solve the governing equations at every iteration of the denoising process. This design makes the method applicable to problems requiring computationally expensive numerical simulations and enables faster sample generation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model not only significantly reduces the deviations compared with standard diffusion models but also achieves further reductions when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation decouples PDE evaluation from training, conditioning on zero deviation at sampling, yielding faster, more physically faithful spatiotemporal samples and boosting accuracy beyond standard diffusion and existing physics-constrained methods.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion models generate visually plausible samples but often violate underlying physical laws; enforcing governing equations is computationally challenging if done at every diffusion step.
AI.method: Train a diffusion model conditioned on the degree of deviation from correct dynamics, using self-generated data augmentation; at sampling, fix the deviation condition to zero; decouple PDE evaluation from diffusion training/sampling; enables handling expensive simulations.
AI.result: Significant reduction in deviation from physics compared with standard diffusion; added reductions when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods; compatible with expensive numerical simulations and faster sample generation.
AI.conclusion: A simple, effective way to enforce physical constraints in diffusion-based generation without solving PDEs during every step, improving physical fidelity and efficiency; complements existing physics-constrained diffusion approaches.

title: Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026. Project page: https://bit-pie.github.io/ESRP/ Code: https://github.com/BIT-PIE/ESRP Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/serendipity800/ESRP-PD
summary: This paper introduces Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning (ESRP), a novel task requiring embodied agents to rearrange furniture in 3D scenes to match a target configuration using only egocentric observations and a top-down target layout. Unlike prior rearrangement tasks, ESRP precludes global state access and introduces mutual object occlusions, reflecting the practical constraints of real-world robotic deployment. These factors make aligning partial egocentric observations with the global target layout particularly challenging for long-horizon planning. To facilitate research, we present ESRP-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark built on OmniGibson featuring over 5,400 scene pairs and 8,200 objects. We define three multi-level metrics to evaluate rearrangement quality and provide four baselines: a hierarchical task-and-motion planning method, a vision-language-model-based method, and two learning-based approaches (IL and RL). Experimental results demonstrate that current methods struggle to complete the task efficiently, highlighting ESRP as a challenging frontier for embodied agents in scene understanding and long-horizon task planning. This work serves as a stepping stone toward deploying intelligent agents in real-world scenarios. Project page: https://pie-lab.cn/ESRP/.

AI.tldr: A new embodied rearrangement task (ESRP) requires agents to rearrange furniture in 3D scenes using only egocentric observations and a top-down target layout, with mutual occlusions. ESRP-Bench on OmniGibson provides 5.4k scene pairs and 8.2k objects; three-level evaluation metrics; four baselines spanning planning, vision-language, and learning approaches. Current methods struggle, highlighting ESRP as a hard benchmark for long-horizon embodied scene understanding and planning.
AI.motivation: Study long-horizon embodied manipulation under partial observability and occlusions to reflect real-world robotics, bridging perception and planning under restricted access to global state.
AI.method: Define the ESRP task and dataset. Build ESRP-Bench on OmniGibson with 5,400+ scene pairs and 8,200 objects. Propose three multi-level evaluation metrics. Provide four baselines: hierarchical task-and-motion planning (TAMP), vision-language-model-based method, and two learning-based approaches (imitation learning and reinforcement learning).
AI.result: Foundational capabilities are lacking: current methods cannot efficiently complete ESRP tasks, indicating a significant gap between perception-to-action planning in constrained observations.
AI.conclusion: ESRP offers a challenging but important benchmark for advancing embodied scene understanding and long-horizon planning, and serves as a stepping stone toward real-world deployment of intelligent agents.

title: UniGeo: A Multi-modal Large Language Model for Text-Guided Cross-View Geo-Localization
summary: Text-guided drone geo-localization aims to identify a target region in a large-scale image gallery from a natural-language description. Existing methods mainly formulate this task as direct matching between an open-ended text query and candidate images. However, incomplete queries and highly similar candidates often make global cross-modal matching insufficient for reliable fine-grained localization. We propose UniGeo, a unified multimodal large language model (MLLM) for text-guided drone geo-localization. Built on a shared vision-language framework, UniGeo jointly supports geo-semantic understanding, cross-view semantic generation, and candidate-level verification. Specifically, it establishes stable correspondences among local scene elements, spatial relations, and language descriptions through geo-semantic learning, and further models semantic mappings between drone and satellite views through cross-view generation. Based on these capabilities, a plug-and-play verification module performs fine-grained discrimination among highly confusable candidates. We further introduce a multi-stage training strategy that progressively learns geo-semantic understanding, cross-view generation, and candidate verification, improving adaptation to text-guided geo-localization. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple retrieval backbones. On GeoText-1652, UniGeo improves R@10 and mAP by 13.59 and 2.83 percentage points, respectively, validating its effectiveness for fine-grained text-guided drone geo-localization.

AI.tldr: UniGeo is a unified multimodal LLM for text-guided drone geo-localization that integrates geo-semantic understanding, cross-view generation between drone and satellite views, and candidate-level verification within a multi-stage training framework, yielding consistent retrieval gains on GeoText-1652.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal text-to-image localization suffers when queries are incomplete and candidates are highly similar; there is a need for fine-grained localization leveraging local scene semantics and cross-view mappings to improve discrimination among candidates.
AI.method: A shared vision-language framework that (1) learns geo-semantic correspondences between local scene elements and language, (2) models cross-view semantic mappings via cross-view generation between drone and satellite views, and (3) includes a plug-and-play verification module for fine-grained candidate discrimination; trained through a multi-stage strategy that progressively learns geo-semantic understanding, cross-view generation, and candidate verification.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across retrieval backbones. On GeoText-1652, R@10 increases by 13.59 percentage points and mAP by 2.83 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: UniGeo demonstrates effective integration of geo-semantic understanding, cross-view generation, and candidate verification within an MLLM framework for fine-grained text-guided drone geo-localization, with notable gains on a standard benchmark and a learning curriculum that enhances adaptation.

title: Agent Mesh: Reliability Primitives for Non-Idempotent Agent Delegation - Identity Adequacy and Evidence Adequacy
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly perform bounded software tasks under an orchestrator that retries, resumes, and budgets them. The machinery such orchestrators reach for is the service mesh's: retry, timeout, and error-rate circuit breaking. We report a failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform over 147 numbered incidents spanning 81 runs, each with a measured cost and, in most cases, a mutation proof reproducing the failure. All three assumptions those primitives rest on are violated in practice, and we quantify the consequences: a loop of fifty-four consecutive successful tool calls no error-rate breaker could see; a progress signal constant by construction, guaranteeing a false trip on the third repair round and driving one run from six of six components to three; twenty-one events accumulated across six invocations of one delegation, making a correct, idempotent component unwinnable; a misrouted failure that woke five components for a two-component fault, leaving three bystanders regressing working code; and twelve incidents in which the enforcement layer blocked correct work, the most expensive costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. We find one cross-cutting cause and its dual. Identity adequacy: in five separate subsystems an identity that failed to discriminate produced a confident wrong answer, and two of them derived the corrective rule independently. Evidence adequacy: a reliability decision may be taken only on evidence capable of moving, attributable to what it measures, and deterministic under identical conditions. From the findings we derive seven reliability primitives whose enforcement unit is the delegation rather than the message, and specify the controlled evaluation the study motivates but does not constitute.

AI.tldr: Service-mesh reliability primitives (retry/timeout/circuit-breaking) fail in production autonomous agents; a failure study exposes systemic issues, cross-cutting causes, and a path toward seven delegation-level reliability primitives.
AI.motivation: To empirically evaluate whether common reliability primitives in orchestration layers hold under real agent workloads, identify failure patterns, and derive design guidance for reliable agentic delivery platforms.
AI.method: Empirical failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform: 147 incidents across 81 runs; each incident with measured cost and often a mutation-proof reproduction; analysis of failure patterns and derivation of reliability primitives.
AI.result: Documented failure patterns include long sequences of successful tool calls unseen by breakers, constant progress signals causing false repair trips, aggregated delegation events preventing idempotent components from succeeding, misrouted failures waking multiple components, and enforcement layer blocking correct work with costs up to 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. Identified cross-cutting causes—Identity adequacy and Evidence adequacy—and proposed seven reliability primitives with enforcement at the delegation level.
AI.conclusion: Reliability enforcement should be anchored at the delegation boundary; findings motivate a controlled evaluation approach and outline directions for future rigorous assessment and design of agentic reliability primitives.

title: Safety by Design: Realized-Cost Constraints for Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions
summary: Contextual bandits are a standard framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications in clinical trials, dosage selection, recommendation systems, and autonomous systems. Safety is central in many of these applications, since a single unsafe decision in settings such as dosage selection or autonomous driving can have catastrophic consequences. A common way to model safety in bandit problems is to associate each action with both a reward signal and a cost signal, and to optimize reward subject to constraints on cost. Most existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring the expected cost of each action to remain below a prescribed threshold. However, this may be insufficient in heteroscedastic settings, where the chosen action affects not only the expected reward and cost, but also the variability of the observed outcomes. We study contextual bandits with one-dimensional continuous actions and stage-wise high-probability constraints on the realized cost. We propose High-Probability Constrained UCB, an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. For linear reward and cost models, we prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, and we extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experiments show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.

AI.tldr: High-Probability Constrained UCB for contextual bandits with realized-cost safety; achieves near-optimal regret in linear settings and extends to general function classes via eluder dimension; empirically reduces safety violations.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical sequential decision making under heteroscedastic outcomes. Existing safety constraints based on expected costs may be insufficient when variability depends on actions.
AI.method: High-Probability Constrained UCB: an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set under stage-wise high-probability cost constraints; applicable to one-dimensional continuous actions; analyzes linear reward and cost models and extends to general function classes via eluder dimension.
AI.result: For linear models, establishes a tight tilde-O(d sqrt(T)) regret bound; extends to general function classes using eluder dimension; experiments show enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces safety violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.
AI.conclusion: Realized-cost safety constraints provide stronger guarantees in heteroscedastic settings; the proposed HPC-UCB approach delivers both near-optimal regret and practical safety improvements, with broader applicability through eluder-dimension analysis.

title: FlashVLA: Streaming Action Decoding for Fast and Asynchronous VLA Inference
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are increasingly promising for robotic manipulation, yet their real-world deployment remains bottlenecked by high inference latency and unstable asynchronous execution. This challenge is particularly pronounced in flow-matching-based VLA models, where action decoding requires multiple iterative steps conditioned on the VLM context. While efficient inference methods improve control frequency and asynchronous methods reduce execution idle time, existing approaches often fail to jointly achieve low-latency inference and accurate, temporally consistent asynchronous execution. We introduce \textbf{FlashVLA}, a streaming action decoding framework that addresses both challenges in a unified formulation. FlashVLA maintains a streaming action buffer with multiple chunks at different noise levels and decodes them using chunk-wise causal attention. This design allows FlashVLA to produce one executable action chunk per inference step. Moreover, its chunk-wise autoregressive formulation implicitly preserves action continuity, enabling smooth asynchronous execution without extra future-state conditioning. Across extensive simulated and real-world experiments, FlashVLA substantially improves inference speed while maintaining strong task performance. It can achieve $\geq$30\,Hz control frequency on a single GPU with smooth asynchronous inference in real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: FlashVLA introduces a streaming action decoding framework for Vision-Language-Action models that achieves low-latency, temporally coherent execution by using a streaming buffer with chunk-wise causal attention, delivering one executable action chunk per inference step and reaching ≥30 Hz on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: High inference latency and unstable asynchronous execution hinder real-world deployment of flow-matching VLA models in robotic manipulation, due to iterative action decoding conditioned on VLM context.
AI.method: Proposes FlashVLA with a streaming action buffer containing multiple chunks at different noise levels and chunk-wise causal attention. It decodes one executable action chunk per inference step and uses a chunk-wise autoregressive formulation to preserve action continuity without requiring future-state conditioning.
AI.result: Significant speedup in inference while preserving task performance; demonstrates ≥30 Hz control frequency on a single GPU with smooth asynchronous inference in real-world deployment, validated across extensive simulations and real robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework that jointly achieves low-latency inference and stable asynchronous execution for VLA models, enabling practical real-world robotic manipulation with flow-matching approaches.

title: GeoMAD: Geometry-Aware Multi-View Anomaly Detection via Deformable Fusion and Distributional Alignment
summary: Multi-view anomaly detection (MvAD) detects defects by exploiting complementary observations from multiple camera viewpoints. The central challenge is to fuse views with sufficient geometric awareness while remaining scalable to multi-class industrial settings. Existing methods typically fall into two extremes: voxel-based fusion provides explicit geometric alignment but requires costly 3D construction and class-specific assumptions, whereas lightweight patch-based fusion is efficient but relies on discrete candidate matching and lacks continuous cross-view correspondence. In this paper, we propose GeoMAD, a unified multi-view, multi-class AD framework that addresses both geometric correspondence deficiency and distributional inconsistency. Our \textit{Cross-view Deformable Fusion Module} (CDFM) learns content-adaptive, view-pair-specific sampling offsets directly on 2D feature maps and arranges them across a multi-scale window pyramid with image-global reference sampling, enabling hierarchical cross-view correspondence without camera calibration, voxel construction, or class-specific 3D supervision. We further introduce \textit{Distributional View Alignment} (DVA), a self-supervised cross-view regularization loss that aligns each view's bottleneck distribution against a per-instance view-centric target, enforcing global consistency without pixel-level correspondence. Together, CDFM and DVA bridge local geometric correspondence and global distributional consistency, providing geometry-aware and distribution-consistent fusion while preserving the efficiency of 2D feature-space learning. Extensive experiments on Real-IAD and MANTA-Tiny show that GeoMAD achieves strong detection and localization performance in unified MvAD.

AI.tldr: GeoMAD is a unified multi-view, multi-class anomaly detection framework that combines a cross-view deformable fusion module for geometry-aware 2D feature fusion with a self-supervised distributional view alignment to enforce global consistency, achieving scalable, calibration-free, multi-class anomaly detection and localization.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap between voxel-based fusion (high geometric alignment cost and class-specific constraints) and patch-based fusion (efficient but with discrete matching and incomplete cross-view correspondence) by enabling continuous, content-adaptive cross-view fusion in 2D feature space without 3D supervision or camera calibration.
AI.method: Introduces Cross-view Deformable Fusion Module (CDFM) that learns content-adaptive, view-pair-specific sampling offsets on 2D feature maps and arranges them in a multi-scale window pyramid with image-global reference sampling to establish cross-view correspondence; introduces Distributional View Alignment (DVA), a self-supervised cross-view regularization that aligns each view's bottleneck distribution to a per-instance view-centric target for global consistency across views.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Real-IAD and MANTA-Tiny show GeoMAD achieves strong detection and localization performance in unified multi-view anomaly detection across multiple classes.
AI.conclusion: GeoMAD provides geometry-aware and distribution-consistent fusion in a scalable, calibration-free 2D feature-space framework for multi-view, multi-class anomaly detection and localization, bridging local cross-view correspondence and global distributional consistency.

title: LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.

AI.tldr: A problem-driven survey of LLM-based agents for time-series, organizing systems by the time-series task rather than components; four categories; analyzes how task requirements shape architecture, tools, and memory; summarizes datasets/environments and performance; provides a task-oriented design guide and identifies open gaps.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for time-series vary across tasks; existing work is component-driven and fragmented; a task-centric taxonomy can better inform design, evaluation, and reuse.
AI.method: Proposes a taxonomy based on time-series problems. Classifies existing systems into forecasting and reasoning; augmentation and synthesis; anomaly detection and diagnosis; and decision support. Examines task-driven influences on architecture, tool usage, and memory. Compiles representative datasets/environments and compares performance under shared settings.
AI.result: A task-oriented design guide for LLM-based time-series agents; mapping of datasets/environments; cross-task performance comparisons; identification of gaps and future directions.
AI.conclusion: The survey advances practical guidance for building LLM-based time-series agents and highlights open research gaps, especially in standard benchmarks and cross-task evaluations.

title: Beyond Client Averaging: A Client-Independent Second-Order Stationary-Bias Component in Stochastic SCAFFOLD
summary:
Existing constant-step analysis of stochastic \Scaf{} identifies a leading $O(γ/N)$ stationary mean bias and shows that higher-order bias can persist as the client count increases, but does not identify the first client-independent contribution at coefficient level. For full-participation stochastic \Scaf{} with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count $H$, and bounded additive gradient noise, we prove, uniformly over $N\ge2$,
  $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{π_{γ,N,H}}[x]-x^\star ={}& -\frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{4f''(x^\star)^2}\fracγ{N}\\ &- \frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{12f''(x^\star)} \frac{(H-1)(5H-1)}{H}γ^2 +O_H\!\left(\frac{γ^2}{N}+γ^3\right). \end{aligned} $$
  Hence client averaging suppresses the leading $O(γ/N)$ bias but does not remove the client-independent $O(γ^2)$ component when its coefficient is nonzero.
  The mechanism is indirect: although the direct control contribution cancels pathwise in the linear global average, the controls still alter within-round local trajectories and their second moments. Fresh gradient noise and persistent control fluctuations therefore generate local second-moment corrections that nonquadratic curvature converts into stationary mean bias. The coefficient vanishes for quadratic objectives. Numerical experiments are consistent with the predicted coefficient, its persistence as client count increases, and the stated joint remainder. The result is restricted to the one-dimensional homogeneous fixed-$H$ setting.

AI.tldr: Identifies the first client-independent contribution to stationary mean bias in full-participation stochastic Scaf with one-dimensional homogeneous clients; shows averaging reduces leading bias O(γ/N) but leaves a nonzero O(γ^2) term unless the objective is quadratic; provides uniform bound over N≥2.
AI.motivation: Understand remaining bias sources in constant-step stochastic Scaf under realistic nonquadratic objectives and client averaging; quantify how local steps and gradient noise interact with curvature to produce stationary bias, beyond the leading γ/N term.
AI.method: Analytical derivation in a one-dimensional, homogeneous client setting with fixed local-step count H, full participation, and bounded additive gradient noise. Uses Taylor expansion around x*, analysis of the stationary distribution π_{γ,N,H}, and uniform bounds to derive E[x]-x* up to higher-order terms. Expresses bias in terms of curvature f''(x*), f'''(x*), step size γ, noise variance σ^2, and H.
AI.result: The stationary mean bias satisfies E[x]-x* = - (f'''(x*) σ^2)/(4 f''(x*)^2) * (γ/N) - (f'''(x*) σ^2)/(12 f''(x*)) * ((H-1)(5H-1)/H) * γ^2 + O_H( γ^2/N + γ^3 ). The leading O(γ/N) term is suppressed by client averaging, but a client-independent O(γ^2) term generally remains when its coefficient is nonzero. The γ^2 term vanishes for quadratic objectives (f'''=0) or when H=1. The remainder is uniformly O(γ^2/N + γ^3).
AI.conclusion: Client averaging reduces the leading γ/N bias but does not eliminate the O(γ^2) component that arises from nonquadratic curvature and gradient-noise interactions, yielding a persistent client-independent bias unless the objective is quadratic or the local-step count is minimal (H=1). The mechanism is via induced second-moment corrections within rounds, not direct pathwise contributions. Numerical experiments align with the theoretical coefficients and remainder; the result is currently restricted to the one-dimensional, homogeneous, fixed-H setting.

title: CLAP: Cross-Embodiment Video World Models are Zero-Shot Physical Simulators
summary: State-of-the-art action-conditioned video models are typically restricted to a single robot embodiment, preventing them from leveraging the vast corpus of heterogeneous video data that contains rich signals for learning generalizable physics. To bridge this gap, we introduce CLAP, a framework for cross-embodiment action-conditioned video generation capable of being trained on diverse, internet-scale videos across human and robotic agents. CLAP is grounded in the insight that universal physical laws govern spatiotemporal dynamics regardless of the actor. However, cross-embodiment learning is non-trivial because action representations vary sharply across robot platforms and are typically absent in human videos. CLAP addresses this fundamental challenge through the following core contributions. First, CLAP reconciles disparate action spaces using end-effector poses, language instructions, and latent actions. Second, to resolve their individual limitations, CLAP introduces a curriculum-based cross-embodiment learning recipe that first learns foundational physical priors across unlabeled video data using latent actions and subsequently grounds them in end-effector action spaces for zero-shot deployment to real-world tasks. Crucially, CLAP approaches or surpasses state-of-the-art single-embodiment video models in challenging environments like DROID. These performance advantages compound via few-shot adaptation to establish a novel paradigm for training single-embodiment video world models. Ultimately, CLAP delivers the most comprehensive suite of action-conditioned video world models to date - spanning diverse action-conditioning spaces (end-effector, language, and latent) and robot morphologies (including cross-embodiment, DROID, Bridge, bimanual YAM robots, and G1 humanoids). We open-source all code and models. Project Website at https://omni-clap.github.io .

AI.tldr: CLAP enables cross-embodiment action-conditioned video generation by learning universal physical priors from diverse, unlabeled videos and grounding multiple action representations (end-effector poses, language, and latent actions) across varied robot morphologies. It matches or surpasses state-of-the-art single-embodiment models, supports zero-shot deployment and few-shot adaptation, and is open-sourced.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitation of single-embodiment video models by exploiting diverse, internet-scale video data to learn generalizable physics for action-conditioned video generation across humans and robots.
AI.method: A curriculum-based cross-embodiment learning pipeline that (i) reconciles disparate action spaces using end-effector poses, language instructions, and latent actions; (ii) first learns foundational physical priors from unlabeled video data with latent actions, then grounds them in end-effector action spaces for zero-shot deployment; (iii) trains across diverse morphologies (including cross-embodiment, DROID, Bridge, bimanual YAM, G1 humanoids).
AI.result: CLAP matches or surpasses state-of-the-art single-embodiment video models in challenging environments (e.g., DROID); performance compounds with few-shot adaptation; delivers a broad suite of action-conditioned video world models across multiple conditioning spaces and morphologies; open-source code and models with a project website.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that universal physical laws governing spatiotemporal dynamics enable robust cross-embodiment video generation; introduces a practical training paradigm for action-conditioned video world models that integrate human and robotic agents, paving the way for broader generalization and deployment.

title: Generative Semantic Scene Completion
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary material (29 pages) is included as an ancillary file. Project page: https://shichen.world/GSSC-project-page/ - Code, models and the PS$^3$ dataset: https://github.com/BillyChern/GSSC-S2D2
summary: Outdoor LiDAR semantic scene completion (SSC) recovers a dense semantic voxel grid from a scan observing 1% of the target volume, under class imbalance beyond 7,000x. We recast SSC as generative semantic scene completion (GSSC): a single discrete-diffusion formulation in three roles. First, paired sparse-dense scene synthesis (PS$^3$) generates matched sparse LiDAR observations with their dense semantic completions, addressing the long tail at its source and yielding the PS$^3$-SemanticKITTI corpus we train on alongside SemanticKITTI. Second, semantic-guided generative scene completion (SGSC) generates the scene from noise with multinomial discrete diffusion, conditioned on the sparse scan through a bird's-eye-view semantic map and a sparse 3D feature stream. Third, the same framework instead refines an existing completion in one flow-matching step: structured source discrete diffusion (S$^2$D$^2$). S$^2$D$^2$ improves the mIoU of SGSC's own output and every external SSC base tested, without base retraining or test-time adaptation. On the strongest base, one step without test-time augmentation reaches 38.8% mIoU on the SemanticKITTI hidden test. To our knowledge that is the best causal, single-sweep, single-sample result on that leaderboard, +2.1 pp over the previous best published score under the same restriction. Four correction steps with eight-view test-time augmentation reach 39.2%, outside that restriction.

AI.tldr: Generative diffusion-based SSC for outdoor LiDAR; introduces PS^3-SemanticKITTI dataset, SGSC, and S^2D^2 refinement; achieves state-of-the-art mIoU on SemanticKITTI with 38.8% single-step, 39.2% with augmentation.
AI.motivation: Overcome severe data sparsity and extreme class imbalance in outdoor LiDAR SSC; leverage discrete diffusion to generate dense semantic scenes from sparse scans; provide paired data to train robust models; improve upon existing SSC pipelines without retraining.
AI.method: Three-part framework: (1) PS^3 for paired sparse-dense scene synthesis producing matched sparse observations with dense semantic completions, creating PS^3-SemanticKITTI; (2) SGSC a multinomial discrete diffusion conditioned on sparse BEV semantic map and 3D features to generate complete scene from noise; (3) S^2D^2 a refinement step that updates an existing completion in one flow-matching step, not requiring base retraining; tested on SemanticKITTI; one-step inference yields 38.8% mIoU; four-step with eight-view TTA yields 39.2%.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines; best single-step mIoU 38.8% on hidden test, +2.1 pp vs prior under same restriction; PS^3-SemanticKITTI enables training; S^2D^2 improves mIoU across SGSC and external SSC bases; no test-time adaptation required for S^2D^2 and base retraining not needed.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion-based SSC is effective for outdoor LiDAR; single-sweep, causal results reach state-of-the-art under restrictions; refinement flow can boost results; dataset extension PS^3-SemanticKITTI broadens training data; results indicate robust handling of class imbalance and sparse observations.

title: The Reasoning Tax: Token Economics of LLM Reasoning Across Task Types and Deployment Contexts
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures and tables, accepted at the 2026 TPCTC Conference and will be published at Performance Evaluation and Benchmarking (Springer)
summary: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable large language models misses a central deployment question: when do extended thinking tokens earn their cost? We introduce the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric that measures the accuracy gain of a reasoning model over a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token multiplier. We define paired and approximated TES variants for model families with reasoning toggles and frontier models without direct non-reasoning counterparts. We then conduct an empirical benchmarking analysis across 151 model-benchmark evaluation runs on seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, and research-level physics. The analysis examines three deployment-facing dimensions: which task structures yield positive marginal reasoning efficiency, how increasing reasoning effort changes TES within model families, and how deployment context changes economic viability. Results show that task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty: sequential inferencechain tasks such as AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench show high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks such as MMLU-Pro show low TES despite their difficulty. We also find systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. Finally, Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) shows that inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) shows how on-premises deployment can change the economics of otherwise costly reasoning workloads. These findings support a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treating it as a universally beneficial mode.

AI.tldr: Introduces Token Economy Score (TES) to quantify the marginal accuracy gain from reasoning in LLMs relative to a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token cost; validates across 151 runs on seven benchmarks; finds that task structure and deployment context strongly influence TES; recommends selective enablement of reasoning by task, effort, and deployment context.
AI.motivation: Accuracy-only benchmarks ignore deployment costs and context; a marginal, token-aware metric is needed to decide when extended reasoning tokens are economical.
AI.method: Define TES as the accuracy gain of a reasoning-enabled model over a non-reasoning baseline, divided by the generated-token multiplier. Develop paired and approximated TES variants for models with reasoning toggles and frontier models lacking a non-reasoning counterpart. Benchmark 151 model–benchmark runs across seven domains (math, code, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, physics). Analyze deployment-facing dimensions: task structure effectiveness, how TES changes with reasoning effort within families, and how deployment context affects economics. Introduce Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) and Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM).
AI.result: Task structure (e.g., sequential inference chains) predicts TES better than nominal difficulty; sequential tasks like AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench yield high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks (e.g., MMLU-Pro) show low TES despite difficulty. TES exhibits diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort, including cases where more thinking lowers accuracy. RCS indicates most inference cost is internal thinking; DCM shows on-prem deployment can alter economics of costly reasoning workloads. Outcome supports a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, required effort, and deployment context rather than assuming universal benefit.
AI.conclusion: TES provides a deployment-aware metric to guide model selection for reasoning; use reasoning where it improves efficiency and effectiveness, and avoid it where marginal gains do not justify cost.

title: On the Indistinguishability of Human v/s AI Generated Text
summary: The rapid improvement of LLMs has made distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing a pressing problem. This challenge is further amplified by paraphrasing tools designed to make machine-generated text appear more "human". We study how access to human writing samples can be used to strategically paraphrase machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Under a multi-sample setting with human and machine responses to the same prompts, we show that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution under simple mixing and stability conditions. Our results derive an explicit convergence rate, extend the analysis to a finite-sample setting, and characterize how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with the desired error.

AI.tldr: Repeated paraphrasing of machine-generated text using human samples converges the machine distribution to the human empirical distribution; explicit rate; finite-sample analysis; scaling laws for human samples and paraphrase rounds.
AI.motivation: Address AI-human text discrimination; examine whether paraphrasing can align machine outputs with human-like style when human samples are available; quantify how many human samples and paraphrase iterations are needed.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis under a multi-sample setting with prompts; model paraphrasing as a mixing/stability operator; prove convergence of the machine distribution to the empirical human distribution; derive convergence rate; extend to finite-sample setting; analyze how sample size and rounds affect error.
AI.result: Under simple mixing and stability assumptions, repeated paraphrasing drives the machine distribution toward the human distribution; the paper provides an explicit convergence rate and finite-sample guarantees; scaling laws for required human samples and paraphrase rounds as a function of target error.
AI.conclusion: Paraphrasing guided by human samples can approximate human-like text distribution with provable rates; results illuminate data collection and process design; future work should relax assumptions and validate empirically.

title: G2D: Generative-to-Discriminative Collaborative Inference for Zero-Shot Image Classification
comment: Accepted at ACM MM 2026. 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Zero-shot classification needs efficient label retrieval and fine-grained visual reasoning, yet discriminative and generative vision-language models fail in complementary ways.When CLIP's top-1 prediction is wrong, the correct label often remains in its top-$K$ shortlist, making disambiguation rather than recall the key challenge.Standalone generative models, however, are hindered by large label spaces and unconstrained outputs.This complementarity motivates separating broad candidate retrieval from fine-grained, image-grounded verification.We propose G2D, a training-free framework that uses a generative VLM to verify CLIP-retrieved candidates against the image.Candidate names and CLIP probabilities provide a structured prior for resolving visually similar classes.Fixed confidence routing, entropy-adaptive candidate sizing, and trie-constrained decoding focus generative reasoning on uncertain samples and ensure one valid output for each input at test time.Across eight benchmarks, G2D achieves 68.85% average accuracy, versus 59.35% for CLIP and 63.11% for the standalone VLM.Across seven generator configurations, candidate-set verification improves average accuracy by 1.08--27.42 percentage points.G2D also transfers to DCLIP, WaffleCLIP, and CuPL, supporting a practical interface between discriminative proposal and generative visual reasoning. Code: https://github.com/Harzva/G2D

AI.tldr: G2D combines discriminative retrieval with a training-free generative verifier to re-rank CLIP-retrieved candidates using image-grounded verification, improving zero-shot classification accuracy across benchmarks and enabling transfer to other VLMs.
AI.motivation: Discriminative models can fail on top-1 errors though correct labels lie in top-K; generative models struggle with large label spaces and unconstrained outputs. A separation of broad candidate retrieval from fine-grained verification can leverage strengths of both.
AI.method: A two-stage, training-free pipeline: (1) CLIP retrieves a short candidate-set with probabilities; (2) a generative VLM verifies each candidate against the image using a structured prior from candidate names and CLIP probabilities. The system employs fixed confidence routing, entropy-adaptive candidate sizing, and trie-constrained decoding to produce a single valid output per input.
AI.result: On eight benchmarks, G2D attains 68.85% average accuracy vs 59.35% for CLIP and 63.11% for the standalone VLM. Across seven generator configurations, candidate-set verification yields 1.08–27.42 point gains. G2D also transfers to DCLIP, WaffleCLIP, and CuPL. Code available.
AI.conclusion: Separating candidate retrieval from generative verification yields practical, training-free gains, enabling tight coupling between discriminative proposals and generative visual reasoning and broad transfer to other VLMs.

title: 6.5% of the Neuro-Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation
summary: We present a six-stage framework for auditing the reproducibility of scientific claims across a research literature within the computer science domain, and instantiate our framework for the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) subdomain. Instantiating the framework on the NSAI subdomain produced a multi-year audit. Stage one retrieved 5,497 records and removed 3,018 duplicates. Stage two screened the 2,479 unique records at title and abstract, identifying 1,365 self-identified NSAI records, then removed a further 61 at full text for off-topic, non-research, no-quantitative-evaluation, or inaccessible-full-text reasons. Stage three sought a verifiable public code artifact for each of the 1,304 eligible records and found none for 849, leaving 455 to enter the artifact inventory and bounded rerun of stages four and five. We fully or partially reproduced 85 studies, 6.52% of the eligible corpus and 18.68% of attempted reruns. We found that 321 attempted reruns were blocked by missing non- code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories. These figures quantify a persistent reproducibility deficit that survives even nominal "code available" declarations, and signal the need for enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles in future NSAI publications. We argue that empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles.

AI.tldr: A six-stage framework to audit reproducibility in CS, applied to neuro-symbolic AI; finds sizable reproducibility deficits despite stated code availability and argues for mandatory, versioned, archived artifact bundles.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility in NSAI literature is limited and external code availability declarations do not guarantee reproducibility; a scalable audit is needed to quantify the deficit and guide policy.
AI.method: Six-stage framework: (1) retrieve records and deduplicate; (2) screen for NSAI relevance; (3) locate verifiable public code; (4) build artifact inventory; (5) bounded rerun of stages; (6) attempt full/partial reproduction and quantify results.
AI.result: From 5,497 records retrieved (3,018 duplicates removed); 2,479 unique after dedup; 1,365 self-identified NSAI; 61 excluded at full text; 1,304 eligible; 849 with missing artifacts; 455 enter artifact inventory; 85 studies reproduced (6.52% of eligible corpus; 18.68% of attempted reruns); 321 reruns blocked by missing non-code artifacts; 42 by missing/unusable code repos.
AI.conclusion: There is a persistent reproducibility deficit in NSAI literature; enforce versioned, permanently archived artifact bundles; empirical NSAI papers should provide complete artifact bundles at submission to improve reproducibility.

title: SAGE: Variate-Wise Semantic Augmentation for Vision-Language Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences, lacking the semantic knowledge that domain experts implicitly leverage, such as the physical meaning of each variable, its statistical behavior, and its temporal dynamics. Recent efforts to bridge this gap fall into two camps. Some rely on large language models at inference time, which is computationally expensive. Others apply uniform textual prompts at the dataset level, ignoring the heterogeneous semantics across individual variates. We propose SAGE (Seeing and Augmenting with Grounded Encoding), an end-to-end CLIP-based framework that jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information. The CLIP text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, while gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and statistical descriptors. In parallel, the frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through a training-only contrastive objective. This dual use of CLIP adds complementary semantic and visual supervision without placing an LLM in the forecasting loop. Across eight long-term benchmarks and M4, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Ablations confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a CLIP-based, end-to-end multimodal framework for multivariate time series forecasting that enhances semantic understanding by grounding textual and visual modalities at the variable level, avoiding LLMs in the loop, and achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: To close the semantic gap in time series forecasting by leveraging domain-level information about variables, their statistics, and dynamics, addressing limitations of LLM-in-the-loop and dataset-wide prompts that ignore variable heterogeneity.
AI.method: jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information using a CLIP-based setup: a text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and per-variable tokens; gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and descriptors; a frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations via a training-time contrastive objective; end-to-end training without an LLM in the loop.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on eight long-term benchmarks plus the M4 dataset; ablation studies show the complementary contributions of multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Grounding time series forecasting in multimodal semantic and visual representations improves accuracy, reduces dependence on large language models, and validates the value of per-variable semantics in forecasting.

title: Glass Surface Detection Grounded in 3D Visual Geometry
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Glass surface detection (GSD) is critical for scene understanding and reconstruction, and yet remains challenging due to the transparency and reflectivity of glass surfaces. Existing GSD methods typically rely on 2D appearance cues, which may fail in geometrically ambiguous scenes. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift: grounding GSD in 3D visual geometry to explicitly model the physical existence of glass surfaces. Our method first distills rich 3D priors from the visual geometry grounded transformer (VGGT) and generates glass-aware 3D representations. It then exploits multi-tasking learning with a novel glass detection head, consisting of two core modules: a Frequency Self-Attention Module (FSAM) that identifies glass-specific spectral features for glass surface localization, and a Geometry Grounding Block (GeGB) that selectively grounds 2D features in 3D geometry for glass surface segmentation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven standard GSD benchmarks, generalizes well to video/multi-modal data, and substantially improves reconstruction in glass scenes. Code is available in https://github.com/YT3DVision/VGGT_GLASS.

AI.tldr: Grounds Glass Surface Detection (GSD) in 3D geometry by distilling VGGT priors and introducing glass-specific 2D-3D fusion modules, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with good cross-modal generalization.
AI.motivation: 2D appearance cues are insufficient for transparent/occlusive glass surfaces due to geometric ambiguity; leveraging 3D visual geometry priors can explicitly model the physical existence of glass and improve robustness.
AI.method: Distill 3D priors from Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) to form glass-aware 3D representations. Employ a multi-task glass detection head with two modules: (1) Frequency Self-Attention Module (FSAM) to identify glass-specific spectral features, and (2) Geometry Grounding Block (GeGB) to ground 2D features into 3D geometry for segmentation.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on seven standard GSD benchmarks, demonstrates strong generalization to video and multi-modal data, and substantially improves reconstruction quality in glass scenes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 3D-geometry grounded approach with FSAM and GeGB effectively leverages 3D priors and spectral cues to robustly detect glass surfaces across diverse settings, enabling improved scene understanding and reconstruction; code is released.

title: SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents executing complex, long-running procedural skills. Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history. Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

AI.tldr: Replaces append-only histories with a mutable, explicit execution state (SKILL.state) for long-horizon LLM agents, improving accuracy and dramatically reducing token consumption.
AI.motivation: Tackle latency and context-poisoning from growing prompt histories in autonomous procedural agents; enable scalable, long-duration reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce a runtime that, at each step, provides the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation; discard intermediate reasoning after a validated state update; architecture-agnostic and evaluated across diverse datasets, models, and environments.
AI.result: Improved task accuracy across settings and substantial reduction in cumulative token usage, demonstrating scalability of explicit execution state.
AI.conclusion: Explicit execution state is an effective, architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills, mitigating prompt growth and latency.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Control of CAV Platoon Joining Maneuvers in Mixed Traffic
summary: Connected and automated vehicle (CAV) platooning offers a promising approach to improving road safety and traffic capacity. However, platoon control in real-world traffic is challenging due to uncertainty and heterogeneous driving behaviors. Reinforcement learning (RL) has strong potential for addressing such control problems, but its practical deployment raises challenges related to safety and learning efficiency. This paper proposes a generic modeling and simulation framework for investigating CAV platoon joining maneuvers and comparing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control algorithms. The problem is particularly challenging in mixed-traffic environments, where CAVs coexist with human-driven vehicles exhibiting heterogeneous longitudinal and lateral behaviors. The objective is to achieve safe and efficient joining maneuvers by either incorporating penalties for risky behaviors into the learning process or using an external safety controller to constrain the learned policy. An agent-based modeling framework coupled with the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) simulator is used to evaluate Deep Q-Network (DQN), Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Results show that PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN, achieving a joining success rate of approximately 98 % and a collision rate below 1 %, largely due to risk-related penalties incorporated into the reward function. However, this improved performance requires more decision steps to complete the maneuver, revealing a trade-off between safety, joining effectiveness, and decision efficiency. An external safety controller effectively prevents collisions, although its interventions may reduce joining efficiency. The results highlight the importance of jointly considering safety and efficiency when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic.

AI.tldr: PPO-based DRL framework for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic; PPO outperforms DQN/DDQN; safety penalties or external safety controller to ensure collision-free joining; trade-offs between safety, efficiency, and decision steps.
AI.motivation: Address safety and efficiency in CAV platoon joining under uncertainty and heterogeneity of human-driven vehicles; evaluate DRL algorithms in a realistic mixed-traffic setting.
AI.method: Agent-based modeling with SUMO; compare DQN, DDQN, PPO for platoon joining; incorporate risk penalties or external safety controller; evaluate performance metrics (joining success rate, collision rate, decision steps).
AI.result: PPO achieves ~98% joining success and <1% collisions; longer decision horizon; risk penalties essential; external safety controller prevents collisions but may reduce joining efficiency.
AI.conclusion: RL-based platoon joining can be safe and efficient when appropriately reward-penalized or constrained; safety-efficiency trade-offs are critical; external safety controllers are effective but may impede performance; framework supports systematic evaluation in mixed traffic.

title: Cross-Architecture Knowledge Distillation from a Vision Foundation Model to a Lightweight Visual State Space Model for Tea Leaf Disease Classification
summary: Automated tea leaf disease classification supports precision agriculture, yet deploying accurate models on edge devices remains challenging under tight compute budgets. Self-supervised vision foundation models such as DINOv2 provide strong features but are too large for field deployment, while lightweight models trained from scratch on small agricultural datasets often underfit. We study cross-architecture knowledge distillation (KD) from a fine-tuned DINOv2 teacher (Vision Transformer) to a compact bidirectional Visual State Space Model (LVSSM) student, an underexplored direction because the architectures use fundamentally different token-mixing mechanisms. We identify and fix two training-stability problems that prevent the from-scratch SSM student from learning on limited data: a single large patch-embedding convolution and a fusion layer that severs the residual path. With a progressive convolutional stem and gated bidirectional selective-scan block, the 4.45M-parameter student trains stably. Across three seeds, temperature-scaled logit distillation raises test accuracy from 92.32+/-2.14% to 95.41+/-1.17% (best single run: 96.20%; macro-F1: 94.45%), a +3.09 percentage-point mean gain. The student uses 5.0 times fewer parameters than the 22M-parameter teacher while retaining 98.3% of its accuracy. Ablations show that intermediate feature-alignment losses reduce accuracy, making simple logit-level KD the strongest configuration. A fair from-scratch comparison shows the gain is specific to students that start below the teacher. We report per-class metrics, confusion matrices, bootstrap confidence intervals, and FLOPs/latency measurements, and discuss limitations including the single-dataset scope and simplified non-official SSM implementation.

AI.tldr: Cross-architecture KD from a DINOv2 teacher to a compact LVSSM student yields strong tea leaf disease classification on edge devices; logit distillation with stability fixes outperforms feature alignment; 4.45M vs 22M params; ~3.1 pp accuracy gain; single dataset, three seeds.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate edge deployment for automated tea leaf disease classification under tight compute budgets; investigate whether cross-architecture KD can bridge the gap between large foundation models and small edge models.
AI.method: Fine-tune DINOv2 ViT as teacher; train LVSSM student from scratch with KD; address training stability issues: (1) large patch-embedding conv; (2) fusion layer disrupting residual path; implement progressive convolutional stem; gated bidirectional selective-scan block; use temperature-scaled logit distillation; compare with intermediate feature-alignment losses; three seeds; measure accuracy, macro-F1, per-class metrics, confusion matrices, bootstrap CIs, FLOPs/latency; dataset limited to single tea-leaf dataset; fair comparison to teacher.
AI.result: Student achieves 95.41% test accuracy (mean, ±1.17) across three seeds; best run 96.20%; macro-F1 94.45%; 98.3% of teacher accuracy with 5.0x fewer parameters; three seeds show stability; ablations show feature-alignment losses reduce accuracy; logit KD is strongest; FLOPs/latency evaluated; limitations include single dataset and simplified SSM implementation.
AI.conclusion: Cross-architecture KD can efficiently transfer knowledge from large ViT teachers to compact SSM students for edge agriculture; with appropriate stability fixes and logit KD, performance approaches teacher with substantial parameter efficiency; results are promising but need broader datasets and official reproducibility of SSM implementation.

title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
comment: 46 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary information available on request from the authors
summary: Mentalization - the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions to guide one's own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit mentalizing-like behavior in two economic games; performance varies by model family and size, with prompting enhancing strategic reasoning; GPT-5 shows adaptive recursion depth and can exceed human performance in some tasks; cognitive computational modeling provides a formal framework for comparing intelligence across humans and machines.
AI.motivation: To determine whether large language models can guide adaptive behavior via mentalization and to compare mentalizing capacities across model providers and sizes, benchmarked against humans.
AI.method: Two economic games were used with cognitive computational modeling to reveal latent mentalizing strategies in LLMs. Four model families (DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Gemini 2.0 Flash) totaling N=2,099 agents were tested against opponents of varying sophistication. A prompting strategy aimed at eliciting strategic reasoning was evaluated. Human participants (N=251) were included as a reference group.
AI.result: LLMs displayed clear behavioral and computational signatures of mentalizing, with results varying by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, though effects differed by task. GPT-5 agents demonstrated flexible adaptation of recursive depth to opponents and outperformed humans in some settings.
AI.conclusion: There are differing mentalization capacities across LLMs. Cognitive computational modeling is a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines, enabling systematic evaluation of mentalizing capabilities and adaptation to opponents.

title: When Is the Sharp Covariance Envelope Tight? Feature-Only Geometry for Volume-Sampled Least Squares
summary: Prior analyses by Derezinski and Warmuth established all-size sampling identities, selected-OLS unbiasedness, and inverse moments for ordinary volume sampling, while their exact arbitrary-fixed-response loss and prediction-covariance formulas are at the rank-size endpoint s=d. We establish a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance for every full-rank fixed pool, response, and legal budget d <= s <= m under ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares; its coefficient is globally sharp over the full-rank class. Global sharpness does not determine attainability on the pool in hand. Under positive loss, strict-interior budgets, and no coloops, a feature-only margin nu_A gives the exact fixed-design spectral phase: nu_A > 0 if and only if the normalized spectral envelope is strict for every compatible residual, whereas nu_A = 0 if and only if some compatible residual is spectrally tight; the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget. A residual-augmented change of measure supplies the response-aware mechanism and a one-sided quantitative slack bound, while support saturation proves the attainment direction. Critical equal-leverage geometry interprets the boundary, and sound lower certificates yield conservative same-primitive cardinality decisions. Frozen-feature examples show that the certificate is nonvacuous and measure the fixed-pool cost of its authorized reduction. The claims concern conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance, not population generalization.

AI.tldr: Establishes a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance under full-rank fixed pools with ordinary fixed-size volume sampling and selected unweighted least squares; introduces a feature-margin nu_A that characterizes spectral phase, plus a residual-based change of measure and slack bounds; provides criteria for spectral strictness and attainability directions, with lower certificates and geometric interpretations; results pertain to conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened covariance rather than population generalization.
AI.motivation: To rigorously characterize the coefficient covariance and spectral properties of estimators derived from volume-sampled designs across a range of fixed budgets, and to provide verifiable certificates and interpretations for design decisions under fixed pools.
AI.method: Derive a Loewner envelope for the centered coefficient covariance across d ≤ s ≤ m for ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares; analyze global sharpness and attainability; introduce the feature-only margin nu_A to capture spectral-phase behavior; employ a residual-augmented change of measure to connect response and design, and use support saturation and equal-leverage geometry to obtain certificates and bounds; present frozen-feature examples to illustrate nonvacuity of the certificate.
