AI.result: The paper proves that nu_A > 0 iff the normalized spectral envelope is strict for every compatible residual, and nu_A = 0 iff some compatible residual is spectrally tight; the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget. It provides a one-sided quantitative slack bound, an attainment-direction result, and a set of geometric interpretations (critical equal-leverage geometry) with sound lower certificates that guide same-primitive cardinality decisions. The framework yields a conditional (design- and response-aware) view of the centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance, not population generalization.
AI.conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of coefficient-covariance structure under fixed-pool, volume-sampled designs by delivering exact spectral-phase criteria, certificates, and geometric interpretations, while remaining focused on the conditional, fixed-design covariance rather than population-level generalization; they also highlight limitations in equating global sharpness with attainability and provide tools for practical design decisions under budget constraints.

title: Decoupling Planning and Control for Instructable Agents
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. Project page: https://zinengtang.github.io/instruct-to-act/
summary: Recent work shows that pre-trained, instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) perform well at mapping from instructions and observations to high-level plans, but struggle to realize such plans as reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control, but lack open-ended task guidance. In this work, we combine these strengths into a single system, Instruct-to-Act, where we train a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, higher-latency, and high-level text instructions generated by a VLM planner. To train controllers to be language-instructable, we relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. We evaluate our proposed approach across seven embodied environments, including three multi-agent environments where VLM planners coordinate through language while trained controllers serve as their actuators. Under matched observation and action spaces, our decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants, preserves fast control, and lets us swap in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

AI.tldr: A decoupled Instruct-to-Act system combines a VLM planner with a fast world-model controller, trained via synthetic instruction relabeling, delivering low-latency, language-guided control across seven environments and competitive results with baselines.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between high-level, language-guided planning and low-latency, reliable action in unknown environments; enable language-instructable controllers and multi-agent coordination by leveraging strengths of VLM planners and world-model controllers.
AI.method: Train a world-model controller to act at high frequency conditioned on sparse, high-level text instructions from a VLM planner; relabel segments of controller rollouts with synthetic instructions; jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective plus reward-maximizing and world-modeling losses; maintain a decoupled architecture allowing swapping different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning.
AI.result: Outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants; preserves fast control; supports swapping VLM planners without fine-tuning; competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully combines language-guided planning with fast, autonomous control, showing robustness across single and multi-agent settings and offering a flexible, plug-and-play framework for integrating different VLM planners.

title: Ring Forcing: Towards Precise Long-Term Memory for Autoregressive Video Diffusion
summary: Scaling video generation to long durations reveals a critical bottleneck: current models lack robust long-term memory. This deficiency can be studied along two critical aspects: object permanence, the ability to precisely reproduce the appearance of objects upon re-entry; and memory capacity, the ability to process ultra-long context and use information from distant history. Robust long-term memory requires both: object permanence without sufficient context handling limits the temporal scope, while long context length without permanence fails to maintain identity. To address this, we present Ring Forcing, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed to robustly construct and precisely utilize long-term memory. Our ring-structured training strategy enforces retrieval from distant history, effectively reconciling the trade-off between strict historical adherence and generative diversity. To expand memory capacity, we introduce a compression and timestep composition strategy. Under fixed sequence length constraints, this method extends the effective historical span to minutes-long durations and achieves a comprehensive receptive field over the entire history. Furthermore, we present a sparse RoPE mechanism to enable flexible, scalable memory adaptation while fully exploiting pre-trained priors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Ring Forcing achieves superior minutes-long coherence and object permanence, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Introduces Ring Forcing, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed to enable robust long-term memory for minutes-long video generation. Key components include ring-structured training to enforce retrieval from distant history, a compression and timestep composition strategy to extend memory under fixed sequence length, and a sparse RoPE mechanism for scalable memory adaptation. Demonstrates improved minutes-long coherence and object permanence over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: To overcome two core bottlenecks in long-duration video generation: (1) object permanence—the ability to consistently reproduce the appearance of objects upon re-entry, and (2) memory capacity—the ability to process ultra-long context and utilize information from distant history. Under current models, these factors limit temporal coherence and identity preservation in long videos.
AI.method: Proposes Ring Forcing, an autoregressive video diffusion framework with (a) ring-structured training that forces retrieval from distant history to balance adherence and diversity, (b) a compression + timestep composition strategy to extend the effective historical span within fixed sequence lengths, and (c) a sparse Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) mechanism to enable scalable, flexible memory using pre-trained priors. This combination aims to construct and utilize long-term memory more robustly while maintaining tractable computation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show superior minutes-long coherence and object permanence, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art video generation methods.
AI.conclusion: Ring Forcing effectively reconciles long-term historical adherence with generative diversity, expanding memory capacity to minutes-long horizons and enabling robust object permanence in autoregressive video generation.

title: Approved Too Late: Verdict Staleness in LLM-Guarded Self-Adaptive Systems
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Autonomic Computing and Self-Organizing Systems (ACSOS 2026)
summary: A large language model (LLM) guardrail for a self-adaptive system (SAS) may issue an approval that is correct at check time but stale by actuation. This creates an Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazard. We study verdict freshness: whether a guardrail verdict remains valid when used. We distinguish three quantities that answer different questions: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. We introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon from its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without an explicit plant-dynamics model. Using fixed settings documented in the artifact, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. A separate audit of four LLM judges finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream. We formulate a freshness contract: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

AI.tldr: Proposes a freshness-aware guardrail for self-adaptive systems to mitigate time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazards in LLM-driven decisions. It defines three freshness metrics, evaluates them in five SAS environments, and introduces the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS) that estimates validity horizons without explicit plant models. FBS substantially reduces approval expiry, but judge behavior still induces use-time invalidity; the paper formalizes a freshness contract requiring veridical approvals at both check and use times.
AI.motivation: TOCTOU hazards arise when guardrail verdicts become stale by actuation in self-adaptive systems guided by large language models. Ensuring that approvals remain valid at use time is essential for safety and reliability.
AI.method: Define three freshness quantities: (i) all-candidate verdict-change under fixed-action replay; (ii) oracle-labeled expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories; (iii) judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Evaluate across five reproducible SAS environments with a replay shift of eight steps. Propose Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS) that estimates each approval's validity horizon from safe-side margin and recent feature volatility without explicit plant-dynamics modeling. Use fixed artifact settings for reproducibility. Audit four LLM judges to assess judge-conditioned invalidity.
AI.result: All-candidate verdict-change rates: 5.3–48.4% at shift eight. FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval expiry from 3.4–24.7% to 0–1.8% at the same shift. Four-judge audit reveals nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream.
AI.conclusion: A freshness contract is proposed: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time. FBS offers a practical, model-free method to bound verdict staleness, but judge behavior remains a source of risk; future work should further reduce judge-induced invalidity and explore integration with broader safety guarantees.

title: Mitigating Strong-Modality Collapse in Multimodal Learning via Inverted Asymmetric Fusion
summary: Fusing multiple modalities is expected to improve model performance. However, on the MultiHuSE dataset, early, late, and symmetric attention fusion often fail to outperform the best unimodal baseline (text). Pathway isolation of a symmetric attention fusion model reveals that the text-pathway accuracy drops from 74.9% to 56.4% after fusion in one such setting, indicating that the dominant modality can be degraded during integration. We term this strong-modality collapse and argue that it helps explain why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines. We propose Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF), which avoids forcing mutual attention across modalities. The dominant modality is preserved by passing through fusion unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as a contextual anchor. Before fusion, weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. We evaluate IAF on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies: text-dominant datasets (MultiHuSE, UR-FUNNY) and an audio-visual-dominant dataset (MUStARD). Pathway isolation shows that IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, whereas symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25%.

AI.tldr: Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) preserves the dominant modality during multimodal fusion by leaving it unchanged and using weaker modalities as context, aided by modality-aware knowledge distillation; it mitigates strong-modality collapse and improves over the best unimodal baselines across text- and audio-visual-dominant tasks.
AI.motivation: Strong-modality collapse in symmetric/early/late fusion degrades the dominant modality's performance and can prevent multimodal methods from surpassing unimodal baselines; this is observed on datasets like MultiHuSE where text accuracy drops substantially after fusion.
AI.method: Propose Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF): the dominant modality passes through fusion unchanged; weaker modalities attend to the dominant one as a contextual anchor. Weaker modalities are strengthened beforehand via Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. Evaluation conducted on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies (text-dominant and audio-visual-dominant). Pathway isolation used to assess modality preservation.
AI.result: IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across configurations; symmetric fusion can degrade it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF yields up to 8.25% improvement over the strongest unimodal baseline.
AI.conclusion: IAF offers a robust remedy to strong-modality collapse, enabling reliable multimodal gains by protecting the dominant modality while leveraging weaker modalities as contextual anchors; effective across diverse modality hierarchies and datasets.

title: CGS-SLAM: Collaborative Gaussian Splatting based SLAM for Multi-Agent Reconstruction
summary: Recent advances in SLAM have leveraged 3DGS for photorealistic reconstruction and novel view synthesis. However, most methods rely on RGB-D input, which is unavailable on consumer-grade smartphones, and few integrate 3DGS within a collaborative framework. Therefore, we present CGS-SLAM, a hybrid decentralized/centralized system enabling multi-agent 3DGS SLAM using only RGB and inertial data. Each agent performs local tracking with inertial data as a motion prior and reconstructs a scaled map using a metric monocular depth estimator (Depth Pro). Keyframe encodings are shared among agents, enabling dynamic keyframing in regions of spatial overlaps with other agents, enhancing submap alignment. Afterwards, a central server aligns submaps using VGGT as a view alignment model. This bidirectional communication keeps communication cost low during mapping and global reconstruction in difficult GNSS-denied environments. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate competitive tracking performance, improved rendering quality over state-of-the-art methods, and accurate submap alignment.

AI.tldr: Hybrid decentralized/centralized multi-agent SLAM using RGB and inertial data to enable 3DGS-based photorealistic mapping and novel view synthesis with low communication overhead.
AI.motivation: RGB-D input is often unavailable on consumer devices; existing 3DGS SLAM methods are typically single-agent and data-heavy. There is a need for collaborative SLAM that leverages 3DGS while minimizing bandwidth, suitable for GNSS-denied environments.
AI.method: Each agent performs local tracking with IMU as a motion prior and builds a scaled map using a metric monocular depth estimator (Depth Pro). Keyframe encodings are shared across agents to support dynamic keyframing in regions with spatial overlap, improving submap alignment. A central server aligns submaps using VGGT as a view alignment model. Bidirectional communication maintains low mapping bandwidth while enabling robust global reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple datasets show competitive tracking performance, improved rendering quality over state-of-the-art methods, and accurate submap alignment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CGS-SLAM demonstrates a viable hybrid architecture for multi-agent 3DGS SLAM with RGB+IMU input, achieving low communication cost and robust GNSS-denied global mapping, with strong rendering enhancements and submap alignment.

title: Multi-Image Visual Token Pruning in Large Visual Language Models
summary: With the growing demand for processing multiple image sequences in real-world applications, various visual token pruning methods have emerged to mitigate the computational and context length constraints faced by Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs). However, most existing pruning approaches rely on static strategies that struggle to adapt across different architectural LVLMs and multi-image scenarios, and are additionally constrained by their dependence on attention computations that are incompatible with efficient techniques like FlashAttention. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free, Adaptive Visual Token Pruning (AVTP) framework, applicable to diverse LVLM architectures. We strategically determine pruning layers based on empirical analysis of visual attention distributions across various LVLMs, and implement adaptive pruning ratios in multi-image contexts where images of higher importance retain proportionally more tokens. We conduct extensive experiments across different LVLMs to demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of AVTP. Specifically, Qwen3VL-8B achieves 2 times inference speedup while maintaining 96.1\% of its original accuracy on multiple multi-image benchmarks, InternVL3.5-8B retains 94.1\% accuracy, and LLaVA-OV-7B even exceeds its original baseline performance. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/zry13/AVTP}{this link}.

AI.tldr: Training-free Adaptive Visual Token Pruning (AVTP) reduces LVLM inference cost by adaptively pruning visual tokens across layers and images, achieving notable speedups with minimal or even improved accuracy across multiple LVLMs.
AI.motivation: LVLMs face high compute and long context due to processing multiple images; existing pruning methods are static and architecture-specific, and rely on attention computations incompatible with efficient variants like FlashAttention; need a training-free, architecture-agnostic pruning approach.
AI.method: AVTP determines pruning layers through empirical analysis of visual attention distributions across LVLMs; applies adaptive pruning ratios in multi-image contexts (more important images retain more tokens); designed to be training-free and compatible with various LVLM architectures; integrates with attention computations.
AI.result: Across benchmarks: Qwen3VL-8B ~2x speedup with 96.1% accuracy; InternVL3.5-8B 94.1% accuracy; LLaVA-OV-7B surpasses baseline; code release.
AI.conclusion: AVTP demonstrates robustness and effectiveness across architectures and multi-image scenarios; it enables faster inference with minimal loss or even gains; broad applicability without retraining; potential to accelerate LVLM deployment.

title: FaithSieve: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Math Proofs with Faithful Formal Evidence
comment: 32 pages, 3 figures; preprint with appendix and supplementary experimental details
summary: Large language models can now generate complex, multi-step mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation approaches largely depend on model-based natural-language judgments, which often overlook local reasoning gaps. While formal theorem provers like Lean offer a path to rigorous verification, using them to evaluate informal text requires solving locality and semantic mismatches: a prover might bypass a local flaw by proving an overly broad target, or validate an auto-formalized statement that drifts from the original mathematical intent. To address this, we introduce FaithSieve, a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs. FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring, so Lean evidence is incorporated only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the context, objects, and logical form of the original claim. We construct two expert-verified datasets, ProofLoc-Olympiad and ProofLoc-University, to benchmark first-error localization. On the 350-problem Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve using a GPT-5.4 backbone achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, outperforming the direct-judging baseline of 72.29%. Furthermore, on the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark spanning six advanced domains, FaithSieve reaches 84.5% exact accuracy, compared to 75.0% for the direct judge. Our work demonstrates that decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning.

AI.tldr: FaithSieve is a Lean-assisted framework that decomposes natural-language proofs into local units and grounds formal validation with semantic alignment, achieving superior first-error localization on math-proof datasets compared to direct judgment baselines.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of NL mathematical proofs rely on model-based judgments that miss local reasoning gaps. Formal provers offer rigorous verification but struggle with locality and drift between informal claims and formalized targets. A framework that aligns formal evidence with the original intent can improve error localization and evaluation reliability.
AI.method: Decompose coarse proof steps into fine-grained reasoning units, extract typed proof obligations, and verify them via a formal evaluation agent (Lean). Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring to ensure formal statements faithfully preserve context and logical form. Two expert-verified datasets (ProofLoc-Olympiad, ProofLoc-University) benchmark first-error localization across domains.
AI.result: On 350 Olympiad problems, FaithSieve (GPT-5.4 backbone) achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy vs 72.29% for direct judgment. On 200 ProofLoc-University problems across six domains, it reaches 84.5% vs 75.0% for direct judge, demonstrating improved reliability in NL mathematical reasoning evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained decomposition and faithful formal grounding significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of evaluating natural-language mathematical proofs, addressing locality and semantic drift issues in informal reasoning evaluations.

title: A Layer Importance Metric for Quantization Accounting for the Speed-Quality Trade-off in Autoregressive Models
summary: Small language models (sLLMs) are nowadays hosted on devices with limited memory and computational budget. In an autoregressive setup, inference is memory-bandwidth bound: uniform quantization is often detrimental to such models, since their architecture has limited redundancies and only a few layers are not very sensitive to lower precision. We propose a composite metric that combines two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured in terms of a normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using a roofline-based latency analysis). By profiling Gemma 3 1B, we find that Feed-Forward Network blocks and the embedding matrix are the most promising targets for acceleration. For each candidate, we estimate a normalized quality score based on simulated quantization and a normalized speed score based on roofline modeling with no actual execution needed. We combine the two scores in a composite priority coefficient, allowing us to tune the trade-off between speed and quality as needed. Our metric is general and can be used to prioritize individual blocks, their projection sublayers, or transformer layers as a whole. We evaluate our approach on several model architectures, showing that our estimates have at around 4% prediction error for the accelerated speedup. We find that our method generally allocates more resources to the most expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value-based approaches that require expensive approximate inference. Our analytical approach makes sLLM quantization a predictable engineering task.

AI.tldr: A composite metric combines information retention (SQNR-based) and throughput (roofline) to guide quantization/acceleration of sLLMs, prioritizing FFN blocks and embeddings; achieves ~4% speedup-prediction error; generally outperforms some baselines; enables predictable engineering for sLLM quantization.
AI.motivation: Reduce memory bandwidth bottlenecks and provide a predictable, general framework to quantify and prioritize quantization/acceleration targets in sLLMs, especially under strict device budgets.
AI.method: Profile a small language model (Gemma 3 1B) to identify high-impact blocks (FFN blocks, embedding matrix). Construct a composite score by normalizing a simulated-quantization quality metric (SQNR-based) and a roofline-derived speed metric. Combine into a composite priority coefficient to rank blocks or layers; do not execute on hardware but estimate. Validate across multiple architectures and compare against evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, and Shapley-value-based methods.
AI.result: The approach yields around 4% prediction error in accelerated speedup estimates. It tends to allocate more resources to expressive layers. The metric is general, applicable to blocks, projection sublayers, or transformer layers, and reportedly provides a predictable quantization/acceleration pathway without expensive inference.
AI.conclusion: An analytical, predictive metric framework for sLLM quantization that guides resource allocation toward the most expressive components, enabling predictable engineering and potentially better speedups with less search overhead.

title: SpatialCrafter: Single Image World Modeling with Generative 3D Proxies
summary: Explorable image-to-scene generation is essential for applications in gaming, robotics, and virtual reality. Existing methods based on video diffusion model (VDM) commonly rely on incomplete conditioning signals such as sparse point clouds or 2D panoramas, leading to stochastic hallucinations, long-term drifts and suboptimal 3D consistency. We present SpatialCrafter, a novel two-stage framework that addresses these issues by introducing a global 3D proxy for high-fidelity image-to-scene generation. Specifically, we decompose the generation process into global proxy generation and appearance refinement. For proxy generation, we propose a Point-anchored Sparse Structure~(PaSS) Flow module that predicts a spatially aligned and geometrically consistent 3D proxy. For appearance refinement, we re-frame the VDM as a Generative Deferred Refiner which synthesizes high-frequency photorealistic details upon proxy-defined scene geometry. To better integrate the proxy with the pre-trained VDM, we introduce Parallel Geometry Injection and Proxy-Aware Corruption training strategies, which improve robustness to proxy artifacts without disrupting the pretrained generative manifold. Furthermore, as no suitable dataset exists for this explorable scene generation task, we construct a new large-scale dataset of 115K scenes. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first hybrid dataset for image-to-scene generation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that SpatialCrafter outperforms state-of-the-art methods, mitigates long-term drift, and remains robust and consistent under rapid camera motion and extreme viewpoint changes. Code, models, and the newly constructed dataset will be publicly released. See more at https://fangchuan.github.io/SpatialCrafter/.

AI.tldr: SpatialCrafter introduces a two-stage framework for explorable image-to-scene generation using a global 3D proxy. It decouples geometry and appearance via PaSS Flow for proxy generation and a Generative Deferred Refiner for refinement, with training strategies to integrate proxies with pretrained diffusion models. It also provides a new 115K-scene hybrid dataset and demonstrates improved 3D consistency and robustness over SOTA.
AI.motivation: Existing VDM-based image-to-scene methods rely on incomplete conditioning (e.g., sparse point clouds, 2D panoramas), causing stochastic hallucinations, drift over time, and weak 3D consistency. A global 3D proxy can anchor geometry and reduce drift while enabling high-fidelity appearance.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) global proxy generation using PaSS Flow (Point-anchored Sparse Structure Flow) to produce a spatially aligned, geometrically consistent 3D proxy; (2) appearance refinement by reframing the diffusion model as a Generative Deferred Refiner that adds high-frequency details onto proxy-defined geometry. To integrate with pretrained VDMs, introduce Parallel Geometry Injection and Proxy-Aware Corruption training strategies that improve robustness to proxy artifacts. Additionally, construct a large-scale dataset of 115K explorable scenes.
AI.result: SpatialCrafter outperforms state-of-the-art on synthetic and real datasets, mitigating long-term drift and maintaining robustness under rapid camera motion and extreme viewpoint changes; demonstrates high 3D consistency and quality. Public release of code, models, and the 115K dataset.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling scene geometry and appearance via a global 3D proxy enables more faithful, stable explorable image-to-scene generation with better 3D consistency and resilience to viewpoint changes, supported by targeted training strategies and a new large-scale dataset.

title: Thinking on Shots: Consistent Multi-Shot Video Editing with Agentic Reasoning
comment: Project Page: https://wucy0519.github.io/MMLVE/ and see source codes at https://github.com/Wucy0519/MMLVE
summary: While generative AI has significantly advanced video editing, existing methods primarily focus on single-shot or short video clips. Editing long videos with multiple instructions remains a formidable challenge. Naive chunking strategies, e.g., fixed-duration segmentation, often lead to entity fragmentation, severe editing hallucinations, and disrupted temporal continuity. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Multi-Instruction Multi-Shot Long-Video Editing (MMLVE) task, which is structured around three core objectives: Cross-Shot Editing Consistency (CSEC), Multi-Instruction Decoupling (MID), and Zero-Destruction on Spatiotemporal Structure (ZDSS). To tackle these three unique challenges, we introduce an agentic editing framework that leverages the synergy of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to achieve shot-level video decoupling and precise instruction parsing. Furthermore, to comprehensively evaluate this task, we construct MMLVE-Bench, which is an MMLVE-focused dataset characterized by complex real-world spatiotemporal dynamics, high-density heterogeneous instructions, and sparse, random entity distributions. Three MMLVE-focused evaluation metrics are further exploited to assess the quality of the editing results. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our MMLVE-Agent outperforms existing closed-source SOTA approaches (e.g., Seedance 2.0), successfully eliminating editing hallucinations, preserving cross-shot editing consistency, and attaining seamless spatiotemporal transitions.

AI.tldr: Proposes Multi-Instruction Multi-Shot Long-Video Editing (MMLVE) to address long-video editing with multiple instructions, introducing an agentic editing framework that combines LLMs and VLMs, a dedicated MMLVE-Bench dataset, and three evaluation metrics; claims SOTA performance and reduced hallucinations with seamless cross-shot transitions.
AI.motivation: Long videos with multiple editing instructions suffer from entity fragmentation, editing hallucinations, and disrupted temporal continuity when naively chunked. A task and benchmark tailored to cross-shot consistency, multi-instruction decoupling, and preservation of spatiotemporal structure is needed.
AI.method: An agentic editing framework using LLMs and Vision-Language Models to decouple shots and parse instructions at the shot level; construction of MMLVE-Bench with real-world spatiotemporal dynamics and dense heterogeneous instructions; proposed three evaluation metrics for MMLVE; empirical evaluation showing MMLVE-Agent outperforms Seedance 2.0.
AI.result: MMLVE-Agent outperforms existing closed-source SOTA (e.g., Seedance 2.0), eliminates editing hallucinations, preserves cross-shot editing consistency, and achieves seamless spatiotemporal transitions across long videos.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively tackles CSEC, MID, and ZDSS in long-video editing, with a dedicated benchmark and metrics enabling robust evaluation and demonstrating strong empirical performance over prior methods.

title: ProofEvolve: Neuro-Symbolic Evolution for Formal Automated Theorem Proving
summary: Automated theorem proving offers a natural foundation for recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. However, existing neural provers do not fully preserve this recursive structure, where the learning process should be self-improving over time. Existing methods either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. In addition, these methods also heavily rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, even when unsuccessful partial attempts contain useful discoveries. To close the gap, we propose ProofEvolve, a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures with neural models to decisively expand the knowledge boundary. In this framework, the neural model proposes variation operators, including decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations. The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Over the evolution loops, ProofEvolve computes verified closure over the resulting proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Within each problem, ProofEvolve evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive. Across problems, kernel-checked schema extraction adds newly proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library. Proof DAGs inherit the solved results through typed schema recombination, with every residual premise exposed as a new subgoal. This evolutionary process preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness. Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.

AI.tldr: ProofEvolve is a neuro-symbolic framework combining neural variation operators with Lean's kernel to evolve and verify proof DAGs, achieving state-of-the-art solve rates on Lean benchmarks by preserving and reusing verified partial results via a persistent schema library.
AI.motivation: Current neural provers either overwrite knowledge via weight updates or lose verified intermediate deductions, and rely on sparse complete proofs; there is a need for recursive self-improvement with soundness and reuse of partial discoveries.
AI.method: Neural model proposes variation operators (decompositions, repairs, schema recombinations). Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Evolution loops compute verified closures over proof DAGs. Within a problem, evolving partial AND-OR proof DAGs in an archive; across problems, schema extraction adds proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library; typed schema recombination propagates solved results; residual premises become new subgoals; maintains soundness while reusing incomplete attempts.
AI.result: On three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among evaluated proof systems.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective recursive self-improvement of automated reasoning through a verified neuro-symbolic approach, enabling growth of a formal knowledge base and improved proof capability across problems.

title: Scaling Model-Generated Distillation Data Can Make Latent Teacher Traits More Recoverable
summary: Scaling model-generated data is usually viewed as improving distillation: more examples should increase coverage, reduce noise, and produce stronger students. We show a second effect: larger datasets can make subtle teacher-specific signals easier to detect in the trained student, even when examples are off-task and never mention the trait. In a controlled setup inspired by subliminal learning, a teacher induced to express a target trait generates restricted off-task data, such as number-only completions. Students trained on different amounts of independent off-task data are evaluated in a separate domain, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. Our main finding is that larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced trait stand out more clearly in the student's later behavior. Other plausible traits may also strengthen with scale, but the target usually grows more. When the small-scale student already favors the target, scaling mainly amplifies that behavior; when it favors a related or salient alternative, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. Analyses of learned LoRA updates show a parallel trend. These effects appear across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer. Our results suggest that scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, even when the data appears off-task or benign.

AI.tldr: Scaling distillation data reveals a second effect: larger independent off-task data can make subtle teacher-specific signals easier to detect in the student, amplifying or shifting trait transfer even when data is off-task. This effect is robust across model families, traits, and settings, implying need for trait-aware curation and evaluation when using generated data for distillation.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that more data solely improves coverage and reduces noise; to show that dataset scale can enhance detection of teacher-induced traits in students, revealing subtle transfer dynamics that can be amplified or redirected by scale.
AI.method: A controlled subliminal-learning-inspired setup: a teacher induced to express a target trait generates restricted off-task data (e.g., number-only completions). Students are trained on varying amounts of independent off-task data and later evaluated in a separate domain with matched no-trait controls to isolate target-specific transfer. Analyses include learned LoRA updates to study trait transfer and cross-model experiments across model families and trait types.
AI.result: Larger independent datasets amplify the visibility of the teacher's induced trait in the student's behavior; the target trait often grows with scale. If the student already favors the target, scaling primarily strengthens it; if the student leans toward a related or salient alternative, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. Effects generalize across trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer; LoRA updates show parallel trends.
AI.conclusion: Scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, even when data appears off-task or benign, to avoid unintended amplification or misalignment of target traits.

title: TADP: Task-Aware Deformable Prediction for Single-Stage 3D Object Detection
comment: Accepted to the 2023 IEEE Intelligent Vehicles Symposium (IV 2023)
summary: Most single-stage 3D object detectors complete different tasks with the same extracted features. Nevertheless, it is impossible to project features into a common space that is adaptive for all the tasks. We present a novel task-aware deformable prediction (TADP) method for single-stage 3D object detection to solve this problem. Firstly, a triple feature refinement aggregation module is designed to extract three-level features adaptively. Additionally, we design the multi-scale feature aggregation block to fuse multi-scale features in a scale-aware manner. Finally, the prediction of each task is deformed with the designed plug-and-play task-aware deformation head. It can percept the emphasis and interaction of each task. We also designed three different deformation modules. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed deformation head shows good results on other detection methods. The experimental results on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that the car mAP is 80.91%, surpassing many state-of-the-art methods on the KITTI benchmark.

AI.tldr: A task-aware deformable prediction (TADP) framework for single-stage 3D object detection that uses triple feature refinement, scale-aware multi-scale fusion, and task-aware deformation heads; achieves KITTI car mAP 80.91%.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation of using a single shared feature space for multiple detection tasks in single-stage 3D detectors by enabling task-specific emphasis and interaction.
AI.method: Three components: (1) triple feature refinement aggregation module to extract three-level features adaptively; (2) multi-scale feature aggregation block to fuse multi-scale features in a scale-aware manner; (3) plug-and-play task-aware deformation heads with three deformation modules to modulate task emphasis and interaction, improving cross-task adaptability.
AI.result: Empirical results show good compatibility with other detectors and state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, notably car mAP of 80.91%, surpassing many baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TADP framework offers a flexible, task-aware deformable mechanism for single-stage 3D detectors, enhancing cross-task adaptability and performance. It appears generalizable to other detectors, with potential follow-up work focusing on ablations, efficiency, and evaluation across more datasets.

title: Hyperspectral Diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI): A Self-supervised Framework for Hyperspectral Image Inpainting
summary: A novel Hyperspectral diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI) framework for solving the hyperspectral image (HSI) inpainting problem has been presented here. Unlike conventional diffusion-based methods that rely on large-scale pretraining, HyDiff-EI is a test-time optimization framework that learns directly from a single corrupted HSI acquisition. This makes it flexible for different sensor configurations and particularly well-suited for practical remote sensing scenarios where large annotated hyperspectral datasets are limited. To address the ill-posed nature of unsupervised inpainting, we embed equivariant consistency constraints within the diffusion process. By leveraging the inherent geometric symmetries and intrinsic characteristics of HSIs, HyDiff-EI bridges the gap between generative diffusion modeling and self-consistent physical priors. We empirically show that coupling diffusion modeling with equivariant priors substantially enhances noise robustness and generalizability. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets including Chikusei, Botswana, and EMIT demonstrate that HyDiff-EI offers remarkable inpainting quality over existing self-supervised and diffusion-based algorithms in both noiseless and noisy cases.

AI.tldr: A novel test-time hyperspectral image inpainting approach (HyDiff-EI) uses diffusion with equivariant constraints learned on a single corrupted HSI, avoiding large pretraining and improving robustness across sensors; demonstrated on real datasets.
AI.motivation: Address ill-posed unsupervised HSI inpainting under limited data by exploiting geometric symmetries and intrinsic hyperspectral structure to improve generalization and robustness.
AI.method: A test-time optimization framework that embeds equivariant consistency constraints within a diffusion process, leveraging self-supervised priors and hyperspectral geometry to learn from a single corrupted acquisition without large annotated datasets.
AI.result: HyDiff-EI achieves superior inpainting quality compared to existing self-supervised and diffusion-based methods in both noiseless and noisy scenarios, with strong robustness and cross-sensor generalizability demonstrated on Chikusei, Botswana, and EMIT datasets.
AI.conclusion: HyDiff-EI effectively couples diffusion modeling with equivariant priors, bridging generative diffusion with physical priors to enable robust, sensor-flexible HSI inpainting in data-scarce remote sensing contexts.

title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ΔW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: FrameFT introduces a memory-efficient PEFT approach by representing parameter updates ΔW as a sparse coefficient matrix in a shared Fusion Frame basis, which can be algorithmically generated and shared across layers. This reduces trainable parameters and memory while maintaining or improving performance on language (and some vision) tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard PEFT methods like LoRA reduce fine-tuning parameters but require memory scaling with model size O(d r). There is a need for even more memory- and compute-efficient fine-tuning that can reuse a common basis across layers to lower footprint and enable scalable updates.
AI.method: Model ΔW as a sparse coefficient expansion in a Fusion Frame basis. Generate Fusion Frames algorithmically and share them across model layers. Store/optimize only the sparse coefficients, enabling significant memory and compute savings. Provide convergence analysis. Evaluate on supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, primarily language tasks, with some vision-model experiments.
AI.result: FrameFT achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, while using far fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Fusion Frame-based sparse coefficient framing for updates yields memory- and compute-efficient PEFT with competitive performance and convergence guarantees, enabling scalable fine-tuning of large models.

title: Gromov-Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation
comment: Gromov-Wasserstein, Optimal Transport, Flow Matching, Graph Generation, Equivariant Networks
summary: Graphs are invariant under node permutations, motivating the use of permutation-equivariant architectures in generative models. In flow matching, however, symmetry may also enter the source--target coupling: once graph pairs are compared up to node relabeling, the natural Wasserstein geometry is that of the graph quotient space. The Euclidean quotient metric of this space coincides with the Gromov--Monge distance, obtained by optimally relabeling the nodes. We develop this perspective theoretically, showing that quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, including for categorical endpoint prediction. In practice, exact Gromov--Monge alignment is intractable, so we construct minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov--Wasserstein-type relaxations and lower bounds for the inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer assignment between graphs. The resulting procedure changes only the training coupling and is compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures. Across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, these structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets, while our scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

AI.tldr: Reframes graph flow matching under permutation symmetry as learning quotient-space couplings; shows quotient couplings lift to aligned representations at no extra cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant minimizers; uses GW-type relaxations for practical node alignment; improves sample quality at low budgets for continuous graphs and heterogeneous molecules, with scalable models competitive under standard sampling.
AI.motivation: Graphs are permutation-invariant; in generative flow models, the source-target coupling should respect node relabeling. The natural geometry is the graph quotient space, where optimal relabeling leads to a Gromov–Monge-type distance.
AI.method: Theoretically, quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost; symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, applicable to categorical endpoints. Practically, exact Gromov–Monge alignment is intractable, so minibatch couplings are built via efficient Gromov–Wasserstein-type relaxations with lower bounds on inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer graph assignment; training coupling is modified but remains compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures.
AI.result: Structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets for continuous graphs and categorical molecular generation; scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating quotient-geometry and equivariant symmetrization into flow matching enables more faithful, data-efficient graph generation; practical GW relaxations provide tractable approximations that fit standard GNN-based pipelines.

title: LLaVAFlow: Preserving Latent Alignment Flow for Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fine-Tuning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong generalization, visual instruction tuning for downstream tasks inevitably causes catastrophic forgetting, impairing overall generalization. While existing methods regulate weight updates to reduce forgetting, they overlook the fundamental cross-modal alignment in MLLMs. Based on prior work and our observations, we argue that cross-modal alignment is implicitly captured in the information-compression trajectory. To preserve the alignment flow embedded in the trajectory, we propose LLaVAFlow, an information-theoretic distillation framework. First, we compress the mutual information between the extracted relations and MLLM embeddings, encouraging a learnable module to produce a refined alignment flow that benefits downstream tasks. Second, we maximize the mutual information between the extracted alignment flows of the pretrained and fine-tuned MLLMs, enabling the transfer of compact alignment information. Extensive experiments show that LLaVAFlow is an effective plug-and-play framework that preserves alignment flow and enhances both downstream performance and generalization.

AI.tldr: LLaVAFlow uses information-theoretic distillation to preserve cross-modal alignment in multimodal LLMs during fine-tuning, by compressing the mutual information of alignment relations and by aligning the flows between pretrained and fine-tuned models, leading to better downstream performance and generalization.
AI.motivation: Catastrophic forgetting during visual instruction tuning in MLLMs; traditional weight-regularization methods ignore the fundamental cross-modal alignment flow, which is implicitly captured in the information-compression trajectory.
AI.method: An information-theoretic distillation framework. It compresses the mutual information between extracted relations and MLLM embeddings to produce a refined alignment flow via a learnable module, and it maximizes the mutual information between the alignment flows of pretrained and fine-tuned MLLMs to transfer compact alignment information. It is designed as a plug-and-play module.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLaVAFlow preserves alignment flow and improves both downstream performance and generalization; it can be integrated as a plug-and-play component.
AI.conclusion: LLaVAFlow is an effective, generalizable approach for maintaining cross-modal alignment in MLLMs during visual instruction tuning, enhancing performance and generalization across tasks.

title: Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

AI.tldr: Adaptive reasoning allocation in agentic AI can reduce waste and prevent incomplete solutions; over-reasoning increases cost with little benefit, while under-reasoning harms accuracy, as shown on MATH-500 and GAIA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI tasks involve dynamic planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and inter-agent interactions. Fixed reasoning budgets or controls fail to match evolving demands, leading to misallocated reasoning and inefficiency.
AI.method: Define misallocation as over-reasoning vs under-reasoning. Quantify with tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness. Evaluate on MATH-500 and GAIA public validation benchmark. Classify cases and analyze correlations between reasoning level and performance/cost.
AI.result: Over-reasoning correlates with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains; under-reasoning correlates with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These patterns support the existence of a systematic trade-off and the need for adaptive mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Advocate for adaptive reasoning mechanisms in agentic AI to match evolving task demands and reduce waste and error. Call for future work to develop dynamic allocation strategies that respond to planning, tool use, and memory use.

title: Packora: Systematic Design for Generative Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction
summary: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is important in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics, where subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can strongly affect material properties. We present Packora, a flow-based generative model for molecular CSP that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and the lattice from molecular graphs. Packora supports multi-component and organometallic crystals and can condition on any subset of molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information within a single model. Inspired by the CCDC CSP blind test, we evaluate generation and ranking separately, using generation to isolate generator quality and ranking to measure end-to-end performance under a common relaxation and ranking pipeline. We also systematically study architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling, identifying an effective design based on cacheable pairwise reasoning, training objective and numerical solver choices, conditioning dropout, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. Packora outperforms the baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving the best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, as well as higher experimental-form recovery, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking.

AI.tldr: Packora is a flow-based generative model for molecular CSP that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and the lattice, supporting multi-component and organometallic crystals, with conditioning on conformers, stereochemical labels, and space group; achieves state-of-the-art in generation and ranking under blind test.
AI.motivation: Molecular CSP is critical in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics; small changes in conformation and packing greatly affect properties. A joint generator/ranker with flexible conditioning and scalable design is needed, evaluated via a CSP blind test.
AI.method: Flow-based generative model that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and lattice from molecular graphs; supports multi-component and organometallic crystals; conditioning on any subset of molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information within a single model. Architecture includes cacheable pairwise reasoning, specific training objectives and numerical solver choices, conditioning dropout, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. Evaluation inspired by the CCDC CSP blind test, with separate generation and ranking pipelines and a common relaxation and ranking pipeline.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines on both structure generation and ranking; achieves best matched-budget coverage across six generation benchmarks; higher experimental-form recovery, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking.
AI.conclusion: Packora provides an effective CSP generation and ranking framework with flexible conditioning and scalable architecture, achieving state-of-the-art performance on generation and ranking benchmarks.

title: Evaluator-Dependent Patient-Adaptive ECG Lead-Channel Allocation
summary: Patient-conditioned acquisition policies for ECG lead-channel selection can outperform population-wide fixed protocols by tailoring the channel budget to each patient's observed cardiac state. However, the value of acquiring any given channel is defined relative to a downstream diagnostic evaluator, so marginal utilities learned under one evaluator need not transfer when the evaluator is replaced. We study this evaluator dependence empirically on PTB-XL by freezing two policies (ECG-on-Demand and MGA) trained with a controlled arbitrary-mask logistic evaluator, then scoring their unchanged acquisition trajectories with a more predictive masked raw-waveform ResNet1D. Exhaustive search provides metric-matched population-wide fixed comparators separately for each evaluator, enabling a clean interaction contrast. At budget $k=4$ on a held-out evaluation fold, ECG-on-Demand shifts from $D_\mathrm{C}=-0.011$ (favoring adaptive under the controlled evaluator) to $D_\mathrm{S}=+0.029$ (favoring fixed under the strong evaluator), yielding an NLL interaction of $+0.041$ (95% CI $[+0.030, +0.050]$). Across two policies, five budgets, and three probabilistic metrics, all 30 interaction estimates are positive with paired confidence intervals excluding zero. Three post-hoc sensitivity analyses -- common-reference scoring, training the strong evaluator on a mixture of policy-generated and random masks, and evaluator-aligned Strong-MGA policy training -- each preserve a positive interaction interval, making reference-choice and mask-distribution artifacts less plausible explanations. Evaluator-aligned training reduces but does not eliminate the gap. These results indicate that adaptive ECG channel allocation should be developed and validated jointly with its intended diagnostic backbone, and that jointly optimized sensing-diagnosis systems remain an open problem.

AI.tldr: Evaluator dependence undermines transfer of patient-conditioned ECG channel policies; across multiple policies, budgets, and metrics, positive interactions persist but reverse under a stronger evaluator; joint optimisation of sensing and diagnosis is needed.
AI.motivation: The value of acquiring an ECG channel is defined relative to a downstream diagnostic evaluator, so learned gains may not transfer when the evaluator changes. This study empirically tests evaluator dependence on PTB-XL by re-scoring policy trajectories with a stronger predictor and comparing to population-wide fixed baselines.
AI.method: Freeze two learned policies (ECG-on-Demand and MGA) using a controlled arbitrary-mask logistic evaluator. Score their acquisition trajectories with a masked raw-waveform ResNet1D. Construct metric-matched fixed comparators per evaluator via exhaustive search. Evaluate across two policies, five budgets, three probabilistic metrics (NLL and others), with held-out folds. Perform three post-hoc sensitivity analyses: common-reference scoring, training the strong evaluator on a mix of policy-generated and random masks, and evaluator-aligned Strong-MGA policy training.
AI.result: At budget k=4, ECG-on-Demand shifts from D_C = -0.011 (adaptive favored under controlled evaluator) to D_S = +0.029 (fixed favored under strong evaluator), with an NLL interaction of +0.041 (95% CI [0.030, 0.050]). Across two policies, five budgets, and three metrics, all 30 interaction estimates are positive with CIs excluding zero. Sensitivity analyses preserve positive interactions; evaluator-aligned training reduces but does not eliminate the gap.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive ECG channel allocation should be developed and validated jointly with its intended diagnostic backbone. Jointly optimized sensing-diagnosis systems remain an open problem.

title: PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agent runs generate experience that can improve both the current run and future work. Most self-improvement methods process this experience only after execution ends, so they cannot redirect the active run or immediately apply and validate lessons learned from it. We argue that self-improvement should instead be live, using emerging experience both to redirect the active run and to update the persistent harness. Existing agent architectures do not fully support this goal. Single-agent self-correction combines task execution and trajectory assessment within one context, while subagent delegation separates execution but typically cannot redirect an active subagent. We present PILOT, a supervisor-worker harness for live self-improvement through two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering lets a separate supervisor redirect or abort the active worker during execution; and (2) live self-evolution distils procedures and failure modes revealed during execution into reusable skills and memory. Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, PILOT outperforms counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In the self-improvement setting, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens fall by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens rise by 110.3% and 134.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: PILOT enables live self-improvement through a supervisor–worker harness with live steering and live self-evolution, achieving state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across multiple backbones and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current self-improvement methods learn after execution, missing opportunities to correct the active run or build reusable skills from ongoing experience.
AI.method: Introduce PILOT: a supervisor–worker harness with (1) live steering to redirect/abort the active worker during execution, and (2) live self-evolution to distill procedures and failure modes into reusable skills and memory; evaluated on two frozen backbones across three benchmarks (including Terminal-Bench 2.0) against other harnesses.
AI.result: PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, it outperforms counterparts by up to 9.8 percentage points. In self-improvement settings, gains are 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens decrease by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens rise by 110.3% and 134.0%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Live steering and live self-evolution enable effective, efficient live self-improvement of long-horizon agents, demonstrating strong performance across architectures and tasks.

title: Adversarial Training Without Input Gradients via Low-Rank Householder Expansions
summary: This work concerns adversarial training against the small-norm adversarial examples that arise from the inherent input instability of a trained deep neural network. Examples in this class are small as measured in the relative $\ell^2$-norm, and therefore lie in the neighborhood of the input on which the model acts approximately linearly, the regime in which the perturbation remains imperceptible. We first show that such examples can be computed directly from the trained network parameters, without input gradient iterations, by means of a linearization called the low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE). The expansion describes the composed affine map rather than any individual layer, and the directions it identifies are read from the activation pattern already available in the forward pass. We then propose a simple adversarial training scheme built on this construction. No differentiation with respect to the input is performed at any point: training requires only additional forward evaluations, with weight parameters updated by the standard backward pass, and the inner maximization of the usual min-max formulation is eliminated entirely. That such a regularizer exists is our main finding: the methods that dispense with the inner search all obtain their local geometry by differentiating with respect to the input, and we show this is not necessary. The regularizer costs the equivalent of $2.8$ PGD steps per epoch, an $8.7\times$ reduction relative to 40-step adversarial training on MNIST and below the cost of 3-step training. The resulting models match three-step PGD adversarial training for relative $\ell^2$ budgets $\varepsilon \le 0.02$ and 40-step training for $\varepsilon \le 0.012$, falling away beyond, consistent with the locality of the expansion.

AI.tldr: LRHE-based adversarial training: compute small-norm adversaries directly from trained parameters using a forward-pass linearization, enabling a regularizer that avoids input-gradient optimization and speeds training while matching modest PGD robustness under small perturbations.
AI.motivation: Address small-norm adversarial examples arising from input instability near linear regimes, and reduce computational cost by eliminating inner-gradient optimization.
AI.method: Low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE) describes the composed affine map of the network, deriving adversarial directions from the activation pattern in the forward pass. Training uses only forward evaluations for the regularizer; no differentiation w.r.t. input is performed and the inner maximization in min–max is removed; weights updated via standard backward pass.
AI.result: Regularizer costs about 2.8 PGD steps per epoch (≈8.7× faster than 40-step PGD on MNIST). Models achieve robustness comparable to 3-step PGD for ε ≤ 0.02, and to 40-step training for ε ≤ 0.012; effectiveness declines beyond the locality radius implied by LRHE.
AI.conclusion: LRHE-based regularization demonstrates that inner-search adversarial training can be avoided for small-norm perturbations, yielding substantial speedups while preserving robustness within the locality where the expansion is valid.

title: Rethinking Image Processing for the Age of AI: A Problem-First Framework for Scientific Progress
summary: Modern AI has greatly expanded the capabilities of image processing. However, the ready availability of powerful models, public datasets, and benchmark leaderboards has also en- couraged a model-first research pattern: researchers increasingly begin with an available architecture and optimize it on a public benchmark, rather than beginning with the underlying real-world imaging problem. This can produce impressive benchmark results without necessarily improving our understanding or solution of the real problem. This paper argues for a problem-first approach that distinguishes the physical imaging problem, solution principle, statistical estimator, and computational implementation, while clarifying what modern AI can achieve and which fundamental problems remain unsolved. Through case studies of super- resolution and low-light enhancement, we show how benchmark datasets may define tasks that differ substantially from the real-world problems they are intended to represent, and why performance improvements must be interpreted within the conditions under which they are obtained. We propose a six-stage workflow that places problem formulation, image acquisition, information-loss analysis, assumptions, ambiguity, and evaluation before model and dataset selection. The paper also proposes clearer standards for evidence, reproducibility, uncertainty, and claims of state-of-the-art performance. More fundamentally, it calls for a change in research culture and education so that future researchers learn to understand imaging problems deeply and use modern AI to achieve genuine scientific and technical advancement.

AI.tldr: Advocates a problem-first framework for imaging AI that separates problem formulation, image acquisition, information loss, assumptions, ambiguity, and evaluation; argues benchmarks can misalign with real-world problems; proposes a six-stage workflow and clearer evidence standards to improve reproducibility and scientific advancement.
AI.motivation: Model-first AI research in imaging often optimizes architectures on public benchmarks without grounding in real imaging problems, risking misaligned progress and misunderstood limitations. A problem-first perspective seeks to clarify what the physical problem is, what is actually being solved, and under what conditions results hold.
AI.method: Proposes a six-stage workflow: (1) problem formulation, (2) image acquisition design, (3) information-loss analysis, (4) explicit assumptions, (5) ambiguity assessment, (6) evaluation, prior to selecting models/datasets. Uses case studies in super-resolution and low-light enhancement to illustrate misalignment between benchmarks and real problems, and discusses standards for evidence, reproducibility, uncertainty, and state-of-the-art claims.
AI.result: Provides a conceptual framework and practical workflow to realign AI research with underlying imaging problems. Through case studies it demonstrates how benchmark tasks can diverge from real-world problems and how clearer evaluation criteria can improve interpretation of results and reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: A problem-first approach clarifies the capabilities and limits of modern AI in imaging, promotes deeper problem understanding, and calls for changes in research culture, education, and evidence standards to ensure genuine scientific and technical advancement.

title: Multi2AV-Safety: Benchmarking Safety in Multimodal-to-Audio-Video Generation
summary: Audio-video generation is rapidly moving from prompt-driven synthesis toward multimodal conditioning, where text, images, audio, and video can jointly shape the generated output. This shift changes the nature of safety evaluation: harmful intent may no longer reside in any single input, but instead emerge from how otherwise benign or weakly harmful conditions interact across modalities and time. Existing safety benchmarks, however, remain largely prompt-centric or tied to fixed conditioning interfaces, leaving such compositional risks difficult to study systematically. To bridge this gap, we introduce Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark, to the best of our knowledge, to cover all 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances. Evaluation on Multi2AV-Safety reveals systematic weaknesses in representative multimodal safety guards across attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures. Our evaluation reveals two complementary failure modes: harmful semantics can emerge from the combination of individually benign inputs, while explicit harmful cues can become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. Together, these results identify \emph{compositional risk perception} as a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation: current safety guards fail to reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time, even when all conditioning inputs are observable. The dataset will be publicly released in October 2026.

AI.tldr: Introduces Multi2AV-Safety, a multimodal safety benchmark for audio-video generation, covering 11 non-singleton conditioning configurations (T/I/A/V) with 11,024 attack instances; reveals compositional risk perception gaps in current safety guards; dataset released Oct 2026.
AI.motivation: Multimodal conditioning enables safety risks to arise from interactions across modalities and time, making prompt-centric benchmarks insufficient. A systematic framework is needed to evaluate safety across text, image, audio, and video inputs.
AI.method: Constructs 11 conditioning configurations across modalities (T/I/A/V), generates 11,024 attack instances, and evaluates representative safety guards for compositional and time-evolving harm signals; analyzes attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures to identify where guards fail.
AI.result: Reveals systematic weaknesses in multimodal safety guards; identifies two complementary failure modes: (1) harmful semantics emerge from combinations of benign inputs, (2) explicit harmful cues are harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context; demonstrates a gap in compositional risk perception.
AI.conclusion: Advocates for improved multimodal safety evaluation and guards that reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time; dataset will be publicly released in October 2026.

title: Graph-Based Pseudo-multimodal Contrastive Learning for 12-Lead ECG Representations
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. Presented at the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026)
summary:
12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a standard, non-invasive examination widely used for diagnosing coronary artery disease, where clinical interpretation relies on comparing waveform patterns across multiple leads. However, most existing ECG analysis methods focus on single-lead signals or treat each lead independently, and typically process ECG signals as one-dimensional time-series data using CNNs or RNNs. While effective in modeling local waveform changes, such approaches have difficulty capturing inter-lead dependency and global waveform patterns essential for clinical diagnosis.
  To address this limitation, we propose a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework called Graph-CMMC. ECG waveforms are transformed into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to construct complementary representations of the same cardiac activity, enabling a pseudo-multimodal learning setting. Using all 12 leads, Graph-CMMC aligns waveform and GADF representations in a self-supervised manner, while a graph-based relational module is employed to model inter-lead dependency and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
  Experimental results on a multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification task demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to supervised learning methods. These results further suggest the effectiveness of using GADF as a complementary representation and incorporating explicit graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependency for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised graph-based framework for 12-lead ECG using Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images and a graph-relational module to capture inter-lead dependencies, achieving competitive multi-label occlusion classification without labeled data.
AI.motivation: Current ECG analyses often treat leads independently or as 1D signals with CNN/RNNs, failing to capture inter-lead dependencies and global waveform patterns critical for diagnosis; a pseudo-multimodal, graph-based approach could exploit cross-lead relationships.
AI.method: Transform ECG waveforms into GADF images to form complementary representations for all 12 leads; use a pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning setup aligning waveform and GADF representations; employ a graph-based relational module to model inter-lead dependencies and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
AI.result: Experimental results on multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification show competitive performance relative to supervised methods, indicating GADF's effectiveness and the value of explicit inter-lead graph modeling for 12-lead ECG representations.
AI.conclusion: GADF-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning with a graph-relational module is a promising approach for robust 12-lead ECG representations and can approach supervised performance on clinically relevant tasks.

title: MedFG-VQA: Low-Frequency Memory and Graph Attention for Lightweight Medical VQA
summary: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) holds significant promise for clinical decision support, yet faces challenges due to limited annotated data and the high computational demands of existing large vision-language models.
