We propose MedFG-VQA, a lightweight framework that leverages a memory bank to augment DCT-based low-frequency features and employs graph-enhanced cross-attention for effective visual-textual alignment. Specifically, our approach features two key components: Frequency-Memory Fusion (FMF), which enhances low-frequency features by retrieving from a learnable memory bank built on DCT decomposition, and Graph-Aware Cross-Attention (GACA), which aligns visual-textual features via cross-attention and refines them through graph-convolutional aggregation. To address data scarcity, we construct SynMed-VQA, a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising over 2 million question-answer pairs across 9 imaging modalities and 10 major organs, generated with GPT-4o. Extensive experiments on SynMed-VQA and three other standard biomedical VQA benchmarks demonstrate that MedFG-VQA achieves competitive or superior performance compared to much larger models while maintaining significantly lower computational costs, highlighting its efficiency and potential for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: MedFG-VQA is a lightweight Med-VQA framework that combines a frequency-memory fusion module leveraging a learnable DCT-based memory bank with a graph-aware cross-attention module, trained/validated on a 2M+ synthetic dataset SynMed-VQA and several biomedical VQA benchmarks; it achieves competitive accuracy with far lower computational cost than large vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity and high computational demands in medical visual question answering by exploiting low-frequency information and graph-based alignment, and by generating large synthetic datasets to scale training.
AI.method: FMF: retrieve and fuse low-frequency features from a learnable DCT-based memory bank to augment image representations. GACA: cross-attention between visual and textual features followed by graph-convolutional refinement to enforce relational structure and improve alignment.
AI.result: On SynMed-VQA and three standard biomedical VQA benchmarks, MedFG-VQA achieves competitive or superior performance compared with much larger models while requiring substantially less computational resources, indicating strong efficiency and potential for clinical deployment.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain memory augmentation combined with graph-aware cross-attention provides data-efficient, scalable Med-VQA; synthetic data helps mitigate annotation gaps; the approach shows favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-offs that suit clinical settings.

title: DuMateBench: Evaluating Autonomous Agents in Complex Real-World Workflows
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly adopted to complete complex, multi-tool workflows in real-world settings. However, existing benchmarks typically separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate agents in environments that are cleaner and more stable than those encountered in practice. We introduce DuMateBench, a real-session benchmark reconstructed from anonymized and privacy-screened user sessions collected from a large-scale production agent platform. Each task preserves the relevant pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, and is then validated through human verification. The resulting benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning 8 broad scenarios and 17 fine-grained capability categories, with most tasks requiring multiple capability coordination. We execute these tasks in isolated Docker containers injected with three forms of real-world environmental complexity: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy, and assess performance using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol. Experiments across five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial gaps in strict task completion. Complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses further show that performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by the capabilities of the LLM and the surrounding agent framework. The code and data are publicly available at https://dumatebench.com/.

AI.tldr: DuMateBench is a real-session benchmark for autonomous agents, based on anonymized production sessions, featuring 200 tasks across 8 scenarios and 17 capability categories, with real-world perturbations (Insufficient, Unstable, Noisy) and mixed evaluation (deterministic + LLM judge). It reveals sizable gaps in task completion across frameworks and LLMs; code/data are public.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between clean, synthetic benchmarks and messy real-world multi-tool workflows by preserving authentic pre-solution history, configurations, and workspace state, while enabling controlled evaluation under realistic perturbations.
AI.method: Reconstructs tasks from anonymized production sessions, preserving interaction history, configurations, and workspace; validates tasks via human verification; tests tasks in Docker with three perturbation modes; uses a hybrid deterministic and LLM-based judge; evaluates across five agent frameworks and four state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.result: The study finds substantial gaps in strict task completion under real-world perturbations; robustness analyses show performance is jointly influenced by LLM capabilities and the surrounding agent framework.
AI.conclusion: DuMateBench offers a realistic, scalable benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents in more authentic settings, highlighting robustness challenges and guiding future development; code and data are publicly available.

title: ClusterAttention: A training-free speedup of bidirectional attention
summary:
This paper introduces ClusterAttention, a general training-free speedup of bidirectional attention layers. Existing sparse attention methods either rely on structure in the input, such as order in language or spatial proximity in images, or use slow clustering processes amortized over several forward passes. ClusterAttention instead uses a fast recursive clustering method that adapts to the geometry of the keys and queries in each attention head to produce useful clusters. This method allows setting the size of the clusters arbitrarily. We utilize this by setting all clusters to be a fixed size that is a power of two, allowing the block-sparse attention to run at the same latency per query-key interaction as dense attention on GPUs. We also derive an expression for the output error in sparse attention, that explains the counterintuitive experimental finding that tight clusters can lead to larger errors than random clusters. We then derive the error when excluded clusters are compensated through their centroids, and show that this error shrinks with tighter clusters. We integrate this compensation into the method.
  On large-scale tabular data ClusterAttention speeds up TabPFN-3 arXiv:2605.13986 by two to six times, while retaining at least 99% of the dense accuracy. To our knowledge, it is the first training-free method that can be successfully applied in the setting of unstructured input and a single forward pass. For video generation with Wan 2.1-14B T2V arXiv:2503.20314 , ClusterAttention achieves output closer to dense attention and a larger speedup (1.8x versus 1.4x) compared to SVOO arXiv:2603.18636 , a leading method developed specifically for this domain, both run without offline calibration.

AI.tldr: ClusterAttention is a training-free, geometry-adaptive block-sparse attention that uses fixed-size, power-of-two clusters per head to match dense-attention latency on GPUs; it includes a theoretical error analysis and demonstrates substantial speedups with minimal accuracy loss on tabular and video-generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational cost of attention without relying on input structure or offline calibration, enabling fast, single-pass inference on unstructured data.
AI.method: A fast recursive clustering method that adapts to the geometry of keys/queries per attention head. Clusters are fixed-size (power of two) to enable uniform latency with dense attention. Includes centroid compensation for excluded clusters and derives an error expression to predict sparse-attention error; compensation is integrated into the method.
AI.result: On TabPFN-3, 2× to 6× speedups with at least 99% of dense accuracy; first training-free method for unstructured input with a single forward pass. On Wan 2.1-14B T2V, achieves 1.8× speedup and outputs closer to dense than SVOO (1.4×), both without offline calibration.
AI.conclusion: ClusterAttention provides a practical, training-free pathway to fast, accurate attention by geometry-adaptive clustering and centroid compensation, with proven gains across tabular and video-generation tasks and a solid theoretical account of the induced error.

title: From Reasoning to Pixels: Grounded Medical Multimodal LLMs for VQA and Segmentation
summary: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA), their reliance on global image features often lacks precise pixel-level grounding, thereby limiting clinical trustworthiness. To bridge the semantic gap between high-level clinical reasoning and spatial localization, we propose \textsc{\textsc{MedREAL}} (\textbf{Med}ical \textbf{RE}asoning-driven \textbf{A}nswering and \textbf{L}ocalization), a unified framework that seamlessly aligns linguistic reasoning with spatial grounding. Specifically, \textsc{MedREAL} introduces \textbf{S}eg \textbf{A}nchored \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{P}ooling (SARP) to distill task-relevant semantic evidence directly from \texttt{[SEG]} tokens within the MLLM's hidden states. Furthermore, a \textbf{R}easoning-to-\textbf{V}isual (R2V) fusion mechanism is proposed to effectively inject these reasoning-aware features into a segmentation pipeline for accurate mask decoding. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct MedRAVS-13K, a comprehensive dataset comprising 13,824 expertly validated samples across four diverse imaging modalities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{MedREAL} significantly outperforms state-of-the-arts, achieving 68.49\% gIoU and 70.47\% cIoU on benchmark evaluations. By generating evidence masks that are strictly consistent with textual diagnoses, \textsc{MedREAL} provides a robust, interpretable framework for reasoning-driven medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: MedREAL unifies reasoning and spatial grounding for medical visual tasks by extracting task-relevant evidence from [SEG] tokens (SARP) and fusing it into segmentation (R2V), aided by MedRAVS-13K. It achieves strong pixel-level grounding and interpretable evidence masks, outperforming SOTA on standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Bridge the semantic gap between high-level clinical reasoning and precise spatial localization to enhance trustworthiness and interpretability in Multimodal Large Language Models for medical imaging.
AI.method: SARP distills task-relevant semantic evidence from [SEG] tokens within the MLLM's hidden states. R2V fusion injects reasoning-aware features into a segmentation pipeline for accurate mask decoding. A new dataset, MedRAVS-13K (13,824 samples across four imaging modalities), supports evaluation.
AI.result: MedREAL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 68.49% gIoU and 70.47% cIoU on benchmark evaluations. It also produces evidence masks strictly consistent with textual diagnoses, enabling interpretable reasoning-driven analysis.
AI.conclusion: MedREAL provides a robust, interpretable framework that tightly couples linguistic reasoning with spatial grounding in medical image analysis and offers a valuable dataset for future research.

title: AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling
comment: 31 Pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables, Accepted as a main conference paper at EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.

AI.tldr: AgentJudgeBench systematically evaluates LLM-based judges for agentic tool-calling on workflow DAGs; reveals a task-difficulty ceiling, mixed effects of ground-truth, limited efficacy of popular mitigations, and model-specific guidance for reliable evaluation.
AI.motivation: Fill a gap in evaluating reliability of LLM judges for structured, dependency-driven workflows. Provide a benchmark that quantifies alignment across DAG topologies, difficulty levels, generators, and judges, including ground-truth exposure and mitigation strategies, to inform reliable evaluation of agentic systems.
AI.method: Construct 3,808 instances across six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers; evaluate five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Test mitigation strategies including chain-of-thought, judge temperature, and structured evaluation rubrics; assess ground-truth exposure; conduct a human validation study to identify human-aligned judges.
AI.result: Judge alignment declines with task difficulty; alignment is 1.5x faster without ground truth. On hard, ground-truth-free queries, all six judges converge to a 77–82% band, indicating a structural ceiling driven by task difficulty. Ground-truth exposure can reduce alignment for some models (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Gemini-2.5-Pro) due to over-anchoring. Chain-of-thought and judge temperature have negligible effects; structured rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 percentage points but do not generalize uniformly across judge–generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference; a human validation study finds GPT-OSS-120B most human-aligned, while without GT frontier judges perform only marginally within the shared ceiling.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM judges exhibit fundamental limitations for evaluating agentic systems. Practical guidance includes using structured rubrics to boost alignment, being cautious with ground-truth exposure due to possible over-anchoring, and selecting models judiciously (e.g., QwQ-32B with GT for programmatic alignment; GPT-OSS-120B as a human-aligned judge). Overall, ceilings driven by task difficulty rather than model size constrain reliability, underscoring the need for robust evaluation pipelines and complementary human-in-the-loop validation.

title: TEMPLAR Wales: A georeferenced environmental and toponymic dataset of Welsh settlements
summary: Place names provide persistent records of how landscapes have been described and organised, but their quantitative reuse requires explicit separation between mapped places, lexical annotations and environmental measurements. TEMPLAR Wales is a georeferenced environmental-toponymy dataset comprising 3,757 settlement records across Wales. The resource links a reproducible settlement frame to deterministic lexical screening and settlement-level environmental attributes through stable identifiers. It contains 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements, generated from a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements, while retaining exact- and prefix-token matches and their provenance separately. Environmental attributes describe river and coastal proximity, elevation and local terrain context at multiple spatial scales, land cover and neighbourhood woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements derived from independent elevation products. The dataset is distributed as four relational tables accompanied by a field-level data dictionary, source-provenance register and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirms relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between independent terrain sources and reproducible reconstruction of the frozen release. TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical and environmental landscape studies, GIS and spatial data analysis without treating computational lexical detections as verified etymologies or contemporary environmental measurements as historical landscape reconstructions.

AI.tldr: Templar Wales provides a georeferenced, reproducible toponymy dataset linking lexical place-name elements to settlement positions and environmental attributes across Wales, distributed as four relational tables with provenance and licensing, enabling robust linguistic geography and environmental studies while avoiding etiological claims.
AI.motivation: To enable quantitative reuse of toponymic data by explicitly separating mapped places, lexical annotations, and environmental measurements, and to provide a reproducible, deterministic dataset for linguistic geography and historical landscape research.
AI.method: Create a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements; perform deterministic lexical screening; link 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements to stable identifiers; extract environmental attributes (river/coast proximity, elevation, terrain context, land cover, woody cover) at multiple scales from independent elevation products; organize into four relational tables with data dictionary, provenance, licensing; validate relational integrity and reproducibility.
AI.result: A dataset comprising 3,757 settlement records, 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements; stable identifiers; documented environmental coverage; strong agreement between independent terrain sources; reproducible reconstruction of the frozen release; four relational tables with metadata.
AI.conclusion: Provides a reusable foundation for toponymy, linguistic geography, historical/environmental landscape studies and GIS; clarifies that lexical detections are not etymologies and environmental measurements are not historical reconstructions; supports reproducible analyses and transparent provenance.

title: A Geometry-Driven, Framework-Agnostic Optimization for Object Pose Estimation
summary: Current object pose estimation research remains predominantly model-centric, focusing on architectural innovations and post-processing refinements. This paper introduces a data-centric optimization by proposing a novel, physically grounded rotation representation through principal axes alignment. Our method aligns the object's coordinate system with its inherent geometric axes, derived from inertial properties, yielding three key advantages: Inherent Stability-leveraging the energy-minimizing property of principal axes provides a robust representation that is less sensitive to noise and occlusions; Symmetry-Aware Canonicalization-explicitly resolving rotational ambiguities for symmetric objects at the data level, which fundamentally eliminates label confusion during network training; and Framework Agnosticism-the optimization is applied purely at the dataset level, ensuring plug-and-play compatibility with existing networks without any architectural modification. We validate the framework across diverse category-level and instance-level models. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent and significant accuracy improvements, while preserving the integrity of the baseline network. This work establishes a new, geometry-driven direction for enhancing pose estimation, circumventing the need for complex network redesign.

AI.tldr: Data-centric pose estimation via principal-axis alignment: a symmetry-aware, dataset-level rotation canonicalization that improves robustness without changing network architectures.
AI.motivation: To reduce model-centric complexities and label noise in pose estimation by aligning rotations to the object’s inherent geometric axes and resolving symmetry-induced ambiguities at the data level, enabling plug-and-play improvements across existing networks.
AI.method: Derive a rotation representation by aligning the object's coordinate frame with its principal axes (from inertial properties). Apply symmetry-aware canonicalization to resolve rotational ambiguities for symmetric objects. Implement the optimization at the dataset level, not within network architecture, ensuring compatibility with existing models without modifications.
AI.result: Reported consistent, significant accuracy gains across category-level and instance-level models while preserving baseline network performance and integrity; improvements attributed to enhanced stability and clearer training signals from symmetry-aware canonicalization.
AI.conclusion: This work advocates a geometry-driven, data-centric shift in pose estimation, enabling performance gains without network redesign and suggesting broader adoption of inertial-based canonical rotations for robust and unambiguous pose representations.

title: SIGMA: Structured Noise-Effect-Aware Grouped Multi-Agent Aggregation
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces significant challenges in maintaining robust coordination under noisy observations. Although observation disturbances are often introduced independently across agents, their downstream effects on cooperative decision-making can become structured through underlying cooperation structures. We characterize this phenomenon as structured noise effects, where noise-induced decision effects exhibit local correlation among agents with stronger task-related dependencies while remaining globally heterogeneous across different agents and local structures. Existing robust MARL methods, however, rarely explicitly characterize or exploit such structure-dependent noise effects. To address this limitation, we propose SIGMA, a hierarchical collaboration framework that exploits cooperation structures to learn robust representations under noisy observations. SIGMA first organizes agents into adaptive local structures through density-based grouping and performs intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific representation deviations. Inter-group attention then adaptively integrates information across different groups to preserve global coordination while accommodating their heterogeneous contributions. Experiments on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II empirically validate the structured noise effects and demonstrate that SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.

AI.tldr: SIGMA addresses structured noise effects in cooperative MARL by organizing agents into adaptive local groups with intra-group consensus and inter-group attention to enhance robustness to noisy observations.
AI.motivation: Observation disturbances in MARL can produce structured, locally correlated decision effects aligned with cooperation structure; existing robust MARL methods ignore this structure, limiting robustness.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework: (1) adaptive local grouping via density-based clustering, (2) intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information and smooth agent-specific deviations, (3) inter-group attention to integrate information across groups while preserving heterogeneous contributions.
AI.result: Empirical validation on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II shows SIGMA consistently improves robustness to observation noise and maintains competitive performance in noise-free environments.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting cooperation structure with hierarchical aggregation yields robust representations under noise; SIGMA's combination of local consensus and global attention balances local robustness and global coordination.

title: Terrain signatures in Welsh settlement names
summary: Landscapes are named, but whether names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic structure is rarely tested. We analysed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen, source-audited 24-element lexical framework, preregistered outcome-specific models and geographically structured validation. The central comparison contrasted 101 settlements carrying high-terrain elements (\textit{bryn} or \textit{mynydd}) with 139 carrying low-terrain elements (\textit{cwm} or \textit{pant}). High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4 m higher relative to their 2-km surroundings (95\% CI, 10.8--38.1 m; Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.00137). The association remained positive across prespecified 1-, 2- and 5-km neighbourhood definitions and was reproduced using an independently produced elevation source (24.1 m; 95\% CI, 10.6--37.6 m). Adding terrain-name polarity to a non-lexical spatial and settlement baseline reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63\%, 6.22\% and 7.30\% under 10-, 25- and 50-km spatial blocking, respectively, although improvement varied among held-out regions. River-related names provided weaker, directionally consistent evidence, while the preregistered woodland model was non-estimable. Residual spatial structure, unresolved name language and the absence of independent external replication limit interpretation. Selected Welsh settlement-name categories therefore retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, without establishing individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory or transferability to other naming systems.

AI.tldr: Welsh settlement names containing high-terrain elements correlate with higher elevations; terrain-name polarity modestly improves predictive accuracy; effects robust across neighborhood scales but limited by residual spatial structure and lack of external replication.
AI.motivation: Test whether toponyms encode measurable, present-day environmental information beyond broad geographic structure.
AI.method: Analyzed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a 24-element lexical framework; preregistered outcome-specific models; geographically structured validation; contrasted high-terrain (bryn/mynydd) vs low-terrain (cwm/pant); tested across 1-, 2-, 5-km neighborhoods; used independent elevation data; employed Holm-adjusted p-values; evaluated effect on mean squared error (MSE) with and without terrain-name polarity; explored river-related and woodland categories; assessed residual spatial structure and language issues.
AI.result: High-terrain names associated with locations ~24.4 m higher than surroundings (CI 10.8–38.1 m); replicated with independent elevation source (~24.1 m; CI 10.6–37.6); association persisted across 1-, 2-, 5-km neighborhoods. Adding terrain-name polarity reduced geographically held-out MSE by 4.63% (10-km), 6.22% (25-km), 7.30% (50-km). Effects varied by region; river-related names weaker; woodland model not estimable. Residual spatial structure and unresolved language limits interpretation; no external replication.
AI.conclusion: Selected Welsh settlement-name categories retain measurable present-day terrain information without asserting etymology or causal naming; transferability to other naming systems remains unestablished; findings support toponymic encoding of environment but warrant cautious interpretation and external replication.

title: FIDA: Feature Instability-Driven Attack on Self-Supervised Facial Representation
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. However, the systemic risks they pose in face representation have received little attention. The entanglement of identity features in self-supervised face learning presents unique challenges for attack stealthiness. To address this gap, we propose FIDA (Feature Instability-Driven Attack), a novel backdoor attack framework. FIDA uses subtle semantic triggers for injection, but its key innovation is a novel objective called Feature Instability Loss. It trains the encoder to increase the sensitivity of triggered features along perturbation directions sampled during attack optimization . By preventing the backdoor from exhibiting the rigid feature patterns typical of previous attacks, FIDA effectively evades the evaluated perturbation-based defenses. Experiments show that FIDA achieves a high attack success rate and generally preserves benign utility across the evaluated settings , posing a significant threat to real-world multimedia applications relying on facial analysis.

AI.tldr: Introduces FIDA, a backdoor attack on self-supervised face representations using Feature Instability Loss to make triggers more perturbation-sensitive and less detectable, achieving high attack success while preserving benign utility.
AI.motivation: SSL-based face representations are increasingly used but are susceptible to backdoors; traditional attacks reveal rigid, detectable feature patterns. There is a need for stealthier attacks that exploit the entangled identity features in SSL face learning.
AI.method: Develops FIDA, injecting subtle semantic triggers and training with Feature Instability Loss, which optimizes for increased sensitivity of triggered features along perturbation directions sampled during attack optimization, thereby evading perturbation-based defenses.
AI.result: Empirical results show high attack success rates with generally preserved benign utility across evaluated settings, indicating a significant threat to real-world multimedia applications relying on facial analysis.
AI.conclusion: FIDA exposes systemic vulnerabilities in SSL-based face representations through a novel instability-driven objective, underscoring the need for defenses that account for feature instability and identity entanglement and motivating further research on robust, stealthy backdoor defenses.

title: Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation
summary: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). The central contribution is this relational problem formulation, not a novel GNN architecture; CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. The per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.

AI.tldr: Introduces Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) for detecting AI-generated text via cross-sentence-relational signals, instantiated as CSFG (Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph). The method encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition-deviation signals in a learnable GNN, with per-edge deviation δ_ij acting as a false-positive calibrator. Achieves high binary-detection accuracy (97.14%), strong gains over graph baselines, good generalization to unseen LLMs, but degrades when transition variance aligns with human baseline.
AI.motivation: Current AI-generated text detectors rely on token-level statistics or stylometry, which overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. A relational, sentence-pair level signal—inter-sentence transition variance—offers a robust, generalizable cue to distinguish human from AI writing.
AI.method: Formalize Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) as the core problem; instantiate Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG) to operationalize ROR. Build a graph capturing positional, sequential, semantic, and transition-deviation signals; learn edge features with a Graph Neural Network; compute per-edge deviation δ_ij as a surrogate for ROR; use this to calibrate false positives and detect AI-generated text without hand-crafted thresholds.
AI.result: Empirical validation across four benchmarks with p<0.001. CSFG achieves 97.14% binary detection accuracy, outperforming the strongest graph baseline by 11.14 percentage points. False-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in inflated-variance regime; degradation when generators’ transition variance approaches human baseline.
AI.conclusion: ROR is a core relational formulation for AIGT detection; CSFG demonstrates a concrete, effective instantiation using a GNN-based graph encoding of multiple signal modalities. The emphasis is on relational reasoning rather than novel GNN architectures, with strong empirical performance and generalization, though performance may drop for generators whose transition variance mimics human writing.

title: Decentralized Multitask Learning over Learned Task Graphs
summary: This paper investigates decentralized multitask learning over networks when the underlying task relationships are unknown. While existing graph-regularized multitask frameworks typically assume a known structure, practical settings often require learning inter-task dependencies directly from distributed data. We propose a decentralized two-phase strategy that first estimates a generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates, and subsequently exploits the learned graph to enable cooperative multitask diffusion learning. This framework is motivated by a Gaussian Markov random field prior, which gives rise to a decentralized maximum likelihood estimator for the graph Laplacian. The analysis quantifies the Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to the steady-state performance of the multitask diffusion recursion, and introduces a topology sensitivity index to capture the effect of network heterogeneity. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that cooperation enabled by the learned task graph significantly improves performance over non-cooperative learning, while approaching the true-graph baseline when the estimation stepsize is sufficiently small.

AI.tldr: A decentralized two-phase learning framework: learn a graph Laplacian from noisy gradient iterates under a Gaussian Markov random field prior, then use the learned graph for cooperative multitask diffusion; analyzes Laplacian estimation error and its impact on steady-state performance and introduces a topology sensitivity index; simulations show gains over non-cooperative learning and approaching the true-graph baseline as the stepsize shrinks.
AI.motivation: Unknown task relationships in distributed multitask networks; need to infer inter-task dependencies from distributed data without assuming a known graph structure.
AI.method: Phase 1: decentralized maximum likelihood estimation of the graph Laplacian using a Gaussian Markov random field prior based on noisy non-cooperative SGD iterates. Phase 2: diffusion-based multitask learning that leverages the learned Laplacian for cooperation. Theoretical analysis characterizes Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to steady-state performance; introduces a topology sensitivity index to capture network heterogeneity effects.
AI.result: Derivation of bounds on Laplacian estimation error and its impact on diffusion performance; empirical results show cooperation gains over non-cooperative learning and convergence toward the true-graph baseline as the estimation stepsize decreases; simulations corroborate the theory.
AI.conclusion: Learning the task graph enables effective cooperation in decentralized multitask learning, yielding near-true-graph performance when the Laplacian is well estimated; the approach provides a principled way to discover inter-task relationships from distributed data and exploit them for improved learning.

title: Order Matters: A Chinese Multi-Panel Meme Benchmark for Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Many multimodal tasks depend on how visual elements are ordered and composed, not only on recognizing them in isolation. Internet memes are a compact case of this problem: their punchline often depends on a constrained reading order and cross-panel visual--textual cues. While large vision-language models (LVLMs) show strong performance on single-image understanding, it remains unclear whether they can perform sequence-aware reasoning over structured meme layouts, especially in Chinese social media. We introduce CMPM, a Chinese Multi-Panel Meme benchmark with 1,214 annotated samples covering five structural types, ordering dependency, panel-order constraints, and optional comment context. We formulate a two-layer evaluation: Task1 probes structure typing and order-sensitive panel sequencing (with a context ablation setting), and Task2 evaluates Chinese meme explanation generation with human ratings on five 1-3 Likert dimensions (visual, panel, humor, context, and faithfulness). We benchmark five representative LVLMs under a unified protocol. Results indicate that canonical-display accuracy is not by itself evidence of order understanding: the primary shuffled condition produces a sharp accuracy drop, revealing a persistent gap in order-sensitive multimodal reasoning. Task2 preferences place Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 above the open models, while comment context yields only a small and mixed Core4 gain. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: CMPM introduces a Chinese Multi-Panel Meme benchmark with 1,214 samples across five structural types to evaluate order-sensitive, panel-aware reasoning in LVLMs. A two-layer protocol (structure typing + order-sensitive sequencing; plus a meme-explanation task with human ratings) reveals current LVLMs struggle with cross-panel ordering, with only modest gains from context. Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 outperform open models, and code/data will be released.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in evaluating sequence-aware multimodal reasoning in memes, particularly in Chinese social media, where punchlines rely on constrained reading order and cross-panel cues.
AI.method: CMPM dataset (1,214 samples) covering five structural types. Two-layer evaluation: Task 1 – structure typing and order-sensitive panel sequencing with a context ablation setting; Task 2 – Chinese meme explanation generation rated by humans on five dimensions (visual, panel, humor, context, faithfulness). Benchmark across five representative LVLMs under a unified protocol.
AI.result: Canonical-display accuracy alone misleads about order understanding; a shuffled condition causes a sharp accuracy drop, highlighting gaps in order-sensitive multimodal reasoning. Task 2 shows Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5领先 open models; adding comment context yields only small, mixed gains.
AI.conclusion: CMPM exposes current LVLM limitations in order-sensitive reasoning for Chinese memes and provides a benchmark and protocol for evaluating and improving such capabilities; code and data will be released after acceptance.

title: Five Primitives for Governing Autonomous AI Agents at Runtime
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Describes an implemented system in private pilot deployment; four of five primitives implemented
summary: Enterprise deployments of autonomous AI agents inherit a control model built for human users and long-lived services, and the fit fails in three specific ways: agent principals are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing faster than provisioning; their actions are selected by a model rather than programmed, so the set of things they may attempt is not known in advance; and the population is discovered rather than provisioned, because anyone who can call an API can create one. We argue that governing such agents is a runtime problem -- not a model-alignment problem and not a build-time problem -- and we derive five primitives from the questions that must be answered before an action takes effect and after it has: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain. For each we state what fails if it is absent and why the others cannot structurally supply it. We describe an implementation in which an agent's action is mediated against policy before it takes effect, authorised against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger a third party can verify with the vendor out of the loop. We report what the architecture costs: the enforcement point sits on the request's critical path, identity requires a sidecar per workload, and fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial. We are explicit about implementation status: four primitives are built and running in private pilots, and the fifth is built as separate tooling and not yet integrated into the request path. We keep it in the set deliberately: a five-part decomposition that exactly matches what its authors happened to build is not a taxonomy but a description of a codebase.

AI.tldr: Practical runtime governance for autonomous AI agents using five primitives (discovery, identity, governance, attestation, supply chain); implemented as policy-mediated actions with per-tenant vocabularies and a hash-linked signed ledger; four primitives operational in private pilots; fifth tooling separate, not yet in the request path.
AI.motivation: Enterprise deployments assume persistent principals and programmable actions; for agents that appear/disappear and are model-driven, runtime governance is needed to constrain actions before they take effect. Build-time model alignment is insufficient.
AI.method: Define five primitives and their failure modes; implement enforcement that mediates agent actions against policy before effect; authorize actions against per-tenant vocabulary; log actions in a hash-linked signed ledger verifiable by a third party; architectural components include a request-path enforcement point and a sidecar per workload; treat supply-chain primitive as separate tooling not yet integrated.
AI.result: An architecture with explicit primitives; four implemented and running in private pilots; fifth exists as tooling; cost estimates include enforcement-on-path overhead, per-workload sidecar overhead, and potential availability impact due to fail-closed mediation.
AI.conclusion: The five-primitives decomposition mirrors the actual codebase rather than a taxonomy; runtime governance is necessary for agent actions; the current status shows progress but full integration across the request path is incomplete.

title: Benchmarking_Fast_Domain_Adaptation_for_Unsupervised_Speech_Units
summary: Representation learning has attracted great atten- tion and managed to reach good performances as a pretraining method for downstream tasks or as a first step towards unsu- pervised speech modeling. Yet, little is known about how such methods deal with out-of-domain speech and how could they be adapted in a few shot to new domains. This is important especially for accented speech where one observes a long tail of accents that diverge from the standard ones. We introduce ABX- Accent, a benchmark based on the AESRC dataset that features 10 different accents of English. It includes a small (< 10 hours) unlabelled training set in each of the accents and adaptations of the Zero Resources Challenge ABX evaluation metrics to each of the accents. We illustrate this benchmark with a baseline model that uses adaptive domain normalization to fine tune a pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding model on the accents. This method is first developed on LibriSpeech using a male/female split. When applied to the new benchmark, the proposed method yields a relative improvement of 23.6% on across-speaker ABX scores on average compared to non adapted models. The data and metrics will be open sourced upon paper acceptance

AI.tldr: ABX- Accent introduces a benchmark for 10 English accents with small unlabeled adaptation data; a baseline adapts a pretrained CPC model via adaptive domain normalization and reports ~23.6% relative improvement on across-speaker ABX; data/metrics to be released.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how representation learning for speech handles out-of-domain/accent variability and how to enable few-shot adaptation to new accents.
AI.method: Create ABX- Accent benchmark from AESRC with 10 accents, each having <10 hours unlabeled data and accent-specific ABX metrics; fine-tune a pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) model using adaptive domain normalization; baseline developed with LibriSpeech male/female split; evaluate across-speaker ABX scores.
AI.result: Relative improvement of 23.6% on across-speaker ABX scores on average over non-adapted models; data/metrics to be open sourced after acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive domain normalization facilitates domain adaptation to accented speech in a few-shot regime; ABX- Accent provides a standardized platform for evaluating such methods and may be extended to more accents and languages; data and benchmarks to be released.

title: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
summary: We present an extension and comprehensive real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system designed to accelerate end-to-end scientific research across hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript generation. Moving beyond in silico hypothesis generation, this specialized configuration transitions Co-Scientist into an execution-grounded research partner advancing closed-loop scientific workflows across materials science, biology, and computer science. In materials science, Co-Scientist interfaced with a semi-automated chemical vapor deposition reactor to design a safe precursor route for MXenes; experimental execution produced a lamellar 2D material sharing key structural similarities with the Ti3C2Tx MXene lattice, although further experiments are needed to confirm the atomic structure. Leveraging Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid, lab-in-the-loop execution, it also tailored growth recipes to laboratory constraints in minutes, enabling single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors. In biology, Co-Scientist predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli across inducer (IPTG) gradients from sparse imaging data, quantitatively matching unpublished wet-lab morphological measurements. In computer science, Co-Scientist autonomously discovered an inference-time scaling architecture that outperformed six frontier models on HealthBench (Hard and Professional) while reducing potential clinical harm under blinded physician evaluation. Finally, a double-blind study of end-to-end generated papers with 30 domain experts across 450 reviews demonstrates that Co-Scientist's reliability modules reduce hallucination and plagiarism while improving research safety. Together, these results demonstrate progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Extension of Co-Scientist to execution-grounded, closed-loop research across materials science, biology, and CS with real-world validations and safety enhancements.
AI.motivation: Bridge hypothesis generation with end-to-end experimentation and manuscript generation to accelerate discovery while improving reliability and safety.
AI.method: Integrates Gemini-based AI with lab hardware (semi-automated CVD reactor), lab-in-the-loop optimization (growth recipes for MXenes and TMDCs), in vivo/in vitro phenotype prediction from sparse data, autonomous inference-time architecture search, and a double-blind expert evaluation of generated papers.
AI.result: Demonstrated design and execution of a safe precursor route for MXenes with lamellar material; achieved monolayer growth of MoS2/MoSe2/WS2 in minutes; predicted bacterial phenotypes aligning with measurements; discovered inference-time scaling architecture outperforming six frontier models; double-blind reviews show reduced hallucination/plagiarism and improved safety.
AI.conclusion: Evidence suggests Co-Scientist can function as a real-world, closed-loop scientific partner across disciplines, though some results require further experimental confirmation, and broader validation is needed for atomic-structure verification and clinical safety considerations.

title: Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used objective for aligning language models from preference data, with the coefficient $β$ commonly interpreted as controlling the KL constraint to a reference policy. We show that $β$ entangles two distinct roles: it governs the effective inverse preference-noise scale and simultaneously rescales the optimization dynamics, coupling this scale with the effective step size. As a consequence, at a fixed learning rate the achieved policy deviation is non-monotone in $β$: it vanishes in a dead zone at small $β$, reaches a peak at an intermediate value, and decreases again for larger $β$. Moreover, standard DPO loss values are not comparable across $β$: runs with nearly identical loss curves can differ several-fold in KL divergence from the reference model. This entanglement obscures the role of $β$, increases sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. We propose a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for $β>0$, while making the inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized centered-softplus objective also admits a continuous $β\to0$ endpoint that reduces to a linear preference-margin objective.

AI.tldr: Beta in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) serves two coupled roles: it sets the inverse preference-noise scale and also scales the optimization dynamics, making policy deviation non-monotone in beta at fixed learning rate and causing loss values to be incomparable across betas. A centered-softplus reformulation is proposed, which is argmin-equivalent for beta>0, decouples these effects, and provides a continuous beta→0 endpoint that reduces to a linear margin objective.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the dual roles of beta in DPO, improve interpretability and comparability across beta values, and reduce sensitivity to hyperparameters and learning-rate schedules.
AI.method: The authors analyze the DPO objective to show the entanglement between beta, noise scale, and optimization dynamics. They introduce a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for beta>0, explicitly decoupling inverse noise scale from learning-rate effects, and they derive a beta→0 endpoint that yields a linear preference-margin objective.
AI.result: Demonstrates that at fixed learning rate, policy deviation is non-monotone in beta, with a dead zone at small beta, a peak at intermediate beta, and a decrease at large beta. Standard DPO losses are not comparable across beta because the KL divergence to the reference varies independently of the loss value. The centered-softplus reformulation yields an objective where inverse noise scale and learning-rate effects are explicit and independently tunable, and it provides a continuous beta→0 endpoint reducing to a linear objective.
AI.conclusion: Centering the softplus objective yields an argmin-equivalent formulation to DPO for beta>0, enabling independent control of noise scale and learning rate, improving interpretability, hyperparameter robustness, and learning-rate scheduling. The beta→0 limit offers a simple linear-margin objective.

title: Self-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models without Teacher
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), which leverages a pre-trained, specialized teacher model to provide dense supervisory signals, has achieved significant success in Large Language Models (LLMs) and has recently been adapted to flow matching models. However, this paradigm suffers from two major issues: First, training a separate, task-specific teacher for every new objective incurs high computational costs. Second, the discrepancy between teacher and student distributions often leads to compounding errors along the generation trajectory. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{Self-OPD}, a teacher-free OPD framework for flow matching models that turns the student's own self-exploration into step-wise supervision. At each timestep, Self-OPD branches the deterministic next-state prediction into $K$ stochastic SDE candidates, rolls them out with the ODE sampler, and compares their rewards against a deterministic self-reference baseline to obtain normalized advantages. The velocity field is optimized with an all-branch pull-push objective, where high-advantage branches attract the student and low-advantage branches repel it under direction-aware attenuation and SDE-variance normalization. For multi-objective alignment, Self-OPD fuses normalized scores at the reward level, avoiding direct gradient conflict. Experiments on single and mixed reward benchmarks show that Self-OPD outperforms prior RL and OPD methods without task-specific teachers.

AI.tldr: Self-OPD is a teacher-free on-policy distillation framework for flow matching that uses the student’s own stochastic rollouts via K SDE branches and a pull-push objective to align multiple rewards, surpassing teacher-dependent baselines without task-specific teachers.
AI.motivation: To address two drawbacks of on-policy distillation: (1) high computational cost of training task-specific teachers, and (2) distribution mismatch between teacher and student causing compounding errors.
AI.method: At each timestep, predict the next state deterministically; branch into K stochastic SDE candidates; roll them out with an ODE sampler; compare rewards against a deterministic self-reference baseline to obtain normalized advantages. The velocity field is updated with an all-branch pull-push objective, where high-advantage branches attract and low-advantage branches repel, using direction-aware attenuation and SDE-variance normalization. For multi-objective alignment, fuse normalized scores at the reward level to avoid gradient conflicts.
AI.result: Empirical results on single and mixed reward benchmarks show Self-OPD outperforms prior RL and OPD methods without task-specific teachers.
AI.conclusion: Self-OPD demonstrates that teacher-free, self-guided on-policy distillation can achieve competitive or superior performance for flow matching models and multi-objective alignment, with potential cost reductions.

title: Style as a Confound: False Positives in AI Detection of Non-Native Academic Writing
summary: AI text detectors are increasingly employed in academic settings, but it remains unclear whether their outputs reflect AI authorship itself or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. Previous studies have reported high false-positive rates (FPRs) for non-native English writing, but population-level comparisons confound authorship with differences in topic, domain, and writing style. Professional editing provides a useful setting for examining this issue because it changes the linguistic form of manuscripts while preserving authorship and content. We examined 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, to assess how editing affects detector responses controlling for content and authorship. For the 13 AI text detectors, FPRs for human-written texts varied widely, from 0.0% to 100.0%. Responses varied across detectors: the same edits increased AI scores in some detectors but decreased them in others. Notably, score changes correlated with the extent of editing. The findings identify professional editing style as a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs, rather than establishing a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, raising concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings.

AI.tldr: Editing changes linguistic form without changing authorship; AI detectors show varied, detector-dependent responses to edits; across 13 detectors, false-positive rates for human-written text range widely, and the magnitude of score changes correlates with editing extent, indicating editing style as a key confounder for detector outputs.
AI.motivation: To determine whether AI detectors detect AI authorship or broader linguistic features by exploiting professional editing as a controlled setting that alters form while preserving content and authorship.
AI.method: Analyze 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018–2025): non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions; evaluate 13 AI detectors; compare false-positive rates and score changes; assess correlation with extent of editing.
AI.result: False-positive rates for human-written text varied from 0.0% to 100.0% across detectors. Detector responses to edits were inconsistent across detectors: some detectors' scores increased, others decreased. Magnitude of score changes correlated with the extent of editing.
AI.conclusion: Professional editing style is a major confounding variable in AI detector outputs, compromising fairness and reliability in academic settings; results do not robustly separate text origin from linguistic style; future work should account for editing style or develop detectors robust to such confounds.

title: Performance Foundations of Parallel & Distributed Reasoning Language Models
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and other RL-style post-training paradigms have been used for aligning large language models (LLMs) with reasoning standards. The resulting recent Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, o3, and Kimi k1.5 show that such RL-style post-training ("RL-for-LLMs") can substantially improve chain-of-thought reasoning, long-horizon planning, and self-correction. However, the computational footprint of these systems is massive: state-of-the-art RLM training requires millions of GPU-hours and tightly coupled multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware far beyond classical supervised LLM training. This makes RLM training as much a parallel and distributed systems problem as an algorithmic one. In this work, to facilitate developing RLMs that are simultaneously high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective, we first systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide a compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training algorithmic frameworks: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), as well as their variants. Second, we develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies for RL-for-LLMs, covering both traditional techniques (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, context, and expert parallelism) as well as novel forms of parallelism and optimization techniques for multi-model RLM training, for example disaggregated placement, stage fusion, hybrid parallelism, and asynchronous execution. We harness the work-depth model of parallel computing to make our taxonomy and its insights rigorous and portable. Finally, we analyze existing RLM frameworks and we distill practical guidelines and outline open research directions for building scalable, fast, and cost-effective RLMs.

AI.tldr: Proposes a compute-centric framework for RL-for-LLM systems, delivering a taxonomy of parallelism strategies, a work-depth formalization, and practical guidelines to scale and cost-optimize RLMs (PPO/GRPO variants).
AI.motivation: RLMs can substantially improve reasoning capabilities but impose massive computational footprints and tightly coupled multi-model pipelines. There is a need for scalable, portable, and cost-effective RL-for-LLM tooling.
AI.method: Systematically analyzes PPO, GRPO, and related RL-for-LLM variants from a compute-centric perspective; develops a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, context, expert parallelism) and novel forms (disaggregated placement, stage fusion, hybrid parallelism, asynchronous execution); employs the work-depth model to formalize and generalize these strategies; analyzes existing RLM frameworks and derives guidelines.
AI.result: A rigorous, portable taxonomy of parallelism for RL-for-LLMs; a work-depth-based analytical framework; practical guidelines for scalable, fast, and cost-effective RLM development; identification of optimization opportunities and open research directions.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers actionable guidance and a roadmap of open research directions to advance scalable and economical RL-for-LLM systems.

title: Tether the Subject, Release the Scene: Query-Aware Memory Routing for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Streaming autoregressive video models generate long videos chunk by chunk, using historical memory to maintain consistency. Existing methods typically expose subject and scene queries to history through similar policies. This stabilizes the subject, but can also lock backgrounds, viewpoints, and scene structure to previously generated states even when local motion continues. We call this failure memory-anchored scene under-progression; consistency and motion metrics alone can miss it. We introduce TetherMem, a training-free, query-aware spatiotemporal memory router for frozen video generators. TetherMem separates subject and scene queries and modulates historical access with region- and age-conditioned priors: subject queries retain identity-bearing history, while scene queries reduce reliance on subject history and stale backgrounds. Across 2,400 blinded pairwise judgments from 10 annotators, TetherMem achieves the highest estimated expected preference among eight streaming long-video baselines for overall quality (0.780) and scene progression (0.769). On complete 30-second videos, it sustains changes in background, viewpoint, and scene state while preserving subject recognizability and temporal continuity.

AI.tldr: TetherMem is a training-free memory router that decouples subject and scene queries in streaming video generation to prevent memory-anchored under-progression, achieving higher perceived quality and scene progression while preserving subject identity.
AI.motivation: Current streaming video models expose subject and scene queries to history through similar policies, stabilizing the subject but locking backgrounds and scene structure to past states. This leads to memory-anchored scene under-progression where local motion continues but global consistency lags.
AI.method: Introduce TetherMem: a training-free, query-aware spatiotemporal memory router for frozen video generators. It separates subject and scene queries and modulates historical access with region- and age-conditioned priors. Subject queries preserve identity-bearing history; scene queries reduce reliance on subject history and stale backgrounds.
AI.result: In a blinded study with 2,400 judgments from 10 annotators, TetherMem achieves the highest estimated expected preference among eight baselines for overall quality (0.780) and scene progression (0.769). On complete 30-second videos, it sustains changes in background, viewpoint, and scene state while preserving subject recognizability and temporal continuity.
AI.conclusion: TetherMem addresses memory-anchored scene under-progression without training, enabling stable identity preservation alongside dynamic scene changes in frozen video generators.

title: Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training
summary: Large language models offer broad capabilities, but adapting them to evolving domains, tools, and requirements often entails repeated post-training. Autonomous systems automate parts of this process by proposing updates, training candidates, and using evaluation feedback to select subsequent proposals. As evidence accumulates, a central problem emerges: which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training has changed the parent model? An update's effect depends on its parent, data, and training stage. Treating past success as context-free permission can waste compute. If the resulting child is promoted, it can also degrade the subsequent training trajectory. We formulate this problem as conditional experience transfer and introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training. BCIT binds an observed effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed. Fully trained candidates still face a shared adoption rule, and only observed events extend memory. On one 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates exhibit heterogeneous target and retention effects across the evaluated contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives. These results support treating experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training.

AI.tldr: BCIT introduces boundary-calibrated intervention transfer to authorize reuse of past update evidence in autonomous post-training, linking effects to source context, applying checks and bounded trials to prevent negative transfer; it reduces harmful updates and improves equal-budget final-model quality on a 4B model across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: A core challenge in autonomous post-training is that past update evidence may become non-actionable as the parent model and training data evolve; naive reuse wastes compute and can harm progress. BCIT formalizes conditional experience transfer to safely reuse knowledge.
AI.method: BCIT binds observed update effects to source context, applies applicability conditions, vetoes updates with named hard conflicts, and uses bounded training trials to obtain current-state evidence when needed; adopts a shared adoption rule for fully trained candidates; only observed events extend memory.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a 4B model adapted to finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling shows heterogeneous target and retention effects across contexts; with matched candidates/evidence/compute, BCIT reduces harmful updates and yields higher equal-budget final-model quality than competing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Treat experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training; BCIT demonstrates safer, more effective reuse of past updates by context-bound reasoning and bounded evaluation.

title: Soft Active Electromyography Interface for Machine Learning-Enabled Silent Speech Recognition
summary: Silent speech recognition (SSR) provides an alternative communication pathway in the absence of audible speech. However, conventional approaches are limited by the need for constant facial attachment, privacy concerns, and unstable signal acquisition. Here, we propose a soft, active electromyography (EMG) interface that enables word-level SSR using machine learning. Worn on the hand, the device uses a fingertip electrode that can be positioned near the lips to acquire EMG signals only when needed. The interface integrates liquid metal (LM) interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit (FPC) electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation to ensure high mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network trained on these stable signals achieved a mean accuracy of 97.2 $\pm$ 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary, demonstrating robust linguistic discrimination. Furthermore, real-time drone control validates the practicality of this approach in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails. This study highlights the potential of soft, wearable EMG systems as secure and intuitive human-machine interfaces.

AI.tldr: Soft, wearable finger EMG interface enables word-level silent speech recognition with high accuracy and privacy advantages; demonstrated 97.2% accuracy on 30 words across 3 subjects and real-time drone control.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of conventional SSR (facial attachments, privacy concerns, unstable acquisition) by introducing a discreet, skin-compliant EMG interface that can be worn on the hand and engaged only when needed.
AI.method: Developed a soft active EMG interface worn on the hand with a fingertip electrode near the lips. It uses liquid metal interconnects, transparent flexible PCB electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation for mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network is trained on stable EMG signals to classify a 30-word vocabulary. Evaluation includes three subjects and a real-time drone control demonstration.
AI.result: Mean accuracy 97.2% ± 1.3% across three subjects for 30-word vocabulary, indicating robust linguistic discrimination. Real-time drone control demonstrates practical applicability in noisy/privacy-sensitive environments where voice recognition fails.
AI.conclusion: Soft, wearable EMG systems show promise as secure, intuitive human–machine interfaces for silent speech recognition, enabling private, unobtrusive control in environments where vocal communication is undesirable.

title: AraMS-28k: The Largest Publicly Released Line-Level Dataset of Historical Arabic Manuscripts with Margin and Insertion-Anchor Annotations
comment: Data and code available at this https URL and this https URL. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22095333 Code: https://github.com/ArchaText/AraMS-28k-Dataset
summary: We introduce AraMS-28k, the largest publicly released line-level dataset of genuine historical Arabic manuscripts, comprising 14 books, 3,043 pages, and 28,600 annotated text lines (27,971 main-text, 629 margin). Thirteen books are hand-copied manuscripts spanning three script traditions -- Naskh, Ruq'ah, and Maghrebi -- and one is a lithographed printed edition included to broaden format diversity. Each line is labelled as main-text or margin, and margin lines that have an unambiguous attachment point in the main text are further annotated with an insertion anchor, recovering the manuscript's true non-linear reading order at line-level granularity -- to our knowledge the first such annotation released for a historical Arabic manuscript corpus. Because reference transcriptions are fully vocalised while manuscript hands are typically undiacritised, we release both the raw diacritised transcription and a diacritic-normalised counterpart for every line. The dataset was constructed with RefLAM, a reference-grounded annotation pipeline that aligns multimodal-LLM OCR against independently sourced clean transcriptions and routes every line through human review, combining automatic verification with expert oversight. We describe the construction and quality-control process, present the annotation schema, report dataset statistics at both the corpus and per-book level, and provide baseline HTR results using Kraken and HATFormer, including a cross-script generalisation gradient from in-distribution pages to fully unseen books. AraMS-28k is released with page images, line-level annotations, and fixed train/val/test splits under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to support reproducible research on Arabic manuscript recognition, layout analysis, and reading-order recovery.

AI.tldr: AraMS-28k is the largest public line-level dataset of authentic historical Arabic manuscripts (14 books, 3,043 pages, 28,600 lines). It annotates main-text vs margin lines, with margin anchors to recover non-linear reading order, and provides both vocalised and diacritic-normalised transcriptions. Built with the RefLAM pipeline, includes baseline HTR results (Kraken, HATFormer), and is released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with fixed splits.
AI.motivation: To enable robust OCR, layout analysis, and reading-order recovery for historical Arabic manuscripts by providing a large, diverse, high-quality line-level dataset that includes margin annotations and non-linear reading order, addressing gaps in existing resources.
AI.method: 13 hand-copied manuscripts across Naskh, Ruq'ah, Maghrebi (plus one lithographed edition) were annotated at line level as main-text or margin. Margin lines have insertion anchors to recover the manuscript’s non-linear reading order. Transcriptions are provided in both fully vocalised and diacritic-normalised forms. RefLAM, a reference-grounded annotation pipeline, aligns multimodal-LLM OCR with clean transcriptions and routes lines through human review, combining automatic verification with expert oversight. Annotation schema, corpus statistics, and per-book metrics are described, with baseline HTR results using Kraken and HATFormer and a cross-script generalisation gradient.
AI.result: AraMS-28k comprises 28,600 annotated lines (27,971 main-text, 629 margin) across 14 books, including 13 hand-copied manuscripts in three script traditions and one lithographed edition. It provides page images, line-level annotations, and fixed train/val/test splits under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The dataset enables reading-order recovery via margin insertion anchors and supports both vocalised and diacritic-normalised transcriptions. Baseline HTR results demonstrate cross-script generalisation from in-distribution pages to unseen books.
AI.conclusion: The dataset advances reproducible research in Arabic manuscript recognition, layout analysis, and reading-order recovery, showcasing the effectiveness of the RefLAM pipeline and establishing a substantial resource for cross-script OCR and manuscript layout studies.

title: Graph-Guided Selective Unlearning for Language Models: Controlling Support Routes Beyond Forget Seeds
summary: Enterprises fine-tune language models on proprietary data that may later require removal due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations. Selective unlearning removes requested knowledge while preserving model utility, offering a practical alternative to full retraining, but existing methods treat the explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope. This is insufficient when target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. We propose GRAPHSU, a graph-guided controller that expands the deletion scope beyond forget seeds by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors. On the Task of Fictitious Unlearning (TOFU), a synthetic author-profile question-answering benchmark, and PISTOL, a structural-unlearning benchmark built around interconnected factual samples, with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over a matched seed-only baseline, demonstrating that effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes, not just forget seeds.

AI.tldr: GRAPHSU expands deletion scope by graph-guided propagation of forgetting signals, outperforming seed-only unlearning on TOFU and PISTOL benchmarks with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; achieves substantial reduction in leakage while maintaining utility.
AI.motivation: Selective unlearning relying only on forget seeds misses adversarially recoverable knowledge via paraphrases or related examples; enterprise data requires broader deletion of influence.
AI.method: Build a weighted support-route graph linking training samples; propagate deletion pressure from forget seeds through high-risk neighbors; apply graded forgetting strengths; evaluate on synthetic TOFU and PISTOL benchmarks with two models.
AI.result: GRAPHSU achieves lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points vs seed-only baseline; demonstrates importance of controlling support routes for effective unlearning.
AI.conclusion: Controlling the broader support network is essential; GRAPHSU offers a practical, scalable approach to enterprise unlearning.

title: Unifying Detection and Adaptation in Task-Free Continual Learning
summary: To mitigate catastrophic forgetting in downstream continual learning (CL) for large language models (LLMs), existing methods typically constrain parameter updates or introduce task-specific adaptation modules. However, these methods often rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{Fi}sher-guided \textbf{uni}fied (\textbf{FiUni}) framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation. FiUni is motivated by a key observation about the Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models: the orthogonality among the principal subspaces of its Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation, estimated from a small number of downstream task samples, can reflect the similarity between different tasks. Based on this observation, FiUni constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA), while matching the Fisher principal subspace of each incoming batch window with historical subspaces. This enables FiUni to adaptively determine whether to reuse existing knowledge, expand a related subspace, or create a new subspace, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation.
