Experiments show that FiUni can effectively infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: FiUni proposes a Fisher-guided unified framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation in task-free continual learning for LLMs, using FIM subspaces from K-FAC to guide LoRA updates and dynamically balance knowledge reuse and isolation.
AI.motivation: Address catastrophic forgetting in continual learning for LLMs under task-free settings, where explicit task boundaries are unavailable; existing methods rely on task boundaries or full fine-tuning, which is impractical for scalable, real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Compute Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) subspaces from a small set of downstream task samples via K-FAC; build frozen subspaces that guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA); for each incoming batch window, align its Fisher subspace with historical subspaces to determine whether to reuse, expand, or create a new subspace, thereby enabling batch-level task detection and adaptive parameter sharing/ isolation.
AI.result: Empirical results show FiUni can infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance relative to advanced task-aware CL methods while using fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: FiUni offers a dynamically adaptive, parameter-efficient framework for batch-level task detection in task-free CL, balancing knowledge reuse and isolation through Fisher-subspace alignment and LoRA-guided updates.

title: KISS-GS: 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Kept Simple
summary:
Scene reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become common, however deployment remains painful as the uncompressed file sizes can be massive. Current 3DGS compression systems combine multiple strategies for file size reduction, which can obscure where gains come from and limit component reuse across training pipelines. To make the gains more transparent, we propose KISS-GS, a modular compression pipeline named after the principle of keeping things simple, designed to decouple compression entirely from training.
  Given a 3DGS scene reconstructed with vanilla 3DGS, we are able to reduce it through compaction by 15.7x using a combination of state-of-the-art pruning schemes. Then we encode it into an image-based format designed for simple, ubiquitous decoding. With the SOG-XT format, we propose a novel extension to Self-Organizing Gaussians with two main contributions: (i) Self-organizing 2D Codebooks and (ii) Parallel Representative Assignment Smoothing (PRAS), which leverages the symmetry of quaternion and scale parameterizations to produce 2D attribute grids more amenable to encoding.
  This encoding reduces scene size by 6.6x. We show that optional encoding-aware fine-tuning yields a further 2.2x. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our simple and modular approach thus achieves a total of 85x to 319x reductions in the size of the scene over uncompressed vanilla 3DGS, setting new benchmarks for real-world scenes and surpassing tightly integrated methods in rate-distortion. Decoding relies solely on web-native image formats, and the modular design makes each stage easy to combine with future advances in reconstruction and compaction.
  Code and project page: https://fraunhoferhhi.github.io/KISS-GS/

AI.tldr: Modular compression pipeline (KISS-GS) for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples compression from training, achieving 85x–319x size reductions via pruning, an image-based SOG-XT encoding with Self-Organizing 2D codebooks and PRAS, plus optional encoding-aware fine-tuning; decoding uses web-native image formats with a reusable design.
AI.motivation: Uncompressed 3DGS scenes are extremely large; there is a need for transparent, component-wise compression that can be reused across training pipelines without tightly coupled gains.
AI.method: Three-stage approach: (1) prune-and-compact a vanilla 3DGS scene to drastically reduce data; (2) encode into an image-based SOG-XT format with two innovations—Self-organizing 2D codebooks and Parallel Representative Assignment Smoothing (PRAS) leveraging quaternion/scale symmetry; (3) optional encoding-aware fine-tuning; decode with standard web image formats; modular design enables plugging in future advances.
AI.result: Reported 85x to 319x total reduction in scene size over uncompressed vanilla 3DGS across standard benchmarks; achieved best-in-class rate-distortion relative to tightly integrated methods; decoding relies on widely supported image formats; code and project page released.
AI.conclusion: A simple, modular pipeline can surpass tightly integrated, monolithic compression methods by decoupling compression from training and leveraging task-aware encoding innovations; the approach offers broad compatibility and extensibility for 3DGS workflows.

title: AgentFold: Closed-Loop Agentic Search for Protein Folding Model Design
summary: Scientific LLM agents have shown promise in literature reasoning, tool use, and experiment planning, but it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific machine-learning systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. We study this question in protein folding, where progress requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation. We present AgentFold, a multi-agent framework that formulates folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, AgentFold proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates model variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores both successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches. On an engineering-scale protein-folding codebase comprising more than 2,000 lines of code, AgentFold explores approximately 80 model variants using approximately 5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. Under a matched computational budget, AgentFold improves the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperforms a random-search control. Beyond model improvement, the resulting intervention traces reveal recurring empirical design patterns: stable gains tend to arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, whereas direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training. The code and experimental resources are publicly available at https://github.com/lmqfly/AgentFold.

AI.tldr: AgentFold uses an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven loop to search, implement, and validate code changes in a protein-folding framework (ESMFold), using a Monte Carlo Tree Search–style policy to allocate compute. It reports a 7.5% lDDT improvement over Codex proposals using ~80 variants, ~5k GPU-hours and 170M tokens, and reveals design patterns for stable gains.
AI.motivation: To determine whether scientific LLM agents can autonomously improve tightly coupled scientific ML systems via executable code changes and expensive validation, focusing on protein folding where architectural edits must balance accuracy, efficiency, and domain interpretation.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework forms a closed-loop search over executable code variants starting from ESMFold. Agents propose hypotheses, implement and debug code changes, evaluate model variants, analyze outcomes, and store interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates compute across high-scoring search branches. Evaluations run on a roughly 2,000-line codebase, exploring ~80 variants with ~5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. The framework records both successful and failed interventions.
AI.result: On a mid-sized protein-folding codebase, AgentFold explored ~80 variants, used ~5k GPU-hours and 170M tokens, and achieved a best lDDT improvement of 7.5% over independent Codex proposals, outperforming random search. It also identifies recurring empirical design patterns for stable gains and destabilization factors.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that autonomous LLM-driven agents can perform executable code-level improvements in a complex scientific ML system, and provides actionable design insights and reproducible resources (code and data).

title: Emotional Preferences as Goal-Priority Regulation
summary: A core question in decision-making for agents is whether the relative priorities of competing lower-level objectives can be determined by emotional preferences autonomously generated by higher-level goals, rather than being externally prespecified. Under changing external environments and evolving internal states, emotions play an important functional role in regulating the relative priorities of competing goals. Inspired by the goal-directed theory of emotion, this paper studies how such preference regulation can be computationally realized through reinforcement learning. We first propose a conception of emergent emotional preference: a high-level goal autonomously induces state-dependent preferences over competing lower-level objectives. This conception is built upon a framework consisting of a multi-objective reinforcement learning inner controller and an outer preference generator. The inner controller provides a repertoire of preference-conditioned goal-directed behaviors, while the outer preference generator learns a mapping from the current state to objective preferences through reinforcement learning on a high-level goal. We operationalize emotional preference as a state-dependent regulation of relative goal priorities that emerges through optimization. Furthermore, we characterize the policy space induced by preference regulation and derive an upper bound on the optimality gap in terms of the representation error of the inner behavioral repertoire. We show that the gap vanishes when the optimal policy can be represented by the available preference-conditioned policies. Experiments in self-constructed multi-objective exploration environments show that the learned preference function exhibits contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, and temporal persistence, and outperforms the evaluated fixed-preference and handcrafted-preference strategies.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hierarchical RL framework where a high-level goal autonomously induces state-dependent emotional-like preferences over lower-level objectives; provides theoretical bounds on optimality gaps and demonstrates adaptive, context-sensitive trade-offs that outperform fixed or handcrafted preferences.
AI.motivation: To understand whether emotion-like preference regulation can emerge from higher-level goals and improve decision-making under changing environments without externally specifying objective priorities.
AI.method: A two-tier architecture: an inner multi-objective RL controller that yields a repertoire of preference-conditioned policies, and an outer preference generator that learns a state-to-preference mapping via RL guided by a high-level goal. Formalizes emergent emotional preference as state-dependent regulation of objective priorities; derives policy-space bounds and an upper bound on the optimality gap in terms of inner repertoire representation error.
AI.result: Derived an upper bound on the optimality gap; the gap vanishes when the optimal policy is representable by the available preference-conditioned policies. Empirical results in self-constructed multi-objective exploration environments show contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, and temporal persistence, with performance better than fixed-preference and handcrafted-preference baselines.
AI.conclusion: Emergent emotional preferences are computationally realizable and advantageous for adaptive, context-aware decision-making; the framework provides both theoretical guarantees and empirical support for autonomously regulated relative priorities in RL.

title: Per-View Gaussian Predictions Enable Training-Free Distractor Filtering in Feed-Forward 3DGS
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs an explicit Gaussian representation from multiple input images in one network execution, making 3D reconstruction increasingly accessible for casual captures. However, such captures frequently contain transient objects that appear in only a subset of the views. Such content can be encoded into the per-view Gaussians associated with the inputs that observe it and remain in the combined representation despite being observed by no other input. As a result, it may produce blurred, duplicated, or floating artifacts in novel views. We introduce a training-free filtering procedure that exploits this per-view prediction structure. For each input, we exclude its associated Gaussians and render the same camera using the remaining representation, revealing content that is inconsistent with the other inputs. Feature similarity forms candidate regions, and rendering-based verification retains only candidates whose removal reduces reconstruction error in the other input views. The procedure operates on a single frozen prediction without retraining or scene-specific optimization. Across three reconstruction models and two distractor benchmarks, it consistently improves novel-view quality with varying numbers of input views. On clean scenes, evaluations across four models show that the original reconstructions are largely preserved.

AI.tldr: Training-free per-view Gaussian filtering reduces artifacts from transient objects in multi-view Gaussian Splatting reconstructions, improving novel-view quality without retraining.
AI.motivation: Transient objects appearing in only a subset of input views can be encoded into per-view Gaussians, leaking into the combined representation and causing blurred, duplicated, or floating artifacts in novel views; a non-learning post-processing filter is needed to remove such content.
AI.method: For each input view, remove its associated Gaussians and render with the remaining representation. Use feature similarity to identify inconsistent content as candidate regions; verify candidates by rendering to check whether removing them reduces reconstruction error in other views. Operates on a frozen predictor, no retraining or scene-specific optimization. Evaluated across three reconstruction models and two distractor benchmarks; improves novel-view quality with varying numbers of input views; preserves original reconstructions on clean scenes.
AI.result: Consistent improvement in novel-view quality across multiple models and datasets. On clean scenes, the original reconstructions are largely preserved, indicating the filter tends to avoid over-editing in non-occluded content.
AI.conclusion: A versatile, training-free post-processing filter for 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates transient-content artifacts without retraining, with demonstrated robustness across models and datasets.

title: Discovering Relationships in Data Lakes Using Large Language Models: An Industrial Case
summary: Data lakes rely on metadata to remain usable, yet this meta data is often limited or weakly informative for column relationship discovery, especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels. We propose ColRel, a two-stage method that builds column embeddings from metadata and data available at ingestion time. In difficult cases, such as coded schemata, business dictionaries help better interpret column names and support the generation of short natural-language descriptions used in the second stage. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset show that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings.

AI.tldr: ColRel is a two-stage approach that combines ingestion-time metadata and data with short natural-language descriptions to discover column relationships in data lakes, aided by business dictionaries for coded schemas; it excels in semantically related, weak-signal settings, evidenced by benchmarks and an ERP dataset.
AI.motivation: Metadata in data lakes is often insufficient for reliable column relationship discovery, especially with ERP-derived datasets containing coded or abbreviated schema labels.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) build column embeddings from ingestion-time metadata and data; (2) generate short natural-language descriptions (helped by business dictionaries for coded schemata) to improve relationship discovery.
AI.result: ColRel shows strong performance in semantically related, weak-signal settings on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset.
AI.conclusion: Integrating metadata-driven embeddings with data signals and interpretable NL descriptions, aided by business dictionaries, enhances column relationship discovery under weak-signal conditions, improving usability of data lakes for ERP-derived data.

title: Tabular Deep Learning for Algorithmic Trading: Cross-Regime Bayesian Optimisation for Equity Signal Generation
summary: Algorithmic trading now represents a market exceeding $20 billion, where even marginal gains in signal robustness can translate into economically significant returns. Existing evaluations of equity prediction models do not explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection. Five model classes are trained on daily observations from approximately 300 large-cap US equities over eleven years, with Bayesian optimisation configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection is associated with out-of-sample generalisation, as signal precision remains above the random baseline across all four quarters of the test period, and portfolio performance slowly degrades under simulated input noise before collapsing beyond a defined threshold. No individual tabular deep learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees, but combining XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation produces a Hybrid ensemble with an annualised return of 51.26%, a Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and a statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p = 0.011). A near-zero beta indicates this outperformance is driven by stock selection, not market exposure. Alternative data plays a secondary role once technical and fundamental features are accounted for, as well as contributing more strongly on the short side than the long, and varies by model class. An interactive application makes these results explorable in real time, with live data integration the remaining step toward practical deployment.

AI.tldr: A regime-aware hyperparameter search enhances robustness of equity-prediction models; a Hybrid XGBoost+TabNet ensemble delivers strong risk-adjusted returns with low market beta.
AI.motivation: Explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter optimization to improve out-of-sample generalization under regime shifts.
AI.method: Five model classes trained on daily data from ~300 large-cap US equities across 11 years; Bayesian optimization targeted trading performance across three market regimes; assessed out-of-sample generalization and input-noise robustness; combined XGBoost and TabNet via rank aggregation into a Hybrid ensemble; evaluated an interactive real-time explorable result.
AI.result: Regime-robust hyperparameters improve out-of-sample generalization as signal precision remains above random baseline across all test quarters; portfolio performance degrades under simulated input noise only beyond a defined threshold; no single tabular deep-learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees; Hybrid ensemble (XGBoost+TabNet with rank aggregation) achieves annualized return 51.26%, Sharpe 2.44, CAPM alpha 0.423 (p=0.011) with near-zero beta indicating stock selection dominates performance; alternative data plays a secondary role, more impactful on the short side and varying by model class; results can be explored via an interactive application with live data integration as a next step.
AI.conclusion: Regime-aware hyperparameter optimization yields robust, economically meaningful performance with low market exposure, supporting practical deployment pending live data integration.

title: RubricRM: Generative Reward Modeling via Dynamic Rubrics for Image Generation and Editing
summary: Reward models play an essential role in aligning visual generative models, yet most existing visual reward models use a single scalar score or rely on fixed criteria that cannot adapt to different instructions. This limits both interpretability and task sensitivity, especially for text-to-image generation and instruction-based image editing, where different inputs require different evaluation dimensions. We propose RubricRM, a pairwise generative reward modeling framework that first produces an input-specific rubric with evaluation dimensions, weights, and scoring criteria, and then applies the rubric to score candidate images. We train dedicated RubricRM models for text-to-image generation and image editing using a two-stage training pipeline: supervised fine-tuning teaches the model the rubric-based scoring paradigm, while GRPO further improves scoring through fine-grained dimension-level rewards. Experiments on multiple generation and editing benchmarks show that RubricRM outperforms existing specialized reward models and remains competitive with strong proprietary MLLM judges despite using smaller backbones. Our models, data, and code are available at https://github.com/zijiankan/RubricRM.

AI.tldr: RubricRM creates input-specific rubrics for image evaluation and uses a two-stage training (supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO) to score text-to-image generation and image editing, outperforming existing reward models and approaching proprietary judges with smaller backbones; code available.
AI.motivation: Current visual reward models rely on single scalar scores or fixed criteria, limiting interpretability and task sensitivity for diverse inputs in text-to-image generation and image editing.
AI.method: For each input, RubricRM generates an evaluation rubric with dimensions, weights, and scoring criteria, then applies it to candidate images. Training is two-stage: (1) supervised fine-tuning to teach rubric-based scoring, (2) GRPO to improve scoring via fine-grained dimension-level rewards. Separate RubricRM models are trained for text-to-image generation and image editing.
AI.result: RubricRM outperforms existing specialized reward models and remains competitive with strong proprietary MLLM judges despite smaller backbones, across multiple generation and editing benchmarks. The work provides data and code at the linked repository.
AI.conclusion: RubricRM enables adaptable, interpretable, input-specific reward evaluation for visual generation tasks, achieving strong performance with smaller models and offering a practical release of data and code for replication.

title: DEEPCHART: How Far are LLMs from Faithful Data-Science Chart Generation?
summary: Faithful chart generation in real-world data-science workflows requires grounding visualizations in scattered evidence, computing chart-ready quantities, and rendering them accurately. Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible, instruction-compliant charts, yet data-level hallucinations remain difficult to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts. To measure this gap, we introduce DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances drawn from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. DEEPCHART formulates chart generation as an Extract--Reason--Visualize pipeline and evaluates source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stage by stage. Experiments with state-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors common in realistic long and multimodal settings. These findings suggest that larger context windows alone are insufficient; faithful chart generation also requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering. Our benchmark and associated resources are available at https://github.com/tangdouer1005/DeepChart.

AI.tldr: DEEPCHART is an expert-annotated benchmark for task-conditioned chart generation, framing it as Extract--Reason--Visualize to evaluate source data extraction, data reasoning, and rendering; findings show visually plausible charts can mask data-level errors, underscoring the need for reliable extraction and reasoning beyond larger context windows.
AI.motivation: To address data-level hallucinations in AI-generated charts that appear visually plausible but may misrepresent underlying numbers, especially in long, noisy, multimodal contexts.
AI.method: Assemble 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances from real-world sources; annotate with ground-truth data and reasoning steps; evaluate in three stages (source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, chart rendering) within an Extract--Reason--Visualize pipeline.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that despite plausible visuals, extraction and reasoning errors are common in long multimodal settings; larger context windows alone are insufficient for faithful chart generation.
AI.conclusion: DEEPCHART provides a benchmark and resources to study faithful chart generation, emphasizing evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning as prerequisites to accurate rendering.

title: Cone Extended Rayleigh Quotients for Directed Graph Learning: Minimax Spectral Certificates, Sensitivity, and Adaptive Control
summary:
Directed graph learning naturally leads to trainable nonsymmetric propagation operators with distinct right and left spectral structures. Building on the two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils \[ B_θ-λG, \] we develop a learning-oriented methodology for spectral certification, sensitivity analysis, and control without requiring symmetry, nonnegativity, or cone preservation. In the positive-orthant setting, computable lower and upper cone bounds provide an a posteriori enclosure of a distinguished cone level, while smooth soft-min/max surrogates preserve rigorous one-sided bounds with explicit approximation errors and remain differentiable with respect to the trainable parameters.
  For a simple interior level, the right and left modes satisfy \[ Dλ_C(B)[H]=v_C^T H u_C, \] yielding first-order optimal graph-supported interventions under prescribed perturbation budgets and motivating adaptive spectral control. Numerical experiments demonstrate the applicability of the approach beyond cone-preserving operators and in directed learning settings. Signed nonsymmetric perturbations reveal a transition from interior eigenpairs to boundary complementary quasi-pairs, including non-spectral cone levels, while controlled experiments show that symmetrization can remove predictive information carried solely by edge direction.
  On the directed Cora citation network, adaptive recomputation of the right--left sensitivity reduces the distinguished spectral level by approximately $21.5\%$ under a cumulative edge-weight reduction budget of $0.5\%$, with no observed change in test accuracy for the trained model and data split considered.

AI.tldr: Two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for directed graphs enables spectral certification, sensitivity analysis, and control without symmetry; provides computable cone bounds and differentiable surrogates; validated on Cora with a notable reduction in a distinguished spectral level and no loss in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Directed graphs yield nonsymmetric propagation operators with distinct right/left spectral structures. There is a need for rigorous spectral guarantees, sensitivity analysis, and control mechanisms that do not require symmetry, nonnegativity, or cone-preservation.
AI.method: Develop a two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils B_θ-λG. Provide computable lower/upper cone bounds in the positive orthant; employ smooth soft-min/max surrogates with explicit approximation errors that stay differentiable in trainable parameters. Derive first-order sensitivity Dλ_C(B)[H] = v_C^T H u_C for interior levels and enable adaptive spectral control. Demonstrate applicability beyond cone-preserving operators and in directed learning; study perturbation regimes including signed nonsymmetric perturbations and impact of symmetrization. Validate on directed Cora with adaptive recomputation of right–left sensitivity.
AI.result: Establishes an a posteriori cone enclosure for a distinguished cone level, with differentiable bounds and explicit error; shows transitions from interior eigenpairs to boundary quasi-pairs under perturbations; symmetrization can erase edge-direction information. In Cora, adaptive recomputation reduces the spectral level by ~21.5% under a 0.5% edge-weight budget, with no test-accuracy change.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends spectral guarantees and adaptive control to directed (nonsymmetric) learning without symmetry or cone-preservation assumptions. It enables provable, differentiable spectral interventions and broad applicability beyond cone-preserving operators, demonstrating practical impact on directed graph learning.

title: Geo-LoRA: Geometry-Aware Subspace Evolution for Low-Rank Adaptation in Continual Learning
summary: Rehearsal-free class-incremental learning (CIL) with LoRA adapters remains challenging because the low-rank subspaces updated across tasks evolve without geometric control, causing unstable shared representations and repetitive collapse of task-specific updates into previously occupied directions. We introduce Geo-LoRA, a geometry-aware framework that explicitly regulates how low-rank subspaces, both shared and task-specific, evolve during continual learning. For the shared branch, Subspace Projection Preservation (SPP) constrains consecutive updates to follow smooth trajectories on the Grassmann manifold, and Adaptive Core-Slack Alignment (ACSA) decomposes transitions into principal and residual components, aligning the former while modulating the latter to balance stability and plasticity. For the task-specific branch, Median-Calibrated Block Overlap (MCBO) imposes a statistical constraint via normalized projection overlap, penalizing excessive reuse to mitigate subspace crowding. These constraints jointly regulate the evolution of all LoRA subspaces across layers and tasks without introducing additional adapter types beyond standard LoRA. Geo-LoRA provides a principled geometric formulation for continual low-rank adaptation and consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets and different task lengths.

title: Categorizer Automata for Discounted-Sum Payoffs
summary: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is a fundamental operation in artificial intelligence. We introduce the categorizer automaton, a deterministic automaton that reads an infinite sequence of rewards and identifies which of finitely many bins contains its discounted sum. Categorizer automata generalize comparator automata, the special case of two bins, which have already proven useful in quantitative synthesis. Our main technical contribution is the construction of a categorizer automaton whose state space is linear in the number of bins, rather than exponential as obtained by a cross-product of comparator automata. We then apply categorizer automata to Markov decision processes, where they allow one to synthesize policies that maximize the expected utility of a discounted-sum payoff for utility functions that may be discontinuous. For piecewise-constant utility functions, the resulting algorithm is exact and runs in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions, a class that includes any utility with bounded slope between finitely many jumps, it again runs in pseudo-polynomial time and yields an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy. We also show that the synthesis problem considered is PSPACE-hard already for piecewise-constant utilities.

AI.tldr: Introduce categorizer automata to classify discounted sums into finitely many bins with linear-state complexity, enabling efficient MDP policy synthesis for discontinuous utilities; generalizes comparator automata and achieves exact/pseudo-polynomial algorithms, with PSPACE-hardness for piecewise-constant utilities.
AI.motivation: Mitigate state explosion when binning continuous discounted sums and enable synthesis for MDPs with discontinuous utility functions.
AI.method: Construct categorizer automata whose state space scales linearly with the number of bins (unlike exponential cross-products of comparator automata). Apply to MDPs to synthesize policies that maximize discounted-sum payoff utilities. Develop exact algorithm for piecewise-constant utilities and pseudo-polynomial-time epsilon-optimal algorithms for piecewise-Lipschitz utilities.
AI.result: Exact algorithm for piecewise-constant utilities; pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm for both piecewise-constant and piecewise-Lipschitz utilities, yielding epsilon-optimal policies for the latter; PSPACE-hardness of the synthesis problem even for piecewise-constant utilities.
AI.conclusion: Categorizer automata provide a compact, efficient framework for binning discounted sums and enabling synthesis with discontinuous utilities; they achieve favorable state complexity and preserve decidability, though some hardness results persist (PSPACE-hard).

title: TRACE-CRC: Trajectory-Adaptive Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Step Channel State Information Prediction
comment: Published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), volume 329, Conformal and Probabilistic Prediction with Applications (COPA 2026)
summary: Reliable prediction of time-varying channel state information (CSI) is essential for efficient wireless communication. Each CSI frame is a matrix-valued representation of the wireless channel response, and a sequence of CSI frames forms a temporal channel trajectory. Modern deep learning-based CSI predictors, however, often provide only point predictions and lack calibrated uncertainty estimates. This limitation is particularly problematic in multi-step CSI prediction, where the target is a sequence of future CSI matrices, and downstream decisions such as beamforming or scheduling may fail if any part of the predicted trajectory is unreliable. We propose trajectory-adaptive calibration and error profiling with conformal risk control (TRACE-CRC), a method for trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification in multi-step CSI prediction. TRACE-CRC constructs Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI matrices and controls the risk that at least one future frame is uncovered. Instead of calibrating each future step independently, TRACE-CRC combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control. Empirically, TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with substantially smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while avoiding the trajectory undercoverage of compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.

AI.tldr: TRACE-CRC provides trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification for multi-step CSI prediction by building Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted matrices and using trajectory-adaptive calibration with learn-then-test conformal risk control to ensure trajectory-level coverage with tighter bounds.
AI.motivation: In multi-step CSI prediction, point estimates lack calibrated uncertainty and trajectory-level reliability is critical for downstream decisions; existing stepwise calibrations can under- or over-cover entire trajectories.
AI.method: Trajectory-adaptive calibration and error profiling with conformal risk control (TRACE-CRC) constructs Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI frames, avoids per-step independent calibration, and combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control to guarantee trajectory-level coverage.
AI.result: Empirically, TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with significantly smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while mitigating trajectory undercoverage observed in compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.
AI.conclusion: TRACE-CRC provides efficient, trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification for multi-step CSI prediction, enabling reliable trajectory-level decisions with tighter, calibrated uncertainty bounds.

title: TempJail: Temporal Jailbreak Attacks against Image-to-Video Generation Models
summary: In recent years, image-to-video (I2V) generation models have made remarkable progress in subject consistency and temporal coherence, enabling high quality video synthesis. However, these advances also introduce new safety risks. Existing studies mainly focus on jailbreak attacks involving single frame violations, while largely overlooking the temporal dimension unique to video generation models. In this paper, we investigate three attack scenarios and uncover a temporal vulnerability in I2V systems: unsafe semantics may emerge not from a single frame, but from semantic composition over time. We further identify two key challenges in such attacks: temporal abstraction and semantic camouflage. To address these issues, we propose TempJail, a novel temporal jailbreak framework for I2V systems. For temporal abstraction, we decompose a target malicious caption into an initial frame visual condition and a temporal text instruction. For semantic camouflage, on the image side we model semantic injection as controlled latent perturbation in diffusion sampling and introduce gradient guidance from pretrained encoders. On the text side, we rewrite the caption into an innocuous ``subject-action-scene'' template that bypasses safety filters while preserving temporal guidance. In the black-box inference phase, these two modalities jointly enable malicious semantics to be gradually triggered over time. Experiments on closed-source commercial models, including Kling, Seedance, Veo and PixVerse, show that TempJail improves attack success rate over prior state-of-the-art methods by 23.3\% under GPT-5.2 evaluation and 22.0\% under human evaluation. Our codes are available at \href{https://github.com/luqi-glory/TempJail}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: Identifies temporal vulnerabilities in image-to-video (I2V) systems and proposes TempJail to induce unsafe semantics over time via temporal composition, combining caption decomposition and latent perturbations with text rewrites; achieves higher attack success on several models.
AI.motivation: Safety risks in I2V arise from temporal dimension; prior work focuses on single-frame jailbreaks, neglecting how unsafe semantics can emerge through semantic composition over time.
AI.method: TempJail framework: (1) decompose a malicious caption into an initial frame visual condition and a temporal text instruction; (2) image-side: controlled latent perturbation in diffusion sampling with gradient guidance from pretrained encoders to inject semantics; (3) text-side: rewrite caption into an innocuous subject-action-scene template that preserves temporal guidance and bypasses safety filters; (4) black-box inference to trigger malicious semantics gradually over time.
AI.result: Attack success rate improved by 23.3% under GPT-5.2 evaluation and 22.0% under human evaluation, compared to prior state-of-the-art; validated on closed-source models Kling, Seedance, Veo, PixVerse; code released on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Temporal semantics introduce a new class of safety risks in I2V; TempJail demonstrates practical exploitation of temporal composition and underscores the need for temporal-aware defenses and robust safety mechanisms across I2V systems.

title: AI Control Scientist: LLM-driven Agentic System for Automated Control Design
summary: Control system design is critical for modern industry, such as chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control. However,traditional control design workflows rely heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To this end, this paper proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS), the first large language model (LLM)-driven agent capable of automatically generating optimized controller from language design requirements. Specifically, a Task Modeling Agent interprets user requirements to engineering constraints; a Controller Design Agent generate candidate controller structures and executable code; and a Parameter Tuning Agent refine controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed agentic system can automatically generate multiple representative control systems, outperforms existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency. This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, paving the way for model predictive control and other advanced control systems design.

AI.tldr: An LLM-driven agent system (AICS) automatically generates optimized controllers from language requirements using three specialized agents, improving design success and optimization efficiency over automated baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional control design is manual, expert-driven, and parameter-intensive, hindering efficiency and scalability; AI automation can automate design from requirements and support advanced control methods like MPC.
AI.method: Proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS) architecture with Task Modeling Agent, Controller Design Agent, and Parameter Tuning Agent. The Task Modeling Agent converts user requirements into engineering constraints; the Controller Design Agent proposes controller structures and generates executable code; the Parameter Tuning Agent optimizes controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria. Empirical evaluation shows automatic generation of multiple representative control systems and superior performance to baselines.
AI.result: AICS outperforms existing automated baselines in design success rate and optimization efficiency; demonstrates feasibility of fully agent-driven control design.
AI.conclusion: This work could transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, enabling adoption of MPC and other advanced control system design approaches.

title: Ultra Low-Power, Lightweight, Probabilistic RSS-Based Path Reconstruction: A System for Landscape-Scale Bee Tracking
summary: Applications in fields such as movement ecology, Internet of Things or robotics share the need for systems that localize devices that are too small and power constrained to implement GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite Systems). Alternative low-power localization methods often rely on only measurements of RSS (Received Signal Strength) to infer the AoA (Angle of Arrival) of a transmitted radio frequency signal, but are limited by range and the power demand of the large number of RSS measurements required to infer an accurate AoA. In this paper we address these issues with a novel RSS-based method for tracking ultra lightweight and low-power moving receivers across a complex landscape, achieved by using a minimal number of RSS measurements from simple rotating high-gain transmitters with a range of 300m, and applying probabilistic modelling to infer their AoA. The receiver's movement path is then modelled using a Gaussian process and reconstructed using doubly stochastic variational inference, resulting in approximately 15m accuracy tracking of receivers weighing 38mg (including power source) over a scalable landscape range while consuming less than 180uW, increased to approximately 10m accuracy at less than 600uW by taking more RSS measurements. We anticipate that this method will support fields such as the behavioural study of flying insect species, which we demonstrate by applying the system to track Bombus terrestris nest return flights.

AI.tldr: Novel RSS-based AoA tracking for ultra-light, low-power receivers using rotating high-gain transmitters (range ~300 m). Combines probabilistic AoA inference with Gaussian process motion modeling, and doubly stochastic variational inference for path reconstruction. Achieves ~15 m accuracy at <180 μW (38 mg device) and ~10 m accuracy at <600 μW with more RSS samples; demonstrated on Bombus terrestris nest return flights. Supports scalable, low-power localization in ecology, IoT, and robotics.
AI.motivation: Need for localization of extremely small, power-constrained devices where GNSS is infeasible. Traditional RSS-based AoA methods require many measurements and higher power; there is a demand for accurate, low-power tracking across complex landscapes for applications such as movement ecology and insect behavior studies.
AI.method: Use minimal RSS measurements from rotating high-gain transmitters (range ~300 m) to probabilistically infer Angle of Arrival (AoA). Model receiver motion with a Gaussian process and reconstruct the trajectory using doubly stochastic variational inference.
AI.result: Achieves approximately 15 m localization accuracy for 38 mg receivers at power under 180 μW; accuracy improves to about 10 m when power increases under 600 μW by collecting more RSS measurements. Demonstrated on tracking Bombus terrestris nest return flights, indicating applicability to real-world moving fauna tracking over scalable landscapes.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables accurate, energy-efficient tracking of ultra-lightweight devices over large areas using RSS-based AoA with probabilistic and Bayesian inference, supporting applications in behavioral ecology and related fields where GNSS or high-power localization is impractical.

title: Aphanta: Diagnosing Task-Aligned Image-Edited Intermediates for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Explicit visual intermediates can help multimodal large language models (MLLMs) externalize spatial evidence and updated visual states, but their utility depends on whether an image editor can faithfully realize the required transformation. We introduce \textbf{Aphanta}, an automated task-discovery and closed-loop diagnostic framework for the MLLM -> image editor -> MLLM pipeline. Aphanta evaluates three conditions---direct reasoning, reasoning with an editor-generated intermediate, and reasoning with an idealized reference intermediate---to separate potential visual headroom from the practical utility of current editors. Across 20 candidate tasks and multiple editor--MLLM combinations, we find that utility is strongly task-conditioned. Gains concentrate in visual cue injection, grounding, and counterfactual state realization, whereas intermediates requiring symbol-sensitive construction or structural extrapolation are substantially less reliable. On the selected positive-task subset, our consolidated Qwen pipeline improves the mean task score from 0.343 to 0.445 ($+10.2$ points; $+29.7\%$ relative), while the full study also retains filtered and unsuccessful tasks to expose the boundary. These results position image editing as a specialized visual workspace rather than a universal reasoning mechanism, and establish Aphanta as a reusable protocol for measuring task--representation alignment, editor realization, and downstream pipeline utility.

AI.tldr: Aphanta is a diagnostic framework to measure when MLLMs can benefit from image-editor intermediates by comparing direct reasoning, editor-generated intermediates, and idealized reference intermediates across 20 tasks and multiple editor-MLLM setups; utility is highly task-dependent and editors act as a specialized visual workspace rather than universal reasoners.
AI.motivation: To quantify and disentangle the practical utility of image editing as an externalized visual state for multimodal LLM reasoning, separating editor-fidelity constraints from theoretical potential.
AI.method: Evaluate three conditions (direct reasoning; reasoning with an editor-generated intermediate; reasoning with an idealized reference intermediate) within a closed-loop MLLM→image editor→MLLM pipeline. Test across 20 candidate tasks and multiple editor–MLLM combinations; report task-level and aggregated scores, including a positivity subset and boundary-exposing filtered/uncompleted tasks; use a consolidated Qwen pipeline for improvements.
AI.result: Utility is strongly task-conditioned. Gains concentrate in visual cue injection, grounding, and counterfactual state realization; intermediates requiring symbol-sensitive construction or structural extrapolation are less reliable. On the selected positive-task subset, mean task score rises from 0.343 to 0.445 (reported as +10.2 points, +29.7% relative). The full study also presents filtered and unsuccessful tasks to reveal boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Image editing acts as a specialized visual workspace rather than a universal reasoning mechanism. Aphanta offers a reusable protocol to measure task–representation alignment, editor realization, and downstream pipeline utility across MLLM–editor systems.

title: Inductive Correlation Clustering with Graph Neural Networks
summary:
Correlation Clustering (CC) is a natural formulation of clustering in combinatorial optimization, which uses a graph representation of the input and does not require a pre-specified number of clusters. Given $n$ objects and a pairwise similarity function, the goal is to cluster the objects so that similar objects are put in the same cluster and dissimilar objects are put in different clusters. Despite its versatility, existing CC algorithms suffer from significant scalability issues and are inherently transductive: i.e., the algorithm must be executed from scratch for any new problem instance.
  In this work, we bridge this gap by leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to solve Inductive Correlation Clustering, a novel generalization of the CC problem designed to handle unseen graph instances. By learning to exploit common structural patterns and node features during training, our framework generalizes to new graphs drawn from the same distribution with minimal computational overhead with respect to standard algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach through extensive experiments. Our framework not only excels in the inductive setting, e.g., lowering the inference time up to $5$ order of magnitude, while maintaining an approximation ratio within $~10\%$ of the best baseline solution, but also achieves competitive results on standard (transductive) CC benchmarks. Finally, we showcase a practical application of our framework as a learnable pooling mechanism for graph classification. Our results indicate that our method serves as an efficient pooling layer, enhancing the ability of GNNs to capture hierarchical structural information in networks.

AI.tldr: A GNN-based inductive framework for correlation clustering (CC) that generalizes to unseen graphs, enabling scalable inference with near-baseline accuracy and offering a learnable pooling layer for graph classification.
AI.motivation: CC is powerful but inherently transductive and not scalable to new instances. There's a need for inductive, scalable CC that can leverage graph structure and node features across instances.
AI.method: Train a Graph Neural Network to exploit structural patterns and node features to perform Inductive Correlation Clustering on unseen graphs from the same distribution; yields fast inference with minimal overhead compared to standard CC solvers and can be used as a learnable pooling layer for graph classification.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong inductive performance: inference time up to 5 orders of magnitude faster; approximation ratio within ~10% of the best baseline; competitive results on transductive CC benchmarks; demonstrates the framework as an effective pooling operator for graph classification.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers scalable, inductive CC through GNNs, with practical benefits for graph pooling and classification, while preserving competitive clustering quality.

title: Virtual iEEG from Scalp EEG: Charting the Landscape of Source Imaging, Intracranial Inference and Reconstruction
summary: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides temporally precise and spatially specific access to neural activity from focal and deep brain regions, but its invasiveness and restricted anatomical coverage limit routine use. These constraints have motivated scalp-to-intracranial inference, termed virtual iEEG when model outputs carry iEEG-defined event, feature, representation, or contact-level waveform semantics. This review presents a target-centred framework distinguishing event inference, feature translation, and waveform reconstruction, while separating predictability from observability, identifiability, fidelity, and utility. Evidence is evaluated according to cohort independence, anatomical and spectral coverage, train--test separation, and target-patient adaptation. Current studies support inference of selected intracranial events, low-frequency components, and task-related representations, but not unique recovery of arbitrary contact-level activity. Stronger validation requires appropriate controls, source-imaging baselines, uncertainty assessment, and incremental-utility testing. Future progress depends on independent paired datasets and prospective evidence that virtual iEEG adds value beyond scalp EEG and EEG source imaging.

AI.tldr: Virtual iEEG is a framework to infer intracranial neural events and representations from noninvasive data, showing selective success in inferring certain events and low-frequency content but not full recovery of arbitrary intracranial activity; robust validation and independent paired datasets are needed to show added value over scalp EEG and EEG source imaging.
AI.motivation: Intracranial EEG offers precise spatiotemporal neural signals but is invasive with limited coverage; there is a need for noninvasive methods that capture iEEG-like semantics (events, features, waveforms) to extend clinical and research access.
AI.method: Proposes a target-centered framework that categorizes inference tasks into event inference, feature translation, and waveform reconstruction. Distinguishes predictability, observability, identifiability, fidelity, and utility; assesses evidence along dimensions such as cohort independence, anatomical/spectral coverage, train-test separation, and target-patient adaptation.
AI.result: Current studies demonstrate inference of selected intracranial events, low-frequency components, and task-related representations, but fail to uniquely recover arbitrary contact-level activity. Validation needs controls, source-imaging baselines, uncertainty assessment, and incremental-utility testing.
AI.conclusion: Progress toward noninvasive virtual iEEG hinges on independent paired datasets and prospective evidence that virtual iEEG provides added value beyond scalp EEG and EEG source imaging; stronger validation and utility testing are required.

title: SymbolLKG: Towards Verifiable Logical Reasoning via Logical Knowledge Graph and Symbolic Solvers
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in natural language understanding, yet they struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, frequently suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing solutions like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) lack rigorous verification mechanisms, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often misses the complex, structural dependencies inherent in logical tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a Neuro-Symbolic architecture that integrates a Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with dynamic solver routing. Specifically, we introduce an ontology-based LKG that treats logical rules and constraints as first-class topological nodes, enabling explicit modeling of dependencies extracted from text. We further design a Logic Router to dynamically dispatch tasks to the optimal symbolic engine, which is supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism. Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.

AI.tldr: A Neuro-Symbolic framework that combines an ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph with a dynamic solver routing mechanism and topology-aware retrieval to improve logical reasoning in LLMs, achieving higher accuracy and providing verifiable reasoning paths over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at natural language but struggle with strict, multi-step logical reasoning and are prone to hallucinations. CoT lacks formal verification, and standard RAG misses complex structural dependencies in logic. A principled integration of symbolic logic with neural models, leveraging topological reasoning, could improve accuracy and provide verifiable explanations.
AI.method: Introduce an ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) where logical rules/constraints are topological nodes to capture dependencies extracted from text. Develop a Logic Router that dynamically dispatches tasks to the most suitable symbolic engine. Employ a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism to supply structurally relevant information.
AI.result: Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks show the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, achieving higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates the viability of neuro-symbolic integration for verifiable, accurate logical reasoning in LLMs and offers a scalable path to robust reasoning systems beyond conventional prompting and RAG approaches.

title: Diffusion Policies for Short-Horizon Planning in Robot Crowd Navigation
summary: Robot crowd navigation requires safe and efficient decision-making under dense, dynamic, and multimodal human--robot interactions. Existing reinforcement-learning methods typically output a single reactive action at each timestep, which limits their ability to represent diverse short-term avoidance strategies. We propose Planning Diffusion Policy Optimization (PDPO), an offline-to-online reinforcement-learning framework that uses a diffusion policy to generate short-horizon action chunks for crowd navigation. PDPO is first pretrained on collision-avoidance demonstrations and then fine-tuned online with PPO by treating the denoising process as an internal decision process. During execution, the policy generates a five-step action chunk and applies it in a receding-horizon manner. Furthermore, we observe an evaluation artifact in common crowd-navigation benchmarks: without explicit boundary constraints, learned agents may leave the valid domain and bypass dense crowds. To address this, we introduce a setting in which boundary violations are treated as collisions. Experiments show that PDPO obtains an improved success rate over strong baselines, and ablations demonstrate that action chunks are especially important for the modified bounded benchmark.

AI.tldr: PDPO uses a diffusion policy to generate short-horizon action chunks (five steps) for dense crowd navigation, pretrained on collision-avoid demonstrations and online-PPO fine-tuned; it treats boundary violations as collisions to fix an evaluation artifact; shows higher success rates than baselines, with action chunks particularly impactful in bounded benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods often output a single action per timestep, limiting the expression of diverse, short-horizon avoidance strategies in dynamic, multimodal crowds; there is also an observed evaluation artifact where agents exit the valid domain. The work aims to enable richer action planning and robust navigation under bounded constraints.
AI.method: Introduce Planning Diffusion Policy Optimization (PDPO): a diffusion-based policy that generates five-step action chunks. Pretrain offline on collision-avoidance demonstrations, then fine-tune online with PPO by using the denoising process as an internal decision sequence. Execution uses a receding-horizon approach with five-step chunks, and boundary violations are treated as collisions during evaluation.
AI.result: PDPO yields higher success rates than strong baselines on crowd-navigation tasks. Ablation studies show that generating action chunks (instead of single actions) is particularly beneficial in the modified bounded benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based short-horizon action chunk generation, coupled with offline-to-online RL (PDPO), effectively improves safety and performance in dense crowd navigation, and addressing boundary-violation artifacts is crucial for robust benchmarking.

title: MVC-Bench: Benchmarking Calibration of Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Reliable evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) and medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) requires calibrated confidence, particularly under realistic clinical conditions. However, existing efforts mainly focused on improving accuracy, leaving calibration in the medical domain underexplored. To this end, we propose MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark for medical image classification with VLMs and Medical-VLMs. MVC-Bench assesses the calibration across three axes: (i) robustness to modality, backbone, and domain shift (ii) effectiveness of calibration strategies and prompt-tuning methods (iii) stability under prompt-template and random-seed variations. The benchmark covers eight different backbones, three medical modalities, including fundus imaging, histopathology, and chest X-ray under in-domain and domain shift settings. It compares post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods, together with six prompt-tuning methods. Across more than 1638 controlled experiments, we report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, and further report results with complementary calibration measures, including Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE). We further investigate the underlying causes of miscalibration in VLMs and Medical-VLMs and propose a simple train-time calibration method, Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, which achieves lowest ECE on 10 out of 12 settings in in-domain and remains competitive under domain shifts. Collectively, MVC-Bench provides a structured evaluation framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.

AI.tldr: MVC-Bench: a calibration-centric benchmark for medical VLMs; evaluates confidence calibration across modalities, backbones, and domain shifts; analyzes prompt-tuning strategies and calibration methods; introduces a simple train-time regularization (MCM) achieving strong in-domain calibration and competitive cross-domain performance.
AI.motivation: Calibrated confidence is critical for safety in medical AI. While accuracy has been the focus, calibration under realistic clinical conditions (modality, backbone, domain shifts) remains underexplored for vision-language models and Medical-VLMs.
AI.method: Evaluate eight backbones across three medical modalities (fundus imaging, histopathology, chest X-ray) under in-domain and domain-shift settings. Compare post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot methods, using six prompt-tuning strategies. Report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, with Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE) as supplementary metrics. Conduct 1638 controlled experiments. Propose Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization as a simple train-time calibration method that achieves the lowest ECE on 10 of 12 in-domain settings and remains competitive under domain shifts.
AI.result: Extensive empirical evaluation reveals the effectiveness and limitations of different calibration strategies and prompt-tuning approaches. MCM yields the best in-domain ECE on the majority of settings (10/12) and maintains competitive performance under domain shifts. MVC-Bench offers a structured framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.
AI.conclusion: MVC-Bench provides a comprehensive and extensible benchmark to assess and improve calibration in medical VLMs. The proposed MCM regularization is a simple, effective calibration technique that enhances in-domain reliability and remains robust under distribution shifts, informing safer deployment of medical VLMs.

title: LiveSim: Simulating Environment-Shaped Users in Multi-Agent Live-Stream Ecosystems
summary: User behavior simulation with large language models~(LLMs) is increasingly used to support multi-agent ecosystem simulation. Existing simulators typically rely on static user profiles inferred from historical observations, which become inadequate in socially intensive environments such as live streaming where interaction dynamics continuously reshape user behavior. We propose \textbf{LiveSim}, an LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation. It represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses and progressively refines them through trajectory-grounded interactions, where discrepancies between simulated and observed trajectories reveal missing environmental shaping effects. These signals are further extracted as transferable environment-behavior patterns and accumulated in a collective behavioral memory to improve user-level behavioral fidelity and support ecosystem-level simulation. Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data validate the effectiveness of LiveSim in improving user-level behavioral fidelity and enabling ecosystem-level analysis of risk evolution and platform intervention effects.

AI.tldr: LiveSim is an LLM-based framework that models users as editable hypotheses in a live-stream ecosystem, refining them via trajectory-grounded interactions and a collective memory of environment-behavior patterns to improve user-level fidelity and enable ecosystem-level risk analysis.
AI.motivation: Static, history-only user profiles fail to capture evolving, socially complex dynamics in live streams. There is a need to model adaptive user behavior and environment-behavior coupling to better assess risk and platform interventions.
AI.method: Represent each user as an editable behavioral hypothesis. Use trajectory-grounded interactions to identify missing environmental shaping effects. Extract transferable environment-behavior patterns and store them in a collective behavioral memory. Use these to improve user-level fidelity and support ecosystem-level simulation and analysis.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data show improved user-level behavioral fidelity and enable analysis of risk evolution and intervention effects at the ecosystem level.
AI.conclusion: LiveSim provides an adaptive, memory-augmented LLM-based framework for dynamic social ecosystems, with potential for scalable user modeling and richer ecosystem-level insights into risk and interventions.

title: TraceBench: Controlled Evaluation of LLM Agents for Time-Series Root-Cause Attribution
summary: LLM agents are increasingly applied to anomaly detection and root-cause analysis in time-series observations collected from real-world systems; however, their performance on these tasks has not been systematically evaluated under controlled conditions. We introduce TraceBench, a simulation-based framework for generating controlled root-cause attribution tasks. In each generated task, an agent receives time-series observations produced by simulating a physical dynamical system and must determine whether a system parameter was altered during the simulation and, if so, which one. Using TraceBench, we generate tasks from three interpretable mechanical systems and systematically evaluate four LLM agents across controlled experimental conditions, yielding new insights into how these agents analyze time-series observations from dynamical systems. Our results show that agents benefit substantially from domain context and explore data primarily through numerical console output rather than visualizations. We also find that agents generally perform worse when required to produce a Python script that maps each time-series sample to a predicted root-cause label than when they submit predictions directly. We release our datasets, agent trajectories, experimental results, and a leaderboard on our website, tracebench.github.io.

AI.tldr: TraceBench is a simulation-based framework that creates controlled root-cause attribution tasks from time-series of dynamical systems, enabling systematic evaluation of LLM agents on anomaly detection and fault localization; four LLMs are evaluated under varied conditions, revealing domain context helps, agents rely more on numerical console output than visualizations, and producing Python mappings is harder than direct predictions; datasets and leaderboard are released.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of systematic, controlled evaluation of LLMs for time-series anomaly detection and root-cause attribution in real-world dynamical systems; a controlled benchmark is needed to isolate factors affecting performance and to compare different agents.
AI.method: Develop TraceBench to generate time-series tasks from three interpretable mechanical dynamical systems; vary experimental conditions; evaluate four LLM agents on root-cause attribution (whether a parameter was changed and which one); compare responses produced as predictions versus Python scripts; analyze reliance on domain context and data representations; release datasets, agent trajectories, results, and a leaderboard.
AI.result: LLMs benefit from domain context and primarily explore data via numerical console output rather than visualizations; performance is worse when required to generate a Python script mapping samples to root-cause labels than when submitting direct predictions; study provides new insights into how LLMs process time-series from dynamical systems.
AI.conclusion: TraceBench enables controlled evaluation of LLM agents on time-series root-cause attribution; domain-context enhances performance, but tooling choices (direct predictions vs code) influence effectiveness; datasets, trajectories, results, and leaderboard are publicly released to spur further research.

title: Differentiable Jitter Correction using Deep Learning-based Image Quality Metric for Phase-Contrast Micro-CT
summary: This paper proposes a fully differentiable jitter correction method for X-ray phase-contrast micro computed tomography using a deep learning-based image quality metric that estimates and compensates per-projection rigid jitter directly from the acquired projection data, without a pre-scan motion-free reference. The approach builds on a gradient-based auto-focus strategy adapted to parallel-beam geometry. A set of candidate objective functions is benchmarked in a controlled study, and the sensitivity of the visual information fidelity (VIF) metric to the jitter artifact is verified with the target phase-contrast data. To operate without a clean reference, a compact 3D convolutional neural network is trained to predict the VIF score from a single corrupted volume. A spatially selective total variation penalty applied exclusively to the image background is introduced to penalize spurious high-frequency structures that otherwise emerge during optimization. Experiments on biological specimens acquired at different synchrotron beamlines are conducted. Evaluation uses jitter motion applied to simulated and experimentally acquired projection data. The result confirms that the integrated pipeline reliably recovers fine structural detail lost due to jitter, with generalization demonstrated across morphologically distinct samples.

AI.tldr: A differentiable jitters-correction pipeline for X-ray phase-contrast micro-CT using a deep-learning image-quality metric (VIF) to optimize per-projection jitter without a reference, via gradient-based auto-focus, a 3D CNN predictor of VIF from corrupted volumes, and a background total-variation penalty; validated on biological specimens across beamlines and with simulated/experimental jitter.
AI.motivation: Correct projection-stage jitter in X-ray phase-contrast micro-CT without access to a motion-free reference, enabling restoration of fine structural details and reliable imaging across varied samples and beamlines.
AI.method: A gradient-based auto-focus jitter correction in parallel-beam geometry; evaluation of multiple objective functions using a perceptual VIF metric; a compact 3D CNN predicts VIF from a single corrupted volume to operate without a clean reference; a spatially selective background TV penalty suppresses spurious high-frequency structures; experiments on biological specimens at synchrotron beamlines with jitter applied to simulated and real data.
AI.result: The integrated pipeline reliably recovers fine structural detail lost due to jitter and generalizes across morphologically distinct samples, with validation on both simulated and experimentally acquired data across multiple beamlines.
AI.conclusion: A differentiable, reference-free jitter-correction framework leveraging a learned VIF objective and background TV regularization; effective across samples and beamlines, enabling robust enhancement of phase-contrast CT without requiring pre-scan motion-free references.

title: BekchiAI: Measuring, Observing, and Controlling LLM Agents in One Click
summary: Large language model agents reason, call tools, and act autonomously over many steps, but their agentic skills-correctly sequencing tools, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, and grounding generated arguments-are hard to measure with accuracy-only leaderboards. We present BekchiAI, which addresses both sides: a benchmark for measuring agentic skill and a platform for observing and controlling live agents. The BekchiAI-Benchmark, a suite of 13 tool-using ReAct agents across 7 task categories (arithmetic, structured/SQL, security detection, URL grounding, planning, orchestration, and tool-policy), totalling 2,057 deterministic, committed test tasks. Every task is verifier-checkable gold answers are computed by running canonical SQL against a real database, computing the exact schedule of a directed acyclic graph (DAG), or evaluating closed-form lambdas including adversarial security samples paired with deliberately imperfect signature scanners so a score reflects the model's own judgment, not the copying of an oracle. We define a small set of behavioral metrics beyond accuracy-tool-call adherence, URL hallucination and source-match, and per-model token cost and report a four-model comparison (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b) whose story is in the per-family spread, not the aggregate. The benchmark runs are executed using the provided evaluation scripts. BekchiAI-Platform is a complementary web-based observability and control layer for deployed agents, providing full token and latency telemetry as well as remote run termination. The benchmark, evaluation tools, and platform are publicly released.

AI.tldr: BekchiAI introduces a benchmark and platform to quantify and observe agentic skills in tool-using LLMs, featuring 2,057 deterministic tasks across 7 domains, verifier-grounded gold answers, behavioral metrics, and a cross-model comparison; both benchmark and platform are publicly released.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of leaderboards in reliably measuring agentic competencies (tool sequencing, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, grounding argued outputs) and to provide an observable, controllable environment for live agents.
AI.method: BekchiAI-Benchmark comprises 13 tool-using ReAct agents evaluated on 7 task categories (arithmetic, structured/SQL, security detection, URL grounding, planning, orchestration, tool-policy) with 2,057 deterministic tasks. Gold answers are verifier-checkable via canonical SQL, exact DAG schedules, or closed-form lambdas including adversarial samples. Behavioral metrics beyond accuracy (URL hallucination, source-match) and per-model token cost are reported. BekchiAI-Platform offers a web-based observability/control layer with token/latency telemetry and remote run termination. Public release of benchmark, tools, and platform.
AI.result: The paper reports a cross-model comparison across four models (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b) and emphasizes that performance patterns lie within model families rather than in aggregate, highlighting the value of granular behavioral metrics and reproducible evaluation circuitry.
AI.conclusion: BekchiAI provides a scalable, reproducible framework to measure and govern agentic AI behavior, combining a rigorous benchmark with live observability tools, and is openly released to the community.

title: When Interference Graphs Evolve: Doubly Robust Estimation of Dynamic Peer Effects
summary: Peer effects are difficult to estimate when interaction graphs evolve because pre-assignment network history, dynamic peer exposure, and post-assignment network change have distinct causal roles. We introduce a controlled contrast framework that indexes potential outcomes by own treatment, temporally aggregated peer exposure, and a post-assignment evolution summary. Differences between the resulting means define own-treatment, peer-exposure, controlled network-evolution, and joint controlled contrasts rather than a mediation decomposition. We develop the Dynamic Network Doubly Robust estimator, DynaNet-DR, which combines a temporally factorized propensity with normalized augmentation. Under consistency, summary sufficiency, sequential exchangeability, positivity, nuisance convergence, and weak dependence, its canonical estimator is consistent when either the outcome regression or the propensity estimator is consistent. The reported implementation adds representative-score prediction, fixed clipping, and finite-sample stabilization. Semi-synthetic benchmarks on fixed real temporal graph sequences show favorable estimation accuracy among methods targeting the full profile. These benchmarks assess summary-indexed contrasts rather than counterfactual edge generation, and the MathOverflow study is an observational illustration under the stated assumptions.

AI.tldr: Introduces a controlled-contrast causal framework for dynamic networks and the DynaNet-DR estimator, enabling consistent estimation of own-treatment, peer-exposure, and network-evolution effects via summary-indexed contrasts under standard causal assumptions; validated with semi-synthetic benchmarks on real temporal graphs.
AI.motivation: To estimate peer effects when interaction graphs evolve; pre-history, exposure, and post-assignment network changes have distinct causal roles, complicating standard mediation and diffusion analyses.
AI.method: Define potential outcomes indexed by own treatment, temporally aggregated peer exposure, and a post-assignment evolution summary. Develop DynaNet-DR, combining a temporally factorized propensity with normalized augmentation; include representative-score prediction, fixed clipping, and finite-sample stabilization.
