Rely on consistency, summary sufficiency, sequential exchangeability, positivity, nuisance convergence, and weak dependence for identifiability, achieving double robustness where either outcome regression or propensity is consistent.
AI.result: Canonical estimator is consistent if either the outcome regression or the propensity estimator is consistent. Semi-synthetic benchmarks on fixed real temporal graph sequences show favorable estimation accuracy for methods targeting the full profile. Benchmarks focus on summary-indexed contrasts rather than counterfactual edge generation; MathOverflow study serves as an observational illustration under the stated assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a robust framework for estimating dynamic peer effects with evolving networks via summary-indexed contrasts, offering a practical estimator (DynaNet-DR) with double robustness and demonstrated accuracy on semi-synthetic benchmarks; it extends causal inference in networks beyond edge-level counterfactuals.

title: Multi-Person Human Motion Forecasting in Complex Scenes
summary: Accurately forecasting the movement of people in complex scenes requires reasoning over the past and present state of the entire environment. In this context, effectively incorporating object information and social interactions into a unified framework remains particularly challenging. To address this, we propose Object-Conditioned Social Diffusion (OCSD), a conditional diffusion model that integrates motion history, multi-person interactions, and object cues into a single framework. OCSD uses an object-conditioning mechanism that modulates denoising at every timestep, enabling fine-grained human-object reasoning, and a social encoder that models the interactions between all humans in the scene. As a result, our model naturally handles varying group sizes, complex social interactions, and supports sampling multiple plausible futures. Extensive experiments show that OCSD achieves state-of-the-art results on the Humans in Kitchens (HiK) and HOI-M3 benchmarks. It reduces the two-second path error by 121.5 mm (31.3%) on HiK and 130.5 mm (33.2%) on HOI-M3 compared to prior work, and produces more realistic long-term forecasts.

AI.tldr: OCSD is a diffusion-based trajectory predictor that conditions on object cues and social interactions to forecast multi-person motion; achieves state-of-the-art results on HiK and HOI-M3, with notable reductions in short-term path error.
AI.motivation: Forecasting multi-person movement in complex scenes requires a unified approach that leverages past motion, social interactions, and object cues. Challenges include varying group sizes, intricate human–object relationships, and producing multiple plausible futures.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model (OCSD) that integrates motion history, a social encoder for inter-person interactions, and an object-conditioning mechanism that modulates denoising at every diffusion timestep. This enables fine-grained human–object reasoning and natural handling of different group sizes while supporting sampling of multiple plausible futures.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on HiK and HOI-M3. Reduces two-second path error by 121.5 mm (31.3%) on HiK and 130.5 mm (33.2%) on HOI-M3 compared with prior work; yields more realistic long-term forecasts.
AI.conclusion: Object-conditioned diffusion with a social encoder effectively fuses history, social dynamics, and object cues, delivering accurate and plausible multi-person trajectory forecasts in complex environments.

title: C-Unseen: Weak Signal Detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs via LLM Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the AI4SE 2026 Special Track, held within the WISE 2026 Conference
summary: Weak signals are early, low-visibility indicators that precede significant changes before those changes become established. Existing detection methods, based on keyword frequency, topic modeling, or untyped graph topology, fail to capture the semantic and relational structure through which such signals manifest. In this paper, we propose C-Unseen, a self-interpretable framework for weak signal detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs). We define a weak signal as a rare, semantically coherent subgraph that proliferates across consecutive TKG snapshots. The framework operates through two modules: a Rare Subgraphs Extractor, in which an LLM identifies subgraphs whose content is in tension with the dominant snapshot narrative via chain-of-thought reasoning, and a Weak Signal Alerter, in which the persistence of these rare subgraphs is tracked across time steps to isolate true weak signals. Experimental results demonstrate that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: C-Unseen advances weak signal detection in dynamic temporal knowledge graphs by a self-interpretable two-stage framework. It first uses an LLM-based Rare Subgraphs Extractor to identify semantically rare subgraphs that conflict with the dominant narrative, then tracks their persistence with a Weak Signal Alerter to confirm true signals, outperforming keyword, topic, and graph baselines.
AI.motivation: Weak signals are early indicators of major changes but are elusive to traditional detection methods that rely on keyword frequency, topic models, or untyped graphs. Capturing semantic and relational structure in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs) is essential to detect such signals.
AI.method: Two-module framework: 1) Rare Subgraphs Extractor: an LLM with chain-of-thought reasoning evaluates subgraphs and flags content that is in tension with the dominant snapshot narrative, yielding rare, semantically coherent subgraphs. 2) Weak Signal Alerter: tracks the persistence of these subgraphs across consecutive DTKG snapshots to isolate true weak signals.
AI.result: Experimental results show that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines on detecting weak signals in DTKGs.
AI.conclusion: C-Unseen provides a self-interpretable, two-stage approach to weak signal detection in DTKGs, leveraging semantic tension in rare subgraphs and their temporal persistence to identify true signals.

title: Common Geodesics Do Not Guarantee Fisher Consistency of the Structured SVM: Minimal Counterexamples and a Tree-Metric Classification
summary: A known necessary condition for Fisher consistency of the structured support vector machine requires the task loss to be a metric for which every output triple has a common geodesic point. We show that this condition is not sufficient for the canonical coordinate-wise argmax decoder. A four-output unit star admits an exactly optimal score vector whose maximizers are all strictly non-Bayes, and four outputs are minimal among metrics satisfying the condition. We then completely classify positively weighted tree metrics whose vertex set is the output space: argmax consistency holds if and only if the tree is a path. The failure on branching trees is confined to boundary distributions; every tree retains the argmax property at every full-support distribution. Among metrics satisfying the common-geodesic condition, five outputs are necessary and sufficient for a full-support counterexample; $K_{2,3}$ is the smallest member of an infinite $K_{m,n}$ family. We additionally give a full-support counterexample for the three-dimensional Hamming cube. All optimality claims have exact primal-dual certificates. The counterexamples expose a concrete decoder gap: in this polyhedral setting, an embedding can guarantee the existence of a calibrated link without validating a prescribed argmax link on every surrogate-risk minimizer.

AI.tldr: Common-geodesic metric condition is not sufficient for argmax consistency of the canonical coordinate-wise decoder in structured SVMs. The paper classifies when argmax consistency holds for tree-structured output spaces (only if the tree is a path); exhibits minimal counterexamples (four outputs for general metrics; five outputs for full-support under the condition); identifies K_{2,3} as the smallest in an infinite K_{m,n} family; provides a full-support counterexample for the 3D Hamming cube; all optimality claims come with primal-dual certificates; reveals a decoder gap where calibrated embeddings can exist without a validated argmax link on every surrogate minimizer.
AI.motivation: Clarify Fisher consistency (risk consistency) for structured SVMs and the sufficiency of the common-geodesic condition for argmax decoding. Determine minimal structures that violate argmax consistency and map precise boundaries (path vs branching trees; boundary vs full-support distributions).
AI.method: Theoretical, constructive analysis using explicit counterexamples (four-output star; analysis of positively weighted tree metrics; boundary vs full-support distribution analysis; polyhedral/dual certificates for optimality; examination of K_{m,n} families and the 3D Hamming cube).
AI.result: The common-geodesic condition is not sufficient for argmax consistency. Argmax consistency holds iff the output-space tree is a path. Branching trees fail only on boundary distributions; full-support distributions preserve argmax. Five outputs are needed for a full-support counterexample under the condition; K_{2,3} is the smallest in the Km,n family. A full-support counterexample exists for the 3D Hamming cube. All claims have primal-dual certificates. The results reveal a decoder gap: calibrated embeddings do not guarantee the argmax link on every surrogate-risk minimizer.
AI.conclusion: The study delineates precise boundaries for argmax consistency in structured SVMs with metric losses. It shows that common-geodesic is necessary but not sufficient, highlights the special role of path-structured outputs, and emphasizes the need to consider boundary behavior and global surrogate minimization in decoder design. It also exposes a concrete gap between calibration and argmax validation in polyhedral embeddings.

title: Anatomy-Guided Foundation Model Adaptation with Within-Case Prototype Supervision for Standard Plane Detection in Fetal Ultrasound Blind Sweeps
summary: Detecting the fetal abdominal circumference standard plane in low-cost obstetric blind sweeps is a highly imbalanced frame-classification problem: positive frames account for under 3% of a sequence, form short contiguous segments, and are poorly handled by off-the-shelf ultrasound and vision foundation models. We propose AnatoProto, a lightweight sequence-level framework that adapts a frozen BiomedCLIP encoder to fetal blind sweeps through four components: (i) anatomy-weighted spatial pooling that uses nnU-Net abdominal-region probabilities as a spatial prior to reweight BiomedCLIP patch tokens, so frozen semantic features are aggregated onto anatomically meaningful regions; (ii) a within-case prototype loss that pulls each frame embedding toward the mean of positive frames of the same sweep, exploiting case-level structure unavailable at the frame level; (iii) a three-stage cascade refinement (frame->segment->case-level rejecter) that lifts the prediction unit from noisy frames to structurally-constrained segments; and (iv) a hybrid prediction head that jointly models per-frame stability and inter-frame boundary transitions to suppress boundary false positives. On the ACOUSLIC-AI benchmark, AnatoProto reaches a test F1 of 67.72, outperforming the strongest foundation-model baseline (FetalCLIP + PRS, F1 = 54.52) by +13.20 F1 and the strongest video temporal-action-detection baseline (TriDet + PRS) by +15.76 F1. A synergy study, backed by embedding geometry and paired-bootstrap confidence intervals, shows that the prototype loss and anatomy-weighted pooling are not additive: applied alone the prototype loss reduces recall by 12 points, but combined with anatomy-weighted pooling it increases recall by 6.5 points -- a sign-flip we trace to the accuracy of the within-case prototype.

AI.tldr: AnatoProto is a lightweight sequence-level framework that adapts a frozen BiomedCLIP encoder to fetal blind sweeps, using anatomy-weighted pooling, within-case prototype loss, cascade refinement, and a hybrid head to tackle imbalanced frame-level detection of fetal abdominal circumference standard planes; it achieves substantial F1 gains on ACOUSLIC-AI and reveals non-additive interactions among components.
AI.motivation: To overcome extreme frame-level class imbalance, short positive segments, and poor generalization of off-the-shelf models in fetal ultrasound plane detection by exploiting anatomical priors and sequence-level structure.
AI.method: Four components: (i) anatomy-weighted spatial pooling reweights BiomedCLIP patch tokens with nnU-Net abdominal-region probabilities; (ii) within-case prototype loss pulls frame embeddings toward the sweep-level positive-frames mean; (iii) three-stage cascade refinement (frame -> segment -> case-level rejecter); (iv) hybrid prediction head modeling per-frame stability and inter-frame boundary transitions.
AI.result: On ACOUSLIC-AI benchmark, AnatoProto achieves test F1 = 67.72, beating FetalCLIP + PRS (F1 = 54.52) by +13.20 and TriDet + PRS by +15.76. A synergy study shows the prototype loss and anatomy-weighted pooling interact non-additively: prototype loss alone reduces recall by 12 points; combined with anatomy-weighted pooling it increases recall by 6.5 points, linked to within-case prototype accuracy.
AI.conclusion: AnatoProto effectively addresses severe sequence-level imbalance in fetal plane detection, delivering substantial performance gains and revealing important non-additive component interactions.

title: Evaluating human and LLM screening workflows in a conceptually complex scoping review: Recall--workload trade-offs and run-to-run consistency
summary:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for screening in evidence synthesis, where false negatives can remove relevant studies before full-text assessment. We compared human and LLM title-and-abstract screening workflows in a preregistered study embedded in a conceptually complex scoping review.
  Methods. After a conservative title-only screen, 1,131 records were screened by one review lead, four trained assistants screening non-overlapping subsets, and seven complete LLM runs using different models and processing configurations, including a nominally identical repeat run. We compared retained workload, operational recall against 316 verified eligible records, agreement, run-to-run consistency, and procedural burden. Because eligibility was verified only for records advanced and assessed in the parent review, recall estimates were operational.
  Results. No workflow recovered all verified eligible records. The human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records while achieving 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 file batches achieved the highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7% of records. All-at-once configurations recovered fewer eligible records than corresponding file-batch configurations. Two nominally identical GPT-5.4 file-batch runs agreed on 91.7% of records but differed on 94 records, including 29 verified eligible records retained by only one run.
  Discussion. LLM screening performance depended on the implemented workflow, not model identity alone. Processing configuration, workload, record-level variation, and human-LLM decision integration are therefore substantive properties of deployed systems. For high-recall tasks, LLMs are better suited to validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows than autonomous exclusion.

AI.tldr: LLMs can support screening in evidence synthesis but no single workflow achieved perfect recall. Performance depends on workflow design (file-batch vs all-at-once), workload, and human-LLM integration; high-recall tasks should employ validated, auditable, human-supervised processes rather than autonomous exclusion.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how different LLMs and processing configurations perform against human title/abstract screening in a preregistered, conceptually complex scoping review.
AI.method: Preregistered study screening 1,131 records after a conservative title-only screen; one lead reviewer, four trained assistants with non-overlapping subsets, and seven complete LLM runs across multiple models/configurations (including repeat runs). Evaluated operational workload, recall against 316 verified eligible records, agreement, run-to-run consistency, and procedural burden; recall is operational since eligibility was verified only for records advanced in the parent review.
AI.result: No workflow recovered all verified eligible records. Human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records with 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 file batches had 83.9% recall but retained 56.7% of records. All-at-once configurations performed worse than file-batch. Two nominally identical GPT-5.4 file-batch runs agreed on 91.7% of records but differed on 94 records, including 29 verified eligible records retained by only one run.
AI.conclusion: Performance hinges on workflow rather than model identity alone. Configurations such as processing strategy, workload distribution, record-level variation, and human-LLM decision integration are critical. For high-recall tasks, LLMs are better used in validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows than for autonomous exclusion.

title: Profit based evaluation of machine learning for nitrogen recommendations in winter wheat
summary: Nitrogen rates for winter wheat are set before the season, under unknown prices and weather. The standard UK advice does not respond to prices, yet recent price swings moved the most profitable rate by tens of kilograms per hectare. Machine learning is often proposed as the fix. However, it is usually judged on prediction accuracy, and accurate prediction does not by itself make the recommended rate more profitable. Our insight is to score nitrogen advice directly by the profit it forgoes on measured yield response curves. We build a test bench on 892 such curves from two long running UK experiments, and sweep the nitrogen to grain price ratio to cover all price scenarios. On this bench, machine learning fails as a predictor. No model recovers the best rate within farm tolerance, and the benchmark noise shows none can. At normal prices, every model also loses to the standard advice on profit. The gain sits elsewhere. A simple correction step applied after the model cuts profit losses by a quarter, while better models and extra features give no gain. The same frozen correction cuts losses by 43% at the second site without any retraining. A hybrid of standard advice plus a damped correction removes bias and trims rare large losses. The same price sweep also prices emission cuts, at a cost comparable to current carbon prices. Machine learning therefore pays as a profit scored correction to standard advice, not as its replacement.

AI.tldr: ML is not a replacement for standard N advice; profit-based evaluation shows simple post-hoc corrections can outperform ML-based predictions; cross-site corrections show robustness.
AI.motivation: Improve nitrogen-rate recommendations for winter wheat under price and weather uncertainty; standard UK advice ignores price signals and recent price swings; evaluate whether ML improves profitability rather than just predictive accuracy.
AI.method: Build a test bench from 892 yield-response curves from two UK experiments; sweep nitrogen-to-grain price ratio to simulate price scenarios; compare ML models to standard advice using profit-based metrics; test post-model corrections (simple damped correction, frozen correction) and hybrids; evaluate cross-site applicability and inclusion of emissions pricing.
AI.result: ML fails to identify the optimal rate within farm tolerance; at normal prices, ML underperforms standard advice on profit. A simple post-model correction reduces profit losses by ~25%; a frozen correction across a second site halves losses by ~43% without retraining; a damped correction blended with standard advice removes bias and large losses; emissions pricing can be included with cost comparable to current carbon prices. Overall, ML adds value as a profit-scored correction rather than as a direct replacement for standard guidance.
AI.conclusion: Profit-based evaluation reveals ML’s value primarily as a correction tool to standard nitrogen advice, not as a full replacement. Simple, robust correction mechanisms can yield meaningful gains and cross-site transferability, while more complex models offer limited additional profit without retraining or additional features.

title: Video-OPSD: Exploiting Privileged Visual Evidence for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Video Large Language Models
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has recently emerged as an effective post-training paradigm that improves policy optimization through dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher. Despite its promise, OPSD remains largely underexplored for Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing methods typically construct privileged teachers by augmenting their context with additional information while keeping the primary input unchanged for both teacher and student. Video reasoning, however, offers a distinct source of privileged supervision within the primary input itself: long videos contain substantial temporal redundancy, and only a small subset of frames provides the evidence necessary to answer a question. Building on this observation, we present $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$, an OPSD framework that exploits privileged visual evidence for both self-teacher construction and knowledge transfer. First, our Evidence-Grounded Self-Teacher conditions the teacher exclusively on annotated evidence frames while the student continues to reason over the complete video. This focused visual input enables the teacher to provide more informative supervision. Second, our Evidence-Guided Token Optimization adaptively weights token-level distillation according to each reasoning token's reliance on privileged visual evidence, thereby emphasizing perceptually grounded reasoning. Experiments across video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show that $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$ consistently improves upon Standard OPSD across multiple backbones and achieves performance comparable to GRPO while requiring substantially less training time, establishing an effective and efficient post-training approach for Video-LLMs.

AI.tldr: Video-OPSD: a post-training self-distillation framework for Video-LLMs that uses evidence frames as a privileged teacher input and adaptive token-level distillation to emphasize reasoning grounded in visual evidence, yielding improved performance with less training time.
AI.motivation: To enhance on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for Video-LLMs by exploiting privileged supervision embedded in the primary video input, leveraging the fact that only a subset of frames carries the necessary evidence for reasoning, thereby reducing unnecessary computation and improving supervision quality.
AI.method: 1) Evidence-Grounded Self-Teacher: the teacher is conditioned only on annotated evidence frames while the student processes the full video; 2) Evidence-Guided Token Optimization: dynamically weights token-level distillation according to each reasoning token's dependence on the evidence, emphasizing perceptually grounded reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical results on video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show Video-OPSD consistently outperforms Standard OPSD across multiple backbones and matches the performance of GRPO while requiring substantially shorter training time.
AI.conclusion: Video-OPSD is an effective and efficient post-training paradigm for Video-LLMs, leveraging privileged visual evidence to improve policy optimization and reducing training cost without sacrificing performance.

title: Learning-Augmented Online Allocation under Unreliable Advice: Robustness, Exposure Fairness, and Distribution Shift
summary: Learning-augmented algorithms improve online decisions using predictions, but unreliable advice may harm efficiency and fairness. We study an online allocation problem with finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints. We propose a robust and fair rule combining advice with a conservative fallback and fairness correction. Under bounded-error assumptions, we prove consistency and robustness with loss proportional to prediction error. Experiments show stability under adversarial advice and significant reductions in exposure disparity.

AI.tldr: A robust learning-augmented online allocation rule is proposed that blends predictions with a conservative fallback and fairness correction to handle finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints. The approach yields provable consistency and robustness under bounded prediction error, with experiments showing stability against adversarial advice and reduced exposure disparity.
AI.motivation: Mitigate the risk of unreliable predictions in learning-augmented online allocation, ensuring efficiency and fairness when decisions are irreversible and exposure must be managed.
AI.method: Introduce a robust and fair rule that fuses expert predictions with a conservative fallback and a fairness-correction mechanism. The analysis proves consistency and robustness with loss scaling with prediction error under a bounded-error model; experiments test behavior under adversarial advice and measure exposure disparity.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves stability under adversarial advice and substantially reduces exposure disparity, with theoretical guarantees tying loss to prediction error.
AI.conclusion: A robust, fair, learning-augmented online allocation framework is developed, providing provable guarantees under bounded errors and practical improvements in fairness and stability in the presence of unreliable predictions.

title: HALO: A Heterogeneity-Aware Language-Aligned IMU Foundation Model for Open-Set Human Activity Recognition
summary: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using inertial measurement units (IMUs) enables a wide range of applications, yet the field still lacks a unified model that can generalize across diverse subjects, devices, and activities. Training such a model is difficult due to two key challenges: sensing heterogeneity -- differences in sampling rates, channel configurations, and sensor placements -- and poor generalization to unseen activities and label vocabularies. We introduce HALO (Heterogeneity-Aware Language-aligned Open-set model), a domain-specific IMU foundation model that addresses both challenges through a two-stage training framework. Stage 1 pretrains the IMU encoder with heterogeneity-aware self-supervised learning, including adaptive-pooling tokenization, channel-independent feature extraction, and contextualized sensor conditioning that injects natural-language sensor descriptions into each channel embedding. Stage 2 aligns this IMU encoder with text embeddings via synonym-aware soft contrastive learning, enabling open-set recognition via cosine-similarity retrieval without per-dataset classifiers. Trained on 10 public HAR datasets and evaluated on 7 held-out datasets, HALO outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines on all 8 aggregate metrics, and still leads on 3 of 4 settings under baseline-matched inputs. Despite using only ~35M trainable parameters -- 10x fewer than the latest foundation model MOMENT (341.2M) -- HALO improves zero-shot open-set accuracy, measured over all 87 training labels, by 13.7 percentage points. On two further datasets with severe distribution shift, every model including HALO collapses zero-shot. A video demonstration of HALO's performance in real world is available at https://youtu.be/rooVKragtFU

AI.tldr: HALO is a heterogeneity-aware IMU foundation model for HAR that uses a two-stage training approach to handle sensing heterogeneity and open-set label vocabularies; achieves strong zero-shot/open-set performance with ~35M params, beating baselines across 10 HAR datasets, but fails under severe distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Need a unified HAR model that generalizes across devices, sensors, and activities and handles unseen labels without dataset-specific classifiers.
AI.method: Stage 1: heterogeneity-aware self-supervised pretraining with adaptive-pooling tokenization, channel-independent features, contextualized sensor conditioning with language descriptions. Stage 2: synonym-aware soft-contrastive alignment of IMU encoder with text embeddings to enable open-set recognition via cosine similarity retrieval without per-dataset classifiers.
AI.result: Evaluated on 10 public HAR datasets with 7 held-out; outperforms five baselines on 8 aggregated metrics; leads on 3 of 4 baseline-matched inputs; ~35M parameters vs MOMENT 341.2M; improves zero-shot open-set accuracy across 87 labels by 13.7 percentage points; on two highly distribution-shifted datasets, all models fail to retain zero-shot performance.
AI.conclusion: HALO demonstrates effective heterogeneity handling and open-set recognition with a lightweight model; suggests strong potential for generalized HAR, though sensitivity to severe distribution shift remains a limitation.

title: Beyond Classification: Task-Dependent Learnability under Privacy-Motivated Image Transformations
summary: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) in computer vision often rely on noise or image perturbations to protect visual data while securely processing it, creating a trade-off between task performance and protection. This trade-off is commonly evaluated using image classification, which primarily captures semantic separability and remains robust despite significant geometric, spatial layout or local boundary alterations. As a result, it is too simplistic as a proxy for generic vision tasks. Exhaustive downstream-task evaluation, however, is computationally expensive because models must often be trained for each PET transformation and parameter setting. We therefore propose a compute-aware multi-task protocol for evaluating PETs in model training. It combines lightweight proxy tasks that target complementary aspects of visual structure while remaining simple and fast to compute. Across irreversible privacy transformations, key-based block primitives, and learnable image encryption schemes, we demonstrate that PETs with similar classification accuracy can differ substantially on other tasks. The outcomes highlight the need for PET evaluation protocols that move beyond classification-only reporting.

AI.tldr: Proposes a compute-aware multi-task protocol with lightweight proxy tasks to evaluate PETs in computer vision beyond classification; shows that PETs with similar classification accuracy can differ across other tasks, arguing for broader evaluation beyond classification-only reporting.
AI.motivation: Classification accuracy is an insufficient proxy for PET quality; exhaustive downstream-task evaluation is expensive, yet necessary to capture task-compatible privacy degradation.
AI.method: Introduce a compute-aware multi-task evaluation protocol that uses lightweight proxy tasks targeting complementary aspects of visual structure; evaluate across irreversible privacy transformations, key-based block primitives, and learnable image encryption schemes.
AI.result: PETs with similar classification accuracy can exhibit substantial differences on other tasks; the protocol reveals non-obvious task-specific performance variations across different PET methods.
AI.conclusion: Adopt evaluation protocols that move beyond classification-only reporting, enabling faster, broader, and more reliable assessment of PETs across diverse vision tasks.

title: AI agents in Algorithmic Electricity Markets: On the Emergence of Tacit Collusion
summary: As electricity market participants increasingly adopt learning-based agents for their bidding strategies, electricity markets are becoming algorithmic. Evidence from algorithmic markets in other domains shows that tacit collusion can arise purely through independent learning. Moreover, electricity markets are typically oligopolistic and feature repeated interaction among a small number of participants, making them structurally susceptible to non-competitive behavior. In the face of these observations, this paper investigates the hypothesis that tacit collusion may emerge in electricity markets where participants' actions are controlled by autonomous learning-based algorithms. We model strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring, and model the participants' emergent behavior using multi-agent reinforcement learning. We propose a multi-dimensional set of criteria (going beyond profit comparisons against Nash equilibria) to assess whether the resulting behavior constitutes tacit collusion. Our experimental results showcase that such a danger is realistic for electricity markets: there are cases where agents do learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes that are supportive of tacit collusion indicators, even though the agents were never instructed to collude.

AI.tldr: Learning-based bidding agents in electricity markets can inadvertently create tacit collusion, even without explicit instruction to collude, under repeated interactions and imperfect public monitoring.
AI.motivation: As markets become algorithmic and oligopolistic, there is a real risk that independent RL agents learn strategies that sustain supra-competitive outcomes. A robust detection framework is needed beyond simple profit comparisons to Nash equilibria.
AI.method: Model the setting as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring and study emergent behavior via multi-agent reinforcement learning. Propose a multi-dimensional set of criteria to assess tacit collusion beyond profit-based Nash tests, and run experiments with autonomous learning agents.
AI.result: The experiments show that agents can learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes supportive of tacit collusion indicators, even when no collusion is explicitly programmed or directed.
AI.conclusion: Tacit collusion is a realistic concern in algorithmic electricity markets. The paper offers criteria to detect it and highlights the need for market design and regulation to address potential non-competitive outcomes arising from autonomous learning.

title: Importance Scoring of Transformer Attention Heads in Learning Tabular Data
summary: Computationally demanding and opaque deep learning models can be better understood and optimized by analyzing how they transform data. While deep transformers have been widely studied in computer vision and natural language processing, their application in tabular data remains relatively underexplored. This paper presents one of the first applications of an importance-scoring metric to interpret multi-head transformer models in learning from tabular data. Experiments conducted on 40 diverse tabular datasets demonstrate robustness to head drops based on the proposed head importance score. In 72.5\% of experimental examples, the model remains most resilient to performance drops when heads with the lowest importance scores are gradually removed. In contrast, removing the most important attention head first results in the greatest reduction in classification performance. A closer look at individual head importance scores across six attention layers reveals that important heads are scattered across layers, with no consistent layer-specific trends. In contrast to the image and language domains, the importance of individual attention heads varies considerably across tabular datasets with different schemas and feature spaces. The proposed importance score can improve efficiency and redundancy within transformer architectures. We make the source code for measuring the importance of individual attention heads publicly available.

AI.tldr: A head-importance scoring metric for multi-head transformers on tabular data reveals that pruning low-importance heads preserves performance in most cases (72.5% of instances), while removing highly important heads degrades accuracy; importance varies across datasets and across layers, enabling potential pruning for efficiency; code released.
AI.motivation: Address interpretability and efficiency gaps for transformer-based models on tabular data by extending head-importance analysis to the tabular domain and understanding how attention heads contribute to learning across diverse schemas.
AI.method: Introduce a head-importance scoring metric for multi-head transformers and evaluate it on 40 tabular datasets. Systematically drop heads in order of importance and analyze performance impact across six attention layers to observe distribution of important heads and dataset dependence. Provide publicly available source code.
AI.result: Most resilience observed when removing low-importance heads (72.5% of experiments). Removing the most important head first yields the largest drop in classification performance. Important heads are dispersed across the six layers with no consistent layer-specific pattern. Head importance varies substantially across datasets with different schemas and feature spaces. The proposed score can improve efficiency and reduce redundancy in transformer architectures; code released.
AI.conclusion: The head-importance metric is a useful tool for interpreting and pruning tabular-domain transformers, enabling efficiency gains while highlighting dataset-dependent variability in which heads matter most.

title: Counterfactual Bias Testing for Application Tracking System
summary: Automated candidate-job matching systems are increasingly classified as high-risk AI under emerging regulation, yet auditing them for demographic bias is expensive: classical correspondence-audit studies require hand-crafted resumes and manual submission, which does not scale to fast pipeline retraining cycles. This paper presents a general, reusable methodology that (1) uses task-specialized LLM agents to synthesize identity-neutral base resumes and inject controlled demographic treatments across five protected-characteristic axes (sex/gender, age, residence, language, disability), producing a K x (1+N) correspondence-audit matrix; (2) qualitatively flags inferred protected characteristics per an EU AI Act-aligned prompt; (3) ranks candidates against a job description via a fine-tuned sentence-embedding model and cosine similarity; and (4) computes a nine-metric fairness suite spanning counterfactual (score delta, mean absolute rank change, flip rate), group-fairness (top-K retention, four-fifths/impact ratio), and merit-aware (Recall@K, nDCG@K, equal opportunity, equalized odds) families, each with bootstrap confidence intervals, significance tests, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, culminating in an automated PASS/INVESTIGATE/FAIL report with a composite risk score. On an example corpus of 5 job orders, 100 base candidates, and 10 demographic treatments (90 metric x variant evaluations): score shifts, top-K retention, and merit-aware rate gaps stay within tolerance for every treatment, but a rank-stability metric (MARC) and nDCG@K each surface borderline findings - including one on the neutral baseline itself - that a score- or retention-only view would miss. The results argue for multi-metric, multi-family auditing over any single aggregate score, and for LLM-agent-generated audits as a practical, low-cost complement to human-curated audits for any candidate-job matching pipeline.

AI.tldr: A scalable, LLM-based correspondence-audit framework for bias in automated candidate-job matching, using synthetic identity-neutral resumes, demographic treatments across five axes, a nine-metric fairness suite, and automated PASS/INVESTIGATE/FAIL reporting; multi-metric approach reveals additional insights beyond score/retention metrics.
AI.motivation: Auditing high-risk AI in recruitment is expensive and not scalable; need scalable, reusable methodology aligned with EU AI Act; balance fairness, merit, and practicality in pipelines.
AI.method: (1) LLM agents synthesize identity-neutral base resumes; inject demographic treatments across sex/gender, age, residence, language, disability; (2) infer protected characteristics per EU AI Act prompt; (3) rank candidates vs job with fine-tuned sentence embeddings and cosine similarity; (4) compute nine-metric fairness suite across counterfactual, group, merit-aware families with CIs, significance tests, BH correction; report as PASS/INVESTIGATE/FAIL with composite risk; dataset: 5 jobs, 100 candidates, 10 treatments.
AI.result: In a sample, score shifts, top-K retention, merit-aware gaps within tolerance; MARC and nDCG@K reveal borderline findings, including some on baseline; demonstrates value of multi-metric auditing to catch issues a single metric would miss.
AI.conclusion: Multi-metric, multi-family auditing is necessary; LLM-agent audits offer a practical, low-cost complement to human audits for candidate-job matching pipelines.

title: Circuit Condensation: Post-Training that Concentrates a Behavior's Causal Circuit
summary: One approach to mechanistic interpretability explains behavior through circuits: the components and connections that carry it. Frozen discovery often returns hundreds of edges, making them hard to inspect, compare, or verify exhaustively. We introduce Circuit Condensation, which post-trains models to concentrate behaviors into smaller causal graphs. Each round prunes low-attribution edges and trains a low-rank adapter to match the original through what remains, retaining the cut only if task performance and general capability survive. Across four behaviors and eight models, condensed circuits are smaller than the strongest frozen baseline in 30 of 32 settings, by $8.1\times$ on average and up to $316\times$. Repeating the search without weight updates produces larger circuits in 29 of 32 settings, showing that weight updates, rather than search alone, drive the reduction. Testing every subset of 19 circuits finds 11 that cannot be reduced and reveals removable edges in the rest. Pair ablations expose dependencies between edges, showing that their effects cannot be understood independently. On indirect object identification, condensation isolates 24 heads, 17 of them with documented roles, against 61 heads and 36 undocumented ones for the matched frozen circuit: a sufficient sub-circuit of the published mechanism rather than a reconstruction of it. The resulting circuit tracks the original model's next-token distribution and predicts its errors.

AI.tldr: Circuit Condensation compresses mechanistic interpretability circuits into smaller, faithful subcircuits via iterative pruning and low-rank adapters, achieving substantial size reductions while preserving task performance across multiple models and behaviors.
AI.motivation: Make mechanistic explanations inspectable, comparable, and verifiable by focusing on essential causal edges rather than hundreds of edges from frozen discovery.
AI.method: Iteratively prune low-attribution edges; train a low-rank adapter to match original behavior on the remaining edges; keep pruning only if performance and general capability survive; compare with weight-free search; assess dependencies and ablations; analyze heads and subcircuits.
AI.result: In 30 of 32 settings condensed circuits are smaller than the strongest frozen baseline by average 8.1x, up to 316x; weight updates drive reduction; 11 of 19-circuit subsets cannot be reduced; 24 heads (17 documented roles) identified vs 61 heads (36 undocumented) in frozen; subcircuits track the next-token distribution and predict errors.
AI.conclusion: Weight updates are crucial for condensed circuits; the approach yields smaller, interpretable subcircuits that retain behavior and reveal dependencies and documented functionalities, aiding interpretability and verification.

title: Automated 2D and 3D Segmentation of AMD and DME Lesions in OCT
summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic macular edema (DME) are leading causes of vision loss, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the standard modality for detecting and monitoring the subtle lesions that drive treatment decisions. Most deep-learning segmentation work for OCT is validated only in-domain, leaving generalization to clinical data collected under different acquisition protocols largely untested. This work develops and systematically ablates four lesion-segmentation pipelines -- 2D and 3D variants for AMD and DME -- reaching Dice scores of 0.76 to 0.82 with strong volumetric and surface calibration (r vol, r surf greater than or equal to 0.97 across all four pipelines) on an in-domain validation set. The ablation process establishes a full-volume, calibration-aware adoption standard that catches mechanisms an ordinary slice-level evaluation would keep, and identifies ensemble composition as the most consistent driver of improvement. To test generalization, the models are evaluated on OLIVES, an external clinical cohort with no lesion-level ground truth, using a proxy-metric framework built around biomarker AUROC, central subfield thickness (CST) correlation, and longitudinal concordance. Predictions track clinical biomarkers outside the training distribution, though less strongly than in-domain -- evidence for, not validation of, automated lesion-burden tracking as a clinical tool.

AI.tldr: Four lesion-segmentation pipelines (2D/3D for AMD and DME) achieve in-domain Dice 0.76–0.82 with strong calibration (r_vol, r_surf ≥ 0.97); ablation shows full-volume calibration-aware evaluation and ensemble composition as robust drivers; generalization tested on OLIVES with proxy metrics (AUROC, CST correlation, longitudinal concordance); results show alignment with clinical biomarkers but not yet validated for automated lesion-burden tracking.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in OCT lesion segmentation generalization across diverse clinical acquisition protocols and the limitations of slice-level or in-domain validation; establish a calibration-aware adoption standard and assess external generalization.
AI.method: four pipelines (2D/3D AMD and DME); full-volume, calibration-aware evaluation; ablation study; ensemble analysis; external validation on OLIVES using proxy-metric framework based on biomarker AUROC, CST correlation, longitudinal concordance; no lesion-level ground truth available in OLIVES.
AI.result: In-domain Dice 0.76–0.82; high calibration r_vol, r_surf (≥0.97); ensemble improves performance; OLIVES shows predictions track clinical biomarkers but with weaker strength; not a full validation of automated lesion-burden tracking.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a calibration-aware adoption standard and demonstrates ensemble as a stable driver; highlights potential for external generalization but emphasizes need for lesion-level ground truth or stronger proxies; suggests future work on cross-cohort validation and robust clinical utility assessment.

title: A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering
summary: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating five VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. Representing tables as images at native resolution matches text in both performance and efficiency, but downscaling them makes models compensate the loss in readability with longer, less effective reasoning traces that cancel the expected savings. Highly downscaled tables, however, preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-step method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those at native resolution. On long documents, our method saves 41% of total tokens and gains 7 accuracy points over single-step QA with native resolution tables. It also uses 15% fewer tokens than the most efficient single-step compressed configuration, with no accuracy loss.

AI.tldr: Pixel-level table compression can reduce token costs in VLM QA over multi-table docs; native-resolution tables give best accuracy and efficiency; a two-step training-free method—first selecting relevant tables from compressed context, then reasoning over them at native resolution—achieves substantial token savings with no loss in accuracy.
AI.motivation: To understand how image-based context compression affects table understanding in long, real-world documents and to identify strategies that preserve QA performance while reducing token usage.
AI.method: Assess five visual-language models across two QA benchmarks and five visual-token budgets, comparing native-resolution vs various pixel-compressed table representations. Explore a training-free two-step approach: (1) detect which tables are needed from a pixel-compressed document, (2) perform reasoning on the selected tables at native resolution.
AI.result: Tables at native resolution achieve parity with text in both QA accuracy and token efficiency. Downscaled tables reduce readability, forcing longer reasoning traces that negate token savings; very aggressive downscaling can still signal relevance. The proposed two-step method yields a 41% reduction in total tokens and +7 accuracy points versus single-step native-resolution QA, and uses 15% fewer tokens than the best single-step compressed setup with no accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Pixel compression is viable for long-document QA when combined with a lightweight, two-step strategy that uses compressed context to select relevant tables and native-resolution reasoning for final answers, enabling substantial token savings without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Making Latent Evolution Explicit: Operator-Structured Transitions for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies by predicting how task-relevant scene states may evolve under interaction. Recent WAMs increasingly perform such prediction in latent representation spaces, avoiding full appearance-level generation while preserving control-relevant information. Yet latent transitions are commonly realized with Transformer-based predictors whose inductive structure is centered on token interaction rather than temporal evolution. We study transition realization as an architectural choice distinct from predictive representation and prediction-policy coupling. We introduce the Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON), which models latent evolution in a learned observable space through context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing. Grounded in the controlled Koopman generator view of evolution, LEON organizes context-dependent transition variation around a shared evolution-operator structure while retaining a complementary path for additive change. Controlled dynamical systems verify the resulting evolution-specific inductive bias and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Across two WAM formulations that integrate latent prediction into the policy differently, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness while remaining effective under full transition replacement. These results establish transition realization as a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs.

AI.tldr: LEON provides Latent Evolution Operator Network to model latent state transitions in WAMs using context-modulated operator propagation and additive forcing, improving closed-loop performance and robustness.
AI.motivation: Current world-action-models (WAMs) rely on Transformer-based predictors focused on token interactions rather than genuine temporal evolution; there is a need for an architectural transition mechanism that captures latent evolution within learned observables.
AI.method: Introduce LEON, a latent evolution operator that models latent evolution in a learned observable space via context-modulated propagation and additive forcing; grounded in a controlled Koopman generator view; uses a shared evolution-operator structure with a complementary forcing path; validated with controlled dynamical systems and two WAM formulations.
AI.result: Across two WAM formulations, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness and remains effective under full transition replacement, establishing transition realization as a key architectural choice in latent WAMs.
AI.conclusion: Transition realization is a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs; LEON provides evolution-specific inductive bias through operator propagation and forcing, generalizing across WAM variants.

title: EditaLive! Unified Character Video Editing for Live Streaming
summary: Conventional video editing primarily focuses on scene-level content, whereas live streaming places greater emphasis on the human subject. However, directly applying existing video-editing methods to human-centric live streaming remains challenging, as they may introduce facial-expression inconsistencies and typically depend on multiple offline inference steps, making them unsuitable for real-time interaction. We propose EditaLive, a novel framework for real-time streaming character video editing. In detail, we start from a pretrained image animation model (Wan-Animate), which naturally decouples appearance from motion, and repurpose it as the base model for instruction-based human-centric video editing by reference frame editing and video reconstruction via the collected CharEdit-50K dataset. Besides, we adapt the model from offline bidirectional to causal streaming generation, and design an aligned self-rollout distillation strategy that compresses the model into a two-step sampler, where fixed RoPE and align forcing reduce training--inference discrepancies, and first-frame preserved sparse attention filters redundant historical information to mitigate appearance drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EditaLive delivers state-of-the-art editing performance with faithful preservation of facial expressions and low-latency real-time streaming inference.

AI.tldr: EditaLive is a real-time, human-centric video-editing framework for streaming that repurposes a pretrained image-animation model (Wan-Animate) into a causal streaming generator via aligned self-rollout distillation and a two-step sampler, leveraging the CharEdit-50K dataset to achieve low-latency, facial-expression faithful edits with reference-frame editing.
AI.motivation: Conventional video editing emphasizes scene content and relies on offline steps, causing facial-expression inconsistencies and impracticality for real-time streaming. There is a need for real-time, instruction-based, human-centric video editing for interactive streaming.
AI.method:
- Start from Wan-Animate to decouple appearance from motion and adapt it as the base model for instruction-based editing via reference-frame editing and video reconstruction using CharEdit-50K.
- Convert offline bidirectional generation to causal streaming generation.
- Propose an aligned self-rollout distillation that compresses the model into a two-step sampler with fixed RoPE and align-forcing to reduce training-inference gaps.
- Introduce first-frame preserved sparse attention to filter redundant historical information and mitigate appearance drift.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show state-of-the-art editing performance with faithful facial-expression preservation and low-latency streaming inference.
AI.conclusion: Edits can be performed in real time while preserving identity expressions, thanks to the two-step sampler and attention techniques; the approach demonstrates strong potential for real-time, human-centric streaming editing and paves the way for practical deployment.

title: From Atomic to Agentic: Towards Interpretable Evaluation of LLMs' Agentic Mathematical Capabilities
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are evolving from performing end-to-end mathematical reasoning to integrating agentic intelligence. However, most existing math benchmarks evaluate only final answers. This outcome-oriented evaluation provides limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic, failing to guide the transformation of LLMs into robust agents. To bridge this gap, we present a process-level benchmark designed to evaluate the inherent agentic mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Our framework aligns problem-solving agentic behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. We design a comprehensive suite of planning, action, and feedback tasks across both textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations via controlled LLM rewriting. Experiments reveal that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles. This demonstrates that process-level evaluation is crucial for interpreting the true potential of LLMs and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents.

AI.tldr: A process-level benchmark evaluates agentic mathematical reasoning in LLMs, revealing differences in reasoning capabilities beyond end-to-end accuracy using a taxonomy of atomic math skills and a pipeline for planning, action, and feedback across textual and multimodal contexts.
AI.motivation: End-to-end accuracy alone cannot diagnose internal reasoning failures or guide robust agent design; a process-level view is needed to understand and improve LLM-based mathematical agents.
AI.method: Introduce a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities; design planning, action, and feedback tasks in textual and multimodal settings; implement an automated pipeline to synthesize trajectories and annotate with controlled LLM rewriting, enabling fine-grained process-level evaluation.
AI.result: Models with similar final accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles; process-level evaluation provides diagnostic insight into LLMs and informs the development of next-generation mathematical agents.
AI.conclusion: Process-level evaluation is essential for interpreting the true potential of LLMs in agentic mathematics and guiding the development of robust mathematical agents.

title: MM-Spectrum: Multimodal Multi-spectral Molecular Structural Elucidation with a Stable MoE Framework
summary: Inferring molecular structures from multimodal spectroscopic measurements requires integrating complementary yet highly heterogeneous signals. However, the common paradigm of directly concatenating multispectral sequences can exhibit anomalous performance degradation, primarily due to pronounced heterogeneity and the resulting multimodal imbalance across modalities. As a remedy, we propose MM-Spectrum, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework tailored for multimodal multispectral spectra-to-structure elucidation. To better match the information characteristics under multispectral imbalance, MM-Spectrum introduces an explicit modality-aware routing mechanism that exposes spectral identity to the router in addition to token content representations. Moreover, it incorporates shared and interaction experts, together with heterogeneous expert capacities, to extract multispectral modality-unique and cross-modal synergistic information while suppressing noise-induced interference. Across full-modality, bimodal, and missing-modality settings on molecular structural elucidation, MM-Spectrum achieves consistent and substantial improvements, supported by ablation studies and interpretability analyses.

AI.tldr: MM-Spectrum is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model for multimodal spectral data that handles heterogeneity and imbalance via a modality-aware router, multiple expert types, and heterogeneous capacities, yielding robust improvements across full, bimodal, and missing-modality settings in molecular structure elucidation.
AI.motivation: Multimodal spectroscopic data are highly heterogeneous across modalities. Naively concatenating signals leads to performance degradation due to modality imbalance and noise; there is a need for a model that can selectively route information by modality and allocate resources to modality-specific and cross-modal interactions.
AI.method: Propose MM-Spectrum, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework with a modality-aware routing mechanism that exposes spectral identity to the router in addition to token content, plus shared and interaction experts with heterogeneous capacities to capture modality-unique and cross-modal information while suppressing noise.
AI.result: Across full-modality, bimodal, and missing-modality settings on molecular structure elucidation, MM-Spectrum achieves consistent and substantial improvements, supported by ablation studies and interpretability analyses.
AI.conclusion: A modality-aware, capacity-diverse sparse MoE framework effectively mitigates multimodal imbalance and improves multispectral spectra-to-structure elucidation, enabling reliable inference even with missing modalities.

title: ReViCo: Unveiling the Limitations of VLMs in Visual Text Understanding via Error Correction
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown great success in general visual tasks, yet they still struggle to deeply understand text within images. In this paper, we introduce ReViCo (Real Visual Correction), a benchmark designed to evaluate VLM text understanding through a novel task of visual text error correction. ReViCo challenges models to identify and fix text errors in real-world images, which requires a profound understanding of the interplay between visual text and its surrounding visual context. We benchmark various VLMs using two distinct paradigms: prompt-based strategy and targeted model training, both aimed at pushing the limits of current models. Our experiments reveal a striking performance gap between even the best VLMs and human, and further analysis also shows that most models struggle to accurately perceive the visual text, resulting in frequent correction errors. By highlighting these gaps, ReViCo provides a new benchmark foundation for developing more robust and text-aware VLMs.

AI.tldr: ReViCo benchmarks VLMs on visual text error correction to measure how well they understand text in images.
AI.motivation: address the persistent difficulty VLMs have in reading and interpreting textual content embedded in images and its interaction with visual context.
AI.method: introduce ReViCo benchmark; evaluate via two paradigms (prompt-based and targeted fine-tuning); run across multiple VLMs; analyze gap vs humans; report error rates in visual text perception and correction.
AI.result: best VLMs still far from human performance; many models misread or misperceive text; correction errors frequent; prompts and training help but limited.
AI.conclusion: ReViCo offers a new standard for developing more robust, text-aware VLMs and highlights the need for improved visual text comprehension.

title: GraphMemix: Query-Aware Evidence Forests for Long-Term Multimodal Agent Memory
summary: Organizing long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging because existing methods either suffer from expensive question-agnostic offline summaries or naive embedding similarity matching that introduces incomplete and redundant context. To address these issues, we propose GraphMemix, a combinatorial-optimization graph memory framework that models memory organization as query-aware evidence-forest construction. Specifically, our method consists of three key components:(1) candidate graph construction, which expands multi-view seed memories through schema and semantic relations to acquire query-aware original context; (2) evidence utility and activation costs, which decouples direct memory support from anchor-conditioned relation verification to suppress redundant or conflicting information; and (3) forest optimization, which jointly selects a forest-format memory context under a maximum evidence budget and its reliable relational structure. By organizing memory into a query-relevant subgraph, the method avoids substantial lifecycle cost and recovers low-similarity complementary evidence. Experimental results across four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements with different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.

AI.tldr: GraphMemix proposes a graph-memory framework that builds a query-aware evidence forest to organize long-term multimodal memory, reducing lifecycle cost while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long-term multimodal memory faces high costs and incomplete/redundant context when using offline summaries or naive embedding similarity; there is a need for query-aware, evidence-based memory organization.
AI.method: Three components: (1) candidate graph construction expands multi-view seed memories via schema and semantic relations to obtain query-aware original context; (2) evidence utility and activation costs decouple direct memory support from anchor-conditioned relation verification to suppress redundancy/conflicts; (3) forest optimization jointly selects a forest-format memory context under a maximum evidence budget and a reliable relational structure.
AI.result: Experiments on four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks show significant improvements across different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.
AI.conclusion: GraphMemix organizes memory into a query-relevant subgraph (evidence forest), reducing lifecycle cost while recovering low-similarity complementary evidence; supports scalable, accurate long-term memory for multimodal agents.

title: QuantumBoostNet: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Enhanced Accuracy in Cardiac Ultrasound View Identification
summary: Accurate identification of the correct view or angle in cardiac ultrasound (echocardiogram) is a critical component of cardiologic imaging. This step is essential for precise anatomical interpretation, reliable measurement, and the reduction of clinical errors. Although computer vision has advanced significantly, most state-of-the-art models perform well on standard benchmarks but often yield suboptimal results in specialized medical imaging tasks due to the high level of noise present in the data. QuantumBoostNet, a hybrid classical-quantum architecture, is introduced to address these challenges. This model integrates a classical backbone with two heads: one classical and one quantum, with the quantum head implemented as a parametrized 10-qubit quantum circuit. Training occurs in two stages, with an adaptive transition between heads governed by a mixing parameter that monitors loss dynamics. Extensive experiments indicate that, despite the limited number of qubits that can be simulated, QuantumBoostNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art classical and hybrid classical-quantum models in cardiac ultrasound view identification, achieving a relative improvement over the best competitor. QuantumBoostNet also demonstrates superior performance on established image classification benchmarks and exhibits robustness to noise. These findings support the continued development of hybrid classical-quantum models for specialized medical imaging applications.

AI.tldr: Hybrid classical-quantum neural network (QuantumBoostNet) with a 10-qubit quantum head and two-stage training improves echocardiogram view identification, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and showing robustness to noise.
AI.motivation: Address the noise and data quality challenges in specialized medical imaging and explore whether a quantum head can enhance view identification accuracy beyond classical models.
AI.method: A classical backbone with two heads (classical and quantum). The quantum head is a parametrized 10-qubit circuit. Training proceeds in two stages with an adaptive head-switching mechanism governed by a mixing parameter that tracks loss dynamics.
AI.result: QuantumBoostNet consistently outperforms leading classical and hybrid models in cardiac ultrasound view identification, achieving a relative improvement over the best competitor. It also performs well on standard image classification benchmarks and demonstrates robustness to noise, despite the limited qubit count.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid classical-quantum architectures hold promise for specialized medical imaging tasks by enhancing accuracy in noisy data and providing a viable path for quantum-assisted medical image analysis; warrants further exploration and larger-scale validation.

title: Magpie: Real-Time World Renderer for Interactive Games
summary: Modern game development relies heavily on conventional graphics pipelines. High-quality visual content requires modeling, material authoring, animation, lighting, effects, and runtime optimization, making asset production expensive and extending the development cycle of game prototypes. Recently, video foundation models are beginning to change film and video production, but games differ from linear media, they require not only continuous and realistic imagery, but also stable and reproducible gameplay rules, object states, and interaction outcomes. We present Magpie, a real-time generative world-rendering system for interactive games. Magpie separates gameplay execution from visual generation. Designers define scenes and rules in a game engine. At runtime, the Game Engine resolves player actions and maintains world state, while an independent Render Server generates visual output from white-box frames produced by the engine. Magpie provides a system-level implementation path for applying generative models to real-time game rendering. It preserves gameplay designability and reproducibility, and reduces the dependence of early game prototypes on complete visual assets.

AI.tldr: A two-tier architecture decouples gameplay logic from visual generation to enable real-time, generative rendering in games while preserving reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Asset-heavy traditional pipelines hinder rapid prototyping; generative visuals risk nondeterminism and gameplay drift, necessitating a design that maintains stable world states and interactions.
AI.method: Magpie splits execution: the game engine maintains world state and resolves player actions; a separate Render Server consumes white-box frames from the engine and synthesizes visuals using generative models, enabling real-time output without compromising designability.
AI.result: Provides an architectural path for applying generative models to real-time rendering in games, preserving reproducibility and designability and reducing the need for fully authored visuals in early prototypes.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling gameplay from rendering enables leveraging generative models in interactive environments while highlighting considerations for determinism, latency, and toolchain integration in future work.

title: DSA: Evidence-Aware LLM-Agent Orchestration for Multi-Market Stock Research
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Code available at https://github.com/ZhuLinsen/daily_stock_analysis
summary: Large language models can summarize financial information, but an operational stock-research system must first assemble heterogeneous evidence, expose unavailable data and model capabilities, and control how generated opinions affect a final report. We present DSA, an evidence-aware orchestration framework for multi-market stock research with large language model (LLM) agents. DSA organizes the workflow into evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation with selected context and diagnostics. A default report profile and an optional agentic profile share evidence and model-routing services but use profile-specific output validation and risk safeguards. In the agentic profile, core role outputs are processed by role-specific parsers, whereas Strategy Skill opinions undergo an additional signal-eligibility partition before synthesis; disagreement is supplied explicitly to the decision agent, followed by a conservative risk override. The reference implementation includes six regional market paths, fifteen bundled Strategy Skills, hosted and local model routes, and multiple execution and delivery surfaces. At a frozen software snapshot, a selected manifest of 1,457 portable offline backend contract tests passed; 596 cases were retrospectively mapped to six contract families central to the reported LLM-agent architecture. This evidence establishes implementation conformance for the tested software contracts, not superior report quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.

AI.tldr: DSA provides an evidence-aware orchestration framework for LLM-assisted multi-market stock research, emphasizing governance, evidence acquisition, and model routing with agentic and default profiles; includes modular paths and strategy skills; evidence of contract-level conformance rather than performance gains.
AI.motivation: To address operational needs of stock research systems that require assembling heterogeneous evidence, exposing data/model capabilities, and controlling how generated opinions influence final reports.
AI.method: Evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation; two profiles (default and agentic) with shared services but different output validation and safeguards; agentic outputs go through role parsers and Strategy Skill partitioning; disagreement conveyed to decision agent with risk override; reference implementation with six regional paths, fifteen Strategy Skills, offline backend tests; manifest of 1,457 tests; 596 mapped to contract families.
AI.result: Evidence establishes implementation conformance for tested software contracts; does not assess reporting quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.
AI.conclusion: DSA enables governance-aware, evidence-backed LLM-driven stock research workflows across markets; emphasizes conformance and repurposes rather than claiming improved investment outcomes.

title: Beyond Parallel Blindness: Information Floors and Model Gaps in Block Drafting
summary: Block drafters propose several tokens in one forward pass, before earlier target tokens are realised. Their rejection mixes two losses: missing within-block path information and imperfect modelling of observable information. Accepted length cannot distinguish them. We separate the two with an information floor, the minimum expected rejection at a specified conditioning order; rejection above this floor is the model gap. Estimating both from target rollouts across four domains, four open-weight targets, and a frontier API target yields three findings. First, the all-parallel floor reaches $0.286$ at the final slot on Qwen3-4B, limiting even the best proposal to $71\%$ per-slot acceptance. Second, one realised token removes $86$--$100\%$ of this floor, a locality also recovered by an independent mutual-information analysis. Third, current drafters remain far above their floors: the final-slot model gap accounts for $43$--$64\%$ of DFlash rejection and $85$--$92\%$ of DSpark's oracle-conditioned rejection. These findings separate the value of short-range conditioning from proposal quality.

AI.tldr: Introduces an information floor to separate two sources of rejection in multi-token drafting: missing within-block path information vs. imperfect observable information modelling. Empirically bounds all-parallel rejection, shows realising tokens reduce the floor, and that most rejection stems from the final-slot model gap rather than short-range conditioning.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the contributions to rejection when drafting multiple tokens in parallel: the loss from missing intra-block path information and the loss from not modelling observable information well. An information floor provides a lower bound on rejection for a given conditioning order, enabling measurement of a separate model gap.
AI.method: Define the information floor as the minimum expected rejection at a specified conditioning order. Estimate both the floor and the model gap from target rollouts across four domains, four open-weight targets, and a frontier API target. Analyze per-slot acceptance, effect of a realised token, and corroborate with mutual-information analysis. Compare floors and gaps across domains (DFlash, DSpark) and models (e.g., Qwen3-4B).
AI.result: Findings: (1) The all-parallel floor reaches 0.286 at the final slot on Qwen3-4B, capping best per-slot acceptance at 71%. (2) A single realised token eliminates 86–100% of this floor, indicating strong locality, echoed by mutual-information analysis. (3) Current drafters stay well above their floors: the final-slot model gap accounts for 43–64% of DFlash rejection and 85–92% of DSpark’s oracle-conditioned rejection. Collectively, these results separate the benefits of short-range conditioning from proposal quality.
AI.conclusion: The information-floor framework successfully separates two sources of rejection in multi-token drafting, enabling clearer attribution to proposal quality versus short-range conditioning. The findings emphasize the dominant role of the final-slot model gap in observed rejections and show that realising tokens strongly mitigate the floor, guiding future improvements in drafting strategies and evaluation metrics.

title: Ancient-Bench: A Comprehensive Multi-millennial, Multi-medium, and Multi-script Benchmark for Ancient Chinese Artifact Text Recognition
summary: Ancient Chinese artifact text recognition is fundamental to heritage digitization, and benchmarks for ancient texts are essential for evaluating current model capabilities. However, existing benchmarks suffer from ''fragmentation'', manifested in limited temporal coverage, limited medium diversity, and incomplete script types. Therefore, we present Ancient-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 2,700 images for ancient Chinese artifact text recognition, featuring three dimensions: Multi-millennial (spanning 3,000 years of character evolution), Multi-medium (covering nine artifact categories), and Multi-script (encompassing seven historical script forms). To enable consistent and fair evaluation across heterogeneous media, we further define three annotation standards tailored to the medium-specific characteristics of ancient texts: symbol standardization, character standardization, and parsing standardization. Extensive experiments on Ancient-Bench covering general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and OCR-specialist models reveal that ancient Chinese artifact text recognition remains fundamentally unsolved, with persistent challenges in variant characters, specialized symbols, and hallucination. The dataset is available at https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/Ancient_Bench.

AI.tldr: Ancient-Bench provides a 2,700-image benchmark for ancient Chinese artifact text recognition across 3 dimensions (time: 3,000 years; media: 9; scripts: 7) with tailored annotation standards for fair cross-medium evaluation, revealing persistent challenges in recognition and hallucination for both general VLMs and OCR-specialist models.
