AI.motivation: Address fragmentation in existing ancient-text benchmarks by offering a comprehensive, multi-dimensional dataset to enable consistent, fair evaluation across diverse media, time periods, and historical scripts.
AI.method: Curate a large, multi-attribute dataset (Ancient-Bench) and define medium-specific annotation standards (symbol, character, and parsing standardization). Evaluate both general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and OCR-specialist systems on the benchmark.
AI.result: Experiments indicate that ancient Chinese artifact text recognition remains fundamentally unsolved, with persistent difficulties in variant characters, specialized symbols, and model hallucination across media and scripts.
AI.conclusion: Ancient-Bench is a valuable resource for standardized evaluation across time, media, and scripts, but the task remains challenging, highlighting the need for improved models and annotation schemes.

title: ASIL: Replacing Screenshot-and-Click with Structured State and Semantic Actions
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 19 pages, 7 figures: 9-page main paper followed by limitations, ethics, acknowledgments, references, and appendices A-E. Project page: https://sharryxr.github.io/ASIL/
summary: Powerful code agents can execute scripts, call tools, and manage files, yet many important applications remain accessible primarily through graphical user interfaces. We argue that screenshot-and-click is an inefficient interface for software-operating agents: screenshots are state-incomplete, and GUI actions are brittle, semantically weak, and poorly matched to long-horizon planning. We introduce ASIL (Agent-Software Interaction Layer), an agent-native interface that exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, realized through the deepest feasible access path for each application. We instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and a benchmark of 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks. ASIL reaches above 80 with closed models while executing fewer than five actions per task. Under a repaired runtime and a 50-step screenshot budget, the same tasks yield 6.6 and 26.6 strict success under screenshot-and-click control, rising to 15.0 and 53.3 on an easier OSWorld-comparable band. Against application-native interfaces on matched tasks, ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 strict points but only matches draw.io's MCP content contract. The structured modality also suits training: small-scale SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4, and resource-limited on-policy RL further raises them to 74.4 and 82.2.

AI.tldr: ASIL provides a structured, executable-action interface for software agents via JSON observations, enabling robust long-horizon planning across 15 apps and 380 tasks; it outperforms screenshot-based control and approaches app-native interfaces on some tasks, with notable training benefits.
AI.motivation: To overcome the inefficiency and brittleness of screenshot-and-click interfaces for autonomous software agents by exposing software through structured, semantic actions and observations that align with long-horizon planning.
AI.method: Instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and a benchmark of 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks. Expose software via structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, using the deepest feasible access path for each app. Evaluate with closed models, a repaired runtime, fixed screenshot budgets, and OSWorld/comparable bands. Compare against screenshot-and-click and app-native interfaces; assess training impact via SFT and RL.
AI.result: ASIL achieves >80 performance with closed models while using <5 actions per task. With a repaired runtime and a 50-step screenshot budget, tasks yield 6.6 and 26.6 strict success under screenshot-and-click; OSWorld-comparable band yields 15.0 and 53.3. At parity with app-native interfaces, ASIL surpasses LibreOffice UNO API by 28-38 strict points but only matches draw.io MCP. Training-friendly: SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4; RL further raises to 74.4 and 82.2 under resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: Structured, executable-action interfaces like ASIL enable more efficient, scalable agent operation across diverse software and provide clear training advantages, outperforming screenshot-based control and often exceeding app-native APIs on structured tasks.

title: Understanding Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning: Broader Reasoning Coverage than GRPO
summary: Evolution Strategies (ES) have recently emerged as a memory-efficient post-training paradigm for LLM reasoning. However, the optimization behavior of ES remains understudied, making it hard to define its advantage scope compared to mainstream post-training paradigms (e.g., Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)). By systematically investigating ES dynamics and mechanisms, this paper first identifies a performance advantage of ES over GRPO, theoretically and empirically showing that ES can lead to broader reasoning coverage, thereby better exploiting the reasoning capabilities of pretrained LLMs. Theoretically, we show that verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity across the ES population is helpful to higher Pass@K performances. Empirically, unlike GRPO, which exhibits entropy collapse, ES improves Pass@1 while attaining higher Pass@K than GRPO. We further develop a sequential GRPO-ES training strategy that combines GRPO's strength in Pass@1 with ES's gains in Pass@K. Second, we find that despite substantial whole-model parameter drift, the task-performance gains of ES are only contributed to a sparse subset of larger-magnitude updates. This functional sparsity suggests that large parameter movement need not imply widespread functional change, and held-out evaluations further show that it does not necessarily lead to catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we study how hyperparameter design affects the effectiveness of ES, demonstrating that ES requires a smaller population size in a larger LLM. These findings position ES as a distinct reasoning post-training paradigm rather than a less effective, memory-efficient alternative to GRPO.

AI.tldr: ES delivers a distinct, memory-efficient post-training paradigm for LLM reasoning with broader reasoning coverage and higher Pass@K than GRPO; when integrated with GRPO (GRPO-ES), it yields stronger Pass@1 and Pass@K; ES shows functional sparsity despite large parameter drift; smaller population sizes suffice for larger LLMs.
AI.motivation: To systematically study the optimization dynamics of Evolution Strategies (ES) in LLM post-training and compare its advantages to Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), aiming to delineate ES's reasoning coverage, stability, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity across the ES population; empirical evaluation comparing ES and GRPO on Pass@K; development of a sequential GRPO-ES training strategy; analysis of parameter drift to assess functional sparsity; ablation studies on hyperparameters, notably population size, across different LLM scales.
AI.result: ES achieves broader reasoning coverage and higher Pass@K than GRPO, with no entropy collapse and improved Pass@1 when combined with GRPO-ES. Functional updates are sparse in magnitude yet affect task performance, reducing risks of catastrophic forgetting. A smaller population suffices for larger LLMs.
AI.conclusion: ES constitutes a distinct reasoning post-training paradigm with unique dynamics and advantages over GRPO. When strategically integrated with GRPO, it can exploit broader reasoning capabilities, and careful hyperparameter design (notably population size) is essential for larger models.

title: Temporal Sensitivity Analysis of Tessera Embeddings
summary: Many Earth Observation applications need land-use/land-cover maps that are both precise and frequently updated, yet the strongest Earth Observation foundation models build their embeddings from a full year of observations. We present a controlled study of the temporal sensitivity of Tessera, one of these leading foundation models, for land-use/land-cover mapping. Keeping the encoder frozen, we recompute its embeddings over varying observation windows, from a full year down to a single day. We use them as inputs to a linear probe and a UNet segmentation head, benchmarking both of them against from-scratch networks on LUCAS, DynamicEarthNet, and PASTIS-R datasets. We show that the value of the embeddings is task-dependent. Where classes are separated by phenology, as for the crop types of PASTIS-R, they reach a mean Intersection-over-Union of $58.3$, about $46\%$ above the best from-scratch model. Where classes are temporally stable (e.g., forests in DynamicEarthNet and LUCAS), embedding-based and from-scratch models match only under full supervision. On both datasets, Tessera embeddings remain markedly more label-efficient. Degradation under shorter temporal windows is gradual and class-dependent. Contracting the window from one year to one month costs $39\%$ of the segmentation accuracy on PASTIS-R but only $5\%$ on DynamicEarthNet. Single-day embeddings still classify land cover in LUCAS at $3.4$ times the chance level. Our study shows that temporal coverage is therefore a tunable cost rather than a fixed prerequisite, opening regimes such as near-real-time mapping and faster land-use/land-cover refresh cycles.

AI.tldr: Temporal sensitivity of Tessera embeddings for land-use mapping shows tunable trade-offs: strong performance on phenology-driven classes with shorter windows, and label efficiency persists, enabling near-real-time mapping with varying class dynamics.
AI.motivation: Understand how temporal coverage affects foundation-model embeddings for LULC mapping and whether near-real-time updates are feasible by adjusting observation window length.
AI.method: Freeze the Tessera encoder and recompute embeddings over observation windows ranging from 1 year to 1 day. Use these embeddings as inputs to a linear probe and a UNet segmentation head, comparing against from-scratch models on LUCAS, DynamicEarthNet, and PASTIS-R datasets.
AI.result: Phenology-driven classes (PASTIS-R crops) achieve IoU 58.3, ~46% higher than best from-scratch. For temporally stable classes (DynamicEarthNet, LUCAS), embedding-based and from-scratch models only match under full supervision. Embeddings are more label-efficient. Degradation with shorter windows is class-dependent: 1 year → 1 month costs 39% on PASTIS-R, 5% on DynamicEarthNet. Single-day embeddings can classify LUCAS at 3.4x chance level.
AI.conclusion: Temporal coverage is a tunable cost rather than a fixed prerequisite, enabling near-real-time mapping and faster LULC refresh cycles; embedding-based methods excel for phenology-driven classes and offer label efficiency, with trade-offs for stable classes.

title: A Multi-Modal AI Framework for Real-Time Queue Prediction, Management and Optimisation in Intelligent Border Control Systems
summary: In the present work an efficient border control management procedure is proposed. Compared to operational queue management systems, whose operations are based on mostly static data, the proposed work takes into account dynamic traffic conditions, thus enabling optimal performance, even in cases of uncertainty. To this end, we are proposing a multi-modal Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework, tailored to th needs of border control systems, which enables real-time queue prediction, management, and resource optimization. The novel proposed approach integrates heterogeneous data sources and presents them through a unified representation by employing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for queue forecasting. Furthermore, it leverages Model Predictive Control (MPC) and scheduling optimization to derive actionable control policies, which in turn can be presented to border control officers. The proposed work has been evaluated using synthetic data simulating realistic traffic. The evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces queue prediction error by up to 35% and average waiting time by 30%. Accordingly, the average throughput increases by nearly 20%, compared to ARIMA and rule-based methods. The abovementioned results show the effectiveness and efficiency of combining AI architectures with optimization techniques for proactive and adaptive border traffic management.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal AI framework for real-time border control queue forecasting and optimization using LSTM forecasts and MPC-based scheduling; evaluated on synthetic data with notable improvements over ARIMA and rule-based approaches.
AI.motivation: To replace static queue management with dynamic, data-driven decisions under uncertainty to reduce wait times and increase throughput at border checkpoints.
AI.method: Integrates heterogeneous data sources into a unified representation; uses LSTM for queue forecasting; applies Model Predictive Control and scheduling optimization to derive actionable control policies for border officers.
AI.result: On synthetic data, achieves up to 35% reduction in queue prediction error, 30% reduction in average waiting time, and ~20% throughput gain versus ARIMA and rule-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective integration of AI forecasting and optimization to enable proactive, adaptive border traffic management.

title: Parameter-Efficient pretrained-CT-to-MRI Transfer for Rectal Cancer Segmentation: Performance-Calibration Trade-offs
comment: Accepted to the Medical Image AI in Radiation Therapy (MIART) Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Accurate rectal cancer segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for adaptive radiotherapy and tumor response assessment, but deployment also requires computational efficiency and informative, calibrated uncertainty estimates. We therefore introduce SWIFT, a SWin pretrained model wIth parameter-eFficient and Tumor-aware fine-tuning for rectal cancer segmentation. A Swin V2 encoder pretrained on 10,444 public 3D CT volumes using a DINOv2-style objective was adapted to T2-weighted MRI through four cumulative configurations: full fine-tuning (SWIFT), decoder compression (SWIFTe), low-rank adaptation (SWIFTe-LoRA), and a four-member LoRA-decoder ensemble (SWIFTe-LDE4). Geometric accuracy, tumor detection, radiomic agreement, and probability calibration were evaluated on a held-out 247-case test set from a single-institution cohort acquired using 1.5 or 3 Tesla GE scanners. Compared with SWIFT, SWIFTe reduced total parameters by 70.1% (from 72.8M to 21.8M) and increased tumor detection rate from 89.9% to 93.9%, while achieving a slightly lower median surface DSC (0.61 versus 0.62) and improved radiomic agreement. In a separate SWIFTe ablation, removing tumor-aware augmentation reduced detection from 93.9% to 89.9% but increased surface DSC from 0.61 to 0.64, demonstrating a detection-boundary-agreement trade-off. SWIFTe-LoRA used 14.6% of SWIFTe's trainable parameters while retaining similar segmentation performance. SWIFTe-LDE4 achieved the lowest calibration errors among the four configurations after temperature scaling (expected calibration error, 0.217; Brier score, 0.222), although the absolute expected calibration error indicates residual miscalibration. Similar efficiency-calibration patterns were observed using the public VoCo checkpoint, supporting robustness across pretrained initializations rather than external clinical generalizability.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient SwinV2-based framework (SWIFT family) for rectal cancer MRI segmentation using four fine-tuning configurations, achieving competitive performance with far fewer trainable parameters and improved calibrated uncertainty, evaluated on a single-institution 247-case test set with CT-pretrained initialization.
AI.motivation: Need accurate, fast, and well-calibrated segmentation for adaptive radiotherapy and tumor response assessment, addressing computational efficiency and uncertainty estimation while leveraging pretrained models across imaging modalities (CT pretraining adapted to MRI).
AI.method: Pretrain a Swin V2 encoder on 10,444 public 3D CT volumes using a DINOv2-style objective. Adapt to T2-weighted MRI via four configurations: (1) SWIFT: full fine-tuning; (2) SWIFTe: decoder compression; (3) SWIFTe-LoRA: low-rank adapters; (4) SWIFTe-LDE4: four-member LoRA-decoder ensemble. Evaluate geometric accuracy, tumor detection, radiomic agreement, and probability calibration on a held-out 247-case test set from a single institution using GE scanners (1.5T/3T).
AI.result: SWIFTe reduced total parameters by 70.1% (72.8M→21.8M) and improved tumor detection from 89.9% to 93.9', while yielding a marginally lower median surface DSC (0.61 vs 0.62) and better radiomic agreement. In ablation, removing tumor-aware augmentation lowered detection to 89.9% but raised surface DSC to 0.64, indicating a detection-boundary trade-off. SWIFTe-LoRA used 14.6% of SWIFTe’s trainable parameters with comparable segmentation. SWIFTe-LDE4 achieved the lowest calibration errors after temperature scaling (ECE 0.217; Brier 0.222), though residual miscalibration remains. Public VoCo results showed similar efficiency-calibration patterns, suggesting robustness across pretrained initializations rather than external clinical generalizability.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that parameter-efficient, tumor-aware fine-tuning of a CT-pretrained SwinV2 encoder enables competitive rectal cancer MRI segmentation with strong calibration, using a range of configuration options (including LoRA-based adapters and ensembles) to balance accuracy, efficiency, and uncertainty quantification. External validation across institutions and scanners is warranted to confirm generalizability.

title: Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder
summary: Multimodal representation learning has been shifting from traditional two-tower architectures to large language model (LLM)-based embedders due to their strong instruction-following capabilities. Despite this progress, existing approaches primarily focus on language and image modalities, which also remain the dominant modalities for user-conditioned interactions in current embedders. In this paper, we propose the first Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder (OmniUE), which not only learns a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio by leveraging intermediate-layer representations from dedicated learnable tokens, but also supports omni-interactive querying, enabling users to provide inputs in the form of text, visual regions of interest, and audio spans. Within OmniUE, visual and audio segmenters process diverse user interactions and integrate them with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation. To evaluate OmniUE's omni-interactive capabilities, we introduce OmniCHOIR, benchmarking models for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval based on the given text, video, and audio as well as unimodal or multimodal interaction prompts. OmniUE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, with average improvements of 10.5% on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on our omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark. We believe that jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying paves the way toward universal embedders.

AI.tldr: OmniUE is the first omnichannel, omni-interactive universal embedder that learns a unified text–video–audio embedding space using intermediate-layer representations from dedicated tokens and supports query-by-text, region, and audio-span inputs via an omni-LLM; it is evaluated with OmniCHOIR and achieves strong gains on multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of prior multimodal encoders that focus on text and image by extending to audio and video and enabling omni-interactive querying, yielding a universal, user-conditioned embedding framework.
AI.method: Use intermediate-layer representations from dedicated learnable tokens to build a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio. Visual and audio segmenters process user interactions (text, regions, audio spans) and integrate with an omni-LLM to produce any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation.
AI.result: OmniUE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across textual-interactive video benchmarks (+10.5%), audio tasks (+1.1%), visual-interactive benchmarks (+83.7%), and the omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark (+24.1%).
AI.conclusion: Jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying enables universal embedders and broader multimodal interaction capabilities.

title: SSMB: Self-Supervised Local Feature Detection under Motion Blur
summary: Keypoint detection under motion blur remains a significant challenge, as blur distorts local image structure and degrades the repeatability of feature localization. Existing approaches either rely on computationally expensive deblur-then-detect pipelines that may introduce restoration artifacts, or learn to regress the image positions of handcrafted keypoints extracted on sharp images, which reflects the assumptions of the handcrafted detector rather than what is truly repeatable under blur. We present SSMB, a deblur-free, self-supervised keypoint detector for motion-blurred images that requires neither handcrafted detectors nor external pseudo-labels. SSMB introduces the Local Discriminability Enhancement (LDE) module, which restores fine-grained local discriminability after global feature mixing. Training is performed in two stages. First, geometric pretraining on synthetic shapes bootstraps spatially discriminative keypoint detection without any external detector, just from the rendered geometry. Second, blur-aware training on real sharp-blur image pairs learns blur-invariant detection through a multi-component self-supervised objective that enforces cross-domain consistency, geometric alignment, and spatial coverage. Extensive evaluations on keypoint detection, image matching, relative pose estimation, and visual localization under motion blur demonstrate that SSMB establishes a new state-of-the-art among sparse keypoint detectors, consistently outperforming both supervised and self-supervised baselines across all tasks. Code, models, and datasets will be publicly available upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: Deblur-free, self-supervised keypoint detector for motion blur (SSMB) with Local Discriminability Enhancement; two-stage training (synthetic geometric pretraining; blur-aware self-supervised fine-tuning); achieves state-of-the-art across keypoint detection, matching, pose estimation, and localization without handcrafted detectors or external pseudo-labels.
AI.motivation: Motion blur reduces keypoint repeatability and accuracy. Deblur-then-detect pipelines are prone to restoration artifacts and handcrafted detectors may not be optimal under blur. A deblur-free, self-supervised approach aims for robust, repeatable keypoints under blur.
AI.method: Introduce SSMB with a Local Discriminability Enhancement (LDE) module to recover fine-grained local discriminability after global feature mixing. Two-stage training: (1) geometric pretraining on synthetic shapes to bootstrap spatially discriminative keypoints without external detectors; (2) blur-aware training on real sharp-blur image pairs with a multi-component self-supervised objective enforcing cross-domain consistency, geometric alignment, and spatial coverage.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show SSMB achieves state-of-the-art performance among sparse keypoint detectors across tasks: keypoint detection, image matching, relative pose estimation, and visual localization under motion blur; consistently surpasses both supervised and self-supervised baselines.
AI.conclusion: SSMB provides a deblur-free, self-supervised solution that outperforms existing approaches for motion-blur robust keypoint detection. The LDE module and the two-stage training are key factors in achieving robust, repeatable keypoints without external labels or handcrafted detectors; code and data will be released.

title: A Contract-Centered Architecture for Scalable and Manageable Agentic Runtimes
summary:
Enterprise AI deployment is a coordination problem across business units, application and AI teams, testing, platform engineering, infrastructure, security, operations, and data governance. Use-case benchmarks show whether one agent completes one task, but not how changing capabilities, models, runtime mechanisms, capacity, and enterprise data should be owned, changed, admitted, or evidenced together.
  We present four responsibility objects as shared organizational contracts: Skill (reusable, versioned capability and workflow asset), Harness (runtime compiler and governor), Scaffold (execution/control boundary and NFR owner), and a stack-external data substrate under independent CIO-governed semantics and telemetry. The runtime core is A = <S, H, X>, with the data substrate outside that stack.
  The central contribution is one bounded, falsifiable hypothesis, P1 (cost-aware capability-capacity separability): within a declared operating region, changing activated capability preserves the capacity-response interaction within a preregistered equivalence margin, while changing compatible Scaffold capacity preserves capability semantics up to a non-inferiority margin, and the required controls stay within a declared enforcement budget. Six design conditions become measured obligations whose coverage, violations, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions determine whether P1 is decidable.
  We propose a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment (balanced order, reset/washout, repeated seeds and failure regimes, cluster-aware uncertainty) with a four-state verdict: supported, falsified, conditional-engineering, or inconclusive. This paper contributes a contract-bounded runtime architecture, a source-preserving data substrate, and a falsifiable measurement protocol. It reports no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured result.

AI.tldr: Proposes a contract-based enterprise AI runtime architecture with four responsibility objects and a falsifiable hypothesis (P1) about cost-aware capability-capacity separability; outlines a cluster-period randomized crossover measurement protocol; reports no experiments or results yet.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI deployment is a complex coordination problem across business units, AI teams, and governance layers. Current use-case benchmarks fail to specify how to own, modify, and evidence capabilities, runtime mechanisms, data, and controls at scale.
AI.method: Introduce a bounded runtime architecture A = <S, H, X> and four responsibility objects: Skill (reusable capabilities), Harness (runtime governor), Scaffold (execution boundary and NFR ownership), and a data substrate governed independently. Propose six design conditions and a falsifiable hypothesis P1. Recommend a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment with four-state verdicts to evaluate P1.
AI.result: The abstract reports no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured result.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a contract-bounded runtime architecture and a source-preserving data substrate, plus a falsifiable measurement protocol to decide P1; positions this as a theoretical/propositional contribution rather than an empirical study.

title: Unsupervised Adaptation of 3D CT Foundation Models for 3D CBCT Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the EMA4MICCAI workshop at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Code, trained models, weights, and liver annotations are available at https://github.com/mirabll/FARR3D/
summary: Accurate 3D segmentation of cone-beam CT (CBCT) is critical for interventional and radiation therapy applications, yet it remains limited by two compounding challenges: the scarcity of annotated CBCT data and the large domain shift from diagnostic CT. Interventional CBCT exhibits fundamental modality differences from conventional CT, driven by acquisition and physics effects as well as contrast-specific vascular content, thereby limiting effective cross-modality model transfer. We propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) framework based on redundancy-reducing feature alignment, enabling 3D CBCT segmentation with no target-domain annotations or inference-time adaptation. Our framework is architecture-agnostic, seamlessly adapting both CNN-based and ViT-based foundation models. We evaluate our method on two challenging CT-CBCT liver segmentation benchmarks: one for interventional vascular procedures and one for radiation therapy, demonstrating that even large-scale pretrained segmentation networks require explicit feature-space bridging to generalize across acquisition modalities, and that our approach consistently outperforms existing pretrained foundation model and UDA strategies. To support reproducibility and benchmarking, we release the liver segmentations for a public CBCT dataset, along with the code, trained models, and weights.

AI.tldr: An unsupervised domain-adaptation framework using redundancy-reducing feature alignment enables 3D CBCT segmentation without target annotations, bridging cross-modality gaps from diagnostic CT to interventional CBCT; architecture-agnostic for CNN and ViT; validated on two liver segmentation benchmarks, outperforming pretrained models and other UDA methods; includes public release of data, code, and models.
AI.motivation: Cross-modality domain shift between diagnostic CT and interventional CBCT, compounded by limited annotated CBCT data and modality-specific content, hampers transfer of pretrained segmentation networks.
AI.method: Unsupervised domain adaptation via redundancy-reducing feature alignment that bridges feature spaces between CT and CBCT. Architecture-agnostic, works with both CNN-based and ViT-based foundation models, with no target-domain annotations or runtime adaptation.
AI.result: On two challenging CT-CBCT liver segmentation benchmarks (interventional vascular procedures and radiotherapy), the method consistently outperforms existing pretrained foundation-model and UDA strategies, highlighting the need for explicit feature-space bridging for cross-modality generalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective cross-modality 3D segmentation without target labels or test-time adaptation and is generalizable across backbone architectures; the authors also provide public data and code to support reproducibility.

title: pro-team at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship and Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Vocabulary-Constrained Filtering for Ontology Learning
summary: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite significant progress in Large Language Models (LLMs), which can hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations. In the LLMs4OL 2026 Challenge, we address both the End-to-End Flagship Task (Task A) and Ontology Extension Reuse Task (Task B) using an offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline. Our system employs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval, selecting the top-5 examples for Task A and top-2 for Task B. A left-truncated context-windowing strategy preserves task instructions within long prompts. For Task B, generated triples undergo deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering, retaining triples when at least one endpoint belongs to the sample's closed term/type vocabulary and removing duplicates of the initial ontology. The approach achieves Semantic Graph Similarity of 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 of 0.9200, and Taxonomy Discovery F1 of 0.8540 on Task B, while Task A achieves 0.7416 Semantic Graph Similarity. However, no non-taxonomic relations are extracted, highlighting limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.

AI.tldr: Offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting for ontology learning (LLMs4OL 2026) addressing Task A (End-to-End Flagship) and Task B (Ontology Extension Reuse) with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval; left-truncated context to preserve instructions; Task B uses deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering and deduplication against the initial ontology. Results: Task A SGSimilarity 0.7416; Task B SGSimilarity 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 0.9200, Taxonomy Discovery F1 0.8540; no non-taxonomic relations extracted; major limitation is closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.
AI.motivation: Mitigate hallucinations and format inconsistencies in LLM-driven ontology construction, address both end-to-end generation and extension with retrieval augmentation, and evaluate with ontology-centric metrics.
AI.method: Offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting. Demonstrations retrieved using all-MiniLM-L6-v2; select top-5 examples for Task A and top-2 for Task B. Use left-truncated context window to preserve task instructions in long prompts. For Task B, apply deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering to keep triples where at least one endpoint belongs to the sample's closed vocabulary and remove duplicates against the initial ontology.
AI.result: Task A SGSimilarity 0.7416; Task B SGSimilarity 0.8692; Term-Typing F1 0.9200; Taxonomy Discovery F1 0.8540.
AI.conclusion: Strong performance on Task B with taxonomy-oriented metrics; Task A shows moderate performance; key limitation is absence of non-taxonomic relations due to closed vocabularies; future work should explore richer relation vocabularies and more flexible filtering.

title: Vision-centric generative AI models: A software-hardware perspective
summary: Vision generative artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most rapidly advancing areas of deep learning. The explosion of multimodal models has made them widely associated with text-to-image applications running on large datacentres. However, vision generative models are equally needed in applications that operate under strict hardware constraints at the edge, including autonomous vehicles, agricultural sensors, and mobile devices. In this Perspective, we argue that progress in vision generative AI has been driven by output quality, with hardware evolving reactively to accommodate growing model demands. We quantify the parameter cost and energy efficiency of these models across a range of accelerator platforms, and map four generative model families against seven real-world application domains. Finally, we advocate a software-hardware co-design approach, where deployment constraints are considered from the start of the design process, ensuring that the "right model" runs on the "right hardware" to serve the "right application", making generative AI deployment sustainable and accessible across a much broader range of platforms.

AI.tldr: A perspective on aligning vision generative AI deployment with edge hardware through software-hardware co-design, emphasizing energy-efficient, domain-mapped model choices.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between rapid model capabilities and edge/deployment constraints; enable sustainable, accessible deployment across platforms.
AI.method: Analytical quantification of parameter counts and energy efficiency across accelerator platforms; mapping of four generative model families to seven real-world application domains; advocacy of a software-hardware co-design approach.
AI.result: Provides quantified metrics and a deployment map; demonstrates the need for co-design; outlines guidelines to pair the right model with the right hardware for each domain.
AI.conclusion: Promotes software-hardware co-design from the outset to achieve scalable, sustainable, and accessible deployment of vision generative AI.

title: LAAF: A Layered Accountability Architecture Framework for LLM Applications
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) operate in hospitals, courtrooms, banks, and public service desks, where fluent, confident outputs are treated as authoritative even when ungrounded or incorrect. When such an output contributes to harm, who is answerable, and through what mechanisms can responsibility be traced, explained, and acted upon? Following PRISMA guidance, five databases were searched from January 2022 to March 2026 against four review questions; of 4,512 records identified, 122 primary studies were included, together with 12 regulatory and standards documents analysed as primary sources. The review consolidates a sociotechnical account of accountability as an actor-forum relation resolved into five dimensions, and synthesises mechanisms across four families: technical controls, human oversight, organisational governance, and documentation and traceability, each with a maturity assessment. The corpus is read through a four-layer classification device spanning provenance, application logic, human oversight, and governance and redress, cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring. Both are mapped onto the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations have applied since 2 August 2026, the NIST AI RMF with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance in healthcare, consumer finance, education, and the public sector. Four persistent gaps emerge: under-specification of human oversight, absence of shared accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, and limited empirical evaluation, alongside five structural tensions that no surveyed instrument resolves. The review closes by consolidating the classification device into an integrated accountability architecture, LAAF, with cybersecurity aligned to the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025); it is a synthesis of the surveyed evidence rather than a validated artefact.

AI.tldr: PRISMA-based review of accountability for LLMs in high-stakes settings, proposing a five-dimension sociotechnical framework and four mechanism families, plus a four-layer classification and the LAAF architecture, mapped to major international standards; identifies persistent gaps and tensions and offers an integrated but unvalidated artefact.
AI.motivation: To address how responsibility for LLM-driven harms in domains like healthcare, law, finance can be traced, explained, and acted upon, by synthesizing sociotechnical accountability across governance, technical controls, human oversight, and documentation.
AI.method: Systematic literature review guided by PRISMA; searches across five databases from Jan 2022–Mar 2026; 4,512 records identified, 122 primary studies included; plus 12 regulatory/standards documents; four-layer and five-dimension classification; cross-mapped to EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance; maturity assessment for each mechanism.
AI.result: Identify five accountability dimensions (sociotechnical actors, forums, etc.) and four families of mechanisms (technical controls, human oversight, organizational governance, documentation/traceability), implemented via a four-layer classification (provenance, application logic, human oversight, governance/redress) with cross-cut by traceability and monitoring. Mapped to major standards; highlights four persistent gaps (oversight under-specification, lack of shared metrics, disciplinary disconnect, scant empirical evaluation) and five structural tensions; proposes an integrated LAAF accountability architecture aligned with OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025).
AI.conclusion: The work synthesizes evidence into an accountability architecture rather than delivering a validated artefact; provides a framework to guide governance and future empirical work, with alignment to prominent standards and cybersecurity practices.

title: PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate exceptional visual reasoning capabilities, yet their inference costs escalate rapidly with the proliferation of visual tokens. Existing visual token pruning methods exhibit two fundamental limitations. First, most approaches operate exclusively post-vision encoder, leaving the substantial latency of the visual encoding phase unoptimized. Second, under strict token budgets, these methods often fail to jointly preserve holistic visual contexts and fine-grained details, leading to performance degradation. To address these bottlenecks, we propose PACE (Pixel-Adaptive Condense and Extract), a training-free inference framework that accelerates both the vision encoder and the Large Language Model (LLM) via a unified Condense-and-Extract paradigm. During the Condense stage, an Adaptive Pixel Compressor (APC) evaluates visual information density prior to encoding, adaptively downsampling redundant inputs, curtailing encoder computation while preserving global context and essential visual cues. In the Extract stage, a Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor (DDAE) selectively retains visual tokens via a fusion of internal visual signals from the encoder and semantic signals from the LLM, safeguarding task-critical details. By integrating PACE into Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the model retains 93.8% of its original performance while utilizing only 10% of the visual tokens, yielding a 3.1x speedup in time to first token (TTFT). Our code is available at https://github.com/jjL357/PACE.

AI.tldr: PACE: a training-free inference framework that accelerates both the vision encoder and the LLM by a unified Condense-and-Extract paradigm. It uses an Adaptive Pixel Compressor to downsample inputs based on information density, and a Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor to select tokens by fusing encoder signals with LLM semantics. Reported results include retaining 93.8% of baseline performance with only 10% of visual tokens, and a 3.1x speedup in time-to-first-token on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
AI.motivation: Current visual token pruning methods either operate only after the vision encoder, leaving encoder latency unaddressed, or under strict token budgets fail to preserve both global visual context and fine-grained details. A training-free framework that optimizes both stages and jointly preserves holistic context and critical details is needed.
AI.method: Condense stage: Adaptive Pixel Compressor assesses information density pre-encoding and adaptively down-samples inputs to reduce encoder computation while preserving global context. Extract stage: Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor selects visual tokens by integrating internal encoder signals and semantic signals from the LLM, preserving task-critical details. The approach is integrated into Qwen2.5-VL-7B as PACE.
AI.result: Empirical results show 93.8% of original performance with 10% of visual tokens, and 3.1x speedup in time-to-first-token (TTFT). Code is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: PACE demonstrates that joint, training-free condensation and extraction of visual tokens can substantially accelerate both vision encoding and LLM reasoning with limited performance loss, offering a practical path for deploying efficient VLMs.

title: TransMeme: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Cultural Meme Transcreation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Internet memes are a pervasive form of multimodal online communication; however, such communication often involves users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Therefore, adapting memes across cultures and languages is a central challenge for enabling mutual understanding in online communication. Unlike ordinary translation or standalone text rewriting, cross-cultural meme transcreation must jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning for the target audience, and maintain coherence between text and image. In this work, we first provide an explicit task analysis of cross-cultural meme transcreation and identify three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent and tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. Based on this analysis, we propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents that are coordinated to address these challenges through cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. The framework strengthens target text adaptation with coordinated feedback to handle difficult cases that require deeper cultural or visual intervention. We evaluate the framework on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation using both human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge. Our method consistently outperforms all baselines across both evaluation settings. In human evaluation, it achieves the best performance on all four dimensions and delivers a 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline, while in LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains the highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% versus 26% for the second-best baseline). Further analysis indicates that each component contributes to the performance. Our error analysis suggests that the remaining bottlenecks lie in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than simple cultural knowledge gaps, pointing to future work on humor transfer.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent framework for cross-cultural meme transcreation (Chinese↔English) addressing culture-specific knowledge, intent preservation, and multimodal consistency; demonstrates clear performance gains over baselines in both human and LLM-based evaluation, with remaining challenges in humor transfer and image–text alignment.
AI.motivation: Memes enable multilingual, multimodal online communication but cultural and linguistic gaps hinder mutual understanding. Cross-cultural meme transcreation must preserve intent, adapt culture-dependent cues, and maintain text–image coherence beyond ordinary translation.
AI.method: Propose a coordinated multi-agent system with specialized roles for cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. Includes coordinated feedback loops to handle difficult cases, and evaluation via human judgments and LLM-as-a-Judge.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation. In human evaluation, achieves best performance on all four dimensions and 33.1% average improvement over strongest baseline. In LLM-as-a-Judge, achieves highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% vs 26% for second-best). Ablation shows each component contributes; error analysis points to humor reconstruction and image–text alignment as bottlenecks rather than mere cultural knowledge gaps.
AI.conclusion: An effective framework for cross-cultural meme transcreation with potential for broader languages; future work should focus on improving humor transfer and tighter image–text alignment.

title: CODE: Cross-Modal Calibration and Dynamic Suppression for Open World Object Detection
summary: Open World Object Detection (OWOD) built on multimodal foundation models often suffers from semantic ambiguity caused by unidirectional text-to-vision matching, while rigid outlier penalties may over-suppress unknown objects near known-class decision boundaries. We propose CODE (Cross-Modal Calibration and Dynamic Suppression), a unified inference-time framework with three complementary components. Cross-Modal Joint Confidence Calibration injects global visual prototypes to calibrate text-driven known-class predictions. Uncertainty-Guided Universal Objectness Enhancement measures classification hesitation from local visual responses to strengthen potential unknown objects. Dynamic Outlier Suppression via Confidence Margin replaces rigid suppression with a margin-aware adjustment that preserves ambiguous out-of-distribution instances. Experiments on the Real-World Detection benchmark demonstrate that, with the OWL-ViT L/14 backbone, CODE achieves 21.7 U-mAP and 40.8 K-mAP in Task 1, surpassing the previous state of the art by 2.6 and 2.3 points, respectively.

AI.tldr: A unified inference-time framework (CODE) for Open World Object Detection that calibrates cross-modal predictions, enhances unknown-object detection, and uses a margin-aware suppression to improve performance on Real-World Detection.
AI.motivation: Semantic ambiguity in text-to-vision matching and overly aggressive outlier penalties hinder open-world detection; a balance between known-class calibration and unknown-object preservation is needed.
AI.method: Three components: Cross-Modal Joint Confidence Calibration aligns text-driven predictions with global visual prototypes; Uncertainty-Guided Universal Objectness Enhancement uses local visual responses to amplify consideration of potential unknown objects; Dynamic Outlier Suppression via Confidence Margin replaces rigid suppression with a margin-aware strategy.
AI.result: On Real-World Detection benchmark with OWL-ViT L/14, CODE achieves 21.7 U-mAP and 40.8 K-mAP in Task 1, surpassing prior SOTA by 2.6 and 2.3 points.
AI.conclusion: CODE effectively reduces semantic ambiguity and over-suppression in OWOD, delivering state-of-the-art open-world object detection performance on the tested benchmark.

title: GRAIN: Bridging Name and Narrative Shifts in Real-World Graph Reasoning through Invariance-Rewarded Agentic RL
summary: Despite their potential in standardized graph tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, extracting topological structures from noisy text is highly fragile for LLMs, which often overfit to surface patterns. Moreover, mitigating these parsing failures via multi-agent systems incurs prohibitive latency. To address this, we propose GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. GRAIN models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward. By validating extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, this reward forces the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. We also introduce GRIT, a benchmark evaluating sensitivity to such linguistic shifts. GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45\% in accuracy with approximately 24\% lower latency. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap of SFT models (from 15.77\% to 7.80\%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.

AI.tldr: GRAIN is a single-agent reinforcement learning framework for robust text-to-graph extraction, using a Structure Invariance Reward to align LLM outputs with ground-truth graphs; supported by the GRIT benchmark, it outperforms multi-agent baselines in accuracy and latency and shows strong OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: LLMs are brittle to shifts in node identifiers and task phrasing; deterministic graph tools are stable but parsing graphs from noisy text is fragile. Multi-agent systems reduce brittleness but incur high latency. A single-agent approach with targeted rewards could achieve robustness and efficiency.
AI.method: GRAIN casts reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline trained with reinforcement learning, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward that validates intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies to discourage memorization of surface patterns.
AI.result: GRAIN achieves 16.45% higher accuracy than multi-agent baselines with ~24% lower latency. It also halves the OOD gap of SFT models (from 15.77% to 7.80%) and remains robust on large-scale graphs beyond training distribution.
AI.conclusion: A single-agent RL approach with a Structure Invariance Reward yields robust text-to-graph extraction, improved efficiency, and better generalization compared with multi-agent baselines. The GRIT benchmark quantifies sensitivity to linguistic shifts.

title: DINOcular: Self-Supervised Visuospatial Representations
summary: We introduce a self-supervised framework for learning joint visuospatial representations from RGB-D observations. While modern vision foundation models are trained almost exclusively on RGB images, many embodied systems have access to explicit depth sensing, which provides geometric information that monocular inputs cannot recover. Our method integrates depth-derived geometric priors with a visual backbone through inter-patch and intra-patch fusion, enabling the model to encode both appearance and spatial structure efficiently. The resulting representation shows promising improvements on 3D awareness while preserving semantic transfer: it outperforms prior methods of comparable scale on multiple 3D geometry benchmarks, and remains competitive when probed for standard RGB-D semantic segmentation tasks.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised framework learns joint visuospatial representations from RGB-D by incorporating depth-derived geometric priors into a visual backbone via inter-patch and intra-patch fusion, enabling efficient encoding of appearance and spatial structure.
AI.motivation: RGB foundation models are trained on RGB only, but embodied systems have access to depth information; leveraging depth can improve 3D geometry understanding and spatial awareness without sacrificing semantic transfer.
AI.method: A self-supervised strategy that fuses depth-derived geometric priors with a visual backbone through inter-patch and intra-patch fusion to jointly encode appearance and spatial structure.
AI.result: The learned representation improves 3D awareness and outperforms comparable-scale methods on multiple 3D geometry benchmarks, while remaining competitive on RGB-D semantic segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating depth priors into self-supervised RGB-D learning yields richer 3D-aware representations without sacrificing semantic transfer, validating depth-aware pretraining for embodied perception.

title: Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering for Graph Anomaly Detection
summary: In recent years, graph anomaly detection (GAD) based on frequency-domain filtering have achieved promising results. However, existing approaches still face three major challenges: First, they use static basic function to constructed graph filter which cannot effectively adapt to the frequency-domain distribution of graph data. Second, they fail to adequately consider the importance information of each attribute in the node feature vector, leading to the loss of fine-grained information. Third, they insufficiently utilize node labels for GAD. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel graph anomaly detection method called JPGFN (Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering Network). First, a Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) is developed to better learn fine-grained node features by feature separation and applying nonlinear transformations to node features across different dimensions. Second, an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module is constructed based on Jacobi polynomials to adaptively capture complex frequency-domain features of graph signals. Finally, a node label constraint module is developed to facilitate the use of node labels and enhance the performance of GAD. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms mainstream approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes JPGFN, a graph anomaly detection framework that (1) learns fine-grained node features via feature separation with nonlinear transformations (FSTNN), (2) uses an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filter to capture complex frequency-domain graph signals, and (3) enforces node-label constraints to better exploit labeled information. It claims superior performance on real-world datasets over mainstream baselines.
AI.motivation: GAD in the frequency domain faces three gaps: (i) static basic graph filters fail to match diverse spectral distributions, (ii) uniform treatment of node features loses fine-grained, dimension-wise information, and (iii) underutilization of labeled information in detection tasks. The work aims to address these by feature separation, adaptive spectral filtering, and supervised guidance.
AI.method: 1) Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) to disentangle and transform node features across dimensions with nonlinearities, improving representational richness. 2) An adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module that parameterizes filters via Jacobi polynomials to flexibly model the graph’s frequency response. 3) A node label constraint module to integrate available label information into the GAD objective, guiding anomaly discrimination.
AI.result: Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets report that JPGFN significantly outperforms mainstream graph anomaly detection methods, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of the proposed components.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively combines dimension-wise feature separation, adaptive Jacobi-polynomial-based spectral filtering, and label-informed guidance to enhance GAD performance, addressing key limitations of prior frequency-domain methods.

title: UniFLM: United Segmentation and Measurement on Fetal Limb Ultrasonic Image
summary: Prenatal ultrasound examination is crucial for assessing fetal limb development and detecting congenital anomalies. However, existing artificial intelligence models often overlook fetal lethal skeletal dysplasias due to the lack of high-quality annotated data and a unified framework for multiple long bones. Moreover, generic segmentation models struggle with the inherent noise and semantic gaps in ultrasound images. To address these challenges, we construct the Fetal Limb Bones (FLB) dataset, comprising high-quality annotations for the humerus, femur, tibia-fibula, and radius-ulna. Furthermore, we propose UniFLM, a unified framework for automatic cross-plane segmentation and measurement. UniFLM incorporates a Semantic-Aware Skip Connection module to bridge the semantic gap between encoder and decoder features, and a Positive Sampling strategy to adaptively filter noise and extract essential semantic information. Finally, a Point Regression Mapping module is introduced to learn clinician annotation patterns for precise bone length measurement. Extensive experiments conducted on the FLB dataset demonstrate that the proposed UniFLM achieves superior accuracy and enhanced generalization capabilities in fetal long bone assessment compared to current state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: A unified framework UniFLM for cross-plane segmentation and measurement of fetal long bones using a new FLB dataset, featuring semantic-aware skip connections, positive sampling, and point regression mapping.
AI.motivation: Tackle lack of high-quality annotated data and a unified framework for multiple fetal long bones; address noise and semantic gaps in ultrasound segmentation; enable accurate bone length measurement.
AI.method: Create the Fetal Limb Bones (FLB) dataset with annotations for humerus, femur, tibia-fibula, and radius-ulna. Propose UniFLM: a cross-plane segmentation and measurement framework incorporating a Semantic-Aware Skip Connection module, a Positive Sampling strategy to filter noise and emphasize semantic features, and a Point Regression Mapping module to learn clinician annotation patterns for precise bone length measurement.
AI.result: Experiments on FLB show UniFLM achieves superior accuracy and generalization for fetal long bone assessment compared with current state-of-the-art models.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a new annotated FLB dataset and a unified, semantically aware framework that improves segmentation accuracy and measurement fidelity in fetal limb assessment, with potential clinical impact.

title: When Tool Outputs Become Commands: Separating Action Induction from Runtime Authorization in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented LLM agents must rely on untrusted runtime Observations to complete open-ended tasks; however, when tool outputs no longer merely provide data but begin to specify concrete actions, they effectively become ``commands'' that can drive real-world side effects beyond user intent. We argue that this risk arises from conflating action induction with execution authorization. To address this distinction, we propose SARA, which treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles and separates action provenance from execution authority. On the Observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics and persistently records action-origin provenance across steps as a review signal; on the execution side, actual tool calls are authorized only against the user objective and audited evidence from authorized successful executions, while satisfying goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support. To preserve this separation across multi-step execution, SARA applies No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority. Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn, SARA limits ASR to no more than \(0.63\%\) across four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional Agent backbones.

AI.tldr: SARA separates action induction from execution authorization in tool-augmented LLM agents to mitigate real-world side effects from tool outputs; uses a context-isolated Action Probe to record provenance, and authorization with No-History-Promotion to maintain a secure execution chain; achieves ASR ≤ 0.63% across multiple agents with competitive task utility.
AI.motivation: Untrusted tool outputs can escalate into concrete actions causing unintended real-world effects. Distinguishing action induction from execution authority reduces risk and enables auditability.
AI.method: Introduce SARA framework with two runtime roles: (1) Observation side uses a context-isolated Action Probe that captures action-inducing semantics and records provenance across steps; (2) Execution side enforces authorization of actual tool calls against user objectives and audited successful executions, satisfying goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support; apply No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering origins; evaluate across AgentDojo and AgentDyn and additional backbones.
AI.result: ASR reduced to no more than 0.63% across four evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility; results are consistent across multiple Agent backbones.
AI.conclusion: Separating action induction from execution authority with provenance auditing and history-promotion mitigates tool-use risk without sacrificing performance, offering a practical framework for safer tool-augmented LLM agents.

title: Sidecar: Training-Free Semantic Reuse for Character-Consistent Free-form Visual Storytelling
summary: Visual storytelling requires generating images that follow a narrative while preserving consistent character identities across frames. In free-form story generation, a character is fully described only when first introduced and is later referred to by a type-level mention or pronoun. Although this setting better reflects natural storytelling, later prompts may omit important identity-related semantics, making character consistency more difficult to maintain. We propose \textbf{Sidecar}, a plug-and-play semantic augmentation module that preserves entity-level information from the initial description and injects the missing semantics into later prompt embeddings. Sidecar requires no additional training and does not modify the architecture of the base diffusion model. Experiments on FreeStoryBench show that Sidecar consistently improves prompt-image alignment and character consistency across multiple SDXL- and FLUX-based baselines, with negligible computational overhead.

AI.tldr: Sidecar is a plug-and-play semantic augmentation module for visual storytelling that preserves entity identity across frames by injecting missing semantics into later prompts, with no training and no architecture changes to the diffusion model; it improves prompt-image alignment and character consistency with negligible overhead.
AI.motivation: In free-form storytelling, characters are fully described at first mention, then referred to by pronouns or type-level mentions. Later prompts can omit identity semantics, causing consistency loss across frames. A training-free method to preserve entity-level information is needed.
AI.method: Sidecar attaches as a semantic augmentation module to prompts, preserving the initial entity-level description and injecting the missing semantics into later prompt embeddings. It requires no model training or architecture changes to the base diffusion model.
AI.result: On FreeStoryBench, Sidecar consistently improves prompt-image alignment and character consistency across multiple SDXL- and FLUX-based baselines, with negligible computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Sidecar offers an effective, training-free approach to maintain character identity in visual storytelling prompts, compatible with standard diffusion-model pipelines.

title: Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
summary: The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid- & post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax & multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $π$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

AI.tldr: Frontier performance can be achieved by many institutions via continual learning on open-weight models; introduces Thomson and shows a π-shaped improvement pattern, enabling SovereignAI under various funding with lower compute; claims competitive performance and reduced forgetting.
AI.motivation: Address asymmetry in frontier-model development and provide a practical, accessible path to SovereignAI using open models and continual learning, enabling more actors to own model, tool infra, and data privacy.
AI.method: Use continual learning on readily available open-weight models with a modern mid- & post-training stack; apply safeguards to preserve plasticity and stability; perform minimal high-impact parameter interventions; contrast with fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation; train Thomson focusing on high-stakes professional work.
AI.result: Thomson achieves competitive performance with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal/tax/multilingualism, Deep Research; exhibits a π-shaped pattern with broad improvements including un-targeted ones, and mitigates forgetting in broad-domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: SovereignAI ownership is viable for more actors; the approach lowers compute and personnel requirements; supports wider adoption of frontier capabilities and governance tools; encourages broader participation in frontier AI development.

title: BPMN4CAI: A BPMN Extension for Modeling Dynamic Conversational AI
comment: Presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), September 2025, Münster, Germany
summary: Conversational AI systems, such as chatbots and virtual assistants, are becoming increasingly important to digital business processes. However, the established Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) standard faces challenges when representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions. This paper addresses this methodological and practical research gap by developing a standard-compliant BPMN extension (BPMN4CAI). Using Design Science Research methodology, this paper develops an approach that systematically extends existing BPMN elements and incorporates specialized components. The applicability and relevance of the BPMN4CAI framework are demonstrated and evaluated through a case study. The results show that the BPMN4CAI extension facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.

AI.tldr: Proposes BPMN4CAI, a standard-compliant BPMN extension for Conversational AI using Design Science Research; demonstrates via a case study that it enables adaptive decision-making, context management, and transparent AI interactions in business processes.
AI.motivation: BPMN struggles to model dynamic, context-sensitive interactions in Conversational AI; a standard-compliant extension is needed to capture these aspects within business processes.
AI.method: Design Science Research (DSR); systematically extend BPMN elements and add specialized components; validate via case study and practical evaluation.
AI.result: BPMN4CAI enables adaptive decision-making, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes; validated through a case study.
AI.conclusion: BPMN4CAI provides a practical, standard-compliant framework to model Conversational AI in BPMN, improving the ability to represent dynamic, context-aware interactions in business processes.

title: Detection of Christmas tree plantations from high-resolution aerial imagery. A case study in the French Morvan
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE JSTARS; currently under revision
summary: Christmas tree plantations are economically relevant, yet a largely unexplored application domain in Remote Sensing (RS). Their delineation is challenging because of high planting density, short rotation cycles, visual confusion with surrounding vegetation, the availability of dense labels for one reference year only, and severe class imbalance at the landscape scale. Although Deep Learning (DL) methods have shown strong potential for vegetation mapping, existing approaches are typically designed for forests, generic plantation systems, or orchards, and do not explicitly address the structural specificity and hard-negative confusion that characterize Christmas tree plantations. In response to these challenges, this work makes three main contributions: (i) it frames Christmas tree plantation mapping as a distinct rare-target semantic segmentation problem; (ii) it introduces a Hard Negative Mining (HNM) strategy to improve discrimination against confusing background patterns; and (iii) it evaluates the proposed framework across complementary levels, including supervised testing, temporal transfer, and large-scale validation. On the 2020 test set held out, the best model, DeepLabV3 with a ResNet-34 encoder, achieves an IoU of 0.733 and an F1-score of 0.846. HNM substantially improves precision-recall behavior, increasing the area under the precision-recall curve from 0.204 to 0.913. Temporal inference further shows meaningful transferability, reaching IoU/F1 values of 0.751/0.858 on 2017/2018 and 0.691/0.817 on 2023. Large-scale validation further highlights the intrinsic difficulty of the task, as Christmas tree plantations occupied only a very small fraction of the extent of the common evaluation, corresponding to 1,498.4 ha (1.72\%) in 2017/2018 and 1,782.2 ha (2.04\%) in 2023 out of 87,309.4 ha in total.

AI.tldr: Frames Christmas tree plantation mapping as a rare-target semantic segmentation task, introducing Hard Negative Mining (HNM) to improve discrimination against confusing background, and validating across supervised, temporal, and large-scale evaluations; achieves strong metrics and highlights dataset imbalance as a key challenge.
AI.motivation: Christmas tree plantations are economically relevant but underexplored in remote sensing. Challenges include high planting density, short rotation cycles, visual confusion with surrounding vegetation, sparse per-year labels, and severe class imbalance at landscape scale. Existing DL methods target forests, plantations, or orchards but do not address the unique structural and negative-background confusion of Christmas tree plantations.
AI.method: Modeling as rare-target semantic segmentation and implementing a Hard Negative Mining (HNM) strategy to suppress confusing background patterns. Evaluation includes supervised testing on a 2020 test set, temporal transfer to 2017/2018 and 2023 data, and large-scale validation. Primary model: DeepLabV3 with a ResNet-34 encoder.
AI.result: On the 2020 test set, IoU = 0.733 and F1 = 0.846. HNM improves precision-recall, increasing PR-AUC from 0.204 to 0.913. Temporal transfer yields IoU/F1 = 0.751/0.858 (2017/2018) and 0.691/0.817 (2023). Large-scale validation shows targets occupy a small fraction of the landscape: 1,498.4 ha (1.72%) in 2017/2018 and 1,782.2 ha (2.04%) in 2023 out of 87,309.4 ha total.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that framing Christmas tree plantation mapping as a rare-target segmentation problem with a Hard Negative Mining strategy can substantially improve discriminative performance and temporal transferability. It also underscores the intrinsic difficulty of large-scale detection due to extreme class imbalance, suggesting further improvements in handling rare targets and background confusion.

title: Calibrated Enough to Know, Not Calibrated to Act: Fabricated Evidence Makes LLM Agents Commit to the Unknowable
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, pre-registration and all cached model outputs: https://github.com/Pranav-1100/confidence-calibration-evaluation . Also archived at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22043517
summary: An LLM agent shown a professional-looking market panel commits to a directional call on a provably unpredictable question far more often than one asked the bare question: across 12 frontier models, commitment rises from 6.5% to 54.0% as evidence is escalated. It commits just as readily when every number on the panel is invented: fabricating the entire display, so nothing the model can see is true except the question itself, still lifts commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%, statistically indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by genuine market data. What unlocks confident action is not information but the authority of its packaging. The failure is narrow and locatable. Incapacity is not the answer: on matched answerable questions attached to the same panels, the same models answer essentially always, at near-perfect accuracy. Nor is it belief - stated probabilities barely move across the gradient that swings action by 48 points, and score worse than a climatological baseline. Missing judgment isn't it either: asked to classify a question's knowability before acting, models call it irreducible 90% of the time and then commit on just 0.4% of those. The act/don't-act gate is what fails, and the effect is concentrated in a few models rather than universal. Because the gate is separable, it can be trained. Supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases, predominantly dice, coins, jars and timers, drives commitment to 0.0% on the original cases and transfers to three unseen domains. It does not survive everything: the gate holds exactly when the response format leaves room to reason, and rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it otherwise answers correctly. The gate is trainable and context-fragile, and deployment needs both halves of that sentence.

AI.tldr: LLM action hinges on an act/don't-act gate driven by the packaging/authority of the task, not by knowledge or belief; the gate is trainable and context-sensitive; evidence increases commitment even with fabricated data; rigid formats reduce reasoning room and can worsen outcomes.
AI.motivation: To understand why LLMs commit to directional calls on unpredictable questions, and to characterize the underlying gate controlling action vs. inaction separate from factual knowledge.
AI.method: Evaluate 12 frontier LLMs on market-panel tasks with genuine and fabricated data; measure commitment as evidence escalates; test answerable vs. irreducible knowability; manipulate response formats; train a 3B model on synthetic tasks (dice, coins, jars, timers) to probe transfer to original and unseen domains; assess robustness of the gate.
AI.result: Commitment to directional calls increases with evidence even when the panel is fabricated; the act/don't-act gate, not incapacity or belief, drives action; the gate is separable from knowledge and is trainable but context-fragile; a supervised fine-tune on synthetic tasks reduces commitment on original cases but transfers to unseen domains; rigid formats that constrain reasoning remove the gate's room to operate and can inflate confidence.
AI.conclusion: Action control in LLMs rests on a trainable, context-sensitive gate tied to task presentation. Deployment should address both training the gate and preserving room for reasoning; interfaces and prompts must avoid overly authoritative packaging that can trigger unwarranted commitments; behavior is heterogeneous across models and domains.

title: R2M-Bench: Evaluating Revisit Memory via Relative Consistency in Interactive Video World Models
summary: High similarity between first-visit and return frames does not necessarily show that a video world model remembered the scene; the intervening rollout may simply have changed very little. This ambiguity makes absolute revisit scores sensitive to rendering stability, repetitive content, and failed motion. We introduce \emph{R2M-Bench} (\textbf{R}elative \textbf{R}evisit \textbf{M}emory Benchmark), a benchmark of observable revisit-selective consistency. For every detected return, R2M-Bench compares the revisit pair with two controls from the same rollout: a gap-matched non-revisit pair that measures generic temporal stability and a short-range pair that estimates short-horizon consistency. These comparisons produce \emph{MemoryGain} (MG), the revisit advantage over the temporal baseline, and the \emph{Normalized Memory Ratio} (NMR), which normalizes this advantage by the short-to-baseline dynamic range.
