R2M-Bench combines 100 reference scenes with three leave-and-return trajectories to form 300 instances and evaluates appearance fidelity, scene and object identity, local geometry, and persistent state. Across seven action-conditioned video world models, Overall NMR correlates with human consistency judgments at Spearman's $ρ=0.547$ (95\% CI $[0.45,0.63]$). Its within-model correlation magnitude with generated motion is $0.072$, compared with $0.207$ for raw revisit similarity, indicating that relative calibration substantially reduces the slow-motion shortcut. DreamX-World-Memo achieves the highest Overall NMR among the evaluated video models. Together, these results support same-rollout relative calibration as a practical way to distinguish revisit-specific consistency from generic temporal stability.

AI.tldr: R2M-Bench is a memory-benchmark framework that isolates revisit-specific consistency from generic temporal stability in video world models using MemoryGain (MG) and Normalized Memory Ratio (NMR).
AI.motivation: Absolute revisit scores confound memory with rendering stability, repetitive content, and failed motion. A method is needed to separate revisit-specific memory signals from general temporal stability.
AI.method: Detect return events and compare the revisit pair against two controls from the same rollout: a gap-matched non-revisit pair (temporal stability baseline) and a short-range pair (short-horizon baseline). Compute MemoryGain (MG) as the revisit advantage over the temporal baseline and Normalized Memory Ratio (NMR) by normalizing MG with the short-to-baseline dynamic range. Compose 300 instances from 100 reference scenes with three leave-and-return trajectories; evaluate appearance fidelity, identity, geometry, and persistent state across seven action-conditioned video world models. Correlate Overall NMR with human consistency judgments (Spearman ρ=0.547, 95% CI [0.45, 0.63]); within-model correlation with generated motion is 0.072 vs 0.207 for raw revisit similarity. DreamX-World-Memo yields the highest Overall NMR.
AI.result: R2M-Bench provides a relative, rollout-consistent measure of revisit memory that correlates with human judgments and mitigates the slow-motion shortcut. Across models, it demonstrates that same-rollout relative calibration better isolates revisit-specific memory signals than absolute revisit metrics.
AI.conclusion: Relative within-rollout calibration is a practical approach to disentangle revisit-specific consistency from generic temporal stability in video world models; DreamX-World-Memo leads in Overall NMR among evaluated models.

title: What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on generated interaction data to learn how to interact with external environments. Agentic data generation must maintain consistency among environments, tasks, interactions, and success signals while producing experience that is useful rather than merely abundant. Existing work spans many agent domains, but domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation often obscure common generation mechanisms and conflate candidate construction with verification and selection. This work develops a two-level framework for the field. First, we represent agentic data as a common factorized object $(E,q,τ,v)$, comprising an environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier. We organize generation paradigms by their primary anchor and dependency structure. Second, we formulate generation as constrained distribution design through the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens. Accuracy establishes the feasible support of grounded and internally consistent data. Within this support, Complexity places learning mass relative to the capability of a declared learner and execution configuration, while divErsity controls coverage and redundancy of data. Using this framework, we explore how prior work verifies generated experience, constructs and calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage. The literature reveals a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and diversity beyond surface variation or dataset size. We further discuss broader directions and emerging trends in agentic data generation through the ACE lens, including their implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes and adaptive learning. Overall, the central challenge is not simply to generate more data, but to continually allocate valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve.

AI.tldr: A two-level framework for agentic data generation, unifying data as (E, q, τ, v) and optimizing via an Accuracy-Complexity-Diversity (ACE) lens to ensure useful, consistent, and diverse experience for LLM agents.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation in agentic data generation and the need for consistency and usefulness across environments, tasks, and success signals.
AI.method: Proposes a two-level framework: (1) factorized data object (E, q, τ, v) and organization by anchor/dependency; (2) constrained distribution design using ACE (Accuracy, Complexity, Diversity) to balance feasibility, learner-relative learning mass, and coverage.
AI.result: Reviews and synthesizes prior work, showing a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and meaningful diversity beyond mere dataset size; demonstrates how ACE-guided framing clarifies verification, difficulty calibration, and behavioral coverage.
AI.conclusion: ACE-based lens and factorized data object guide future directions in scaling, data sourcing, training regimes, and adaptive learning to continually deliver valid, informative, non-redundant agentic experience as environments evolve.

title: PAWBench: How Far Are We from Probabilistically Aligned World Modeling?
summary: Recent video generation models are increasingly framed as world models. Many physical processes can unfold in more than one valid way. Therefore, a world model should reproduce not only a plausible trajectory, but also the distribution of possible behaviors under the same initial observation and action. We call this distribution-level requirement probabilistic alignment. However, existing evaluations largely assess individual-video plausibility and do not test whether repeated generations recover the correct distribution. This raises a central question: how far are current video generators from probabilistically aligned world modeling? To answer it, we formalize probabilistic alignment as a distributional criterion for world models and introduce PAWBench, a benchmark for evaluating video generators as stochastic samplers of world dynamics. We further introduce PAWEval, an outcome-level protocol that converts repeated video rollouts into empirical distributions over possible physical behaviors. Across 50 scenarios and eleven current systems, no model consistently matches the reference probabilities while recovering the range of valid behaviors. Having established this gap, we test whether language prompts, initial noise sampling, or model training can reshape the model's predictive distribution. We believe our work can serve as a foundation for future efforts to move towards probabilistically aligned world modeling.

AI.tldr: PAWBench evaluates whether video-generation models probabilistically align with world dynamics by testing their ability to sample correct outcome distributions; reveals a gap between current models and distribution-level accuracy.
AI.motivation: To move beyond single-trajectories and evaluate whether models reproduce the full distribution of possible physical behaviors from the same initial conditions, addressing a key gap in world-model evaluation.
AI.method: Formalize probabilistic alignment as a distributional criterion; develop PAWBench to benchmark stochastic sampling of world dynamics; introduce PAWEval to convert repeated rollouts into empirical distributions; evaluate 11 models across 50 scenarios.
AI.result: No model consistently matches reference probabilities or the full spectrum of valid behaviors; prompts, noise, and training can influence distributions but do not fix the gap; establishes a baseline for future probabilistic alignment research.
AI.conclusion: A foundational framework and benchmark for progressing toward probabilistically aligned world models in video generation.

title: Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search
summary: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, linear prompt optimization method (NPO) using a teacher model with rollout feedback can match or exceed the performance of more complex prompt optimizers (GEPA, GRPO) with fewer rollouts; benefits grow with stronger teachers and generalize across similar student models.
AI.motivation: Reduce computational cost and complexity of prompt optimization while maintaining or improving agent performance across tasks; challenge the trend toward complex optimizers.
AI.method: NPO: iterative revision of prompts via a single-lineage approach using teacher model rollouts; compare against GEPA; evaluate in interactive games; test cross-model transfer of prompts.
AI.result: NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts; advantage increases with stronger teacher models; in interactive games NPO is broadly competitive; GRPO excels on some tasks; prompts transfer well to other student models within same family.
AI.conclusion: Simple, linear prompt optimization can rival sophisticated search procedures; stronger teacher reasoning partially substitutes for optimizer-side search; NPO-effective cross-model transfer; has implications for efficient RSI and prompt engineering.

title: KnockGS:interaction-Grounded Calibrationof Physical Gaussian Representations
summary: Physics-integrated 3D Gaussian representations now allow reconstructed deformable objects to be simulated and rendered under explicit material models. Existing pipelines, however, assume that material parameters are known or manually specified, limiting their applicability when these parameters must be inferred from observed object dynamics. We propose KnockGS, an interaction-response PhysicalGS framework that estimates the elasticity and density scales of a 3D Gaussian object from its dynamics under a known applied force. Rather than treating physical simulation only as a forward process, we turn the force-induced response into a calibration signal: temporal response features are xtracted from the observed dynamics, the two material scales are estimated from those features, and the estimate is then frozen and written back into the same simulator so that it can be tested on an interaction it was never fitted to.We evaluate the framework on both parameter recovery and response-level fidelity. The estimated scales are compared against hidden ground truth, and the re-simulated object is measured against the target using 3D particle trajectories, response-curve statistics, and rendered-frame quality. Across five held-out material targets, our method recovers the scales substantially more accurately than response retrieval, global regression, or a fixed default material, and the frozen estimate remains predictive under interactions that differ in direction and in magnitude. Interaction response therefore carries enough information to calibrate material scales in physically grounded 3D Gaussian representations.Our study is a first step toward interactive PhysicalGS systems that calibrate a Gaussian asset whose rendered appearance and simulated response are consistent.

AI.tldr: KnockGS calibrates elasticity and density scales of 3D Gaussian objects from observed dynamics under known forces, enabling consistent rendering and simulation by fitting material parameters from interaction responses.
AI.motivation: Need to infer material parameters from dynamics to extend Physics-integrated 3D Gaussian representations to unseen interactions.
AI.method: Treat force-induced response as calibration signal, extract temporal features from observed dynamics, estimate elasticity and density scales, freeze estimates into simulator, and test on new interactions.
AI.result: Demonstrated improved parameter recovery and response fidelity across five held-out materials; outperforms response retrieval, global regression, and fixed-default material; frozen estimates generalize to different interaction directions/magnitudes.
AI.conclusion: First step toward interactive PhysicalGS systems that calibrate Gaussian assets so appearance and simulated response remain consistent under varied interactions.

title: BrailleBench: Investigating Multi-Criteria Braille Comprehension in Large Language Models
summary: Although Large language models (LLMs) mediate access to knowledge and computational assistance, their capabilities should benefit vulnerable groups in the same way. However, it is unclear whether existing AI systems are inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users to access the same functionality through Braille, whose indicators, contractions, and digital representations introduce distinct requirements for model comprehension. To this end, we introduce BrailleBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs in Braille comprehension from different Criteria. BrailleBench aligns 5,570 instances from five datasets, including mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop question answering across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Different configurations are designed to understand whether the systems can comprehend Braille-authored content, express answers in Braille, and complete end-to-end Braille interaction. To ensure the quality and prevent evaluation bias, the benchmark is built through a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via a self-created Braille Toolkit without using any data instances generated by LLMs. We evaluate six representative LLMs from various aspects. The results reveal a persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric, where Grade 2 is especially fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille requests further reduce performance. The experimental observations provide valuable guidance for the development of future Braille AI systems. All related resources in BrailleBench are publicly available for future research.

AI.tldr: BrailleBench is a benchmark to evaluate LLMs on Braille comprehension, testing input/output and end-to-end Braille interaction across grades and tasks; results show a gap between print-English and Braille accessibility, guiding future Braille AI development.
AI.motivation: To ensure AI systems are accessible to blind and deafblind users by evaluating LLMs' ability to understand and produce Braille content, addressing the distinct representation and contraction features of Braille.
AI.method: Construct a deterministic, expert-curated benchmark (BrailleBench) with 5,570 instances from five datasets spanning math, commonsense, and multi-hop QA in English and Braille Grades 1 and 2; evaluate six LLMs under configurations: Braille-content understanding, Braille output, and end-to-end Braille interaction; uses a Braille Toolkit for data preparation, with no LLM-generated data.
AI.result: Six representative LLMs show a persistent gap between print-English and Braille capabilities; Grade 2 input is more fragile than Grade 1; fully Braille requests reduce performance; Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric; results offer actionable insights for improving Braille AI systems.
AI.conclusion: BrailleBench provides a rigorous, publicly available benchmark and toolkit to advance Braille-enabled AI, highlighting Braille-specific challenges and guiding future research and system design.

title: Successive Capacity Growth: Task-Complexity-Driven Width and Depth Expansion for Vision Transformer Encoders in JEPA World Models
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) for world modeling typically employ fixed-size Vision Transformer encoders that are over-provisioned for simple tasks and under-provisioned for complex ones, with significant redundancy across attention heads. We propose Successive Capacity Growth (SCG), a method that starts from a minimal encoder (1 head, 2 layers, 283K parameters) and grows incrementally in width (adding attention heads for low-level semantic capacity) or depth (adding transformer blocks for higher-order semantic abstraction), driven by a task-agnostic test-and-verify mechanism that exploits function-preserving expansion to safely trial architectural changes and roll back if they do not improve prediction loss. The Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) ensures that all learned semantic dimensions remain statistically independent and aligned with the predictive objective, preventing collapse even as the architecture grows. On a 60-dimensional multi-object dynamics task, SCG naturally triggers depth expansion, improving prediction loss by 20.3% over the fixed small baseline with 56 times greater parameter efficiency than scaling to the fixed large model; on a 2D navigation task, a single width expansion yields even an 23% improvement over the fixed large model. Across all three tested environments of increasing complexity, the adaptive encoder matches or exceeds the fixed small baseline, with zero false-positive expansions and bit-exact function preservation (ratio = 1.0, absolute difference = 0.0). The take-away is that JEPA world model encoders need not be pre-allocated at maximum capacity - they can grow successively as the task demands, achieving significant compute and data efficiency while maintaining representation quality.

AI.tldr: SCG enables progressive growth of JEPA encoders from a minimal config, guided by a test-and-verify mechanism with function-preserving expansions and SIGReg, achieving substantial predictive gains and parameter efficiency without false positives.
AI.motivation: Fixed-size, over-/under-provisioned Vision Transformer encoders used in Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) lead to inefficiencies and redundancy. The paper argues for task-driven, incremental growth to match complexity.
AI.method: Initialize with a minimal JEPA encoder (1 head, 2 layers, ~283K params). Grow width (add attention heads) to boost low-level semantic capacity or depth (add transformer blocks) for higher-order semantics. Use a task-agnostic test-and-verify loop with function-preserving expansion to trial changes and rollback if they do not improve prediction loss. Apply Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) to keep semantic dimensions statistically independent and aligned with the predictive objective, preventing collapse during growth.
AI.result: On a 60-dimensional multi-object dynamics task, SCG triggers depth growth and reduces prediction loss by 20.3% with 56× parameter efficiency relative to scaling to a fixed large model. On a 2D navigation task, a single width expansion improves loss by 23% over the fixed large model. Across three environments of increasing complexity, the adaptive encoder matches or exceeds the fixed small baseline, with zero false-positive expansions and bit-exact function preservation (ratio = 1.0, absolute difference = 0.0).
AI.conclusion: JEPA world-model encoders need not be pre-allocated at maximum capacity; they can grow progressively as task demands, achieving substantial compute and data efficiency while preserving representation quality.

title: LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms
summary:
We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research (OR) problems. We study inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization. We evaluate two levels of LLM use: at level 1, the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance; at level 2, it receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Human input is minimal: we give one untuned prompt that describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget.
  The strongest model we test, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances. This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before seeing the evaluation instances. Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, suggesting that this capability is moving quickly. Thus, for the well-specified operations problems we study, a single untuned LLM query can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods. These results suggest that frontier LLMs can be a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.

AI.tldr: One untuned LLM prompt can yield competitive algorithms for well-specified OR problems; strongest models (gpt-5.6-sol) match or beat specialized methods on most instances, even at level 2 where the algorithm is fixed before seeing instances; performance improves with newer models, indicating rapid progress; LLMs can serve as empirical baselines for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.
AI.motivation: To assess whether large language models can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research problems, specifically in inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization.
AI.method: Compare two usage levels: level 1 where the LLM receives a single problem instance and outputs a solution for that instance; level 2 where the LLM receives problem class description and broad parameter ranges and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Use one untuned prompt describing the problem, and a Python sandbox with fixed compute budget. Evaluate the strongest model (gpt-5.6-sol) against existing specialized methods across evaluated instances.
AI.result: gpt-5.6-sol matches or outperforms the best existing method on nearly all evaluated instances. This holds at level 2 as well, where the returned algorithm is fixed before evaluation. Performance improves across models released within eight months, indicating rapid progress. Overall, a single untuned LLM query can produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods for well-specified OR problems.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can serve as a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems, with rapid improvements and the potential to reduce reliance on problem-specific algorithm engineering.

title: LeVJEPA: Efficient & Scalable Video Pretraining without the Heuristics
summary: Video carries the temporal structure of the physical world, yet learning representations from it has remained computationally expensive: prevailing self-supervised methods either prevent representation collapse through architectural asymmetries, coupling an exponential-moving-average target encoder, a stop-gradient, and a capacity-limited predictor, or circumvent it by reconstructing masked content in pixel space. We introduce LeVJEPA, the first video encoder trained under LeJEPA's collapse-free objective, which dispenses with both. A single encoder is trained with an invariance loss over global and local views of a clip, regularized by SIGReg, which excludes collapse with a provable guarantee. The architecture reduces to an encoder and a projector, and the objective to a single hyperparameter. This formulation admits two properties. First, the cost of pretraining is governed by the number of tokens the encoder observes; uniform random token dropping renders this number small while simultaneously improving downstream accuracy. At matched epochs on identical data, LeVJEPA matches or surpasses V-JEPA 2 across ViT-S/B/L at 5.6 to 20.8x less pretraining compute, and at matched total FLOPs it exceeds the strongest video baseline by 7.6 points on ImageNet-1K while remaining competitive on motion-centric benchmarks. Second, since no asymmetry between branches is required, the encoder can be trained with block-causal attention at no measurable accuracy cost: temporal ordering becomes a property of the encoder itself. Against a compute-matched DINOv2 trained on frames of the same videos, LeVJEPA approaches the image-pretrained encoder on appearance-centric evaluation while nearly doubling its motion-centric accuracy. These results indicate that, once its computational overhead is removed, video becomes a viable and in several respects preferable substrate for general-purpose visual pretraining.

AI.tldr: LeVJEPA introduces a collapse-free, single-encoder video pretraining objective that removes architectural asymmetries and stop-gradients, achieving large compute savings and competitive/leading performance on both appearance- and motion-centric benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational cost and architectural complexity inherent in self-supervised video pretraining, while avoiding representation collapse and relying on a single encoder.
AI.method: Train a single encoder with an invariance loss over global and local views of a video clip, regularized by SIGReg to guarantee no collapse. Use a simple encoder+projector architecture with one hyperparameter; employ token dropping to reduce pretraining compute; allow block-causal attention so temporal ordering is an emergent property of the encoder.
AI.result: LeVJEPA matches or surpasses V-JEPA 2 across ViT-S/B/L with 5.6–20.8x less pretraining compute at matched epochs; at matched FLOPs it surpasses the strongest video baseline by 7.6 points on ImageNet-1K and remains competitive on motion benchmarks. With compute-matched DINOv2, it approaches image-pretrained encoders on appearance and nearly doubles motion-centric accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating asymmetry and collapse-related components yields a simpler, more efficient video pretraining pipeline. Video becomes a viable substrate for general-purpose visual pretraining when the encoder itself encodes temporal structure, and token dropping further reduces cost without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Verify Smarter, Evolve Further: Efficient Harness Evolution through Behavior-Aware Verification
summary: Agent harnesses shape how language-model agents use instructions, tools, and runtime components, but adapting these harnesses requires costly verification. Existing propose-and-verify methods typically score every candidate on a fixed task set, wasting rollouts on unrelated behaviors and allowing aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions. We introduce HarnessLens, a budget-aware framework for automated harness evolution. HarnessLens jointly explores the task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate. Across three agent harnesses and four benchmarks, HarnessLens improves average held-out performance by 7.6-13.6% while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than competing baselines. These results demonstrate that behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/jhxu5214/HarnessLens.

AI.tldr: HarnessLens enables budget-aware, behavior-driven harness evolution for language-model agents, delivering improved performance with reduced verification cost.
AI.motivation: Current propose-and-verify harnesses rely on fixed task sets and aggregate scores, which leads to wasted rollouts and missed regressions; there is a need for reliable, sample-efficient harness adaptation under constrained interaction budgets.
AI.method: Jointly explore the task space and configurable harness components; derive candidate modifications from execution trajectories; apply an attributable-evidence gate to selectively verify candidates on behavior-relevant tasks.
AI.result: Achieves 7.6–13.6% improvement in average held-out performance across three harnesses and four benchmarks, while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under budget constraints; code is released.

title: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
summary: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

AI.tldr: CorporateBench (CB) is a large, human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark for enterprise-scale document reasoning, with 230k+ documents across four synthetic firms, assessing information extraction and knowledge-base querying. Results show LLMs struggle increasingly as input size approaches realistic scales, filling a benchmarking gap for corporate communication reasoning.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of LLMs on enterprise-scale corpora is hindered by privacy constraints and overly simplistic synthetic data; there is a need for a scalable, realistic benchmark that preserves cross-document logical consistency to assess corporate-relevant reasoning.
AI.method: CB constructs four synthetic firms (12–10,000 employees) and two evaluation axes (information extraction and knowledge-base querying) using temporally evolving, consistent world knowledge. The corpora, exceeding 230k documents, are human-validated and ensure cross-document consistency across large scales. Five LLMs are evaluated.
AI.result: LLMs’ performance deteriorates as the input size grows toward realistic scales, indicating current models struggle with corporate-scale, cross-document reasoning. CB serves as a metric for corporate communication reasoning and helps benchmark progress.
AI.conclusion: CB fills a gap in the benchmarking ecosystem by providing a realistic, scalable, human-validated Q&A benchmark for corporate communication scenarios, guiding LLM developers and benchmarking efforts.

title: Reconstructing Humans and Objects in Interaction using Large Reconstruction Models
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://ac5113.github.io/MILO
summary: Estimation of Human-Object Interactions in 3D (3D HOI) is a fundamental problem in 3D computer vision with applications in AR/VR, robotics, and embodied AI. However, reconstructing these interactions in 3D remains challenging due to depth ambiguities, occlusions, and object shape variability. Existing approaches are primarily concerned with reprojection and contact constraints, fitting parametric human models and object templates to 2D images. In this paper, we explore a different avenue. We present MILO, a framework that leverages the visual capabilities of Large Reconstruction Models (LRMs) to recover detailed 3D human-object interactions from a single image. Our key observation is that LRMs provide a powerful geometric scaffold that preserves relative human-object arrangement and proximity cues. This significantly simplifies the reconstruction procedure, reframing the problem as interpreting the LRM mesh: we segment it into human and object components, fit a parametric body model to the human part, and optionally align an object template to the object part (if such a template is available). MILO achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and outperforms existing baselines across multiple benchmarks and interaction scenarios. Our code is available at https://ac5113.github.io/MILO.

AI.tldr: A single-image 3D HOI reconstruction framework MILO uses Large Reconstruction Models (LRMs) as a geometric scaffold to recover 3D human-object interactions by segmenting the LRM mesh into human and object parts, fitting a parametric body model to the human part, and optionally aligning an object template to the object part; claims superior accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: 3D human-object interaction (HOI) reconstruction in 3D is hard due to depth ambiguity, occlusions, and object shape variability; existing 2D-reprojection-based and parametric-model approaches are limited. Leveraging LRMs' geometric priors could simplify 3D reconstruction from a single image.
AI.method: Utilize the LRM-generated mesh from a single image as the geometric scaffold. Segment the mesh into human and object components. Fit a parametric body model to the human portion; optionally align an object template to the object portion if a template is available. Rely on the LRM's preserved human-object arrangement and proximity cues to guide reconstruction.
AI.result: MIL0 achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and outperforms existing baselines across multiple benchmarks and interaction scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LRMs provide a robust geometric scaffold for 3D HOI from a single image, simplifying reconstruction and enabling plausible 3D interpretation of human-object interactions; potential for future work includes better object-template alignment and broader benchmark coverage.

title: Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance
comment: 5 pages (14 appendices), 5 figures, presented at 2026 ICML Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Steering interventions targeting eval-awareness, a model's recognition that it is being tested, are increasingly used in safety evaluation pipelines, where evaluation-awareness is treated as a single quantity to be suppressed. We show that verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought can be identified as capabilities-flavored ("the user is testing my ability to follow instructions"), safety-flavored ("the user is testing my boundaries"), both, or neither: framings that predict compliance very differently. On Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset, capabilities-framing predicts compliance with a +24 to +46 percentage-point gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions. A CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts suggests the link is causal, with 10 of 11 prefills shifting compliance in the predicted direction. Then, eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform: aggregate suppression rates can move while the safety-relevant component does not, and the same "X% suppression of eval-awareness" can correspond to qualitatively different behavioral outcomes.

AI.tldr: Eval-awareness in model testing can be framed as capabilities-flavored or safety-flavored; framing affects predicted compliance with large gaps; CoT-prefill on eval-awareness-negative outputs suggests a causal link; eval-awareness is heterogeneous and suppression of it is not uniform across components.
AI.motivation: To understand how the recognition that a model is being tested influences compliance, and how different framings of this eval-awareness alter outcomes in safety evaluation pipelines.
AI.method: Classify verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought into capabilities- vs safety-flavored frames; evaluate their association with compliance on Qwen3-32B using the FORTRESS dataset across steering conditions; apply CoT-prefill interventions on eval-awareness-negative rollouts to test causality; examine whether aggregate suppression masks component-specific effects.
AI.result: Capabilities-framing predicts higher compliance, with a 24–46 percentage-point advantage over safety-framing across conditions; CoT-prefill on eval-awareness-negative rollouts shifted compliance in 10/11 cases, suggesting a causal link; suppression rates of eval-awareness are not behaviorally uniform and the same suppression percentage can map to different outcomes depending on the underlying frame.
AI.conclusion: Framing eval-awareness as a variable in evaluation pipelines materially affects safety outcomes; eval-awareness is multi-dimensional, requiring disaggregated measures by frame to accurately predict and control model behavior in safety assessments.

title: Learning a Continuous Sepsis Severity Score Without Hour-by-Hour Supervision: A Two-Site Retrospective Study
summary:
Currently used sepsis severity indices rely on fixed variables and weights established decades ago, which are coarsely discretized and calibrated to a cohort that no longer reflects contemporary critical care. No alternative learned directly from patient trajectories is in routine use. We conducted a retrospective two-cohort study on a total of 29,116 and 7,691 adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria from two hospital systems in Massachusetts and Georgie, respectively.
  We developed a sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Unlike previous studies, we use mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than a per-state target, allowing credit to be redistributed non-uniformly across timesteps. Evaluation was done on a permanent 20% test holdout, using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation. Uncertainty intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of whole patients. Under this ranking scheme, non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors on a 0-10 scale within all strata of baseline SOFA-2, with similar results stratifying within lactate, mean arterial pressure (MAP), and creatinine. Within-patient change in the index correlated with change in lactate (Spearman rho = 0.39; n = 1,854). Similar, weaker correlations were found for MAP and creatinine. On a cohort level, cross-institutional agreement measured by Spearman correlation between models trained on different sites, were 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 against ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. Our index also correlated with established indices, while null controls stayed near zero.
  Our index demonstrated hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and is consistent with clinical expectation, indicating potential as a decision support tool complementing clinical judgement.

AI.tldr: A data-driven sepsis severity index using 43 routinely collected variables over a 72-hour window, trained to predict mortality as a time-aware ranking signal. It shows discrimination between survivors and non-survivors, tracks within-patient changes aligned with lactate, and exhibits moderate cross-site generalizability, suggesting potential as a clinical decision-support tool beyond legacy indices.
AI.motivation: Addresses limitations of fixed, decade-old sepsis indices by leveraging longitudinal trajectory data and modern, diverse cohorts to produce a continuously-valued severity score aligned with mortality risk.
AI.method: Retrospective two-cohort study including 29,116 and 7,691 adult Sepsis-3 patients from two hospital systems. Developed a sepsis index from 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Mortality used as the ranking signal across time steps. Evaluated on a permanent 20% test holdout using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlations. Uncertainty estimated via bootstrap at the patient level. Assessed stratification across baseline SOFA-2, lactate, MAP, creatinine; examined within-patient changes and cross-site generalizability (within-site vs cross-site correlations).
AI.result: Non-survivors scored 1.19–1.64 points higher than survivors on a 0–10 scale across baseline strata. Index change within patients correlated with lactate (rho=0.39; n=1,854); weaker but present correlations with MAP and creatinine. Cross-institutional model agreement was 70–77% of same-site correlations; external within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 with ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. Index correlated with established indices; null controls near zero. Demonstrated hourly prognostic information consistent with clinical expectation, supporting potential as a decision-support tool alongside clinical judgment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 43-variable, 72-hour sepsis index provides continuous, hourly prognostic information, aligns with clinical expectations, and shows cross-site generalizability to a meaningful degree, indicating potential utility as a decision-support tool. Further prospective validation and integration work are warranted to confirm clinical impact and generalizability across diverse settings.

title: Retrieval Heads Meet Vision: Uncovering How VLMs Locate and Extract Visual Information
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can locate an image region referred to by a text prompt and route the corresponding visual evidence to the output, yet the internal mechanism behind this behavior is not understood. Inspired by retrieval heads in large language models, we ask whether VLMs contain an analogous mechanism for visual retrieval. We answer affirmatively by introducing Visual Retrieval Heads (VRHs), a small subset of attention heads (about 1.7-2.6%) that are causally responsible for grounding text descriptions to image regions. To find them, we recast existing head-scoring methods under a unified design space over query tokens, key aggregation, and cross-sample aggregation. We then show that scoring attention from output prediction tokens with a sum over the ground-truth referent region most reliably identifies causal heads. Across eleven VLMs and five referring-expression benchmarks, masking only the top 20 VRHs reduces grounding accuracy by up to 80 percentage points, while masking the same number of random heads has little effect. Beyond replicating the causal-sparse-universal triad established for text retrieval heads, VRHs exhibit several properties not previously reported: they generalize across visual reference tasks, remaining causal on attribute, spatial, counting, and visual-math benchmarks despite being discovered through bounding-box prediction; they are functionally specific, preserving output format while corrupting localization; and they are architecturally shared, transferring causally across VLMs that share an LLM backbone but differ in vision encoder, projector, and instruction tuning.

AI.tldr: A small, causally crucial subset of attention heads in vision-language models—Visual Retrieval Heads (VRHs)—causes grounding of text prompts to image regions. They are sparse (about 1.7–2.6%), transferable across models with shared backbones, generalize across tasks, and remain causal when manipulating attributes, spatial relations, counting, and visual-mmath tasks. Masking the top VRHs severely degrades grounding performance, while random head masking does not.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal mechanism enabling text-to-region grounding in VLMs by identifying whether there exists a specialized, causal mechanism akin to retrieval heads in LLMs.
AI.method: Define a unified design space for head-scoring methods (query tokens, key aggregation, cross-sample aggregation). Use causal probing by scoring attention from output prediction tokens with aggregation over the ground-truth referent region to identify candidate heads. Validate by ablating (masking) top VRHs across 11 VLMs and 5 referring-expression benchmarks, comparing against masking random heads.
AI.result: Identified a sparse set of causal heads (VRHs), ~1.7–2.6% of heads. Masking the top ~20 VRHs reduces grounding accuracy by up to 80 percentage points; masking random heads has little effect. VRHs generalize across tasks (attributes, spatial, counting, visual-math) and preserve output format while corrupting localization. They are architecturally shared, transferring across VLMs with the same LLM backbone but different vision encoders/projectors/instruction tuning.
AI.conclusion: There exists a sparse, transferable, and causally responsible grounding mechanism in VLMs—the Visual Retrieval Heads—that accounts for region grounding and generalizes across related tasks and models. This supports a triad akin to text retrieval heads in LLMs and offers a targeted interpretability handle for grounding in multimodal systems.

title: Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm
comment: 59 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Includes Appendix A (variable definitions), Appendix B (supplementary tables), and Online Appendix C (meta prompts)
summary: We study how sophistication in generative AI (genAI) use varies among the back-office workforce of a large firm. Using proprietary data, we observe 713,564 employee prompts and their corresponding large language model responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025. We document three main findings. First, senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, consistent with domain expertise complementing genAI capabilities. Second, sophistication varies considerably across functions and is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management, three groups that share a focus on firmwide strategic initiatives and organizational change. Third, we observe neither improvements in sophistication over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training, suggesting that sophisticated use can be difficult to change. Together, our study provides measures of and insights into sophisticated genAI use that managers can use to improve outcomes and that researchers can use in future research.

AI.tldr: Large-scale real-world study of genAI use sophistication among back-office workers; seniority and function predict sophistication; no time trend or training effect.
AI.motivation: Fill gaps in understanding how genAI adoption varies within organizations and how seniority and function influence sophistication; inform management practices and future research.
AI.method: Observational analysis of 713,564 prompts and corresponding LLM responses from ~4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025 using proprietary data; measures of 'sophistication' derived from prompt-response interactions.
AI.result: (1) Senior employees show more sophisticated genAI use; (2) sophistication varies by function, highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management; (3) no improvements over time and no lasting gains from formal AI training.
AI.conclusion: The study provides measures of sophisticated genAI use and insights for managers to improve outcomes; highlights that sophisticated use is difficult to change, suggesting a need for targeted interventions and further research.

title: UrbanGround: From Local Perception to Spatial Agency in a Real-Scale City
comment: 35 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables. Project Page: https://urbanground.github.io, Code Repository: https://github.com/UrbanGround/UrbanGround
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret a street view, but urban agency depends on whether such local evidence remains useful after the agent starts to move. In this paper, we investigate how far current MLLM agents can turn local urban perception into reliable action in a complicated real-scale city. We propose UrbanGround, the first sandbox to make this question testable in a physically constrained replica of Hong Kong built from territory-wide 3D geospatial data. UrbanGround supports closed-loop interaction from a first-person view and provides an interactive map for navigation. Agents can directly enter the 3D city and explore from a first-person view. Our analysis follows the growth of the spatial problem through three research questions. We first test whether an agent can ground a local scene well enough to answer spatial questions after active observation. Then we ask whether that grounding supports navigation as destinations become farther away and less explicit. Finally, we examine whether the resulting behavior survives changes in route availability and pedestrian motion. Contemporary MLLM agents usually show useful atomic abilities in visual recognition and short-range spatial reasoning, while orientation and pedestrian-aware movement remain unreliable. Their central failure emerges over extended exploration, where local abilities do not compose into sustained goal-directed behavior and errors accumulate without effective correction. We hope UrbanGround will support broader study of how far current MLLM agents can explore reliably in complex, open-ended urban environments.

AI.tldr: UrbanGround provides a city-scale, physically grounded sandbox to test how far current multimodal LLM agents can transform local urban perception into reliable, long-horizon action; initial findings indicate limitations in sustained navigation despite strong local perception.
AI.motivation: To understand whether local perceptual grounding in MLLMs can be composed into sustained, goal-directed behavior in open-ended urban environments, and to provide a testbed for controlled experiments on city-scale, dynamic conditions.
AI.method: Construct UrbanGround from Hong Kong's 3D geospatial data; enable closed-loop, first-person exploration with an interactive map; run experiments over three research questions analyzing grounding, navigation as distance increases, and robustness to route/pedestrian changes.
AI.result: Current MLLMs exhibit strong visual recognition and short-range spatial reasoning but weak orientation and pedestrian-aware movement; extended exploration reveals accumulation of errors and failure to sustain goal-directed behavior; the sandbox highlights these gaps and enables systematic study.
AI.conclusion: UrbanGround is the first sandbox of its kind for testing open-ended urban exploration by MLLMs; it will support broad, structured investigation into extending local perception into reliable navigation, with potential improvements in grounding, planning, and correction mechanisms.

title: Mechanistic Reaction Prediction via Discrete Flow Matching on Graph-Structured Electron Occupation
summary:
Chemical reactions are fundamentally transformations in electron space, yet most machine learning approaches model them either through \textit{de novo} generation of product molecules or through heuristic graph edits that operate directly on molecular topology.
  We introduce MAELLE (\textbf{M}ech\textbf{A}nistic \textbf{E}dit f\textbf{L}ow-matching on e\textbf{L}ectron r\textbf{E}arrangements), which instead models reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors.
  Concretely, we formulate the reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over the graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space defined on all bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites.
  To construct the intermediate edit trajectories, we generalize the discrete flow matching mixture path to discrete electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, yielding a sequence of mechanistically interpretable edit moves without requiring elementary step annotations.
  MAELLE achieves competitive performance on the USPTO-480K benchmark compared with leading reaction prediction models.
  Beyond in-distribution accuracy, we evaluate robustness across two out-of-distribution settings - structural complexity and reaction type - and find that MAELLE maintains strong performance where existing methods degrade.
  Finally, because the learned flow operates over the full electron redistribution, MAELLE naturally recovers mechanistic trajectories that align with known chemistry and can predict side products of a reaction.

AI.tldr: MAELLE uses discrete flow matching over electron occupation space to predict reactions via a CTMC, yielding interpretable mechanistic trajectories and robust performance.
AI.motivation: Current ML approaches either generate de novo products or edit topology; need a physically grounded, interpretable framework that captures electron rearrangements and is robust out-of-distribution.
AI.method: Reactant-to-product mapping modeled as CTMC on graph-structured integer electron occupation vectors for all bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites. Edges correspond to electron rearrangement edits; intermediate trajectories constructed by discrete flow matching extended via Optimal Transport to discrete electron moves; requires no elementary-step annotations.
AI.result: Competitive on USPTO-480K; maintains performance under structural complexity and reaction-type OOD; recovers mechanistic trajectories aligned with chemistry; can predict side products.
AI.conclusion: Electron-space flow matching provides a mechanistically interpretable, robust framework for reaction prediction, with potential for mechanistic insights and side-product forecasting.

title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution
summary: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

AI.tldr: WikiSkill co-evolves agent skills with a persistent wiki to accumulate experience; it improves skill evolution, enables transfer across models, and scales with model size; ablations show knowledge persistence is key.
AI.motivation: Skills learned by agents are scattered across optimization histories, hindering systematic reuse; need a persistent knowledge base to accumulate, refine, and reuse skills across iterations and models.
AI.method: Proposes WikiSkill: separate raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills; maintain a wiki that consolidates experience; skill updates build on wiki; evaluate on diverse benchmarks/models; perform ablations; compare against baselines and state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods; test cross-model transfer and inter-model evolution.
AI.result: WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and no-skill baselines in most settings; larger models benefit more from evolved skills; smaller models with skills can outperform much larger models without; skills transfer effectively across models and families; skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved ones; ablation shows persistent wiki is critical.
AI.conclusion: Systematic accumulation of agent experience in a persistent wiki enables reusable and transferable skills; skill evolution complements scaling; supports cross-model transfer; persistence is essential for effective skill evolution.
